# FOREWORD

The French Academy has awarded the full Bordin Prize <note>The Prix Bordin was a prestigious academic prize established in 1835 to encourage high-quality literary and scientific works.</note>, "specifically dedicated to encouraging high literature," to the three published volumes of the complete publication of the *Manuscripts of Leonardo da Vinci*.

The contents of the three volumes remaining to be published will not make one regret such encouragement. The present volume, the fourth of the work, will particularly show what the last of the previous series hinted at: how much the painter of the **Last Supper** <note>original: "Cène"</note> and the **Mona Lisa** <note>original: "Joconde"</note>, as profound and universal a scholar as he was, was a man of great and vivid imagination, in letters and sciences as much as in the arts; it is not useless to insist upon this point. This must have been one of the reasons why Francis I <note>King Francis I of France, Leonardo’s final patron.</note> could not tire of Leonardo da Vinci’s conversation, of whom he said that he did not believe there was another man in the world who knew as much.

The report and observations which accompanied the volume containing manuscripts C, E, and K in June 1888 were intended to serve as a preface to the facsimiles remaining to be edited for the deadline originally set for 1891. It is exactly on its date, announced in that report, that the fourth volume sees the light of day.

It was difficult to arrive at this point within the legal deadlines of the ministerial subscription, while taking every possible care that each new part of the work was, from all points of view, complete in its entirety and very exact in its details¹. Therefore, it is only right that the author state what intelligent and persevering will was required by the House of Quantin <note>Maison Quantin was a prominent French publishing firm known for high-quality art and history books.</note>, leaders and collaborators, to successfully reach this goal.

The fourth volume adds manuscripts F and I (see the preface of the 1st volume, p. 20 [6th], 22 [9th], and 25) to the six from the Institute <note>Refers to the Institut de France, where these specific manuscripts are held.</note> already published. These manuscripts contain many drawings, sometimes in pen, sometimes in red chalk, among which one will notice an energetic face bearing some resemblance to that of the elderly Leonardo da Vinci (see manuscript I, folio 139 [91] verso, note 1, 2nd part), a

---

1. Nevertheless, some errors will undoubtedly be discovered little by little; they will be noted at the end of the sixth volume or, if necessary, at the end of the fifth.

<summary>In this foreword, the editor announces that the project has received the Bordin Prize from the French Academy and emphasizes Leonardo's vast imagination and intellect. He also notes the inclusion of manuscripts F and I, which contain significant drawings and potential self-portraits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Foreword by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien, detailing the specific artistic and scientific contents of the fourth volume of Leonardo da Vinci's manuscripts (specifically Notebooks I and F).</meta>

# FOREWORD

...a dog's head (I, 96 [48] rº), sketches of a man carrying a burden, of a monk, of a tree (I, 113 [35] rº, 34 rº, 37 vº <note>The abbreviations "rº" and "vº" stand for *recto* and *verso*, referring to the front and back of a manuscript leaf.</note>), parts of buildings (I, 110 [62] rº; F, 3 rº), beautiful or curious movements of water and other things (F, 8 rº, 21 rº, 48 rº, 73 vº (mixtures); I, 81 [33] rº, 115 [67] vº). As for the text, one will find complementary parts of most of the subjects treated in notebooks A, B, C, D, E, and K, as well as many parts that are quite new relative to the subjects of said notebooks. Some of these passages are already famous for having been commented upon by Amoretti, by Venturi¹, by Libri²; others have been published in the selected pieces arranged by Mr. J.-P. Richter; still others, and not the least interesting among them, were previously unpublished.

To be convinced of the value and variety of the materials, it will suffice to browse through the tables <note>referring to the indexes or tables of contents</note>, prepared like the previous ones, so as to serve provisionally as a guide, classification, and commentary.

Among the numerous articles listed in these indexes, one will notice—to cite only a few examples—observations on the "actions" for painters <note>original: "actes"; referring to the movements and gestures of figures</note>, colors for painting in oil and fresco³, contrasts, the "azure" <note>the blue atmospheric haze</note> in landscapes, etc., etc.; artistic fabrications; notes on the sky and the world, on the elements; curious discussions touching upon the nature of the stars, the waters, days, nights, and spots of the moon, the praise of the sun and its defense against unjust critics; studies on the causes and origins of petrifications and fossils; remarks on waves, the atoms of solar rays, the sands of Libya, the peaks of the Caucasus, seas, and rivers; on the "splendors," or innumerable droplets of air hiding the stars by day, on the droplet compared to the sphere of water; citations from authors (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Epicurus, Archimedes, Posidonius, Vitruvius, the Arab Avicenna, and Albert the Great, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Dante, Albert of Saxony, Leon Battista Alberti, Michele Marullo, etc.), as well as contemporary figures (Salaì⁴, Leonardo's pupil, Messires Octavian Pallavicino and Mariolo, Pietro Monti, Simon de Calima, etc.), a whole series of extraordinary predictions, "Prophecies," and little stories and jests, fantastic descriptions, notes on Duke Ludovico the Moor <note>Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan and Leonardo’s patron</note>, on the bath of the Duchess of Milan, on a carnival costume and various decorative motifs, others on men compared with animals, on doctors, on loans, grammars and the sciences, reason and experience, practice and theory, then further studies of the Latin language and a Latin-Italian glossary, as well as several letters in a strange, perhaps secret script, borrowed from Oriental scripts (see folio 122 [74] verso, note).

->**E** [Monogram]<-

In this book, we will treat shadows <note>original: "verna"; likely a transcription error for "ombra" (shadow), which is the central theme of Manuscript C.</note> and the sphere of the sun, the air, and the water; and how light passes through these aforementioned media; and the causes of winds, rains, thunder, and lightning; and how vapors move through these media; and the colors that these media possess, and how the color of objects is varied by them. <note>Leonardo is describing "atmospheric perspective"—how the air itself changes the appearance and color of distant objects, a technique he famously applied in the *Mona Lisa*.</note>

<summary>This page lists Leonardo’s intended research topics for Manuscript C, spanning from the mechanics of motion and gravity to the complex physics of light, weather, and atmospheric optics.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, motion, centers of gravity, animal locomotion, optics, atmospheric perspective, meteorology, light and shadow</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the cover of Manuscript F to the first internal pages. While the previous cover page was a general list of scientific interests, Folio 1 begins with a specific date—September 12, 1508—marking Leonardo’s return to Milan. Here, he immediately dives into his dual fascinations: the internal mechanics of the human body (anatomy) and the external mechanics of the physical world (hydraulics and optics).</meta>

## [DATE OF THIS MANUSCRIPT. — DEATH BY OLD AGE. — REINFORCED DIKES].

I. — Begun in Milan on the 12th day of September 1508 <note>original: "Comincato ammilano addi 12 disettembre 1508"</note>.
Death in the elderly, when it occurs without fever, is caused by the veins that go from the spleen to the portal of the liver; they thicken so much in their lining that they close up and no longer allow passage to the blood that should nourish them.
The continuous flow of blood through its veins causes these veins to thicken and become callous in such a way that, in the end, they close up and prevent the blood from flowing.
The spaces or hollows of the veins in animals, through the long passage of the fluid <term>humor: in Renaissance medicine, "humors" were the vital fluids of the body</term> that nourishes them, become callous and eventually close. The hollows of the veins of the earth <note>Leonardo frequently compared the "veins" of the earth (water channels) to the veins of the human body.</note>, through the long and continuous flow of water, tend instead to widen.
Willow roots do not allow the banks of canals to be destroyed; and the willow branches, nourished within the thickness of the bank and trimmed low every year, grow thicker and create a continuous weave of shoots; and thus you have a bank that is <margin>alive and of one piece.</margin>
[ Figure: ] c d a b e f

I'. — Begun in Milan on September 12, 1508. <note>This section in the source was a 19th-century French translation of Leonardo's Italian notes above.</note>
Death in the elderly, without fever, is caused by the veins which, going from the spleen to the portal of the liver, thicken so much in their skin that they close, and no longer give passage to the blood which nourishes them.
The continual course of blood in its veins causes these veins to thicken and become callous, in such a way that at the end they close and prevent the blood from its course.
The spaces *or* concavities of the veins of animals, with the long course of the humor that nourishes them, become callous and in the end narrow. The concavities of the veins of the earth, by the long and continuous course of water, go on widening. Willow roots do not let the dikes of canals be spoiled; willow branches nourished through the thickness of the dikes, then cut low, thicken each year, and are made of [augmented by] continual shoots; and thus you have a living dike of one piece.

1. Leonardo da Vinci’s autograph pagination.
2. The writings of Leonardo da Vinci, by Charles Ravaisson-Mollien.
3 and 4. Text also cited by scholar Jean Paul Richter.
5. Under the ink of the first line, a draft in red chalk can be read: "September 12, 1508." Likewise under the following lines: "the veins... elderly... callous by continuous motion... blood... moves." Also in red chalk: the figure above these lines.

## [LIGHT AND SHADOW].
->(REFLECTIONS.)<-

[Figure:] c a o b e d f
— The surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its object —
THAT PART OF THE SURFACE OF OPAQUE BODIES WILL PARTICIPATE MOST IN THE COLOR OF ITS OBJECT WHICH IS NEAREST TO IT.
Let **a b** [ **a o b** ] be the opaque body, and **c d** the luminous object, and **e f** the shadowy object; I say that the middle of this opaque body, **o**, will participate equally in both objects, and the part **a o** will be more luminous than the part **o b**; it will be more illuminated the closer it is to the light, and likewise the part of this body that is darker, being closer to the shadowy object, will be more shaded.

[Figure:] c a o b e d f
The surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its object.
THAT PART OF THE SURFACE OF OPAQUE BODIES PARTICIPATES MORE IN THE COLOR OF ITS OBJECT WHICH IS CLOSER TO IT:
Let **a b** [ **a o b** ] be the opaque body, and **c d** the luminous object, and **e f** the shadowy object; I say that the middle of the opaque body, **o**, participates equally in one and the other object, and that the part **a o** is more illuminated than the part **o b**; it will be more illuminated the more it is near the luminous one, and likewise the part of the body that is more obscure which is near the shadowy one will be more shaded.

<summary>Leonardo records the start date of this notebook in Milan (1508) and explores the physiological causes of death in the elderly via the thickening of veins, drawing a parallel to the "veins" (waterways) of the earth. He also discusses engineering techniques for dikes using willow trees and defines a law of optics regarding how colors and light are reflected onto opaque surfaces.</summary>
<keywords>Milan 1508, anatomy, aging, circulatory system, hepatic portal vein, hydraulics, canal engineering, willow trees, optics, light and shadow, color theory, reflection</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page marks the true beginning of the Codex Leicester. While the previous note (from Manuscript F) was dated September 12, 1508, the opening of this manuscript is dated April 22 of the same year. Leonardo explains his "chaotic" process of gathering notes from various loose papers with the intent to organize them later—a task he rarely finished. He establishes his fundamental scientific principle: starting with observation (experience) to find the underlying law (reason).</meta>

-> FOLIO 1 (*recto*). <-

On the 22nd day of April, 1508, I began this <note>original: "chominciai questo"</note>

and it is a collection of many papers which I have
copied here, hoping then to put them in their
proper places, in order, according to the subjects
of which they treat. I believe that before
 I reach the end of this work,
I may have to repeat the same thing
multiple times; therefore, reader, do not blame me,
because the subjects are many and the memory
cannot retain them all and say, "This
I do not want to write because I already wrote it."
And if I wished to avoid this, I would fall into the
danger of not writing it at all due to the
long interval already mentioned.

If you wish to treat the subject of water,

Air thickens or becomes rarefied,

no differently than how the water of the sea is thicker

## [WATER (VORTICES). — PLANKS].

2. — This vortex <note>original: "retroso" — Leonardo uses this term for whirlpools or circular water movements.</note> does not have a fixed position —
[ Figure : ] e a b c d
Because *a b* is lighter than *c d*, *a b* cannot provide as much water as *c d* consumes; therefore, by necessity, air enters through *c d* into the space of the quantity of water that represented the difference between the water previously in *c d* and *a b*, and thus the water *c d* remains equal to the weight of the water *a b*.

Thin, wavy boards can be made of wood that will resemble camlets <term>camlet: a costly historical fabric, often made of silk and camel hair, known for its luster</term> and tabis <term>tabi: a "watered" silk or moiré fabric with a wavy pattern</term> and various permanent markings.

On surface vortices and those created at various depths of water; and those that take up the entire depth; and the mobile ones, and the stable ones. On the long and the round ones. On those that change their motion, and those that divide, and those that turn into the ones they join, and those that are mixed with falling and reflected water which keep that water turning.

Which are the vortices that rotate light objects on the surface and do not submerge them. Which are those that submerge them and rotate them on the bottom and then leave them on that bottom. Which are those that detach things from the bottom and throw them back to the surface of the water. Which are the oblique vortices, which are the straight, which are the flat.

---

2. — This water vortex has no steady position.
[ Figure : ] e a b c d <note>original: 1. 2.</note>.
Because *a b* is lighter than *c d*, *a b* cannot provide as much water as *c d* consumes; therefore, by necessity, air enters through *c d* in place of a quantity of water equal to the difference of the water that was at first more in *c d* than in *a b*, and so the water *c d* remains equal to the weight of water *a b*.

One can make, from wood, thin wavy planks that will look like camlets and tabis, and with various stable stains.

On surface vortices and those [which are] created at various heights of the water. Of those that take up all that height, and the mobile ones, and the stable ones. Of the long and the round ones. Of those that change motion, and those that divide, and those that turn into those they join, and those that are mixed with falling and reflected water, and make it turn.

Which are the vortices that make light things rotate on the surface and do not submerge them. Which are those that submerge them and make them rotate on the bottom, and then leave them at that bottom. Which are those that detach things from the bottom and throw them back to the surface of the water. Which are the oblique vortices, which are the straight, which are the flat.

## [PLAN FOR THE TREATISE ON WATER. — SWIMMING. — SHIPS].

When you assemble the science of the motions of water, remember to place under each proposition its practical applications, so that such science is not useless —

On the utility of the choices <note>original: "partiti" — refers to the decisions or tactical maneuvers a person must make.</note> that the swimmer must make regarding the surface eddies of the waters and their vortices which submerge those swimmers. And then, once he is submerged, how he must manage to save himself, and so on. And at the end of each book, observe more remarkable things, such as how to break through the thickness of vortices in any direction. On the choices one must make when swimming in sea waves, and the impact of rocks, and the steering of ships.

---

In putting together the science of the movements of water, remember to put under each proposition its helpers <note>referring to practical applications or supporting proofs</note>, so that such science is not useless.

On the utility of the decisions the swimmer has to take in relation to the surface turnings of the waters and their vortices, which submerge these swimmers. Then how he must govern himself when he is submerged, to save himself, and so on. And at the end of each book, observe more remarkable things, such as breaking the thickness of the vortices in any direction. Of the decisions that must be made while swimming in the waves of the seas, and how to avoid the strikes of the reefs and the governing of ships.

# [STAIRCASE. — WATER (CARRIED OBJECTS. — VORTICES)].

3. — [1$^{st}$ figure:] I 2 C
— [at the top, in red pencil:] brick staircase
— OF OBJECTS CARRIED BY WATER, THAT WHICH IS OF SMALLER SHAPE WILL UNDERGO GREATER REVOLUTION <note>original: "revolutione" — here referring to the spinning or swirling motion caused by eddies.</note>.
This happens because the large revolutions of vortices <note>original: "retrosi" — Leonardo's term for back-currents or whirlpools.</note> are rare in the courses of rivers, while small vortices are almost innumerable; large objects are only turned by large vortices and not by small ones, whereas small objects are turned by both small and large vortices <note>Leonardo is observing that smaller objects are more "obedient" to the chaotic movements of water because they fit within even the tiniest eddies.</note>.
— OF OBJECTS CARRIED BY THE WATER'S COURSE THAT ARE EQUAL IN LENGTH AND WIDTH, THOSE WHICH SINK DEEPER WILL UNDERGO FEWER REVOLUTIONS.
This occurs because these revolutions vary greatly from the surface to the bottom of the water; in the water, depths generate as many revolutions as there are depressions in their causes <note>The "causes" refers to the unevenness of the riverbed or obstacles.</note>. Therefore, by necessity, an object carried by water that sinks deeply is buffeted by many different heights of revolutions; for this reason, it remains hesitant <note>original: "dubbiosa" — literally "doubtful," describing an object that doesn't move decisively in one direction because it is being pulled multiple ways.</note>, and frequently it obeys none of them, and if it does obey, it obeys the most powerful one.
<margin>Of objects equal in shape and quantity, the one that sinks deeper obeys the revolutions of the water less.</margin>

# [LEVERS AND WEIGHTS (PROPORTIONS). — “JUDICIAL” SCALES].

[Figure:] c f g a e b 2 [under e] 4 [under d] 8 [under 4] 8 [under f]
The adversary says here that one must understand the weights of the arms of the scale together with the weight of the bodies joined to those arms; and that by considering this, the opposite centers of these combined weights will have distances proportioned to the pole <note>original: "polo" — the fulcrum or pivot point of the scale.</note> of the scale in the same proportion as those combined weights. To which the answer is yes, and it is proven thus: If each arm of the scale is 4 pounds, *that is* a-b and a-c, I will attach to the middle of a-b a weight of 4, which will make 8 between the attached weight and the weight of the arm; *that is*, the combination of the 2 weights is 8, and the center of gravity of this 8 is in the middle of that arm, at point e. On the opposite arm, at the extremity of that arm, I will place 2 against the 4 of the other arm <note>Leonardo is calculating how to balance a scale when the weight of the arm itself is factored in alongside added weights.</note>, and since the distances of the attached weights are doubled as are their weights, I will now make the "judicial" scale <note>original: "bilaca guditiale" — likely referring to a precision balance or a specific diagrammatic arrangement used for legal or scientific judgment.</note> e-f-g. <header>— FOLIO 3 (recto) —</header>

<note>Folio 3 (recto) contains a study on the physics of rebound (<term>percussion<gloss>the striking of one body against another</gloss></term>) and geometric diagrams.</note>

<note>Sketch of a vaulted or ribbed structure, possibly a bridge segment or architectural vaulting study.</note>

<note>Geometric diagram consisting of a circle with a vertical diameter and intersecting lines, likely related to optics or projection.</note>

If an artillery ball strikes a wall of equal hardness, it will rebound from it with angles equal to its <term>angles of incidence<gloss>the angle at which an object hits a surface</gloss></term>, and this rebound will move as far beyond the angle of rebound as the impact of the ball was into the wall, or into the mud, or into the water. <note>Leonardo is observing that the "law of reflection"—where the angle of approach equals the angle of departure—applies to physical objects like cannonballs just as it does to light.</note>

Any ball that rebounds from any solid surface will rebound at angles equal to one another; that is, the angle of percussion shall be equal to the angle of rebound. This occurs if the rebound is from a single body without any <term>yielding<gloss>original: "cedimento" — the compression or deformation of a surface upon impact</gloss></term>. But if it rebounds from a body that possesses some yielding, it will not rebound at equal angles, but will draw closer to the line of rebound than to the line of percussion; and this difference will be greater as the yielding of the struck body is greater. <note>Here, Leonardo correctly identifies that if a surface is soft (like mud or water), it absorbs some of the energy and changes the trajectory, a sophisticated early observation of inelastic collisions.</note>

[ WATER (10th BOOK.) — THE SUN AND THE AUTHORS ].

Book 10.
On the various depths and convexities placed within reservoirs <note>original: "bottini" — cisterns or water-collection chambers</note> before the water exits them, with various speeds, sizes, depths, widths, and shapes of the openings <note>original: "spiraculi" — literally "breathing holes," referring here to outlets or vents</note>, whether high or low, wide or narrow, with thick or thin walls.

[ Continuation from folio 5 recto ] The reasons for its greatness and power <note>original: "virtu" — the inherent physical force or excellence of a thing</note> I reserve for the fourth book; but I marvel greatly that Socrates blamed that body <note>Leonardo is likely referring to Anaxagoras, who was famously prosecuted for claiming the sun was a red-hot stone, though the idea was often discussed in Socratic circles</note> and that he said it was in the likeness of a fiery stone; and certainly, whoever rescued him from such an error would have done little wrong. But I would wish to have words that might serve me to rebuke those who wish to praise the worship of men more than that of the sun, not seeing in the universe a body of greater magnitude and power than that one. Its light illuminates all the celestial bodies that are distributed throughout the universe. 

All souls descend from it, because the heat that is in living animals comes from the soul, and there is no other heat or light in the universe, as I shall show in the fourth book. And certainly those who have wished to worship men as gods—such as Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and the like—have made a very great error, seeing that even if a man were as large as our world, he would appear like a tiny star, which appears as a mere point in the universe; and seeing also that these men are mortal, and putrid, and corruptible in their sepulchers.

<vocab>
- **Diameter (diamitro):** The width of a circular or spherical body.
- **Opaque (opachi):** Materials that do not allow light to pass through.
- **Pupil (pupilla):** The opening in the eye that receives light.
- **Species (spetie):** In medieval and Renaissance science, the "visible form" that travels from an object to the eye.
- **Diagonal (diagonale):** A line joining two opposite corners of a shape.
- **Similitude (similitudine):** A likeness or image of an object.
- **Luminous rays (raggi luminosi):** Beams of light.
- **Room (camera):** Literally a chamber; used here in the context of the "dark room" or camera obscura.
- **Eyes (ochi):** The organs of vision.

## [WATER (9TH BOOK) — THE SUN AND THE AUTHORS].

5. — Book Nine
Of the water that passes through a reservoir <term>reservoir; original: "bottino" — a cistern or water conduit</term> of which the walls are full of vents <term>vents; original: "spiracu li" — small openings or apertures</term> of various sizes, shapes, and positions at different heights, varying from the entrance to the exit and vice versa; and also of the reservoir of various shapes, depths, lengths, and widths; and of waters more or less powerful, fast, thick, or thin.

->PRAISE | Praise | OF THE SUN<-

If you look at the stars without their rays <note>By "rays," Leonardo refers to the visual "twinkling" or diffraction patterns seen by the naked eye.</note> (as is done by viewing them through a small hole made with the fine tip of a slender needle, placed so it almost touches the eye), you will see those stars to be so tiny that nothing seems smaller. Truly, the great distance causes a reasonable reduction in their size, even though many of them are many times larger than the "star" that is the earth with its water. Now, think what our own star <note>meaning Earth</note> would look like at such a distance, and then consider how many stars could be placed, in both length and width, between those stars which are scattered throughout that dark space. I cannot help but blame many of the ancients who said that the sun had no other size than what it appears to be; among these was Epicurus. I believe he derived such a reason from a light placed in our atmosphere equidistant to the center of the person seeing it; whoever sees it never sees it diminished in size at any distance, and the [ The continuation is on Folio 4 verso ] <note>original: "le ragi [ La suite au folio 4 verso ]"</note>

---

5. — Book Nine [ 9th ]:
Of the water that passes through a reservoir whose walls are full of various vents in size; shapes and places, with various heights, varying from the entrance to the exit, and reciprocally, and also: Of the reservoir of various shapes, depths, lengths and widths, and: Of waters more or less powerful, fast, large and small <note>Referencing J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, p. 491, "Bibliography". Below the first paragraph is a draft in red chalk.</note>.

### PRAISE OF THE SUN.

If you look at the stars without rays (as one does by seeing them through a small hole made with the extreme tip of a fine needle, and placed almost touching the eye), you will see these stars being so tiny that nothing can appear smaller, and truly the long distance gives them a reasonable diminution, although there are many which are a very great number of times larger than the star which is the earth with the water. Think now what our star would appear at such a great distance, and then consider how many stars one would put, both in length and width, between those stars which are sown in the shadowy space. I can never help but blame many of those ancients who said that the sun has no other greatness than that which it shows; among them was Epicurus. And I believe that such a reason [idea] is drawn from a light placed in our air equidistant to the center [of the earth]; whoever sees it never sees it diminished in size at any distance and the [continued on folio 4 verso] <note>Referencing Libri, Vol. III, Note XIV. — J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 879. Dr. M. Jordan, p. 76.</note>.

## [CENTERS OF GRAVITY. — HOW THE STARS ARE SEEN. — CHARLATANS].

[ Figure: ] c a b d e f f
Although **b** is the center of accidental gravity <term>accidental gravity; original: "grauita accidentale" — the weight of an object relative to its position on a balance</term> of the pyramid **e**, and the tip counterbalances the base just as much, the true center of natural gravity, which is at **a**, cannot, I believe, be as close to the central line as the center of the cube is. Because it is further from the balance point of the pyramid **c e**, it would happen that when you balanced the pyramid at that center of natural gravity, the part toward the tip would be heavier than the part toward the base; and the excess that the weight of the tip had over the weight of the base would be discharged onto the cube.

The stars are seen by night and not by day because we are beneath the thickness of the air, which is full of infinite particles of moisture. Each of these, when struck by the rays of the sun, yields its own brightness, and so these innumerable splendors <note>original: "invmerabilis plendori"</note> occupy [the view of] those stars; if such air were not there, the sky would always show us the stars within its darkness.

### [WEIGHT AND GRAVITY. — THE SUN AND EPICURUS].

8. — [ 1st figure : ] a o r t n m
The small attachment <term>attachment; original: "appendicolo" — a small supporting piece or counterweight</term> **a n** supports the excess weight that the tip of the pyramid acquires because its whole is not suspended at its center of accidental gravity <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "natural gravity" (the innate center of mass) and "accidental gravity" (where the weight shifts due to position or added mass).</note>. If this attachment **a n** did not support it, this excess weight of the tip would discharge onto the other pyramid and enter the true center of natural gravity of that pyramid, weighed perpendicularly.

Perhaps Epicurus <note>Epicurus (c. 341–270 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who famously argued that the sun was exactly the size it appeared to be in the sky.</note> saw that the shadows of columns striking opposite walls were equal to the diameter of the column from which the shadow originated. Since the path of the shadow was parallel from its beginning to its end, it appeared to him that the sun, too, must be the same width as that parallel <note>i.e., no wider than the column itself</note>. Consequently, he judged the sun to be no larger than that column, not realizing that such a narrowing of the shadow was imperceptible due to the immense distance of the sun.

If the sun were smaller than the earth, the stars in a large part of our hemisphere would be without light; this contradicts Epicurus, who says the sun is only as large as it appears to be.

### [WATER PENETRATING A BODY OF WATER].

[ Figure : ] c b a n m
The flow and ebb <note>Refers to the movement of tides or the surging of water in and out of a passage.</note> is doubled in the same basin <term>basin; original: "pelago" — a deep, stagnant, or slow-moving body of water like a pool or lake</term>, because it will occur many times at the mouth of that basin before the larger [or smaller?] flow is within the great basin itself. This happens because the wave of the first flow runs strongly into the basin, and during the time that this wave follows its momentum <term>momentum; original: "impeto" — the force or "impetus" of a moving body</term>, the water at the mouth makes its ebb. Before the wave that "engulfs" <note>pénètre dans le golfe; enters the deeper part of the basin</note> feels the ebb of the mouth of the basin **c a**, the flow is reborn at that mouth. In that time, the engulfed wave stops, slowing its momentum as much as the second engulfing of the second wave is reborn. Thus, so many waves engulf themselves that the basin, having risen, returns its waters with momentum behind the flow that retreats from that mouth; it no longer engulfs itself in the third or fourth wave until the first water has "dis-engulfed" <note>flowed back out of the basin</note>.

---

<margin>
1. For the specific meaning of the word "pelago" (lake, pond, sheet of water), see Cardinali, p. 273: "a wide and deep shape, in which the waters remain with little motion... the waters entering the basin do so without percussion."
2. For the specific meanings of the word "impeto" (the Latin *impetus*), see the table of contents of manuscripts E and K (Volume III of this publication).
3. Beneath the ink: sketches and a draft in red chalk. The cross in gray pencil is a reader's mark.
4. Libri, vol. III, Note XII.
</margin>

## [WATER. — THE SUN (EPICURUS. — ECLIPSES)].

Given the thickness of the falling water and its slant, along with the power of the wheel which acts as its object, one seeks: the height of the fall of such water required to make it equal to the power of the wheel that <note>The sentence in the original Italian manuscript ends abruptly here.</note>.

The water that strikes objects sometimes splashes back a great deal, and sometimes a little, and sometimes it flows down; this arises from the objects being narrow or wide, or from the greater or lesser descent in front of those objects, or from the more or less powerful current that strikes such objects.

Epicurus says that the sun is exactly the size that it appears to be; therefore, as it appears to be one foot [wide], we must hold it to be so. It would follow that when the moon obscures the sun <note>a solar eclipse</note>, the sun would not exceed the moon in size, as it actually does; since the moon is smaller than the sun, the moon would then be less than one foot wide. Consequently, when our world <note>the Earth</note> obscures the moon <note>a lunar eclipse</note>, it would be smaller than a toe. This is because if the sun is one foot wide and our earth casts a pyramidal shadow <term>umbra; the cone-shaped shadow cast by a planet</term> toward the moon, it is necessary that the luminous source causing the shadow pyramid be larger than the opaque body causing said pyramid <note>Leonardo is using geometric logic to disprove the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus's claim that the sun is only as large as it looks to the naked eye.</note>.

> 1, 2. Figures appear under the 1st and 2nd paragraphs in red chalk, along with a draft in the same chalk under the 2nd paragraph, starting with: "The water that strikes," and ending with: "the more or less powerful current that strikes such objects."
> 3. J.-P. Richter, Volume II, No. 882.
> 4. The crosses at the top of the page and in front of the last paragraph are readers' marks, made in grey pencil.

# FOLIO 9 (recto)

->[WATER — QUESTIONS]<-

9. — Why the eddies <note>original: "iretrosi dellacqua"</note> of the water are hollowed out in the middle by their revolution.
Why the impressions generated on the surface of the water will maintain themselves for some time while being carried by the course of the waters.
Why the movements of the impressions of the waters penetrate one another without changing their original shape.
Rule of the water ounces <term>a historical unit used to measure the rate of water flow; original: "once dell'acqua"</term>, and what width, depth, and velocity of movement a given space of flow must have in a given time.

# FOLIO 9 (verso)

->[MEASUREMENT OF WATER (17 CASES)]<-

OF THE WATER OUNCE <term>the "once" was a standard measure for distributing water to users, such as farmers or millers</term>, AND IN HOW MANY WAYS IT CAN VARY.
Water which pours through a mouth <note>opening or orifice</note> of the same size can vary in quantity, becoming greater or smaller, in [17] ways.
1st: by the surface of the water being higher or lower above the mouth from which it pours.
2nd: by the water passing with greater or lesser velocity along the bank where that mouth is made.
3rd: by the bottom side of the thickness of the mouth where the water passes being more or less sloped.
4th: by the variety of the slopes of the sides of such a mouth.
5th: by the thickness of the lip of that mouth.
6th: by the shape of the mouth, that is, whether it is round, square, rectangular, or elongated.
7th: by that mouth being placed at a greater or lesser slope of the bank along its length.
8th: by such a mouth being placed at a greater or lesser slope of the bank in its height.
9th: by it being placed in the concavities or convexities of the bank.
10th: by it being placed in a greater or lesser width of the canal.
11th: if the height of the canal has more velocity at the height of the mouth or more slowness than elsewhere.
12th: if the bottom has protrusions or hollows opposite this mouth, or is higher or lower.
13th: whether the water passing through such a mouth catches the wind or not.
14th: whether the water falling out of this mouth falls through the air enclosed on one side, or on all sides except the front.
15th: whether the water that falls enclosed is thick in its vessel or thin.
16th: whether the water that falls while being enclosed has a long or short drop.
17th: whether the sides of the canal where such water descends are smooth or bumpy, or straight or curved.

<margin>
1. See above, folio 8 recto, note 3.
2. See: F. Cardinali, book eight, chap. XVI, p. 419: "On the true measure of the water wave." The water that pours... can vary... in sixteen ways... Several differences (the 9th case is skipped, and the 10th becomes the 9th), and Venturi, *Essai*, etc., p. 23-24. <note>Giovanni Battista Venturi was a physicist who rediscovered the importance of Leonardo's hydraulic studies in the late 18th century.</note>
3. Venturi, *Essai*, etc., p. 23; — Dr. M. Jordan, p. 76.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s systematic study of hydraulics, shifting from the practical observations of river behavior on Folio 8 to theoretical physics. Here, he explores the "hydrostatic paradox"—the idea that pressure at the base of a container depends on the height of the fluid rather than the total volume—and the principles of buoyancy and relative weight.</meta>

# FOLIO 9 (recto)

If water is raised through other [water] by the same weight or force, ensure that the motion of each one would be as if it were alone.

The weights of vessels of equal height and bases, even though the vessels might be of a different capacity and of a different shape, are to be weighed one against the other by the weight of the water resting upon their bases, and not on the lids nor on the sides of these vessels, nor on any part of these vessels, for the reason [given] below.

The weight of vessels of equal height and bases, even if the vessel is of different capacity, has the same weight upon these vessels, that is, at the bottom of these vessels. <note>This is a foundational principle of fluid mechanics: water pressure at the bottom of a container is determined by the depth of the water and the area of the base, not the total volume or shape of the container.</note>

Beyond this, let all the water of vessel J be weighed, and it shall be similar to the weight of the water of vessel L, although the vessel may be much wider at the upper part than at the bottom, because it is of equal height.

And note how the movement of the water in the height of vessel D is as much slower than in the height of the other vessel as the vessel is wider in that part than in the other; so that the weight of the water that moves in one of these vessels is of the same weight as the weight of the other water that moves.

---

# FOLIO 9 (verso)

Also, if water is raised through the air, its weight shall be equal to the weight of that water.

However:
Water moving within water has as much lightening <note>original: "alieggieramento"; referring to buoyancy</note> in itself as the weight of an equal amount of water that it occupies. <note>This is Leonardo's phrasing of Archimedes' Principle: an object immersed in a fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.</note>

Let the water *b f* move within the water *a c d e* and be of equal quality <note>original: "bontà"; referring to its density or purity</note> with the said water; I say that such water does not weigh upon any part of the surrounding water, because whatever weight it has is sustained by the surrounding water, just as the weight of the surrounding water is sustained by the water below, as is proven in the third [book] of *On Weights* <note>original: "de le ponderi"; likely referring to a medieval collection of treatises on statics such as the *Liber de Ponderibus*</note>, because *d* is of the same weight as the surrounding water, therefore it is in itself in equilibrium upon the base.

Therefore, if such water moves among other water and is of the same weight as it, it is not pressured nor moved by the other water.

It follows then that such water *b f* is moved by itself or by some other external force.

If such water is moved by itself, it is necessary that one [part] be heavier than the other, because the movement of waters through other waters proceeds by inequality of weight, whereby the heavier part drives out the less heavy and places itself beneath it, or truly the lighter part is driven out by the heavier and places itself above it.

If such water is of the same weight as its surroundings, then it will not be moved by itself but by another force.

If it is moved by another force, it will be none other than the surrounding water that drives it for other causes, such as the currents, because it will be of the same weight as the surrounding water, and thus will be entirely in equilibrium.

Therefore, water that moves through other waters has no weight, except for that weight which is generated by its motion and by the resistance.

Because the motion of the water is gravity <note>Leonardo is connecting the momentum of moving water to the concept of weight/force</note>, so that the motion of the water shall be weight for itself, and it shall be as much heavier as the motion is faster.

<summary>This page contains Leonardo's theoretical proofs regarding hydrostatic pressure and buoyancy, correctly identifying that water pressure depends on depth and that water within water exists in a state of neutral buoyancy unless moved by density differences or external force.</summary>
<keywords>hydrostatics, fluid mechanics, buoyancy, equilibrium, water pressure, relative weight, Archimedes' Principle, motion, density</keywords>

<header>— FOLIO 10 (recto). —</header>

### [HYDRAULIC DEVICES. — THE SUN (Epicurus. — Experiment)].

10. — Concerning the size and shape of the primary wheel that receives water for aquatic instruments, and concerning their <term>simpula<gloss>small ladles or scoops used to lift water</gloss></term> and other accessories belonging to this wheel.
[ Figure : ]  a  n  r m  o  Sun.

Measure how many suns would fit into its course of 24 hours.
Make a circle and turn it toward the south, just as sundials are positioned; place a rod in the middle so that its length is directed at the center of this circle, and note the shadow that the sun casts from this rod onto the circumference of the circle. Let us say the width of the shadow is exactly *a n*; now, measure how many times this shadow fits into the circumference of that circle, and that same number of times the body of the sun will fit into its course in 24 hours.

[ Figure : ] And here one can see if Epicurus <note>Epicurus was an ancient Greek philosopher who argued that the sun was exactly as large as it appeared to the eye, a view Leonardo is testing here with geometry.</note> spoke [rightly] when he said the sun was as large as it appeared to be; for if the diameter of the sun appeared to be the measure of one foot, and this sun entered one thousand times into its course of 24 hours, it would have traveled one thousand feet—that is, 500 <term>braccia<gloss>an Italian unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or the length of an arm</gloss></term>—which is one-sixth of a mile. Therefore, the sun's course between day and night would have traveled the sixth part of a mile, meaning this "venerable snail" of a sun would have traveled only 25 braccia per hour. <note>Leonardo is using irony here; if the sun were as small as it looks, its speed across the sky would be absurdly slow, like a snail.</note>

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 883.</margin>

<header>— FOLIO 10 (verso). —</header>

### [HOT IRON AND FILINGS. — CONVEX MIRRORS].

Test if hot iron attracts iron filings to itself. <note>Leonardo is investigating whether heat influences magnetic attraction.</note>
[1st fig. : ]  a  o  t  b  p  n  c  s  m  a

ON THE <term>ANGLE OF CONTINGENCY<gloss>The angle between a curve and its tangent line</gloss></term>, THE IMPOSSIBILITY OF GIVING A GENERAL RULE, OR SCIENCE, IS SHOWN HERE, TO EVER BE ABLE TO DO SO.

Even though *p q c* is a given convex mirror, and *b* is a given light source, and *c* is the eye which must see that light source upon the mirror, I say it is impossible to give a general rule for finding the <term>simulacrum<gloss>the reflected image</gloss></term> of that light upon the said mirror. This is because, even though the angles that are placed in the middle of this angle of contingency are equal, the sides at the base of such angles will never be in a regular proportion to one another, as are the sides of the other opposite angle. Because even if the angle *o c n* is equal to the angle *b c m t e s*, the base of one will not be in the same proportion with its straight side as the base of the other is with its straight side. Similarly, it happens that the curved side of one will not be in the same proportion with its straight side as the curved side of the other angle is with its straight side. Thus, every part is discordant because of the <unclear>m</unclear> of their curved side; whereas if it were straight, every part would correspond one to the other.

[2nd fig. : ] a b c d e
See how the 2 triangles *a b c* and *d e c* are proportioned by having all their sides straight; all the sides of the larger are double the sides of the smaller.

<header>— FOLIO 10 (recto). —</header>

### [THE PRINCIPLES OF WEIGHT AND MOTION]

All weights, of whatever shape they may be, will be equal in weight at a distance proportional to their lightness relative to their other counterweight.

You will double the weight of the machine, and so it shall be with its force.

<note>To the right of the middle text is a small circular diagram showing a wheel with a vertical radius.</note>

That machine is of a revolving motion which is surrounding <note>Original: *circunfustante*. This likely refers to a mechanism where weights are distributed around the circumference to maintain momentum.</note>, and from here will start the origin of the counterweights which continually fall to give motion to such a wheel. This would be of infinite motion <note>Infinite motion here is a synonym for perpetual motion.</note>, which would be the cause that brings about in a short time the motion that occurs through surrounding motion. And it seemed to me a thing not to be kept silent, because the motions that are to come are proper to weights; and when such weights are in excess, the motion will not be brief, which case would be in perpetual motion. And here will be demonstrated the art that nature holds in said motions, which do not make themselves known except by force of such art of which I shall speak. Which seemed to me a thing not to be kept silent because the **perpetual motion** that you seek is not of nature; and there will never be a thing that has life, nor will said force ever be without the fall of weights, which fall will be the cause of said motion. From which it follows that said motion will be of infinite vanities <note>Original: *vane*. Leonardo often used this word to describe the "empty" or "failing" attempts of engineers to create perpetual motion machines, which he viewed as scientifically impossible.</note> from which the motion is born through said counterweights.

---

<header>— FOLIO 10 (verso). —</header>

### [STUDIES ON THE PERPETUAL MOTION WHEEL]

If you move the ball which is at equal distances.

<note>Below this line is a large circular diagram representing a wheel for studying perpetual motion through the displacement of weights. It is inscribed with several lines and letters (a, b, c, d, e, f, g).</note>

From the line **.a.**, which is <term>perpendicular<gloss>a line at a 90-degree angle to the horizon</gloss></term> to the center of the wheel, starts the line of the weights that fall outside of such a wheel.

Let **d** be suspended to the wheel of the ball and be at a distance of equal weights, because one is as far to the right as the other is to the left.

That part of said wheel which finds itself sending the weight shall be the weight of infinite times; it shows that said weight always falls above the <term>handle<gloss>Original: "mandre." Refers to a mechanical lead or a device to guide the weight.</gloss></term>; the line of the weight which is perpendicular above the center from which the wheel is born shall send the said motion. From which it follows that said motion will be of infinite vanities, from which the motion is born through said counterweights; but it will always be of equal weight, because said weight will be to said motion, [and] the said motion will always be of one and the same weight.

<margin>
If the ball **.f.** is suspended at **.b.** at equal distances, it will be of equal weight to the center **.a.**; **.g.** are weights at said distances.
</margin>

<header>— FOLIO 11 (recto). — / — FOLIO 11 (verso). —</header>

->[CANALS (CURRENTS AND EDDIES)]<-

II. — [ 1st fig. : ] a b
The different positions of the entry and exit of water across the width of its canals drive the current of this water toward the absolute middle of the width of said canal.

[ 2nd fig. : ] c d
The height and the lowering of the entry and exit of the water in its canal varies the total height of the current in its canal, which ought to have been equally distant from the bank and from the bottom.

If, in a parallel canal, an exit is provided in the bottom for a quantity of water, and a vortex <note>Original: *retroso* (a whirlpool or eddy)</note> is generated above such an exit, one asks about the nature of such a vortex.

---

->[GEOLOGY (FORMATION OF MOUNTAINS AND VALLEYS)]<-

If the land of the antipodes <note>Original: *antipodi*. Leonardo refers to the land on the opposite side of the globe, which was a subject of great speculation during the Age of Discovery.</note> which supports the ocean were to rise and reveal itself far out of that sea, being almost flat, in what way would it then, over time, create mountains and valleys—and stones of various layers <note>Original: *falde* (strata or layers of rock)</note>?

The mud or sand from which the water drains, when it remains uncovered by the floods of rivers, teaches us what is asked above.

The water that would drain from the land uncovered by the sea, when that land rose high above the sea, would—even if the land were almost flat—begin to form various streams through the lower parts of that plain. In starting to hollow them out, they would become receptacles for the other surrounding waters. In this way, in every part of its length, the water would gain width and depth, its flow always increasing until all such water had drained away. These hollows would then become the courses of torrents that receive rainwater; and thus they would go on consuming the sides of 

<margin>these rivers, until the spaces between these rivers would become sharp mountains. And as these hills drained, they would begin to dry and create stones in layers, larger or smaller according to the thickness of the mud that the rivers carried into that sea through their floods <note>Original: *diluvi* (great floods or deluges)</note>.</margin>

---

<note>Historical Note: Leonardo was one of the first to recognize that mountains were not static features created at the beginning of the world, but were formed by the dual processes of sedimentation (mud settling in the sea) and erosion (water cutting through the land). He correctly identified fossils and strata as evidence of ancient sea levels.</note>

<summary>Leonardo examines how the placement of canal inlets affects water currents and proposes a revolutionary geological theory: that mountains and valleys are formed by the erosive power of water and the drying of ancient seabed sediment.</summary>

<header>FOLIO 11 (recto). — FOLIO 11 (verso).</header>

# FOLIO 11 (recto)

To know how great the movement <note>Leonardo uses "moto" (movement) here to refer to the displacement or volume of flow over time.</note> of a certain portion of water will be through a canal that is of a single width and a single depth:

While the water in this canal takes time to pass through a distance equal to its own length, an amount of water will depart from this canal that is equal to its length, and of that same width and depth.
— This is proved by the figure below —

Let the water move at a uniform rate throughout the canal, and in such a way that as much as departs, just as much will return; and the movement of the water shall be the same toward the bottom.

---

# FOLIO 11 (verso)

That which falls in a straight line will have a greater impact <note>Original: *percussione*. Leonardo is studying the physics of force and momentum.</note> than that which falls in an oblique <note>Slanted or diagonal.</note> line, as is seen by the strike of water that falls straight down, because the force of this water falls along a straight line.

<note>Drawing of water falling from a vertical stream and splashing against a horizontal surface, illustrating hydraulic impact.</note>

If the water that falls obliquely is slower than that which falls in a straight line, the impact of that strike will be less.

If the water is of a uniform thickness <note>Meaning a consistent volume or depth of the stream.</note> throughout its course without any variation, the movement will be slower at the bottom than at its surface, because the water at the bottom touches the solid bed <note>Original: *il sodo*. This refers to the fixed, unmoving earth of the canal floor.</note>, and this solid bed resists the movement; the other part of the water touches nothing but water, which does not resist the movement at all. And it will be slower toward the banks for the same reason.

<margin>
Furthermore, the part of the water that is in the middle will be faster because it touches nothing but water which is moved along with it, whereas at the banks it will touch the banks, which will greatly resist its movement.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo defines the principles of hydraulic flow, noting how water volume is conserved in a channel and how friction against the bed and banks slows the current. He also observes that vertical falls produce a more powerful impact than slanted ones due to the directness of the force.</summary>

<keywords>hydraulics, fluid dynamics, friction, water velocity, impact force, canal flow, Leonardo da Vinci physics</keywords>

<header>— FOLIO 12 (recto). —</header>

->[WATER (EDDIES)].<-

12. — On the eddies <note>Original: *deretrosi*. These are back-currents or whirlpools formed when water strikes an obstacle or turns back on itself.</note> of water which many times turn back their whirling motion —

Of incident eddies and reflected eddies. The eddy sometimes increases in power and decreases in diameter, and sometimes decreases in power and increases in diameter — The first movement occurs when the water pours along its bottom; the water that composes the eddy is then faster the lower it is, because it has a greater weight of water above it, and for that reason it becomes faster. Because the water pushes more at the bottom than at the top, it further constricts the vacuum <note>Leonardo often used the term "vacuum" to describe the hollow center of a vortex or whirlpool.</note> at the eddy; it bends because it directs itself toward the exit of the water from its "pool" <term>pelago: a deep body of water or a wide basin within a river course</term>.

---

12. — On the eddies of water which many times turn back their whirling motion.
Of incident eddies <note>Incoming or striking currents.</note> and reflected eddies <note>Currents that have bounced back.</note>. The eddy, sometimes, increases in power and diminishes in diameter, and sometimes diminishes in power and increases in diameter.
The first movement is when the water flows out through its bottom; the water that makes up the eddy is then faster the lower it is, because it has a greater weight of water above it, and for that reason becomes faster; the water, pushing more at the bottom than at the top, narrows the void at the eddy more; it bends because it directs itself toward the exit of the water from its "pool." <note>See above, folio 6 verso, note I.</note>

---

<header>— FOLIO 12 (verso). —</header>

->[WATER (CURRENTS AND EDDIES)].<-

Water on an uneven bottom creates contrary movements from the surface to the bed —
The inequality of the bed of rivers arises from the bends in the banks, or from material fallen from these banks at their base —

[ 2nd figure: ] b n a c
Earth falls from the bank and stops under the water at *a*; the water *b* strikes it and divides; part of it turns back and creates the eddy *n*, and part of it goes to *c*. The water *b c* is of equal speed in its current on side *c*, and where there are eddies—one from top to bottom and one of the water at *n*—light objects stop there; and thus, beneath the current, the water becomes slow from the middle forward. In the beginning, because there is little depth, the current is as fast at the bottom as it is at the surface; and for this reason it uncovers the coarse gravel, then the sand, then the mud, and then the leaves. <note>Leonardo is describing the process of hydraulic sorting, where water velocity determines which materials are eroded or deposited.</note>

---

Water on an uneven bottom makes contrary movements, from the surface to the bottom. The inequality of the bed of rivers arises from the bends of the banks, or from materials fallen from these banks at their base.
[ 2nd figure: ] b n a c
Earth falls from the bank and it stops under the water at *a*, and divides; part of it returns backward and creates the eddy *n*, and part of it goes to *c*—it *departs*. The water *b c* is of equal speed in its current on side *c*, and where there are eddies, one from top to bottom and one of the water at *n*, light things come to a rest; and thus, under the current, the water becomes slow from the middle forward. At the start, because there is little depth, the current is as fast below as it is above; and for this reason it reveals the coarse gravel, then the sand, then the mire, then the leaves.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanics of eddies (vortices) and how riverbed obstacles like fallen earth create complex back-currents. He notes that water velocity and pressure at different depths cause the sorting of riverbed materials, from heavy gravel to light leaves.</summary>

# FOLIO 12 (recto). — FOLIO 12 (verso).

The movement of the air in front of a moving body <note>Original: *mobile*. This refers to any object traveling through a medium.</note> causes the space behind it to be filled by that same [air].

Why the bird cools the air with its wings when it rises and falls in the same spot: the air that is pushed down under the wing is compressed, and the other air which follows above it [takes the place of] some of the air above the wing through the narrow spaces that exist between the feathers at the tip of the wing. This happens because the air enters there very rapidly, and that entering air cools the heat of the blood in such a wing; for such a wing, through its great motion, heats itself significantly. This is because the air is pressed under the wing and escapes above through the aforementioned thin and narrow passages <term>meati: small openings, pores, or gaps, here referring to the spaces between feathers</term>.

<note>Small diagram on the right shows a curved profile, likely a wing study, with airflow lines.</note>

---

Nature has made all animals that have a neck so that they can turn their head.

No substance can give motion by its breath <note>Original: *soffio*. Referring to a blast or current of air/fluid.</note> to another that is thicker or thinner than its own.

How the air, through its movement, draws to itself the cloth <note>Original: *panno*. In this context, Leonardo uses the term to describe a textured surface, possibly animal skin or heavy fabric.</note>; this thing gradually swells because the air moved in a straight line through the exit of the passage has greater force than that which enters it. The multitude of hairs on such a cloth, which stand upright against the air, do not let it enter between them; and therefore the air that strikes those hairs is held back <note>Original: *si rincresce*. In this physical context, it suggests the air builds up or is crowded against the resistance of the hairs.</note> and inflates that skin with the same force with which the air is flung out of the passage, and with which the air comes against said hairs, so that the air comes to cool the cloth and is itself cooled by that cloth.

<note>The following list provides the English equivalents for technical terms used in the manuscript:</note>
**Vocabulary:** movement, moving body, bird, cools, the air, feathers, passages, motion, cloth, hairs.

<summary>Leonardo examines the cooling effect of wing movement in birds and the aerodynamic interaction between air and textured surfaces like feathers or hairy cloth. He notes that rapid movement generates heat which the air then dissipates through narrow gaps.</summary>

# FOLIO 13 (recto). — [MILLS AND WATER VORTICES].

13. — [1st fig.:] d a b c e [Beneath the 1st fig., upside down:] When the pond is empty in the month of June, close the mouths <note>Original: *boche*. These are the sluice gates or inlets.</note> and divert the river that used to flow inside, giving it an outlet into the mill-race.

->**THE ACCIDENTAL VORTEX**<-

A hand turned in a circular motion in a vessel half-filled with water generates an accidental vortex <note>Original: *retroso accidentale*. A vortex created by an external force rather than natural flow.</note> which will expose the bottom of said vessel to the air; and after its motor <note>The "motor" here refers to the hand providing the movement.</note> has stopped, this vortex will continue the same motion, but it will always diminish until the end of the impetus <term>impeto: the momentum or force communicated to the water</term> that its motor gave to it.

->**THE UTILITY OF THE VORTEX**<-

[3rd fig.:] Sea. Sea. Pond. Pond.
[Above the 4th fig.:] Augmentation wheel <note>Original: *rota daumento*. Likely a wheel designed to increase the force or volume of water flow.</note> [Beneath the 4th fig.:] A vessel closed everywhere except at the bottom, where water enters only through the siphon <term>cicognola: a siphon or cranked pipe used to move water</term> brought there from the pond.
[5th fig.:] Of one piece.
[6th fig.:] a b c m rt d fne oh g
Let **abc** be the shore of the sea, **bm** the mouth of the pond, **mf** the pond, **fg** the river that forms the pond, **ohn** a canal taken from the upper part of the river for the mill which holds all the water of the river, **fd** the mill-race, **cde** the narrow canal from the sea to the fall, **rt** the mouth of the siphon, **t** the water vortex, and let the mouth **bm** be closed.
In practice, let the secret of the siphon and the vortex be covered and walled in, and let them be placed far from the sea.

# FOLIO 13 (verso). — [WATER VORTICES].

->**ON THE CONCAVITY AND UTILITY OF WATER VORTICES**<-

1st: That vortex will have a deeper concavity <note>The hollow, funnel-shaped center of a whirlpool.</note> which is generated in water of faster motion.
And that vortex will be of lesser concavity if it is generated in "thicker" <note>Original: *grossa*. Leonardo often uses this to mean denser or more voluminous water.</note> water that is not of the same motion, but is slower and turns toward other courses or is without motion.
2nd: And in water of equal speed, that one will maintain itself with its concavity where a greater thickness of water turns together with its motion.
This is said because many times vortices are generated in a narrow current within a great breadth of slow-moving water; this [slow water], being partly supported by the vortex which is full of air, produces water of thin revolution that turns between itself and the air of the concavity; this lateral water, being of great weight, pushes against the sides of the vortex where it rests and, finding it weak, comes to squeeze it closed.
Turn the page [to folio 13 recto] and note the accidental vortex and its benefits.
[In the margin, 2nd fig.:] Vortex generated by a narrow current in a large pool <term>pelago: a large expanse of water, such as a deep pool or the sea</term> of slow movement.
[3rd fig.:] Vortex caused by a large current in a large pool of slow motion.

14. — HOW, WITH RUNNING WATERS, ONE SHOULD CONDUCT THE EARTH OF THE MOUNTAINS INTO MARSHY VALLEES TO MAKE THEM FERTILE AND TO SANITIZE THE SURROUNDING AIR —

[Figure labels:] a b c e g d f h n s
The branches of the canals which, from the high hills, will be conducted according to their natural course, are those which, through their shifting, carry the soil of these hills to the low marshes <note>Original: *paludi*. Leonardo is describing a process of land reclamation known as 'colmata,' where sediment-heavy water is used to raise the level of swampy ground.</note> and fill them with earth, making them fertile.
Let **a** be the main river that enters the marshes at **bfs**; let the canal then be drawn along the height of the hills **acn**, and from it let various branches be allowed to fall; and wherever it is, by shifting the water to different locations, the rushing descents will erode the terrain, and at the end of their course, they will discharge it into the low marshes. In this way, you can change the fall of the entire canal—which is abundant in water—so much that you will have leveled the ground revealed outside of such marshes.

14. — HOW ONE MUST CONDUCT, WITH RUNNING WATERS, THE TERRAIN OF THE MOUNTAINS INTO THE MARSHY VALLEYS, AND MAKE THEM FERTILE, AND SANITIZE THE SURROUNDING AIR.
<note>This section is a French translation of the Italian text above, likely from a later scholarly edition. The meaning remains the same: using hydraulic power to move sediment for land reclamation.</note>
[Figure labels:] a b c e g d f h n s.
The ramifications of the canals, which will be conducted from the high hills according to their natural course, are those which, with their changes, carry the terrains of these hills to the low marshes, fill them with earth and make them fertile.
Let **a** be the master river which enters the marshes at **bfs**; let the canal then be drawn from the height of the hills **acn**, and let various ramifications be allowed to fall from it; and where it is whole, let it be changed in various places so that its descents will ravine the ground, and at the end of their course, discharge it into the low marshes; thus you will be able to change the fall of the entire canal, rich in water, so much that you will have equalized the ground uncovered outside these marshes.

### [WATER VORTICES].

IF WATER HIGHER THAN THE AIR ACQUIRES WEIGHT, AS SHOWN BY THE 7th [PROPOSITION] OF THE 9th [BOOK], WHAT CAUSE MAKES THE WATER AT THE CÔTÉS OF THE VORTICES <note>Original: *retrosi*. You have the 4th of the 7th which proves that every heavy body <term>grave: a physical body or substance possessing weight</term> weighs only along the line of its motion and nowhere else; and from this you see the very deep vortices in the form of great river-wells <note>Original: *pozi de quali* (wells of which). Leonardo compares the hollow center of a whirlpool to a deep well.</note>, the sides of which consist of water that is everywhere higher than the air of that vortex; and these banks of water weigh nothing except along the line of their motion, during the time they possess the power given to them by their motor <note>The 'motor' is the force or momentum driving the water's rotation.</note>.
Why vortices are generated, and why some are hollowed out in the middle and some are not.
Whether the water that would pour into the concavity of the vortices would fill them or not, or if it would escape through the bottom or enter into the lateral current.
<margin>Which natural vortices are those that deepen significantly and which only a little; which change their location and which are stable; which press toward their center and which rise; which, in their progress, turn in contrary motions and which maintain their motion in a single direction; which double themselves and which do not; which join together in contrary motions.</margin>

IF THE WATER HIGHER THAN THE AIR ACQUIRES WEIGHT, AS THE 7th OF THE 9th SHOWS, WHAT CAUSE MAKES THE WATER AT THE SIDES OF THE VORTICES HIGHER THAN THE BOTTOM OF THE VORTEX, WHICH UNTIL THERE IS FULL OF AIR.

Why vortices are engendered, and why some are hollowed out in the middle and some are not ².

<header>- FOLIO 14 (recto). -</header>

How it is possible that the moon can reflect the sun's light, since she is made of such a dark substance and such dense matter? <note>Leonardo is grappling with a classic problem of his time: how the Moon, which appears to be a dark, rocky body like Earth, can shine so brightly. He eventually concludes that the Moon is covered in water, which acts like a mirror.</note>

<note>Small horizontal sketch between text blocks, possibly representing a horizon or water study.</note>

To know how the eye sees various luminous sources placed at different distances from one another, without one obstructing the other, but allowing all their splendor to be seen through the air without any hindrance; and this is the reason:

that if you place a candle flame in a dark room, and place 2 or 3 or 4 or more, one on one side and others on the other, you will see that every flame sends the ray of its light to one place, and they do not hinder one another, but pass through the same small hole <note>This refers to the *camera obscura* (dark chamber) effect, where light from multiple sources can pass through a single pinhole and remain distinct on the other side.</note> without any hindrance from the air; and every light sends its likeness <note>Original: *similitudine*. In Renaissance optics, this refers to the "species" or the visual image of an object traveling through space.</note> throughout the entire space; and I do not need to make any other comparison than that of the candle flame.

---

<header>- FOLIO 14 (verso). -</header>

<margin>
With what motion the water moves in vessels, moved by a center, which is the movement of the water; because by moving the center of the water, all the rest of the water that is in the vessel is moved in a circle, in which center the water goes sinking down along the line of a body. <note>Leonardo is describing the formation of a vortex (like water draining from a tub), where the central axis of the rotation creates a downward pull.</note>
</margin>

While the earth is not turned toward the sun, no body that is found between this earth and the sun can be illuminated by the sun; on the contrary, it is always in shadow between the earth and the sun, unless it were a body luminous of itself, or one that reflected the light of the other stars that are illuminated by the sun; but this would be a weak and uncertain light, which would not be sufficient to overcome the shadow in which said body is found, and therefore it will always remain dark and will not be seen, except by a reflected light from the body of the earth, which earth is also itself illuminated by the sun, as we shall say below. <note>This is a groundbreaking observation of "Earthshine" (or the *Lumen Sinai*). Leonardo correctly deduced that the dark part of the new moon is visible because of sunlight reflecting off Earth's oceans back toward the moon.</note>

The shadow of the earth and of every other body, and likewise of all the planets.

Note how water moved in the air [follows] various streaks and lines, which all concur with the motion in the vessels.

How every thing moved through the air travels along a line of the same substance.

<note>Drawing of a water vortex within a cylindrical vessel, with a circular top-view diagram positioned above it.</note>

<header>— FOLIO 15 (verso). —</header>

## [WATER FALLS — IMPACTS OF OBJECTS]

**OF WATER FALLS**
First, write about the simple concavities made by simple falls of water. *And then* on a bottom of uniform material. *And then* on a bottom of varied material. Then, place the obstacles in the descent of the water; then the obstacles in the place of impact—that is, on the bottom; then in its reflected motion. And first, at the beginning of the fall, then describe in which part of the banks of the basin the water will take its course. And what materials will be carried away and left in different parts of the bottom of such a basin, and what speed or slowness of motion the water will have in different parts of the surface, and likewise from the surface to the bottom at various heights and widths; and so you shall do until you reach the bottom.

<margin>Giving the impetus <note>Original: *impeto*. In Renaissance physics, this refers to the force or "momentum" residing in a moving body.</note> of a moving body in place of...</margin>

If a moving body <note>Original: *mobile*.</note> rises, carried by its impetus against an oblique surface, and such an oblique surface moves with its own impetus against the moving body without descending, that body will rise to a height on that surface that it would never have reached on its own.

<margin>t n abr sc</margin>
As if the line **a b** were the elevation of the moving body **b**, and its impetus was meant to end in a given time at **c** at the height **r**. I say that if the obliquity **s c** comes to meet it with an impetus made along the line **c n s t**, the moving body that was supposed to stop at height **r** will instead rise to the line **n c**.

<margin>Make this trial of yours in a bucket with wire mesh and have a small bucket made.</margin>

<header>— FOLIO 15 (verso). —</header>

### Of the Nature of Water

Every part of water always seeks its center <note>Meaning its center of gravity, tending toward the center of the Earth.</note>.
Water has no weight in itself unless it falls or unless it weighs upon other water.
Water runs along the steepest path.
Water has within itself a certain <term>cohesive power <note>Original: *virtù tenacie*. Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of surface tension centuries before it was formally defined in physics.</note></term> <unclear>united</unclear> that makes it form spheres <note>i.e., droplets</note> of the same body in the air or upon dust; furthermore, the "skin" of this water does not break.
Furthermore, water has no motion of its own unless it is moved by another’s weight or by its own weight, or because it is drawn by its <term>vacuum <note>Original: *voto*. Referring to the Renaissance belief that nature's "abhorrence of a vacuum" could pull fluids upward.</note></term> or by heat that draws it upward.

Furthermore, water has no odor, nor flavor, nor color, and it is very easily moved by every slight motion of the air.

---

### Of the Pipes of the Pumps

If the pipe is thin and the fire is of great heat, it will be consumed; but if it is cooled from the outside by water, it will be eternal. O you, air that enters through the interior part of that pump, you cool that pipe, and the water that surrounds it from the outside will be that which cools the outside air that strikes the sides of said pipe...

<note>A small sketch on the right side depicts a spherical vessel or bulb with a central vertical pipe, related to the discussion on water and "trombe" (pipes or bellows).</note>
