<header>— FOLIO 16 (recto). —</header>

## [THE WATER OUNCE. — MARITIME CANAL. — TURNINGS, SIPHONS.]

16. — The measurements of the <term>ounces <note>Original: *once*. The "water ounce" was a traditional unit of measurement for water flow, defined by the quantity of water passing through a specific orifice under a certain pressure.</note></term> that are given at the water outlets are greater or smaller according to the greater or lesser velocity of the water passing through that outlet. Double velocity gives double the water in the same amount of time; and likewise, triple velocity in the same time will give a triple quantity of water, and so it would follow successively into eternity.

<margin>Make a lock for the narrow canal that comes from the sea, so as to be able to close it against waves and the rising tide, and to open it with the ebb tide.</margin>
[2nd fig.:] m s fg abc e d m n h [3rd fig.:] acb

**A m n** is the vessel of the accidental <term>vortex <note>Original: *retroso* or *tournant*. A swirling motion or eddy in the water.</note></term>, which has a diameter of one and a half <term>braccia <note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note></term> and is 4 1/7 deep; **ab** is where, at the mouth, it is one and a half braccia—at the mouth, and 2/7 at the bottom—into which the mouth of the <term>little stork <note>Original: *cicognola* (Italian) or *cigognette* (French). This refers to a bent siphoning pipe or a crank-arm mechanism resembling a stork's neck.</note></term> enters by the path **abcd**. And the blade that turns on the pole is faster than the course of the water entering this vessel, or of equal speed, so that the movement of the water accompanies and aids it in such motion. And yet, if you wish to make the blade faster than the movement of the blade **h**, you will endure more labor—that is, the blade will give more labor to its motor. The faster it is than the [flow], the more labor it will endure. And if the speeds of the blade and the water were equal, the blade would feel little or almost no labor, as I have shown in the fifth [book] on <term>birds <note>Original: *volatili*. Leonardo is referring to his manuscript "On the Flight of Birds."</note></term> regarding power and resistance: the power of the beating of the wings and the resistance of the air struck by such wings.
[3rd fig.:] a c b

The "little stork" must push its water behind the movement of the blade **h**, and this pushing must also be done upwards along the line of the obliquity of the blade; and let there be the space of one finger and no more between the vessel and the blade, so that the excessive weight of the water does not impede the movement of that blade. The edge of the blade must be oblique, as the drawing shows.

<header>— FOLIO 16 (verso). —</header>

## [WATER. — HEAVY BODIES RAISED BY FIRE].

[1st fig.:] **abc** The movement of water never makes angles except that of incidence, such as the angle **abc**.
[2nd fig.:] The middle water runs to the lowest part of the falling water.
[3rd fig.:] Of the parts of the same water that spring into the air through different obliquities, that which is less oblique falls back closer to its source.

The upwellings of water made from the bottom to the surface of the <term>deep sea <note>Original: *pelago*. A term used for the open sea or a large, deep body of water.</note></term> never fall back toward the bottom because, not entering the air, they do not acquire weight; and not acquiring weight, they cannot penetrate to the bottom, according to the 7th [proposition] of the 9th [book].
Water always springs up and descends with a movement of discontinuous velocity, and this arises from the air it penetrates and from the air that is mixed with it.
[4th fig.] **Heavy body.** To lift a heavy body with fire in the manner of <term>cupping glasses <note>Original: *coppetta*. A medical instrument used to create a vacuum on the skin using heat.</note></term>, one needs a vessel with a vacuum of one braccio, and a length of ten; let it be strong, and let the fire be applied below it, as is done for a bombard; and suddenly let that opening be closed, then immediately let it be closed at the top. Then the bottom—which has a leather [fitting] like a very strong forge bellows—will rise; and this is a way to lift any great thing.

### FOLIO 16 (recto)

Every element moves by the shortest path to its center.  
Moisture moved by heat draws air to itself.  
Water within the air spreads itself into a **droplet**.  
For the reason that the sphere of water  
may be with the air in whatever part of it.  
Vessels of equal height fill in equal time.  
By which means air moved by heat draws moisture to itself.

### FOLIO 17 (recto). — [WATER EDDIES AND THEIR UTILITY].

17. — [Figure: ] h e d c b a f g s n
->**OF EDDIES AND THEIR UTILITY**<-

The water that passes through the canal *h d n* strikes at *g* and divides in such a way that one part turns backward and circles along the line *g f e*, and along the line *e b g* it still follows the movement it began; but it is full of small eddies <note>original: "minuti retrosi"</note> which penetrate all the way to the bottom because they represent the entire thickness of the water that moves in such a revolution. These small eddies are generated because in that location the water *g f e* encounters the current of *d n*. — This is proven:

->**OF THE BOTTOM**<-
In the part of the bottom *g f e*, nothing remains because here the current of the eddy is greater. In the course *e b g*, some things remain, and those are of mediocre lightness, because here the slow course of the small eddies raises them little from the bottom. On the mound *a*, all light things are discharged because there the movement of the water is slowest. On the mound *c*, heavier things are left because this mound is created by the current of the canal which slows down at the encounter with the said small eddies.

<margin>Why they move outward: because the water is slower in the middle of the eddies than at the sides, and where it is slower, it leaves more light things.</margin>

### [WATER EDDIES. — UTILIZATION OF MARSHES].

[1st fig.:] o c b a n
<margin>[At the top:] OF WATER EDDIES</margin>

It is possible that under the current there is less depth than in front or at the sides. 
Let *o c n* be the current and *a* be an eddy composed of double power, according to the 9th [rule] of eddies. Because, besides its revolution, it strikes the bank and jumps up into the air and falls back onto the other water and penetrates; that which penetrates both strikes and hollows out the bottom with sudden depth because, in addition to the percussion, there is the augering <note>original: "triuellamento," referring to a boring or drilling motion</note> action made by the aforementioned revolution, which then rouses and carries away what the percussion has moved; and it becomes all the more powerful as it becomes more turbid. This is the most powerful way that can be used to move and carry away earth and leave a great depth.
The eddy *b* will be of wide but not sudden depth.

### — FOLIO 18 (recto). —

[AZURE SMOKE. — AERIAL PERSPECTIVE].

18. — When smoke from dry wood finds itself between the eye of the viewer and a dark place, it appears azure <note>original: "azzurro"; Leonardo is describing the Rayleigh scattering effect, where small particles scatter shorter blue wavelengths of light more than longer red ones</note>, *and the more so, the darker the background is.*

Therefore, the air becomes blue because of the darkness that it has behind it. And if you look toward the horizon of the sky, you will see the air is not blue; this arises from its thickness. And so, at every degree that you raise your eye above that horizon up to the sky that is above you, you will find the air becoming darker. This is because a smaller amount of air is interposed between your eye and that darkness. And if you find yourself upon a high mountain, the air will become much darker above you as it becomes thinner between you and the said darkness; and so it will continue at every degree of height until, at the end, it remains dark.

The smoke that comes from drier wood will appear more blue, as it is closer to its source <note>original: "cagone," literally "cause"</note>, and is seen against a darker field while the light of the sun strikes it.

### — FOLIO 18 (recto). —

When the soul <note>original: "animo"; can also be translated as "mind" or "spirit"</note> dwells upon a thing, it remains impressed among other thoughts; and if another new one arrives, that which was there first is not interrupted, but remains in that same disposition until the other is completely annihilated. This which I declare is easily proven in the **auditory faculty** <term>virtù uditiva: the physiological and mental power of hearing</term>, for although the air is struck many times by infinite diverse voices and sounds, they are not confounded with one another, but one after another is heard distinctly. The ear cannot hear more than one voice at a time, and likewise the eye cannot see more than a single **object** <note>original: "obietto"</note> at a time, even though it may see many together; and so it is for smell, taste, and touch.

He who paints a figure, for whatever action it may perform, if he does not well imitate its proper motion and the quality of that motion, he creates a dead work in his art.

---

### — FOLIO 18 (verso). —

<margin>
The movement of reason is very similar to that of light, because light is fast among corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> things, and reason is the fastest among incorporeal <note>non-physical or spiritual</note> things; which, because of its speed, becomes similar to the movement of thought. Therefore the **visual faculty** <term>virtù visiva: the power of sight</term>, which is moved by reason, in the same instant that it touches the surface of the thing seen, it returns to the sense that moved it.
</margin>

<note>Annotations adjacent to studies of hair curls</note>

In the movement
of the water,
observe the motion
of the surface <note>original: "vello," literally "fleece" or "shag," here referring to the textured surface of the water</note> of the water,
which behaves in the likeness
of hair.

Observe the motion of the surface of the water, which behaves in the likeness of hair, which has two movements: one of which follows the weight of the hair <note>the tendency of the hair to hang down</note>, the other follows the line of the **curling** <note>original: "volgimento"; refers to the spiral or turning path of a curl</note>. Likewise, water makes its turnings <note>vortices or eddies</note>, of which one part follows the weight of the current, and the other follows the motion of the **reflex** <note>original: "reflesso"; in fluid dynamics, Leonardo uses this to describe a secondary current or a rebounding flow that creates a vortex</note>.

### [WAVES, INTERSECTIONS, CURRENTS].

19. — [1st fig.:] a b c d e semi-cylindrical waves —
There are as many longitudinal waves created in the water of a canal as there are convexities found along its banks. Waves with square bases are formed by the intersection of the longitudinal waves born at the banks of rivers—just as longitudinal waves **a c** and **b c** intersect across the areas **c d** and **c e**.
[2nd fig.:] a b e f c d
The hollows of square waves are themselves square, as shown by the square wave **a b c d**, and these hollows are surrounded in four places. The square wave is formed as you see in **e b f d**.
Square waves merge into the curvature of cylindrical waves, which, over a long distance, will convert into the straightness of the common course of the water; and they are further merged and destroyed by the many varied thicknesses of the cylindrical waves that arise at the banks or obstacles of such a river.
The movement of water within water changes into as many reflected courses in any direction as there are various slanted obstacles that receive the **incident** <term>incident: the initial motion of a fluid or light ray striking a surface</term> movement of such water.
The obstacles to the water are of various kinds, namely: water struck by water, or by a flexible object, or by a stable one.

### [SURFACE WAVES].

SURFACE WAVES
[3rd fig.:] a b c d e f g h n m
When water strikes another body of water at a sharp angle <note>original: "obbliquità"</note>, the part that strikes first is immediately turned, reflected, and slowed down; that which follows covers it like a thin garment <note>original: "sotile vesta"</note> and runs swiftly over the part that first slowed down, and then it likewise reflects and slows down in the same spot as the preceding water. The water that follows does the same over it, and thus they successively follow their course.
If turbid running water begins at a high level and enters a pool at that same height, it travels a great distance at the height of its initial **impetus** <term>impeto: the force or momentum of a moving body</term> before it sinks or mixes with the other water in the **basin** <term>pelago: originally meaning "sea," Leonardo uses it here to describe a deep body of water or pool</term>.

<note>Editorial references for the verso page:</note>
1. See Cardinali, book two, chapter LXXII, p. 314, plate 9, fig. 39.
2. Ibid., chapter LXX.

## — FOLIO 20 (recto). —

## [WAVES AND CURRENTS]

20. — Definition of the **semi-cylindrical wave** <note>original: "onda semicolunnale"; describing a wave shaped like a cylinder cut in half lengthwise, typical of certain flow patterns</note>, and which part of its width is more or less slanted, and how it begins and ends, and where it is more or less wide or more or less high—otherwise called thick—and the variations that cause it to be large or small, or fast or slow.

Waters will flow one over the other without mixing for a long distance when their entry into the **pool** <note>original: "pelagho"; while this can mean the open sea, Leonardo uses it here to describe a larger basin or body of water where currents meet</note> is higher and faster for one than for the other. <note>original French note: See Cardinali, book two, chapter 71, page 314, plate 8, figure 38.</note>

## — FOLIO 20 (verso). —

## [WAVES AND CURRENTS]

Where the water has little motion, the semi-cylindrical waves will form straight intersections.

And where the water is faster, they will curve.

And where the speed is unequal, their curvatures will be varied toward the end.

[4th figure:] s o q p t d m n e c t k a b l

The water that descends from *p* to *k* and leaps back to *d* will pass under the **dead water** <note>original: "acqua morta"; stagnant or still water that does not participate in the main current</note> of *m-d* without mixing with it or carrying any part of it away.

The water that descends from *p* to *k* will rise back up at *d* without leaving any part of itself at *k*, provided that the entire width of its course is equal. <note>original French note: See Cardinali, book two, chapter 73, page 315, plate 9, figure 340.</note>

### — FOLIO 20 (recto). —

The motion of a moved object through the air is faster in the middle of its course than at the beginning or the end, because such motion is produced by compressed air, which is pushed by the <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "impeto"; the force or energy with which a body moves</note> of the <term>mover</term> <note>original: "motore"; the object or force that initiates the movement</note> which arises from the speed of the motion.

The mover makes the air between itself and the motion thicker <note>original: "più grossa"; denser or more compressed</note>, and because such air escapes with speed, it pushes the object forward.

<note>Studies of aerodynamics and the movement of air, illustrated with small sketches of objects or birds in flight with streamline indicators.</note>

The bowstring by itself has no force, but if the bow pulls it, and the air exerts force on the bow, and the bow on the air, and the air on the <term>arrow</term> <note>original: "frettia"; archaic spelling of "freccia" meaning arrow</note>; thus, for this reason, the motion of the air creates the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spirito"; here used to mean an animating force or vital energy</note> or rather the force.

— FOLIO 21 (recto). —

## [EDDIES AND CURRENTS]

21. — Of <term>eddies</term> <note>original: "retroso" (Italian) / "tournant" (French); a circular current or vortex</note>, some are slower in the middle than at the sides; others are faster in the middle than at the sides. There are others still that turn back in the opposite direction to their primary motion.

The eddy that is slower in the middle than at its sides is one of great circumference; this one deposits a great deal of matter in the center of its circle, leaving it in the shape of a mound.

The eddy that is fast in the center of its circulation carries air and water down to its bottom, which it carves out and bores into like a well <note>The original Italian "pozo" refers to a deep pit or well; Leonardo is describing the drilling action of a whirlpool</note>.

[ Fig. : ] n k m      h

The water that falls from **m** to **h** will carry with it the water that falls from **k** to **h**, by the reflected motion **h n**. This would not happen if the percussion <note>The physical impact or strike</note> made by **k h** upon the bottom did not break the course of the water at **h**.

It is observed through experience that the eyes of cats produce a very large pupil at night compared to the size of a human pupil. ### [LIGHT AND SHADOW]
#### (CONTRASTS)

**22. —** That part of a dark object of uniform thickness will appear thinner when it is seen against a brighter background. <note>Leonardo is observing the optical illusion of irradiation, where bright backgrounds "bleed" into the edges of dark objects, making them look smaller.</note>

[1st figure:] a a b c d b e f g h o

*E s E h* <note>original: "e s e h"</note> is the given body, dark in itself and of uniform thickness: *a b* and *c d* are dark backgrounds, one more so than the other; *b c* is a bright background, as if there were a spot struck [by light] from a sunbeam <note>original: "spiracol di sole"; literally a "breathing hole" or vent of the sun</note> in a dark room. I say that the object *e n e g* <note>also labeled *e h* in the diagram</note> will appear thicker at *e f* than at *g h*, because *e f* has a darker background than *g h*; and furthermore, the part *f g* will appear thin because it is seen by the eye *o* against the background *b c*, which is bright.

The part of a luminous body of uniform thickness and brilliance will appear to be thicker when it is seen against a darker background <note>This is the inverse of the first rule: light objects expand against darkness.</note> *and this luminous body being on fire*.

[2nd figure:] a b c d e f g h n

### [WATER, EARTH, THE CENTER OF THE WORLD. — HEAVY BODIES].

[1st figure:] a b Air. Water. Earth.

Let the earth move in whichever direction it wishes, the surface of the water will never leave its sphere; rather, it will always remain equidistant to the center of the world. <note>By "center of the world," Leonardo refers to the center of gravity. He believes water naturally forms a perfect sphere around this point.</note>

Given that the earth might move away from the center of the world, what would the water do? — It would remain around that center with an equal thickness, but with a smaller diameter than when it contained the earth within it. <note>Leonardo posits that if the solid earth moved, the water would stay centered on the gravitational point, forming a smaller, pure sphere of liquid.</note>

->ON THE BOUNCE<- <note>original: "del balzo"</note>

If a heavy body <note>original: "grave"; a technical term for a weighted object or projectile</note> that descends perpendicularly onto a plane does not strike that plane with the part through which the central line of its gravity passes, the bounce will not occur between equal angles.

A heavy body that strikes an oblique <note>slanted</note> plane, even if it falls upon it in a straight line, will bounce back at equal angles relative to that plane, but not relative to its original line of motion. <note>Leonardo is exploring the laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection relative to the surface struck.</note>

## - FOLIO 22 (recto). -

Every part of the visible object’s **species** <term>species: from the Latin *species*, meaning appearance or form; Leonardo used this to describe the "images" or "likenesses" that objects broadcast through the air to the eye</term> sends rays in a straight line toward observers <note>original: "righuardatj"</note> located at various distances.

<note>Perspective diagram showing rays converging from a rectangular object to a vanishing point, with labels 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'f'.</note>

All the intersections of the nearby rays that intersect between the visible object and the distant observer—such as the intersection of **f** with **a** and **e**, and of **d** with **b**—this intersection will be closer to the object in the case of an observer who is further away. And let this intersection be of a long distance through **a**, **b**, **f**, just as **f** is with **c**; the intersection or "intersectioning" will be the point observed by **f** with **c**.

The intersection of the nearby rays regarding the highest point of the observer will be closer to the eye <note>original: "righuardo"</note> than the intersection of the object **d**.

Thus you would have to mix practice with theory, which would be a confusing and disjointed thing.

No white or black is transparent.

## — FOLIO 23 (recto). —

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's mirror writing on folio 23 recto. The text discusses the nature of force and the movement of water toward the center of the world.</note>

Force is an invisible <term>spiritual power</term> <note>original: "virtù spirituale"; in Leonardo's physics, this refers to a non-material, dynamic energy that governs motion.</note> which, through accidental violence, is caused by motion and placed and infused within bodies that are outside of their natural state and condition. This "life" is of very short duration because it always desires to vanish, and through such a desire, it hastens toward its own ruin, which it expects and waits for from within itself. Because of this, the body in which it is placed never has rest and moves unquietly until it finds its own destruction; thus, it willingly <unclear>loses itself</unclear> and is consumed.

<margin>
I am arguing to demonstrate that the center of the earth is immobile, because I am arguing to prove that water is, by its nature, heavy, and through such heaviness, it always seeks to descend. If water had the Earth as its center, it would not seek to go above the Earth, but would come to rest upon it. This it does not do, because it always seeks the <term>center of the world</term> <note>The geometric center of the universe, which in Leonardo's time was believed to be the ultimate point of gravitational attraction.</note>, and for this reason, the water descends and flows, and through such motion, it wears away the earth.
</margin>

***

## — FOLIO 23 (verso). —

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's mirror writing on folio 23 verso. The text examines the relationship between the Earth's center of gravity and the center of the world, and how water erosion affects terrestrial balance.</note>

Because if the Earth is at the center of the world, it will weigh equally throughout its entire circle. However, if the center of the Earth is not at the center of the world, it will weigh more on one side than the other, and because of this, the Earth would not stay still in that location.

Why water runs to the sea rather than the sea running to the water: because the water is higher than the sea, and the sea is lower than the water.

Why the sea does not enter under the Earth to go to the center of the world, and why the Earth, being perforated <note>Leonardo often compared the Earth to a living organism with "veins" or channels inside.</note>, does not have its cavities filled with water. This arises from the fact that the Earth cannot be anything but still, because the center of its weight is at the center of the world. Since the Earth is surrounded by water, this water does not have the center of its weight at the center of the world, but at the center of the Earth. Thus, the water is heavier in one part than in another, and for this reason, it necessarily flows. Through this movement, it eats away at the earth; and as the earth is consumed, that part of the earth loses the weight it once had. Because of this, the equality of weight in the earth is lost, and because the Earth desires to remain in equilibrium, it moves and lifts itself upward. As a result, the water that was previously consuming it moves away and flows elsewhere.

<note>Text relating to the hydrostatic diagrams below.</note>

If weight **a** weighs one hundred pounds, weight **d** will weigh ten. If we diminish ten pounds from weight **a**, **d** will increase by one; and if we add ten pounds to weight **a**, weight **d** will lose one. It follows that the water will not rise except by as much as weight **d** allows.

<vocab>force, spiritual power, center of the world, gravity, erosion, hydrostatics</vocab>

<keywords>force, center of gravity, planetary equilibrium, erosion, hydrostatics, center of the world, fluid mechanics</keywords>

<header>— FOLIO 25 (recto). —
[WATER. — MAGNIFYING GLASSES].</header>

25. — Of waters falling through the air that intersect with various thicknesses, lengths of motion, and powers.
The reflected motion will never reach the height of the **original motion** of the incident motion, unless it strikes as a wave does against a sea rock.

[Figure 3:] Crystal lens, thick on the sides by a twelfth of an inch <note>original: "un oncia d'un oncia"; literally an "inch of an inch," referring to a specific subdivision of measurement.</note>.
This crystal lens must be clear of spots and very bright; and on the sides, it must be thick by a twelfth of an inch—that is, $\frac{1}{144}$ of a <term>braccio</term> <note>A Florentine unit of length, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note>—and thin in the middle, according to the eyesight of the person who will use it—that is, according to the proportion of the glasses that suit them. And let it be worked in the same mold as those glasses. The width of this plate will be $\frac{1}{6}$ of a braccio and its length $\frac{1}{4}$ of a braccio; thus, it will be 3 inches long and 2 wide—that is, a square and a half. This kind of lens should be used at a distance of one-third of a braccio from the eye, and the same distance from the letter you are reading. If it is further away, the letter will appear larger; in effect, common printed letters will look like the letters on **apothecary boxes** <note>original: "lettera discatole daspetiali"; referring to the large, bold labels on medicinal jars in a pharmacy.</note>.

<margin>This lens is good to keep in a study; but if you want to keep one for outdoors, make it $\frac{1}{8}$ of a braccio long and $\frac{1}{12}$ wide.</margin>

<note>A cross appears in the margin here, likely a reader's mark or a reminder to the author.</note>

<header>— FOLIO 25 (verso). —
[SEA WATERS. — THE EARTH AND THE STARS].</header>

— To the extent that the waves of the sea are higher than the ordinary height of the surface of its water, the bottoms of the valleys between those waves are that much lower; and this is because the great fall of the great waves creates great concavities in the valleys.

->ORDER FOR PROVING THE EARTH IS A STAR<-

First define the eye, then show how the "beating" <note>scintillation or twinkling</note> of any star comes from the eye, and why the beating of these stars is greater in one than in another.
And how the rays of the stars are born in the eye. I say that if the beating of the stars were as it appears in the stars, that beating would show itself to have as much extension as the body of that star; being, therefore, larger than the Earth, such a motion made instantly would be found to be incredibly fast to double the size of such a star. Then, prove how the surface of the air at the boundaries of the **sphere of fire** <note>In the medieval worldview, the 'sphere of fire' was the region above the air and below the moon.</note>, and the surface of the fire at its limit, are those through which the solar rays penetrate, carrying the likeness of the celestial bodies—appearing large when they rise and set, and small when they are in the middle of the sky.

[Figure 1:] o e p smcu knat h [Figure 2:] h f g n d k o m a e.
Let the Earth be **a**; let **n d m** be the surface of the air which borders the sphere of fire; let **h f g** be the path of the moon, or if you prefer, the sun. I say that when the sun appears at the horizon **g**, its rays are seen passing through the surface of the air at unequal angles—that is, **o m**—which is not the case at **d k**; and also, it passes through a greater thickness of air; all of **o m** is denser air.

A shadow cannot exist that is not of one and the same nature, even though one may appear to be of a different quality than another.

Furthermore, one shadow will be of the same nature as another, even if they appear to be of different qualities, because the bodies that hide the light are the same for both.

Every shadow will be of greater or lesser **darkness** <note>original: "foscurezza"</note> according to whether it is placed in a greater or lesser luminosity of the site where it falls. Also, every shadow will be of a greater or lesser quantity <note>meaning its perceived size or density</note> according to whether it is closer to or farther from the object-body from which it proceeds. 

Here, the adversary <note>Leonardo often uses the "adversary" as a rhetorical device to represent a counter-argument or a traditional academic viewpoint he intends to challenge.</note> will say that this happens because of the **air** <note>original: "aria"; here referring to the atmosphere as a medium</note> that is positioned between the eye and the object. This air, being of a nature that interferes with the sight, takes away from the shadow's darkness; and the more remote that darkness is from the eye, the less visible it becomes, in the same way that the air acts upon a patch of greenery: the greenery that is closer to the eye will appear more "green." 

And here I say that the reason stated above is true, but it is not the *only* cause for the total difference in the darkness of the said shadow; for the same shadow, placed in the same site and seen by the same eye, will be of varying darkness.

There is another thing that cannot be denied, and it is this: that the air is clearer in one part than in another, and this is caused by the sun or another bright light. For this reason, the shadow will appear clearer <note>or lighter/less intense</note> when it is in clearer air.

Regarding the darkness of the shadow, the other reason is this: that the air is clearer in one part than in the other. Wherefore I say that the air will be clearer toward the light of the window than at the edges of the walls; and this air, being of a nature to reflect itself into dark bodies, the air will be clearer near the light. It will also be clearer in that same body which is closer to such light. Because the air is clearer in that location, it will be more powerful in **remedying** <note>original: "rimidiare"; in this context, it means to soften or diminish the intensity</note> the darkness of the shadow placed in such a clear-air site. 

From this, it follows that the shadow of a single body, seen by a single eye, will have varying darkness within the same space of clear air, because the part that is closer to the light will be clearer than the other parts of that shadow.

<header>— FOLIO 26 (recto). — [CASES OF MOTION]. — FOLIO 26 (verso). — [ WATER. — SPHERICITY OF THE ELEMENTS. — NATURE ].</header>

26. — [1st fig.:] b a c a [3rd fig.:] first [4th fig.:] second a n

**First:** If a power <note>original: "potentia"; referring to a force or moving cause</note> moves a body for a certain time and across a certain space, the same power will move half of that body, in the same time, twice that distance. **Second:** Or rather: *will move* The same force <note>original: "virtù"</note> will move half of that body across that entire distance in half of that time. **3rd:** Or rather: The same force will move half of that body across that entire distance in half of that time <note>Leonardo repeats the previous case here, perhaps for emphasis or as a draft correction.</note>. **4th:** And half of that force will move half of that body across that entire distance in the same time. **5th:** And that force will move twice that mobile <note>A "mobile" is any object in motion.</note> across that entire distance in twice that time, and a thousand times that mobile in a thousand such times across that entire distance. **6th:** And half of that force will move that whole body across half of that distance in all of that time, and a hundred times that body in a hundredth of that distance *in the hundredth of that distance in the same time*. **7th:** *And mov* And if two separate forces move two separate mobiles in a certain time and a certain distance, the same forces united will move the same bodies united across all that distance in all that time, because in this case the initial proportions always remain the same.

<note>I. Repetition of the previous case.</note>

### ON THE ELEMENT OF WATER
<margin>Here follows the proof of what is said on the opposite side <note>Referring to the arguments on page 27 recto regarding the shape of the Earth and its waters.</note></margin>

I say that no part of the surface of water moves by itself unless it descends; therefore, the sphere of water, having no part of its surface where it is able to descend, must necessarily—by the first axiom <note>original: "conceptione"</note>—not move by itself. *And no*. And if you well consider every minute particle of such a surface, you will find it surrounded by other similar particles which are at an equal distance from one another from the center of the world <note>In the Renaissance view, the "center of the world" was the center of the Earth.</note>, and at the same distance from that center is that particle which is surrounded by them; therefore, by the third axiom, such a particle of water will not move by itself because it is surrounded by boundaries of equal height. And so, *s* every circle of such particles acts as a vessel for the particle that is enclosed within that circle, a vessel which has *a* the circuit of its rims [edges] of equal height; and for this reason, *none* this particle is together with all the other similar ones of which the surface of the sphere of water is composed. It *was not* By necessity it will be by itself without motion, and consequently, *each [of all the particles]* being at an equal height from the center of the world, necessity makes that surface spherical. But underneath, it is not necessary for it to be spherical, as reason and experience show.

What is said of the surface of water that borders the air is understood to be said of the surface of the air that borders the fire, which could be such that it often evaporates in the manner of clouds, as *vap*, drawn by the heat of the sun, just as water is drawn into the air by the same heat in the form of clouds; the same applies to fire drawn by a heat greater than its own—that is, by the sun—it being proven in the 6th that the sun is hot by essence, and not by power <note>original: "virtu"; Leonardo argues here that the sun is inherently hot rather than merely possessing the capacity to create heat through friction or other means.</note>, as many would have it.

The truth of these spheres having thus proven that the flexible elements are spherical, my intention is to descend to Nature *in*, in its universality and in the particulars of each element: first fire, then air, and then water.

<summary>This page contains Leonardo's proportional rules for motion and a geometric proof arguing that the surface of water must be spherical because its particles seek equilibrium relative to the Earth's center.</summary>

-> **On Motions** <-

Because impact <note>original: "colpo"; meaning a blow, percussion, or the meeting of two forces</note> is nothing other than one matter into another matter, because within one matter one thing moves faster than another; and because the air does not resist thin <note>streamlined or small</note> motions more than thick <note>large or broad</note> motions, because thick motions occupy more air than thin ones; because the impact will never occur except through air, and because the air resists thick motions more than thin motions, and this happens because thin air <note>referring here to a small volume of air</note> yields <note>original: "si piega"; literally "bends" or "folds"</note> more easily than thick air; and because thick matter opposes the air more than thin matter; and because the impact will never occur except by one matter into another matter, and this happens because thin air yields more easily than thick air.

And this is proven by the 2nd [proposition] of the 4th [book] of Weights <note>Leonardo is citing a classical or medieval scientific text, likely the "De Ponderibus" (On Weights), a standard reference for Renaissance engineers.</note>: because the air will be so much heavier the closer it is to the line of equality, and this happens because thin air yields more easily than thick air, and this will be heavier the closer it is to the line of equality, as is seen in the beam *a. b.*, for the beam *m. n.* will be so much heavier the closer it is to the line of equality—or you might say the horizontal of *a. b.*—given that the said weights are equal in every gravity and the same weight as the beam of such motion; and the line of that air will be heavier the closer it is to the line of that air made by the line *m. n.*, which is lower than *a. b.*

### — FOLIO 27 (recto). —

### [PLATO. — THE SHAPE OF THE ELEMENTS].

<margin>
27. — [In the margin:] The weight of air when it is within fire has the same proportion as the weight of water when it is within air; and such a percussion <note>In Leonardo’s physics, "percussion" refers to the force of impact or the pressure exerted by one moving fluid against another.</note> would be given by air falling from fire into other air, as is given by water falling from air into other water.
</margin>

Winds can be born from the movement of air within air, just as the movement of water occurs within water; for both are movements of the element within itself, born from the fall of a lighter element, as would be the case with air falling from the region of fire where it might "rain" down.

-> THE SHAPE OF THE ELEMENTS <-

Regarding the shape of the elements: first, I argue against those who deny the opinion of Plato, who said that the elements clothe one another with the shapes that Plato assigns to them <note>Plato argued in his dialogue *Timaeus* that the four elements are composed of regular geometric solids: the tetrahedron (fire), the octahedron (air), the icosahedron (water), and the cube (earth).</note>. They claim that a vacuum would be created between one and the other, which is not true; and here I prove it, but first it is necessary to propose a certain conclusion.

It is not necessary for any element that clothes another to be of equal thickness throughout its entire quantity between the part that clothes and the part that is clothed. **We** clearly see the sphere of water being of various thicknesses from its surface to the bottom; and not only would it cover the cubic earth if it were cubic in shape—that is, having 8 angles as Plato wishes—but it covers the earth which has innumerable angles of rocks covered by water, and various protrusions and cavities, and yet no vacuum is generated between the water and the earth. Furthermore, the air that clothes the sphere of water, along with the mountains and valleys that rise above that sphere, leaves no vacuum between the earth and the air. Thus, whoever said a vacuum is generated has practiced poor reasoning.

One responds to Plato that the surface of the figures he assigns to the elements could not endure.

Every flexible and liquid element necessarily has a spherical surface. This is proven *with the* sphere of water, but first one must establish certain concepts and conclusions.

That thing is higher which is more remote from the center of the world, and that is lower which is closer to said center. Water does not move of its own accord unless it descends, and in moving, it descends. These four concepts, placed two by two, serve me to prove that water which does not move of itself has its surface equidistant to the center of the world—not speaking of drops or *other* small quantities that attract one another like steel attracts its filings, but of large quantities. Conclusion follows opposite.

---

### — FOLIO 27 (verso). —

### [UNJUST REPROACHES OF ANCIENT AUTHORS. — REGULAR BODIES].

<note>[Figures included in original: ] a b c d n e m o f p</note>

Of the five regular bodies <note>The five "Platonic Solids": the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>. Against certain commentators who blame the ancient inventors from whom grammar and the sciences were born, acting like "knights" attacking dead inventors. They themselves have not found a way to become inventors due to their own laziness, and they attend to so many books only to continually find fault with their masters through false arguments.

They say that the earth is <term>tetraciedronica</term> <note>Leonardo uses "tetraciedronica" here to mean a six-sided hexahedron or cube, though the word usually refers to a four-sided pyramid. He clarifies this by saying "that is, cubic."</note>, that is, cubic, that is, a body of 6 bases; and they prove this by saying that among the regular bodies, there is no body of less movement or more stability than the cube. And to fire they attributed the <term>thetra cedron</term> <note>The tetrahedron.</note>, that is, a pyramidal body, which is more mobile (according to these philosophers) than the earth; therefore, they attributed the pyramid to fire and the cube to the earth. 

Now, if one were to investigate the stability of the pyramidal body and compare it to the cubic body, [one would see that] the cube is, beyond comparison, more mobile than the pyramid, and it is proven thus: The cube has 6 sides and the regular pyramid has 4, which are placed here in the margin as *a* and *b*; *a* is the cube, *b* is the pyramid. To define this proof, I will take one side of the cube and one side of the pyramid, which shall be *a b p* and *c d*. I say that the cube *c* will be more suited to revolving movement than the pyramid. Let *e* and *f* below be the start of such movements; I say in effect that, with the base of the cube and the base of the pyramid both resting on the same plane, the pyramid must turn one-third of its quantity <note>Meaning it must rotate 120 degrees to land on its next face.</note> to fall onto its other side, while the cube turns only a fourth part of its circuit <note>Meaning it only needs to rotate 90 degrees.</note> to change to the other side and make it its base. 

It follows from these two demonstrations that I have concluded that the cube completes a full rotation by changing its 4 sides on a single plane, while the triangle or pyramid completes its full rotation over its [3] sides on that same plane. The pentagon will rest on all 5 of its sides, and thus, the more sides a body has, the easier its movement is, because it closer approaches the sphere. Therefore, I wish to infer that the triangle <note>The tetrahedron/pyramid.</note> is of slower motion than the cube, and consequently, the pyramid should have been assigned to the earth and not the cube.

<margin>
[Under the 6th figure:] ...less rotates the pyramid...
</margin>

Here it is seen that the cube alone completes its full turn with a single <term>impeto</term> <note>Leonardo uses "impeto" to describe the momentum or force imparted to an object to make it move.</note> and along a single line, whereas the pyramid does not, as can be seen.

<summary>Leonardo critiques Plato's theory of elements by arguing that regular solids would leave vacuums in nature, while also using geometry to prove that the pyramid is more stable than the cube, contradicting traditional philosophical assignments.</summary>

### HEADER: FOLIO 27 (recto) — FOLIO 27 (verso)

<margin>27
On clouds</margin>

Therefore, air by itself has no color, but is tinted by that darkness which lies behind it; and if the air were of infinite thickness, it would be of a blue color. This occurs because the air is between the darkness and the light that strikes it. If it were of a finite thickness, it would show us the color of the darkness of the cold <note>Leonardo often associated the deep black of the void or upper atmosphere with absolute cold.</note>; and if it were between the sun and the eye, it would appear to us white and shining, as appears in the clouds. These clouds, in the areas <unclear>a little</unclear> further up, appear blue, and those which are between the sun and the eye appear white; and if they are above, they appear white, and from below they appear blue.

The reason for the whiteness of the air is this: air by itself is not transparent, but is full of watery vapors and atoms <note>Leonardo uses "atoms" to refer to microscopic particles or dust motes suspended in the air.</note>, which the light of the sun strikes, causing them to shine. Because the multitude of such atoms is very great, the whiteness of the air is born from this.

<note>Drawing of a triangle with a trapezoidal shape inside, representing a study of light rays passing through an aperture or the projection of a shadow.</note>

**On clouds and their colors.** White clouds that are between the sun and the eye have their brightest parts toward the sun, and their darkest parts toward the eye. If these clouds were <unclear>arranged</unclear> in such a way that the sun was between the eye and them, then those clouds would appear white on the side toward the eye and blue on the opposite side.

<note>Two circular diagrams, likely representing the eye or planetary bodies, with concentric circles and radial lines used to model how light hits a sphere.</note>

Why clouds in the middle of the day are white and toward the evening reddish: this arises because the sun at midday passes through a lesser thickness of air than in the evening, and the vapors are then more thinned out.

---

If the sphere of light <note>The light source.</note> were smaller than the sphere of the shadow <note>The opaque object casting the shadow.</note>, the shadow would always keep growing in thickness and would be of infinite length.

And if the sphere of light were equal to the sphere of the shadow, the shadow would be of the same thickness and of infinite length.

And if the sphere of light were larger than the sphere of the shadow, the shadow would be in the shape of a pyramid and would come to an end in a short space.

The reason for the shadow is this: every opaque body that is placed before the light hinders the passage of the rays of such light, and that space which is behind such a body remains without light, and this is called a shadow.

<note>Diagram of a cube in perspective with projecting lines, demonstrating how an object occupies space and blocks light.</note>

**Of the diversity of shadows.** A shadow is of as many natures as there are natures of the lights that create it. For instance, if the light were equal to the opaque body, the shadow would be equal to that body; if it were larger, the shadow would be smaller; and if it were smaller, the shadow would be larger.

<note>Diagram of a pyramid or tetrahedron.</note>

<note>Diagram of a square.</note>

Furthermore, if there were only one light, it would create only one shadow; and if there were many lights, it would create many shadows, which shadows would be one darker than the other according to whether they are deprived of a greater or lesser number of lights.

28. — 8 or 6
It is proved here that the visual power <note>original: "uirtu uisiua"; Leonardo refers to the faculty or force of sight as an active "virtue" or power.</note> is spread throughout the pupil of the eye.

[1st fig. near the text:] p q t ord abcnmo [2nd fig. in the margin:] s luminous t qr op mn kl abcdefghi pupil of the eye.

In flexible elements <note>By "flexible elements," Leonardo means fluids like air and water.</note>, the descent of a heavy body through a lighter medium is always made along the shortest line.

For flexible elements, the ascent of a light element from within [or: in] a heavier medium is made along a long and winding line <note>Leonardo is observing how air bubbles do not rise straight up through water, but instead wobble or spiral.</note>.

[4th fig., before the 10th line of text:] b water a air

The cause of such movement is proved: let **a** be air rising from the bottom of the deep water <note>original: "focho pelagho"; "pelago" refers to the deep sea or a great body of water.</note> and wishing to go by the shortest line to the surface of that water; but the weight of the water above it wishes to descend, and the water at the sides also wishes to fill that space. Each of these bodies of water is of equal power—that is, the side water is of equal height; it follows that the water highest up, which corresponds to the center of the trapped air, is the one that weighs the most. Therefore, the air is constantly refined <note>meaning the air bubble changes shape or "thins out"</note> into various figures, always fleeing from the heavier water. Because in the figure where **c f g** are found [5th fig.], the water **c e f g** presses more [on the air] than the water **a b c f [h]** or **d a c f [h]**, it will move toward **c f** [from **c** to **h**].

**Why the shadow of any body is of the same shape as that body.**

Every shadow, whether perfect or imperfect <note>By "perfect" shadow, Leonardo usually refers to the *umbra* (the darkest part), while "imperfect" refers to the *penumbra* or shadows diluted by secondary light.</note>, will be of the shape of the object from which it is derived.

When the shadow will be perfect and when it will be imperfect, and why the principle of perspective may be imperfect.

Why the part of the luminous air <note>original: "aria luminosa"; Leonardo considers the atmosphere itself as a medium filled with light that interacts with the shadow.</note> which occupies that shadow is not in such a position that it can make the air perfect, so that the shadow of that thing may be perfect.

It cannot be that the shadow of any body has within itself any part of the shadow of any other body without being a part of that same body. # — FOLIO 29 (recto). —

## [OPTICS AND LIGHT (Rays — Experiments)]

**29.** — [Figure 1: a, b, c, d]
The following is the same as [the 5th figure of folio 28 verso], and it contradicts the proposed experiment. Experience further shows that it is the hairs [eyelashes] of the lower lid that show the rays above the light; by taking a stylus <note>original: "stile"; a small pointed tool or rod</note> and moving it lightly across the lower eyelids, you will see that according to the movement you give those lower eyelids, the rays above the light will move accordingly. This is a manifest sign [evident proof] and an experiment born of reason.

**Furthermore:** Having these rays in the eye, if you move *the head* your face slowly to the right and left, you will see the rays that originate from the glisten [lustre] of the eyelids also begin to turn, and they continually exchange one for another.

This light must be at least 25 <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement (cubit) roughly equal to 23 inches or 58 cm</term> away from the eye. Perform the experiment in a dark place [nocturnal location] with slowness and diligence. Keep the eye narrowed and raise or lower your face until you see the rays both above and below the light at the same time; to do this, lean your head against the wall to keep it very steady.

[Figure 2: a, m, n]
The rays of luminous bodies (when distant from the eye) will appear to be of great length. This is because no object that sends a simulacrum <term>simulacrum: a term Leonardo uses for the "likeness" or image of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term> to the eye comes into greater proximity to the pupil than an object that *touches the impression at the edge of the eye [the eyelid]* which touches the pupil, and from there sends the simulacrum to the eye.

<margin>The rays of luminous objects will appear shorter when those objects are near the eye than when they are far away. This is because the edges [eyelids] of the eyes are half-closed—as those do who wish to see rays around a light—and because the rays cannot expand further than the space seen by the eye. It is necessary that in a small, short space one sees *small* short rays, and across a long space [at a great distance], long rays, as shown above by **a b** and **c d**.</margin>

# — FOLIO 29 (verso). —

## [OPTICS AND LIGHT (Rays — Experiments and Theories)]

<meta>This text is a continuation of the discussion found on Folio 30 recto.</meta>

[Continued from folio 30 recto:]
Our proposition holds true: if the luminous source is at **a** [referring to the 1st figure of folio 30 recto], the first central ray, **a o**, goes straight to the pupil of the eye. The ray below it, **a m**, strikes the convexity of the eyelids further [down] than the hairs [eyelashes] and creates several simulacra. These, as soon as they are created, reflect onto the edge **n**, which forms the thickness of the eyelid. From there, they leap into the "light" <note>original: "luce"; Leonardo uses this term to refer to the pupil or the opening of the eye</note> of the eye along with all the simulacra created by the hairs of the eyelids. These hairs have a somewhat long shape, are separated, and their tips point upward, widening more toward the ends, just as real eyelashes do. 

Now, to conclude our intent, I say place **t s** between the origin below *the light* and your eye; you will thus cut the ray **a m**. Because of this, the ray will not be impressed upon the convexities or curves of the lower eyelids, and consequently, the ray above at **n** will be missing. Therefore, it will be missing in the pupil, because when the cause of the simulacra at **m** is missing, the effects of the rays **m n** will also be missing. Thus, the explanation is given: by blocking the ray below the light, the ray above is entirely lost.

The adversary says here that it seems to him that this simulacrum comes from the luminous source, passes between the eyelashes, and is impressed into the thickness of the edges of the eyelids, and from there they jump to the pupil. He argues the simulacrum appears as rays because it is divided by the hairs through which it passes. To this, one responds that if one were to block the lower simulacrum in that case, the upper rays would not disappear, but— <note>The text breaks off here.</note>

<summary>Leonardo demonstrates through experiments with a stylus and head movement that the "rays" seen around a light source are actually reflections from the eyelids and eyelashes rather than properties of the light itself. He explains how blocking the light hitting the lower eyelid causes the perceived rays above the light to disappear, proving a geometric relationship between the eye's anatomy and visual perception.</summary>

<header>— FOLIO 29 (recto). —</header>

The same thing viewed with both eyes <gloss>literally "lights"</gloss>, and then with one and the other individually, will appear to you as a single form. However, this thing will be more clearly seen with both eyes than with only one. This arises because the impact made by the image <term>spetie: "species" or the formal likeness of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term> upon both optic nerves—which unite at a single point—is doubled. Since these nerves are in the same motion and possess the same power, they unite their strength and create a greater clarity than if there were only a single eye <gloss>literally "light"</gloss>. This is proven by the rule of light, which states that light doubled in the same location doubles its brightness.

<header>— FOLIO 29 (verso). —</header>

<note>Manuscript facsimile of Folio 29 verso (Ms. A), discussing the perception of light and dark objects and the phenomenon of irradiation.</note>

Why the eyes are more capable of perceiving dark things than bright <note>original: "litiose"; likely a misspelling of "luminose" or referring to "blurred/contentious" light</note> ones. This arises because dark things come to the eye by way of a true image <gloss>spetie</gloss>, whereas luminous things come to the eye by way of irradiated rays. These rays create a certain flicker or brilliance which occupies the vision and does not permit one to see the true form of the luminous object. We see this in a sunbeam that radiates through a crack in a window: the illuminated air doubles the visibility of the atoms <note>original: "atomi"; referring to dust motes floating in the air</note> that are within it, making them appear much larger than they do in dark air. The same happens with atoms seen against the sun, which appear like gold, while those in dark air are almost invisible. This also happens to the eyes, which remain harmed and dazzled by the sun's ray, such that for some time they cannot perceive the images <gloss>spetie</gloss> of dark things placed in the same location where those sunbeams were.

<summary>Leonardo explains that binocular vision results in a clearer image because the visual power of both eyes converges at the optic nerves, and he describes 'irradiation,' where bright light blurs the true form of objects and makes dust motes visible.</summary>
<keywords>binocular vision, optic nerves, irradiation, light intensity, dust motes, optics, visual perception</keywords>

### — FOLIO 30 (recto). —

## [LUMINOUS BODIES, VISUAL RAYS AND MIRRORS].

30. — HOW THE RAYS THAT ARE SEEN AROUND A LIGHT SOURCE WHEN NARROWING THE EDGES <gloss>literally "lips"</gloss> OF THE EYES ARE GENERATED WITHIN THE EYE AND NOT ELSEWHERE.
[Figure:] a b n o ts m c
First. Convex mirrors will reflect the rays they receive from a light source to all those locations that see the mirror where that light source sees it.
<margin>[In the margin:] (Figure:) n o p m q. Q is the light source; p is the convex mirror; and the area surrounding the mirror, n m o, sees the entire mirror as it is illuminated by the light q. Therefore, from all parts of the circuit n m o, one will be able to see the image <term>simulacro: an optical likeness or "species" of an object</term> of the light source in that convex mirror. —</margin>
The luminous body sends three images <term>simulacri: representations of the object traveling through the air</term> of itself to the eye. One of them goes straight to the pupil; the other two strike and are broken upon the convexity of the eyelids, and from there they bounce back in contrary motions to the opposite edges of the eyes. From these edges, they bounce back into the pupil <term>luce: literally "light," used here to mean the pupil or the visual faculty</term> and join together below and above the first image with a brightness imprinted from the eyelids in the shape of rays. The light source does this when the eye is narrowed, as when someone takes aim at a target.
It is proven thus: Let the eye be positioned as described, and you will see two clusters of rays around the distant light source, one part of which goes upward and the other downward. If you interpose your finger between yourself and the light source, placing it horizontally somewhat below the light, and you raise your finger toward the light with a slow motion until you meet the base of the light from below, you will then note that immediately such a light source will lose all the rays above it. And if you perform the contrary motion with the finger horizontally, starting above the light and lowering the finger with a slow motion until it meets the top of the light, then you will see all the rays below it disappear. With this, it is proven [The continuation is on folio 29 verso].

### — FOLIO 31 (6 verso). —

# [LIGHT AND SHADOW, VISUAL VIRTUE — STARS]

**THE SPACES BETWEEN THE IMAGES <term>simulacri: visual representations or reflections</term> OF THE STARS UPON THE SURFACE OF THE EYE HAVE THE SAME PROPORTION AS THE SPACES INTERPOSED BETWEEN THE STARS IN THE SKY.**

Although the images of the stars are present across the entire surface of the eye and in every part of it, and each image is superimposed upon every other image—appearing to another eye looking at it as if it were the surface of a mirror—it nonetheless remains true that on the inner side of the pupil, which blocks the incoming image of a star from the outside, that image will not be imprinted on another part of the eye. Instead, it will remain without an impression in the eye, because the site where it was directed is blocked by said interposition.

[3rd fig. :] bcd a e

The sense *b* sees the image of the object *a* at the location *d*, while the eye of another spectator of such an image, placed at *e*, sees the same image in another position—that is, in position *c*—as is proven by the 7th [proposition] of the 2nd [book].

->— FOLIO 31 (recto). —<-

<note>Leonardo's manuscript facsimile (recto) contains astronomical observations on the Moon's light and composition.</note>

The moon has no light of its own, and every part of the moon that faces
the sun is illuminated. Of this illumination, the earth sees
a certain portion, and the part that does not see the sun remains
dark, except for that part which faces the earth,
which is illuminated by the "simulacrum" <term>simulacro: here meaning the reflection or image, specifically "earthshine"</term> of the earth.

This serves to demonstrate how the presence of the moon,
even though it is dark, does not obstruct the view of the
sun; and if it did obstruct it, being reflective <note>original: *resspercussiva*, meaning having the quality of striking back or reflecting light</note>,
it would cause an eclipse of the sun for the earth. And if the air
were not luminous—as it is when the sun is
above it—we would always see the moon as black in the midst
of a dark sky.

Let the eye of the earth be at *b*, the center of the earth, and let the moon
be at *a*; and if the sun were at *c* in a straight line with the eye
and the moon, we would see a direct eclipse of the sun, and such an eclipse
would <unclear>however</unclear> be variable according to the motion of the moon
or according to the aspect of the earth. From this, it follows that if the moon
were made of air or water, it would not reflect the sun but
would always be transparent, or rather the sun would pass through it
and we would see no shadow upon said moon; but we see
the shadow on the moon in every one of its phases <note>original: *mvtatione*, change or phase</note> except when
it is in opposition to the sun, and we see it to be round and always
showing those same <unclear>identical</unclear> spots; therefore, the moon is
a dense and solid body.

The air in itself has no light except for that part
which is illuminated by the sun, which
illumination lights up all the rest of the air
joined with it.

Let the sun be at *a*, directly above the center of the earth
at *b*; the air extends from the center of the earth up to the
crystalline heaven at *c*, from which it results that the air which sees
the sun is entirely illuminated. From this illumination,
that other part of the air which does not see the sun is lit up.
Therefore, if you were at *d* and it were night,
you would see all the air outside of the shadow illuminated;
therefore, you would be in daylight as if the sun were there.
Thus, it would never be night. And if you were to say that the air
were not illuminated by reflection <note>original: *respercussivamente*</note>, the air
at *d* would not see the air at *c*; therefore, the entire
line *c-d* would be dark, which is
false. Therefore, the air reflects the light.

as the center, from which the light reaches the antipodes <term>antipodi: people or places on the opposite side of the earth</term>
and illuminates the air above the night-side.
</margin>

Therefore, the air of the antipodes will be illuminated
just like the air of our own night,
which is illuminated by the reflection of the earth.

## [OPTICS (MIRRORS. — STARS)].

32. — The <term>simulacra: the "images" or "species" that Leonardo believed objects emitted through space to the eye</term> of opaque bodies do not overlap one another as long as the eye that judges them remains without motion.

### [SOLAR RAYS (EXPERIMENTS)].

---

**METHOD FOR EXPERIMENTING ON HOW RAYS PENETRATE LIQUID BODIES**
Have two small vessels <term>zanine<span>A term for small basins or containers.</span></term> made, each of which should be parallel, with one being 4/5ths smaller than the other and of equal height. Then fix one inside the other, as you see in the drawing here, and cover the outside with color, leaving uncovered an opening the size of a lentil. Make a solar ray pass through there, coming from another dark aperture or a window. Then, observe whether the ray passing through the water enclosed between the two vessels maintains its straightness as it does outside, or not, and from this, establish your rule.

To see how solar rays penetrate this curvature of the sphere of the air <note>Leonardo is attempting to simulate atmospheric refraction—how the curve of the Earth's atmosphere bends light from the stars and sun.</note>, have two glass balls made, one twice as large as the other and as round as possible. You can cut them in half and fit one into the other, seal the edges, and fill them with water. Pass the solar ray through them as you did above, and see if this ray bends or curves, and establish a rule for it—and in this way, you can perform infinite experiments.
<margin>[In the margin:] Look, while keeping your eye at the center of the ball, at whether a candle flame maintains its size or not.</margin>

## [THE VISUAL FACULTY].

34. — **ON THE VISUAL POWER** <note>original: "DELLA VIRTU VISIUA"</note>
If all the images <term>simulacri: the visual likenesses or "species" of objects that Leonardo believed traveled through the air to the eye</term> that come to the eye met at an angle, by the definition of that angle they would meet at a mathematical point, which is proven to be indivisible. Therefore, all things seen in the universe would appear as one, and that one would be indivisible; there would be no space between one star and another judged in such an angle. And if experience shows us all things separated with proportional and intelligible spaces, it is because that power where the species <note>visual impressions</note> of things are imprinted is itself divisible into as many parts, large and small, as there are images of the things seen. We conclude, then, that the sense takes the images that are mirrored on the surface of the eye and then judges them within; therefore, they do not meet at a point, and consequently not in an angle.

Every surface of a transparent body, both inside and out, is naturally suited to receive the images of its objects.

In no part of the transparent bodies enclosed by their surfaces is there the power to receive or form any image, but they are well suited to give passage to the images from the surface.

## [ELEMENTS PENETRATING ONE ANOTHER, BEAUTIFUL MOVEMENTS. — WHETHER THE SUN IS HOT].

**BOOK 32. OF THE MOVEMENT MADE BY FIRE** <note>original: "MOTO CHEFFA ILFOCO"</note> penetrating water at the bottom of the cauldron; it runs in bubbles to the surface of that water by various paths and according to the movements that the water makes, struck by the penetration of that fire. With such an experiment, you can investigate the hot vapors that exhale from the earth and pass through the water, twisting because the water hinders their movement, and then those vapors penetrate through the air with straighter movements. You shall do this experiment with a square glass vessel, keeping your eye near the middle of one of the sides; and in the boiling water, you can put some grains of millet <note>original: "panicho," referring to panic grass or millet seeds used as "tracers" to visualize fluid flow</note> with slow motion, because by means of the movement of these grains, you can clearly recognize the movement of the water that carries them with it. And with such an experiment, you can investigate many beautiful movements that happen when one element penetrates another.

<margin>**OF THE SUN.**</margin>

They say that the sun is not hot because it is not the color of fire, but is much whiter and clearer. To those, one can respond that when bronze is liquefied, it is hotter and more similar to the color of the sun, and when it is less hot, it has more the color of fire.

# FOLIO 35 (recto).

## [ON RAINS. — TREATISE ON WATER].

---

35. — BOOK 42 ON RAINS <note>original: "LIBRO 42 DELLE PIOGGIE"</note>
Water that falls from a cloud is sometimes resolved into such lightness that, because of the friction it has with the air, it can no longer divide the air and appears to transform into that very air. At other times, as it descends, it multiplies <note>original: "si multiplica"</note> during its fall because it encounters tiny particles of water which, due to their lightness, were descending slowly; it incorporates these and, at every stage of its descent, acquires a new quantity of water. Sometimes the winds bend the rain and make its descent oblique; from then on, the descent becomes slow and long, and often the water changes into such minute particles that it cannot descend and thus remains suspended in the air.

Write how the clouds are composed and how they dissolve, and what cause raises the vapors of water from the earth into the air; write also of the cause of mists and of thickened air <note>original: "aria ingrossata"</note>, and why the sky appears more blue or less blue at one time than another. Likewise, write about the regions of the air and the cause of snow and hail, and the contraction of water as it hardens into ice, and the creation of new shapes of snow in the air. Mention how trees [take on] new shapes of leaves in cold countries, and how the rocks of ice and frost compose new shapes of herbs with various leaves—this frost acting as if it were a dew disposed to nourish and compose the aforementioned leaves.

<note>Scholarly references: This section appears in Cardinali’s "Treatise on Water," Book 1, Chapter 45.</note>

### 35.— Book 42. ON RAINS.
<note>This section repeats the observations above with slight variations in the original French scholarly transcription, emphasizing the "oblique" path of wind-blown rain.</note>
Water falling from a cloud sometimes resolves into such lightness that it can no longer, because of the friction it has with the air, divide the air, and seems to change into that air. Sometimes in descending it multiplies, because it finds minimal particles of water which by their lightness were slow to descend, incorporates with them, and at each part of the descent acquires a new quantity. Sometimes the winds bend the rain and make its descent oblique; consequently, the descent becomes slow and long, and often it changes into such small particles that it cannot descend and so stays in the air.

Write how the clouds are composed and how they resolve, and what cause raises the vapors <note>original: "vapeurs"</note> of water from the earth into the air, and the cause of fogs and thickened air, and why it shows more azure and less azure one time than another; write likewise of the regions of the air, and the cause of snows and hails, and the tightening of water hardening into ice upon the new figures of snow creating themselves in the air, and the trees with new figures of leaves in cold countries, and the rocks of ice and frost which compose new figures of herbs with diverse leaves, this frost making itself in some way as if it were a dew disposed to nourish and compose the said leaves.

<note>A cross marked in gray pencil appears at the top of the original page, likely a reader’s mark.</note>

# FOLIO 35 (verso).

## [DISTANT LIGHTS. — VISUAL FACULTY].

---

TWO SEPARATE LIGHTS AT A CERTAIN DISTANCE WILL APPEAR JOINED AND UNITED.
Regarding this case, it has been judged by many who study perspective <term>prespectiui: scholars of optics and the science of sight</term> that the air surrounding these lights at a great distance is so illuminated that it appears to be of the same nature as the lights; therefore, the light and the surrounding air appear to be a single body.

What they say is not true. If it were the case that the air surrounding such lights at a long distance became so illuminated that it appeared uniformly bright, this would be even more noticeable from nearby (where the true shape of the light is known) than from far away. Furthermore, if the true knowledge of the light's shape is lost as one moves away because its brilliance diminishes slightly, how much more would that clarity of the air—which is far less bright than the light itself—have to diminish and be lost? Therefore, we shall prove that this apparent increase in size is caused by two images <term>simulacri: visual representations or "ghost" images formed within the eye</term> in the eye.

<margin>The excessive brilliance of a light hinders the eye; when it is close, it diminishes the visual faculty <term>virtu visiua: the eye's power to perceive clearly</term> because the pupil, being offended [by the glare], constricts and thus becomes smaller. But when that light moves further away, that offense to the eye ceases because the light lacks [the same intensity of] brilliance; consequently, the pupil grows <note>dilates</note> and sees a larger light.</margin>

### TWO SEPARATE LIGHTS WILL APPEAR JOINED AND UNITED AT A DISTANCE.
For this case, it has been judged by many of those occupied with perspective that the air surrounding these lights at a long distance is so illuminated that it seems to be of the nature of these lights and [that it is] for this reason [that] the light and the air surrounding them appear to be one and the same body.

What they say is not true, because if it were so, that the air surrounding these lights was illuminated so much at a long distance that it appeared entirely uniformly luminous, this same thing would be more easily recognized [observed] from close up (where one knows the true figure of the light) than from far away; and if with distance, one loses the knowledge of the true figure of the light because it diminishes a little in radiance, how much more would that clarity of the air—which is much less brilliant than the light—have to diminish and be lost! Therefore, we shall prove that this increase is made by two "simulacra" in the eye.

<margin>The excessive brilliance of the light prevents the [sight]; being near the eye, it diminishes the visual faculty, given that the pupil, being wounded, contracts and thus becomes smaller; and when the light moves away, the wound does not occur for the eye because the light lacks brilliance, so that the pupil grows and sees a larger light.</margin>

<summary>Leonardo explores the physics of rain and the formation of atmospheric phenomena like frost and blue skies, then investigates why distant lights appear to merge, attributing it to the physiological response of the pupil rather than the air itself.</summary>
<keywords>meteorology, rain, cloud formation, frost patterns, optics, pupil dilation, visual faculty, perspective, atmospheric color, light intensity</keywords>

## [LUMINOUS BODIES. — OPTICS]

36.— Of objects of equal size placed at equal distances from the eye, the one that is more luminous will appear larger.
— Of equal things equally distant from the eye, the darker one will appear smaller.
->IF THERE ARE TWO LUMINOUS BODIES SOMEWHAT NEAR EACH OTHER, AT A GREAT DISTANCE THEY WILL APPEAR JOINED.<-
This can happen for two reasons; the first is that when one is near these lights, the distance or space that separates them is clearly recognized, and the images <note>original: "simulacri." In Renaissance optics, these were the 'species' or likenesses of objects that traveled through the air to reach the eye.</note> that are imprinted in our eye are still very distinct, and their rays do not yet touch. However, at a great distance, these images become so close that it is not just the rays, but the luminous bodies themselves that seem to touch.
Furthermore: at such a distance, the pupil, which had previously been constricted, begins to dilate because the brightness <note>original: "luce." Leonardo often uses this to mean the intensity or 'éclat' of the light source.</note> of the lights is no longer as powerful as it was when near the eye; and thus the eye, with its enlarged pupil, sees an object appear enlarged to you.
[Figure:] a b c d e n

If the air did not "see" the eye through every part of itself, it would not send to the eye its image through all the air; nor would all the air send its image into the whole eye; thus it sees, though the eye does not see except by a single reason <note>original: "ragiō," referring to a mathematical line or proportion.</note> or rather through a single part of the medium of the eye.
