## [AIR, WATER, WIND, WEIGHT]

BOOK 43. ON THE MOVEMENT OF AIR ENCLOSED UNDER WATER.
[1st fig. :] c d e f n m a b
WHETHER AIR ESCAPES FROM UNDER WATER BY ITS OWN NATURE OR BY BEING PRESSED AND DRIVEN OUT BY THE WATER. The answer is that because a heavy thing <term>heavy thing: "il grave," referring to an object or substance with weight</term> cannot be supported by a light thing <term>light thing: "il lieve," referring to a substance with less density, like air</term>, that heavy thing will go falling and seeking what may support it, because every natural action seeks its rest; thus that water which is above, at the sides, and below, surrounding such air, finds itself entirely pressing upon the air enclosed within it, and all that which is above—d e n m—pushes such air downward. And because the lateral weights—a b e f and a b c d—which surround such air and rest on its sides, result in a greater sum of weight than the water which is above, therefore that air escapes through the corners n and m, or from one side or the other, and goes winding <note>i.e., spiraling or zig-zagging</note> in its ascent.

It requires as much force to move an object against immobile air as it does to move the air against an immobile object. <note>This is a remarkably early statement of the principle of relative motion in fluid dynamics.</note>

I have seen movements of air so furious that they have carried and mixed in their course the largest trees of the forests and the entire roofs of great palaces; and this same fury making a hole with a swirling motion, excavating a gravel bed, and carrying gravel, sand, and water more than half a mile into the air.

The same weight will be supported in the air without motion [if] falling with an oblique motion, it can then raise itself very high with a reflected motion. <note>Leonardo is likely observing the flight of birds, specifically how they use wind and "reflected" (upward) currents to soar without flapping.</note>

<summary>Leonardo discusses how pupil size and eyelids affect the perception of light and images, then shifts to fluid dynamics, explaining why air bubbles rise and noting the equivalence of moving an object through air versus moving air past an object.</summary>
<keywords>optics, pupil dilation, luminous bodies, refraction, fluid dynamics, air bubbles, aerodynamics, relative motion, atmospheric fury, bird flight</keywords>

The opaque body <term>corpo opaco: an object that does not allow light to pass through it</term> diminishes its shadow as much as it is further removed from the luminous body.
---
That part of the shadow will be darker the closer it is to the opaque body.

<margin>
<note>Diagram showing a light source (labeled "light"), an aperture with an eye ("the eye"), and the resulting shadow cone.</note>
If the eye is placed between the light and the opaque body, it will see the shadow of that body occupy the entire light; but if it moves closer to the opaque body, it will see the aperture <term>spiraculo: a small opening or vent through which light passes</term> of that light surrounding the shadow; and if it moves further away from that body, it will still see that same light, but will no longer see the shadow, except that the shadow will never appear to be the same size as the eye.
</margin>

The shadow of that body will be of lesser intensity <note>original: "d'ochulto ualore." Here, "value" refers to the optical strength or depth of the shadow.</note> the smaller it is than that body; but the eye, when distant from it, will seem to see more of that body.
The shadow that is distant will be of lesser intensity because it will see a large part of the circumference of the light near the center of that body, which is a light that is not seen from nearby.

<note>Study of optical perspective and shadow intensity based on the distance from the light source and observer position.</note>

If the eye sees the light diminish while surrounding the shadow, that shadow diminishes; and seeing the light increase while surrounding the shadow, there will be an increase in that shadow.
The shadow that is near the light increases with the increase of that light and diminishes with the diminution of that light; meaning that if the eye moves further away, the shadow diminishes because it sees more light, and if it moves closer, the shadow increases because it sees less light.

The shadow of every body will be larger than the body itself when it is struck by a light source smaller than the opaque body; and if the light is smaller, the shadow will be larger than the body; and if the light is equal, the shadow will be equal; and if the light is larger, the shadow will be smaller.
And the shadow of lesser intensity will be that which is near the proximity of the light, and the shadow further from the light will be darker and of greater intensity.
The shadow that is near the proximity of the light and is darker will be that which is near the opaque body; and if the light is smaller, the shadow will be larger; and if the light is equal, the shadow will be equal; and if the light is larger, the shadow will be smaller.

### [SURFACES OF RIVERS: STRAIGHT OR CURVED]

38. — WHETHER THE SURFACE OF THE WATER OF FLOWING RIVERS IS SPHERICAL OR NOT, OR WHETHER IT IS NECESSARY IN THE UNIFORM MOVEMENT OF WATER THAT ITS SURFACE BE STRAIGHT OR CURVED.

[ 1st fig.: ] b c a o r n

It can be straight or curved, provided that in its movement it moves closer to the center of the world <term>center of the world: the center of gravity or the Earth's center</term>; because if it did not do so, the water would remain motionless—at least when the course is not reflected <note>original: "refresso." Refers to water redirected by an obstacle or backflow</note>, and I do not take this into account because it is a violent <note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent" motion is that which is forced against an object's natural tendency</note> movement.

This is proved: Let *o c r* be a mountain from the summit of which a river descends and flows down to the base of its sphere. This water can descend via the straight line *c o a* and via the curve *c b a*, because its height above the center of the world is greater along the line *c n* than at *o n* or *a n*. The same is true for the curve, which is higher at *c n* than at *b n* or *a n*, so that I conclude it is not necessary for the movement of water to be more curved than straight.

<margin>The water of the arc *c* has a greater slope at the surface than at the bottom, so as not to be of equal thickness. [ 2nd fig.: ] d c b a.</margin>

Water that moves over a convex bottom will be slower than if it moved over a bottom that is flat in itself; and it will be all the slower because it comes from a common source. Even though it is proven that they have a common beginning and a common end, the curved path will be slower as its arc is longer than its chord <term>chord: the straight line connecting the two ends of a curve</term>.

Water that moves from its beginning will, at the end, be as much slower along the arc than the chord as the arc is longer than the chord.

The adversary <note>Leonardo often poses questions from an "adversary" to debate scientific principles</note> says here that the proposed movements will be made in equal time; for although the water flows slower from *a* to *d* than from *a* to *b*, it restores the motion from *d* to *c*, which is more sudden than *b* to *c*. To this, one replies that the water *d c* is thin and fast, and the water *a d* is slow and thick; and although in the end just as much water arrives at *c* from *d* <margin>as at *c* from *b*, that from *d c* is so much thinner and contains less water than the water coming from *b*, because the line *d c* is less oblique than the line *c b*, so that in an equal amount of time, the water of *d c* is less than that of *b c*.</margin>

---

->— FOLIO 38 (verso). —<-

### [REFLECTION OF SOLAR RAYS]

PERSPECTIVE OF SOLAR RAYS
[ 1st fig.: ] a Sun, d o p e r s t the world, b f g h i k l m c water.

SOLAR RAYS REFLECTED BY THE SURFACE OF WAVY WATER MAKE THE IMAGE <term>simulacrum: a reflection or visual representation</term> OF THE SUN APPEAR TO BE CONTINUOUS THROUGHOUT ALL THAT WATER WHICH IS BETWEEN THE WORLD <note>original: "l'universo." Leonardo uses this here to mean the observer's horizon or the Earth's surface</note> AND THE SUN.

This is proved: Let *a* be the body of the sun, let *b c* be the surface of the wavy water, let *d t* be the world that sees this water between itself and the sun. By the 2nd [proposition] of the 1st [book], the image of the sun that comes from the sun to wave *m* is by necessity reflected to *t* and nowhere else; and likewise, the image of the sun that comes from the sun to *f* bounces to *d* and nowhere else. Every wave placed between these two extreme waves does the same; therefore, by necessity, the entire line *d t*, placed in front of such images, is seen *by everyone* and illuminated by all those images where the reflected rays spread out, and at no distance will its brilliance be interrupted, as is demonstrated here.

[ 2nd fig.: ] a c b d e f Sun.

THE IMAGE THAT IS REFLECTED FROM THE WAVE TO THE OBJECT INCREASES IN WIDTH AT EVERY DEGREE OF LENGTH.

The image *f* bounces to *c d*, and the image of wave *e* bounces to *a b*; these two strikes of reflected rays overlap each other at *c b*, and there the light is twice as bright as in *a c* or *b d*.

<margin>38</margin>

### WHY THE AIR IS NOT TINTED BY THE COLOR OF OBJECTS

Air, by itself, does not unite with the colors of the bodies that pass through it, but only receives them into itself just as it receives the species <gloss>images or visual likenesses</gloss> of those bodies. And the reason why the air is not tinted by the color of the objects is this: that colors are potential acts and air is an active corporeity <unclear>active</unclear>. Furthermore, because the air has no color in itself, the action of the colors of objects passes through it without tinting it.

And you would see the same if you passed a ball of snow <note>original: "aciesa," usually meaning lit or burning. Leonardo likely refers to a "brightly white" ball or is using a paradox to illustrate that a cold object passing through heat does not immediately change the medium's temperature.</note> through a heated stove; for that snow will not cool the air through which it passes. Similarly, the action of the color of a flame will neither tint the air nor heat the air through which it passes.

<margin>
The air is not tinted by the colors of the objects that pass through it.
</margin>

<margin>
<note>Diagram of optics: A circle representing an object or the eye, with radiating lines illustrating the paths of light rays or visual "species."</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Because the air has no color in itself.
</margin>

<margin>
<note>Geometric diagram: A curved line (an arc) representing the atmosphere or a lens, showing the path of light through a medium.</note>
</margin>

When the same air is not of uniform density <note>original: "spessita," meaning thickness or density</note>, it will be less clear where it is thicker, and more clear where it is thinner. This is proved by the sunbeam passing through fog: the denser the fog, the less clear the beam will be; and the thinner the fog, the clearer will be the ray of light occupying the same air of uniform density.

<margin>
Because the air is not of the same density in all its parts, it will be less clear where it is thicker and more clear where it is thinner.
</margin>

---

->## FOLIO 38 (verso)<-

<margin>
The space of the air.
</margin>

<note>Diagram: A horizontal baseline with several overlapping arcs labeled with letters. This represents Leonardo’s mathematical attempt to map the varying intensity of light as it travels through different "depths" or layers of air.</note>

A space illuminated by the sun is not of uniform clarity in all its parts, because the air through which the sun's ray passes is not of uniform density. If a ray is made to pass through fog, you will see the ray is clearer where the fog is thicker <note>The beam itself becomes more visible to the eye when there are more particles to reflect the light.</note>, and the ray will be less clear where the fog is thinner. Therefore, the space of air occupied by the shadow of an opaque <term>opaque: a solid object that light cannot pass through</term> body will be of a uniform darkness only if the air is of a uniform density. If the density of the air varies, the darkness of the shadow will vary.

<note>Diagram: The sun (a circle) casting rays down toward a horizontal line representing the earth's surface.</note>

A visual field <note>original: "ochio," literally 'eye,' but here referring to the volume of air seen by the eye.</note> occupied by the same air is not of uniform clarity in all its parts, because the air is not of uniform density. Since the air closer to the earth is thicker than the air further from it, the air is not the same in all its parts; where it is less dense it will be clearer, and where it is denser it will be less clear.

<note>Leonardo concludes with a list of key terms for his study: air, color, species, objects, potentials, corporeity, fog, ray, shadow, opaque, density.</note>

->## FOLIO 39 (recto) — [THE SUN IN THE WATER]<-

39. — **[Figure: Sun g h i k l m n; Water of the ocean a b c d; e f]**

Why the reflection <note>original: "simulacro," referring to the reflected image or visual species of an object</note> of the sun is present throughout the entire sphere of the water that sees the sun, and is present in every part of the aforementioned water.

All the sky that sees that part of the sphere of water which is seen by the sun, sees all that water occupied by the reflection of the sun, and every part of the sky sees everything.

The surface of the water, when without waves, illuminates equally the places struck by the reflected rays of the sun's reflection in the water, there being but a single reflection.

The reflection of the sun is unique within the sphere of water seen by the sun; however, this reflection reveals itself to the entire sky positioned before it. Every point of that sky sees a reflection for itself, and the one who sees it in one position is seen by another in a different position. But this happens in such a way that no single part of the sky sees the reflection in its entirety.

— That reflection of the sun will occupy more space on the surface of the water when it is seen by an eye more distant from it. —

->## FOLIO 39 (verso) — [OPTICS (NATURE AND THE PUPIL)]<-

[Continued from folio 40 recto] ...just as it is throughout the interior of that pupil <note>original: "luce," literally "light," but Leonardo frequently uses this term to refer to the pupil or the opening of the eye</note> just like the rays of the large reflection; the senses perceive no other difference except for a decrease in the brightness of the splendor in its power, but not in its quantity. —

— **That object will appear larger which is seen by a larger pupil <note>original: "luce dochio"</note>, and likewise the opposite is true when the conditions are reversed.** —

This proposition also serves to prove the reason why a light source placed before us does not diminish in size at any distance, but only diminishes in its radiance <note>original: "luce"</note>, and not in its magnitude. —

Nature has designed the pupils <note>original: "popila"</note> of the eyes of all animals—both those of the water and those of the land—so that when they are overcome or altered by a greater or lesser light, these eyes may decrease or increase their pupil, which is the black center. This is done because when excessive light causes an alteration to the eye, the eye or pupil constricts like a drawstring purse <note>original: "auso di borsa," a purse closed by pulling a string</note>. Thus, the large light becomes small in quantity and splendor, proportionally according to its closing or diminution. And when these pupils reach the darkness, they become large, and the diminished light is thus increased according to the growth of such a pupil; and so the size of the bodies seen by such a pupil increases. This mechanism serves so that as the light of a candle moves away from the eye, and the light itself diminishes, the pupil increases, causing the figure of the light to increase.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of optics and astronomy, moving from the reflection of sunlight on water to a geometric analysis of how light from a large body (the Sun) interacts with a smaller sphere (the Earth) and the nature of the shadows produced.</meta>

# - FOLIO 39 (recto) -

<note>Optical study showing a geometric diagram at the top. The diagram illustrates light rays from a large sphere (labeled 'sun') falling on a smaller sphere (Earth). Labeled points include k, j, Q, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h.</note>

Every part of the surface of the other sphere <note>referring to the Earth</note> that is illuminated by the sphere of the sun sees the entire body of the sun, for the reason that if the appearance of the sun were a single point, then only that point on the illuminated sphere struck by that point would see it, and nothing else of the sun.

Among luminous spheres of equal power but unequal size, the smaller one will illuminate more than half of the space <note>referring to the surface area of the receiving sphere</note>, and the larger one will illuminate less. Specifically, where two spheres of equal size and unequal light illuminate one another, the one with the greater light will see a larger space on the opposite sphere than the other sees of its own light. But the one with the lesser light will see a smaller space on the opposite sphere illuminated by the larger one than the space of its own sphere that illuminates the other.

---

# - FOLIO 39 (verso) -

Try to see if, given that the sphere of the sun is luminous in a proportion of light greater than its size relative to the earth, whether the earth's shadow does not end in a <term>pyramid|In Leonardo’s time, 'pyramid' often referred to a perfect geometric cone of shadow</term> but in an improper cone.

If the light of the sphere of the sun could be seen as a single point, and the sphere of the earth could be illuminated by it.

The proportion of the earth's shadow to the sphere of the sun, taking the dark void as a proportion, and is less than one-seventh of the earth's sphere, following a straight line.

Illuminate from the opposite side of the sphere from a point of light, and from within the sphere in the light itself you will see the entire sphere of the sun, of which you will see every part through its own sign <note>likely referring to a geometric ray or perspective line</note>; and both are united with the parts of its body. All the alteration of that sphere which is directly opposite to the sun, and through all that space where the whole sun is visible, [one sees] both extremes of the solar light. One of these shows the sphere of the sun and the part of the light, the weak light <note>original: "debol lume," referring to the penumbra</note>, and the greater light. Of the sun's light, one part is shown, and of one light and the other, one part is shown. Because the sun is not a single point, it illuminates in such a way that if you move point by point through the said dark void, in that weak light you will see, point by point, a greater part of the body of the sun, until the eye of the observer finds itself in alignment.

### [OPTICS AND LIGHT. — THE SUN IN THE WATER].

40. — The image of the sun <note>original: "simulacro," meaning the reflected likeness or visual representation</note> imprinted on the surface of the water produces rays both inside and outside of that water, which illuminate across a long distance as if it were a real light source.

WHY THE IMAGE OF THE LIGHT <insert>made</insert> BY THE CANDLE *re* DIMINISHES UPON THE <term>PUPIL|Leonardo uses the word 'luce' (light) to refer to the pupil or the receptive part of the eye</term> OF THE EYE WHEN MOVING SUCH A CANDLE TO A GREAT DISTANCE FROM THAT EYE, AND YET THE VIEWER DOES NOT JUDGE THAT CANDLE TO DIMINISH EXCEPT IN THE CLARITY OF ITS BRIGHTNESS.

<note>A diagram with labels: n, m, a, c, o, b, r, g, h, l. It illustrates light rays from different distances entering the eye.</note>

**CONCEPTION:**
— THAT EYE WILL BE LESS LUMINOUS WHICH IS ILLUMINATED BY A SMALLER LIGHT, EVEN THOUGH EVERY PART OF THAT PLACE PARTICIPATES IN SUCH LIGHT. —

By this conception and by the proposition above—which I ought to have cited first—we are certain that the luminous source *ng* makes a greater impression in the pupil *nmab* at the position *ab* than it would if it were removed to the distance *hl*; this is because the impression of *hl* falls upon the pupil at *co*, which is much smaller than the first impression *ab*. For this reason, the power of the radiance is diminished, but not the quantity, according to the stated conception. This is because the base and the space of the pupil are touched by the [smaller] image *co* just as much as by the larger image *ab*, so that the radiance of the rays around the image illuminates. <note>The text continues on folio 39 verso.</note>

# — FOLIO 40 (verso) —

### [PONDS NEAR THE SEA].

<note>A figure showing a body of water labeled "pond" (stagno) and another labeled "sea" (mare).</note>

— WHY PONDS ARE FORMED NEAR THE SEA
AND WHY THEIR GREAT EXPANSIONS FLOW INTO THE SEA THROUGH SUCH A NARROW CANAL —
ON THE SIDES OF WHICH IS CREATED SUCH A LARGE EMBANKMENT BETWEEN THE POND AND THE SEA —

The <term>storms|original: 'fortune,' referring to the violent surges or 'fortunes' of the sea</term> of the sea throw a great quantity of sand onto the shore, which rises up along that entire shore, both at the mouth of the pond and elsewhere. When the storm has ceased, the mouth of the pond remains closed by the aforementioned material thrown up by the sea. The water that the pond receives from surrounding rivers, finding no further exit, goes on rising and acquiring weight and power; thus, it either breaks the embankment interposed between itself and the sea, or it overflows across the top. With its pouring out, it consumes as much of that embankment as it touches, and continues this course until it clears away all that material that prohibited its necessary discharge.

Furthermore, it consumes no more than is necessary. In the beginning, it widens considerably because the water flowing over the <insert>cause of the</insert> mouth is thin; but at the end, the course of such water narrows because the flow has become thicker by acquiring depth. This is the reason why the exit of ponds into the sea is always narrow.

<note>Scholarly notes from the original transcription: 1. See F. Cardinali, Book 1, Ch. XXXII, p. 286. 2. A cross in gray pencil appears at the top of the page, a reader's mark.</note>

### [WATER].

---

41. — — No surface of water that borders the air will ever be lower than that of the sea.

The wave created by a <term>moving body|original: 'mobile', any object in motion</term> in front of itself—whether in the air or between the surface and the floor of the water—takes the shape of a half-sphere.

The wave made by a moving body on the surface of the water takes the shape of a half-circle, while toward the bottom, it takes the shape of a quarter-sphere.

Why the movement made by a moving body on the surface of water creates a wave in front of it, but does not create a wave when that body moves between the surface of the water and its floor: this occurs because the water at the surface borders the air, whereas the water between the surface and the bottom borders water above it and water below it. <note>Leonardo is observing how the lack of a "compressible" or "yielding" medium like air affects the way pressure waves propagate underwater.</note>

### [THE EARTH AND THE MOON — SWIMMING AND FLIGHT].

How the Earth is not in the center of the Sun's orbit, nor in the center of the universe, but is indeed in the center of its companion elements, which are united with it. And to anyone standing on the Moon, when it and the Sun are both beneath us, our Earth—with its element of water—would appear to function just as the Moon appears to us. <note>Leonardo correctly identifies that the Earth would reflect sunlight and "shine" like a moon to an observer on the lunar surface.</note>

#### ON THE MOVEMENT OF THE BIRD

Whether the movement of birds without beating their wings (in a continuous descent) is longer by maintaining an <term>oblique|slanted or diagonal</term> path, or by frequently making a <term>reflected motion|a rising or upward-tilting motion after a descent</term>; and if they wish to travel from one place to another, whether they will go faster by making violent <term>incident|downward or diving</term> movements and then rising upward through reflection, repeating this sequence of incidents.

To speak of this subject, you must, in the first book, define the nature of the resistance of the air; in the second, the anatomy of the bird and its feathers; in the third, the action of these feathers in various movements; in the fourth, the power of the wings and the tail when the wings are not beating, using the favor of the wind to guide themselves through various movements.

<margin>Anatomize the bat, and stick to this, and from this, design the machine.</margin> <note>Leonardo favored the bat as a model for his flying machine because its wings are made of a continuous membrane rather than individual feathers, which was easier to replicate with fabric and wood.</note>

#### ON SWIMMING AND FLYING —

Always, when two powers strike against each other, the one that is faster rebounds backward. Thus does the hand of the swimmer which strikes and leans against the water, causing his body to move in the opposite direction; thus does the wing of the bird in the air. <note>This is a remarkably early observation of the principle of action and reaction, which would later be formalized as Newton's Third Law.</note>

Why the eyes of animals are not all round, and why some are longer than they are round.

<margin>
41
</margin>

Here we discuss whether the eye sees by the <term>species|original: "spece"; according to Renaissance optical theory, these are the "likenesses" or "forms" of objects that travel through the air</term> that come from the outside, or if it sees by means of the <term>vitreous sphere|original: "palla vitrea"; the clear, jelly-like lens or body of the eye</term> while naked, and if it is enclosed by a glass-like skin, and if—in order to see—the rays of the eye must pass through the center of the pupil, which is always located in the middle of the iris.

<note>Drawings of the eye in cross-section and front view are situated to the right of the following paragraph.</note>

For animals of nocturnal sight, such as cats, they have the pupil—or you might say the sight—in the shape of a <term>date stone|nocciolo di dactilo</term> or a <term>linseed|ranfello di lino</term>. This occurs because such a "stone" shape can expand much more than a round shape can; in round eyes, a "stone" shape cannot expand as much as itself, so it does not appear as large. <note>Leonardo is observing the slit-pupil of the cat, noting its ability to dilate much more significantly than the circular human pupil to allow in more light at night.</note>

If the line of levelness were straight, and if it were equally distant from the center of the Earth, and if it were distant from that center by the diameter of the Earth, it would come to be—if it were truly straight—lower in the sight of the eyes. <note>Leonardo is grappling with the perspective of the horizon; he suggests that a mathematically "straight" horizontal line would appear to dip at the edges because the observer is standing on a sphere.</note>

Every sight would seem to be in the middle of a valley, and would agree with what I want to say—that is, to think with truth—that if it were truly flat in the shape of a valley, and not flat like the diameters of the Earth, declaring said levelness, it would end up being no more flat than it comes to be.

This is worth what was said above: that the valley would come to be in the said diameters in thought; this is what I want to say, that the Earth, from which it will come out flat, would not come to be in the middle of a valley, but in the middle of a sight.

But because the sight toward the horizon is less than that toward the eyes, for this reason, the said horizons do not come toward the eyes.

If the line of levelness were straight, and if it were equally distant from the center of the Earth, it would come to be—if it were truly straight—lower in the sight of the eyes.

<margin>[To the right:] On the reverse side of the bellies of heifers and oxen <note>original: "vitella edi bo"; the French translator suggests "bo" might mean "bue" (ox) or "becco" (goat).</note>, you will find beautiful parts upon which you shall cast the mixture; prepare them, then pour, and thus, with various materials, you will make several coatings without them drying out. Take a leaf of Milanese cabbage, well-crinkled and large, from the month of December or January, which are very crinkled by the cold and have more minute crinkled parts. Then, take your transparent <term>mixture|a liquid compound, likely a resin or glue-based material that hardens into a solid</term>, and coat this leaf; then coat it with a fixed white mixture, then coat it with black, then with <term>sardonyx|a reddish-brown chalcedony, here likely a colored mixture imitating the stone</term>, and in this way you will create several layers. Let it dry and then cut it from the front into strips to make knife handles. — FOLIO 42 (verso). —

[STATIONARY RIVER COURSES].

---

— CONCERNING THE WATER THAT FALLS FROM THE <term>BARRAGES|original: "chiuse"; Leonardo notes later that this refers to parts of the river where water is enclosed or dammed rather than modern locks</term> OF RIVERS: IT IS THE PART WITH THE MOST POWERFUL FALL WHOSE STRAIGHT COURSE WILL BE CLOSED. —
This occurs because water from a powerful fall digs up the ground in the place it strikes, and discharges it where its course becomes weaker than beneath the reflected motion of the water. This motion, being moved toward the sky <note>i.e., splashing upward</note>, becomes weaker with every degree of movement until finally it loses all its power. As power fails it in this reflection, it allows all the heavy materials taken from the place it struck to fall beneath it. After the flood, the water lowers and finds itself enclosed between the material it previously carried and the bank from which it descended.

CONCERNING WATERS THAT DESCEND IN TORRENTS FROM RIVER BARRAGES, ONLY THAT WHICH <insert>will follow its</insert> WILL PRESERVE ITS STRAIGHT COURSE BEYOND THAT TORRENT, WHOSE FALL WAS WEAKER AND SLOWER. —
This happens because water that moves slowly strikes weakly; from this, it follows that it lifts little from the bottom it strikes, and consequently little material is deposited under the reflected motion. Therefore, after such a torrent, the bank remains low here, and all the water that falls follows its course where the bank is lowest; thus the straight course of all the river’s water is found here along with the water of the weak fall.

### [THINGS CARRIED BY THE WATER].

43. — [ 1st figure : ] a d b c
Concerning things carried by water that intersect each other <note>original: "chessintersegano"</note>: of those where one stream of water enters into another at a level higher than the bed of the other, the thing that is in the deeper water will pass beneath the higher water, and the higher [object] will pass through the water that crosses at a higher level. To put it better: the water **d c** has a bed higher than the water **a b**, and things carried <insert>under</insert> near the bottom of water **a b** will pass under the water **d c** and will follow their straight course together with the water that carries them; and the things carried on the surface will encounter the surface of water **d b** and their straight course will be changed into a curve.

[ 2nd figure: ] a b c d
— *Things carried by water near a winding bottom do not follow the same course as those carried by the same water on the surface.*
A light object <note>Italian: "lieue"; French: "lourd." Leonardo likely meant a "heavy" object (grave) for the bottom line, despite the transcription "lieue" (light). If an object is on the bottom, it is typically denser than the water.</note> is carried along the bottom by the line **a d**, and a lighter object will be carried by the surface of the water along the line **b c**.

-> — FOLIO 43 (*verso*). — <-

### [THINGS CARRIED BY THE WATER].

<margin>
CONCERNING THINGS CARRIED BY WATER WHICH HAVE PART OF THEMSELVES IN THE AIR AND PART IN THE WATER.
</margin>

If the thing carried by the water is half in the water and half in the air, and if that air moves with a speed equal to the speed of the water, then that moving object <term>mobile|any body or object in motion</term> will be at the first degree of speed of movement <note>meaning it moves at the maximum possible speed allowed by the flow without resistance from the air.</note>.

*If the movement of the air is slower than...*

If the air is slower than the movement of the water that moves in the same direction, then the movement of the object will be slower than if those movements of air and water were equal; and it will be slowed down more the more the movements of air and water differ.

If the movement of the air is faster than the movement of the air <note>The Italian text repeats "aria" (air), but clearly intends "water" in the second instance to denote the relative speed of the two mediums.</note> that moves in the same direction, then the movement of the object will become faster, and all the more so as that air is faster than the water.

If the movement of the air against the course of the water is of equal speed to the water against the air, the object will follow the course of the water if it has more contact with the water than with the air—and it will do the opposite if it has more contact with the air than with the water.

— The question is asked whether the water **a b**, striking with its weight upon the buckets <note>original: "cassette," literally small boxes or compartments on a water wheel</note> of the wheel, should be accepted and counted with the other weight of the water that is in the bucket on the struck side, or if it should be judged as a greater quantity by adding the power of the percussion <term>percussion: the force of impact generated by a moving body</term> to it. —
*If this were so, the wheel would lift the water on the opposite side higher than the water that falls, since the blow is not weight, but moves a power of weight almost equal to its own power.* —

# — FOLIO 44 (recto) —

If the force of the striker <term>striker: the 'percussore,' or the body that delivers a blow</term> is equal to the motion of the struck body, that motion will be between that of the force and that of the percussion, and both will be equally diminished <unclear>because</unclear> both are consumed by the equality of the resistance, which will be distributed equally between them both.
And if the force is greater than the resistance, the motion of the percussion will be shorter in proportion to how much slower the resistance is to the motion, which is overcome by the force of the motor or striker, as it possesses greater power <term>power: 'potenzia,' referring here to the mechanical potential or force behind the movement</term>.

<note>Technical sketches illustrating mechanical principles: a cylinder on a vertical axis, several wedge-shaped or block forms, and a wheel with internal vanes (likely a water wheel).</note>
</margin>

The weight of the water that falls along the perpendicular line is entirely upon the place of its percussion; but if the line is oblique <note>slanted or at an angle</note>, part of the water is over that place and part is over the air. This part that is over the air will load its weight upon the part that lies beneath it, which, being between that water and the air, will be perpendicular over the air just as the other is above it. And the air, being quickly overcome, will give way to that water, and the oblique line will be overcome by the force of the weight of the water.

<header>— FOLIO 45 (recto). — [BOOK OF THE TREATISE ON WATER. — WATERS IN THE AIR AND WINDS]. — FOLIO 45 (verso). — [WATERS MEETING IN THE AIR (4 CASES)].</header>

45. — ORDER OF THE BOOK
To explain *lob* <note>original: "lob," likely an abbreviation for "lobi" or "gli," interpreted here as the "cases" or "aspects"</note> the aspects of waters that emerge in the air and their percussions <term>percussions: the impacts or collisions between two bodies of water</term> made with various powers, quantities, lengths of motion, varieties of obliquity <term>obliquity: the angle or slant at which the water moves</term>, and quantities, I will use for comparison the 4 principal winds—namely: North, South, East, and West. With these aspects, I will guide myself in providing knowledge of the aforementioned movements of water in the air, and thus this description will be shorter and more efficient. —

— *If 2 waters of equal thickness emerge in the air at the East, and the more powerful one is higher...*
If two waters of equal thickness and unequal height emerge in the air in a straight line from the East, without doubt one, in descending, will follow the other and will be the more powerful.
If waters of equal thickness emerging in the air meet one another.
If a declining obliquity meets an ascending obliquity at an angle.

### 45. — ORDER OF THE BOOK.
To explain the cases of waters that emerge in the air and their impacts, made with various powers, quantities, lengths of movement, varieties of angles, and quantities, I will compare them to the 4 principal winds, that is: North, South, East, and West, and with these aspects I will govern myself to give knowledge of the aforementioned movements of water in the air; thus this description will be shorter and more [more] efficient.
*If 2 waters of equal thickness emerge in the air at the East, and the more powerful one is higher.....*
If two waters of equal thickness and unequal height emerge in the air in a straight line [in the direction] of the East, without doubt one, in descending, will follow the other, and will be the more powerful.
If waters equal in thickness which emerge in the air meet each other.
If a declining angle meets an angle that rises at a point¹.

[ Fig 1 : ] 4th a b e c f d B c takes from f c, and it leaves nothing of itself.
These are the four ways in which waters, moving in the same aspect, penetrate one another with oblique lines toward the center of the world <note>Leonardo refers to the center of the Earth as the "center of the world," which he understood as the destination of all falling weight</note>, etc.
Various obliquities and thicknesses toward the East with equal thicknesses in the air.
These four demonstrations are sufficient to prove the four principal effects made by waters that strike one another in the air.
Of which the first is that which, being more oblique, penetrates the less oblique, and penetrates it in part, and carries with it the part it struck. In the second demonstration, the less oblique penetrates the more oblique in part, and carries with it the part it struck. In the third demonstration, the more oblique water carries with it the less oblique water entirely.
The fourth does the opposite, seeing that the less oblique water carries the more oblique water with it entirely.

Water of equal thickness will be as much more powerful in its motion as it flows out from a lower point in the vessel where it was enclosed. <note>Leonardo is observing that water pressure increases with depth; the lower the opening in a tank, the faster and more forcefully the water jets out.</note>
Regarding waters that strike each other in the air, the more powerful one penetrates the less powerful one, twisting and carrying with it all the water that falls upon it as well as the lateral water; the remainder follows its natural course.
IT IS POSSIBLE THAT WATER FALLING THROUGH THE AIR UPON WATER THAT POURS FROM A VESSEL INTO THE AIR—THE MORE POWERFUL OF THE TWO—MAY ENTIRELY PREVENT THE STRAIGHT DESCENT OF THE LESS POWERFUL ONE AND ACCOMPANY IT ALONG ITS ENTIRE COURSE THROUGH THE AIR.
As if the water that emerges from vessel *a b* [ 2nd fig. : ] and flows into the air with movement *b c*, is struck by the water *d e* that emerges from vessel *d e* by movement *e f*; I say that the water *e f* will bend in the percussion it makes upon water *b c* and will follow the rest of its course along the line *f m* [n], together with the water *b c*, and none of it will fall along the course it originally began by the path *e f*.

### [WATER — DOGS, THE POOR, AND THE RICH].

47. — Very few are the parts of running water found between its surface and its bottom that flow with the same aspect <note>Meaning they do not move at the same speed or in the same direction</note>.

->a c b d<-

The water **a b** flows along the line of the object under the contrary movement **e c d b**, which, by means of the eddy <note>original: *retroso*; a whirlpool or back-current</note>, has hollowed out the bottom beneath it; in this depth flows the said water **a b**, and it is cleared away with the same speed as the revolution of the aforementioned eddy.

**WHY DOGS WILLINGLY SMELL ONE ANOTHER’S BUTTOCKS.** <note>The original Italian uses the cruder term *culo*.</note> This animal holds the poor in hatred because they eat wretched food, and loves the rich because they have good meals, and especially meat. Now, the excrement of animals always retains some of the virtue <term>virtue: in this context, the nutritional essence or 'power' of the food</term> of its origin, as is shown by the mesenteric veins <note>original: *vene miseraice*; Leonardo refers to the veins that absorb nutrients from the intestines</note> distributed even to the lowest intestines to extract for themselves the virtue that remains in those feces. Now, dogs have such a highly refined sense of smell that with their noses they perceive the virtue remaining in such feces; indeed, if they find these feces in the streets, they smell them, and if they sense within them the virtue of meat or something else, they take them and do not leave them. To return to the question, I say that if they recognize through such smells that the dog is well-fed, they respect it, because they estimate that it has a powerful and rich master; and if they do not sense such an essence of virtue, they estimate that such a dog is of little account and has a poor and wretched master, and therefore they bite such a dog just as they would do <margin>to its master</margin>.

***

### [AIR AND WEIGHT — WATER].

How much air is required to lift different heavy bodies <term>gravi: heavy objects or weights</term> of various materials. How much water will enter a boat to make it sink. Which air supports more: that which is enclosed, or the rarefied air—as is done in cupping glasses <note>original: *coppette*; small glass vessels used in medical bleeding to create a vacuum</note>—or common air, or condensed air—as is done in balls <note>specifically leather balls or bladders</note> inflated by the force of a screw? Without doubt, the rarefied air [supports most], then the common air, and the condensed air resists the least.

Every movement—and every part of the thickness of water that falls from a river into the air—follows the line in which the impetus <term>inpeto: the force or momentum of a body in motion</term> that led it to that fall was first begun.

### [WATER, AIR, WEIGHT, RIVERS].

49. — Of waters of equal depth, the one that is narrower will support less weight.

[ 1st fig. : ] a Weight, Air, Water [ 2nd fig. : ] Weight, Air

The weight supported by the boat sinks it into the water just as much as the water surrounding the boat acquires weight over the air inside that boat, which is equal to the weight supported. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of buoyancy: a floating object displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.</note>

Regarding what was said above, the water here in the smaller vessel surrounding the weight placed upon the air does not weigh upon that air as much as the weight placed above it, as does the water of the larger vessel. This larger vessel is made high enough above the air supporting the weight that it is powerful enough to push the air upward, together with the weight placed on top of it, by the same amount that the weight presses it downward.

The waters have more turbulence <note>original: *revolutione*; referring to eddies or circular motions in the current</note> from the midpoint of their height downward than from that middle region upward. This is due to the many obstacles found at the bottom of rivers, while there are few above, except for those objects <margin>placed on the bottom that rise above these waters.</margin>

### [HOW TO LOAD A SHIP — THE WEDGE — THOUGHTS].

Let a great weight be loaded onto a ship without the use of windlasses, levers, ropes, or any [manual] force.

[ 1st fig. : ] Sea 10,000,0000

[ 2nd fig. : ] a n m b c d [ 3rd fig. : ] c e b o

To load any very great single weight onto a sturdy boat, it is necessary to pull that weight to the seashore, aligning its length toward the sea from the shore. Then, let a canal be made that passes beneath this weight and extends as far beyond it as half the length of the boat that must carry the weight. Likewise, the width of such a canal should be made according to the width of the boat. The boat shall be filled with water <note>used as ballast to sink the boat low enough to fit under the weight</note> and pulled under the weight; then, as the water is removed, the ship will rise to such a height that it will lift the said weight off the ground by itself. Once loaded in this way, you can pull it into the sea and lead it to the place intended for it.

[ 5th fig. : ] The blow struck upon the wedge <term>coin; a triangular tool used to split materials or lift heavy loads</term> causes that wedge to move any great weight.

Blink your eye and look at it again; what you see of it now was not there before, and what was there of it is no more. <note>Leonardo observes that light is a continuous stream; the "old" light vanishes and is replaced by "new" light every moment.</note>

Who is it that remakes it if the maker is continually dying?

## [MOVEMENT OF LIQUIDS. — DOUBLING THE CUBE].

The natural movements of liquids in the air are faster and thinner at the end than at the beginning.
The semi-natural movements made by water between the riverbed and the air will be of equal velocity if the bed of said river is equal in straightness, slant, and width.

Semi-accidental movements made between the bottom of the canal and the air upon a bed of equal slant and width always go slowing down, but they are longer than simple accidental ones, because they go leaning and always discharge part of their weight.

**ON DOUBLING THE CUBE.** — Divide the cube *a b* by the diameter; and because such a division is not a perfect squaring <term>quadratura: the geometric process of constructing a square with an area equal to that of a given figure</term>, square it with the eighth [rule], then take half and place it in *c* and square it, so that it becomes *d*; then return *d* to the imperfect squaring just as that of the first half-cube was; thus, you will do as *s* stands below, to which *s* you add as much again, and you will have made the cube *sub-duplo* <note>meaning a cube with a specific proportional relationship, likely half the volume</note> to the one above.

[7th fig.:] *R* is the said imperfect squared half-cube, *f* is the perfection, *m* is the smaller perfect square, *n* is the imperfect one, and thus they are to be situated in this order.
<margin>The other ancient method cannot prove one square to be double the other as this one can.</margin>

# FOLIO 50 (recto)

## [THE NATURE OF SHADOWS AND LIGHT]

If it is possible for a shadow to be less dark <gloss>original: *mācho oscura*</gloss> than the field where it falls, the shadow of bodies will be of so much less darkness as it is more distant from that body. And this [the shadow] will be of a quality similar to the color of the field where it falls. And it will be less equal in color to its original <note>the object casting it</note>; rather, it will be diluted and will be so much weaker as it is more remote. And because of this, that which is said by the mathematicians will be proven true, etc.

<note>Geometric diagram showing a quadrilateral surface representing a shadow or object, with light rays converging toward a point p, labeled with n, p, and m.</note>

If the sun is larger than the earth: it is possible—and it is entirely the case—that the shadow of the earth becomes so much less [dark] than the field where it falls that it reaches towards nothingness <gloss>original: *uer n'è*, "toward nothing"</gloss>. This is caused by the solar rays <term>razj: rays of light</term>.

The weaker the shadow, the less dark it will be, the further it is from its object. Because to maintain the luminous rays <note>to allow light to infiltrate the shadow</note>, as the rays increase, the shadow is less. The air will be longer <note>more extensive</note>, becoming less dark the more remote it is, because of the air interposed between the shadow and the eye.
The weaker the shadow, the less dark it will be, the more remote it is.

# FOLIO 50 (verso)

## [THE GEOMETRY OF SIGHT AND PERSPECTIVE]

No length of sight can see an entire space except from a single unique point <gloss>original: *ū sol ūico punto*</gloss>. No sight can see an entire space—it is less than that—it can only see as much as the sight employs, which is no more than a single unique point. Because the perpendicular line does not break the points, but the eye does. For this reason, an entire space is seen in a single point, and the eye is weak <note>referring to the limited focal point of human vision compared to the vastness of space</note>.

No sight can see [more] than from a single point, because from a single point the eye does not see less than a single point of so much space, because the eye operates [this way]. And if the eye consists of a single unique point of sight, it will be of such a length of air.

<margin>
**Perspective: of bodies.**
All the points that come from the object to the eye... as the body is further away... and if the points come from the eye to the body, all the points come into the eye through a single point. Because the eye does not see by any sight except from a single unique point. From this, it must be demonstrated that the rays of the eye come to the eye <note>Leonardo is exploring the theory of 'intromission,' where light enters the eye</note>, and through the rays of the body they come to the eye, and through the rays of the eye they go to the body <note>Leonardo here acknowledges the ancient 'extramission' theory where eyes send out rays, but his focus is on the convergence at a single point</note>.
</margin>

51. — The center of every pyramidal gravity is located at the fourth part of its axis <note>the line from the apex to the center of the base</note> toward the base—and if you divide the axis into 4 equal parts and intersect two of the axes of such a pyramid, such an intersection will occur at the aforementioned fourth.

**THE SQUARING <term>quadrature: the mathematical process of finding a square (or here, a cubic volume) equal in area or volume to another shape</term> OF THE LARGER CUBE IS DOUBLE THE SQUARING OF THE SMALLER CUBE; AND EACH BEING RESOLVED INTO ITS 6 PYRAMIDS, YOU WILL FIND THE CENTER OF THEIR NATURAL GRAVITY ON THE LINE THAT DIVIDES THE SMALLER CUBE FROM THE LARGER CUBE.**

Then I place it in **c**, and by the eighth, I square its side **r**, and place it in **d**; then I divide the square **d** by its diameter and put half in **n**, and with the eighth I square the side **n** and put it in **p**; its figure is half of a cube.

->— FOLIO 51 (verso). —<-

->## [ON MOTION]<-

**First:** If a power <gloss>original: *potentia*, referring to force</gloss> moves a body through a certain space in a certain time, the same power will move half of that body in the same time through twice that space.

**Second:** If some force <gloss>original: *virtu*, "virtue" or physical power</gloss> moves a mobile object through a certain space in an equal time, the same force will move half of that object through that entire space in half of that time.

**Third:** If a force moves a body in a certain time through a certain space, the same force will move half of that body in the same time through half of that space.

**Fifth [4th]:** If a force moves a body through a certain *space* <insert>time</insert> through a certain space, it is not necessary that such power moves double the weight in the same space in double the time, [or] half of twice such space, because it might be that such force would not be able to move that object at all <note>Leonardo is recognizing that there is a threshold of force required to overcome friction or inertia</note>.

**Sixth [5th]:** If a force moves a body for so much time through so much space, it is not necessary that half of that force moves that same object in the same time through half of such space, for perhaps it would not be able to move it.

**Sixth:** If two separate forces move two separate objects, the same forces united will move the two joined objects in the same time through the same space, because the same proportion always remains in each part.

— FOLIO 52 (recto). —

->[ON MOVEMENT. — LIGHTNING].<-

<margin>
52. — Fourth.
Local movement
of the celestial
arrow <note>The "celestial arrow" is Leonardo's poetic term for a lightning bolt.</note>
</margin>

If a power moves a body in a certain amount of time over a certain amount of space, half the power will move half of that mobile body in the same amount of time over half of such space.

IF EVERY MOVING BODY FOLLOWS ITS MOTION ALONG THE LINE OF ITS BEGINNING, WHAT IS IT THAT MAKES THE MOVEMENT OF THE ARROW OR THUNDERBOLT BE SINUOUS AND FLEXIBLE IN SO MANY ASPECTS, BEING IN ONE AND THE SAME AIR?

What has been said arises, or can arise, from two causes. The first is that the air, which condenses in front of the lightning’s furious impetus <term>impeto: the force or momentum of a moving body</term>, offers resistance to it, so that the motion comes to bend and is of a reflected rather than a straight-line nature. This is similar to what is shown in the third [chapter] of the fifth [book] on waters, where air sometimes emerges from the bottom of marshes in the form of bubbles <note>original: "sonagli," literally "little bells" or "bubbles"</note> and rises to the surface of the water with a sinuous, curvilinear motion. The second way the sinuous movement of lightning can arise is that the matter of the "arrow" exhales <note>or "projects itself"</note> now to the right, now to the left, now upward, and now downward. This is similar to a spark that jumps from glowing coals; for if the coal exhales from one side, it is because it breaks apart due to the moisture increasing <note>expanding</note> inside it. Being red-hot, it shatters that particle of coal and generates another spark which, at its birth, strikes and pushes back the remainder of the coal. This remainder then does the same in several directions, casting various sparks through the air until it consumes itself. But the first opinion pleases me more, because if the second were true, you would see a single lightning bolt generate many, just as that spark generates many. <note>A mark made by a reader—a cross in grey pencil—appears toward the top of the page.</note>

***

— FOLIO 52 (verso). —

->[WATER (THE SPHERICAL EARTH, UNINHABITABLE. — THINGS CARRIED BY CURRENTS)].<-

If the earth were [perfectly] spherical, no part of it would be uncovered by the sphere of the water.

No flat land will be found upon which the water does not sit in a convex shape, being in the center of that plain; and such water will never have motion toward the extremities of that plain. Therefore, upon a perfect plain, there can be water of various depths.

[ Figure ] <note>A diagram showing the curvature of the earth relative to a perceived flat surface.</note>
n a p u o q 
[ Under the figure: ] What here appears to be flat is actually a steep mountain.

It is impossible to find any flat part on the surface of any very large sea <term>pelagho: from the Greek "pelagos," referring to the deep, open sea</term>.

The low places of the sea floor are perpetual, and the peaks of the mountains are the opposite <note>meaning they are temporary due to erosion</note>; it follows that the earth will eventually become spherical and entirely covered by water, and it will be uninhabitable.

[ 2nd Figure ] <note>A diagram of an object submerged in water currents.</note>
An object carried by the course of the water [is found] in the course of lesser power; if it is oblique <note>tilted</note> toward the bottom, it will move toward the bottom, and thus it will move according to the direction of its obliquity.

Of things carried between two [layers of] water, only that which is in the middle of two currents of equal motion will travel without being turned upside down.

But that object will be in continual revolution between top and bottom if it is placed in the middle of two unequal currents.

That object will be deprived of lateral revolution if it moves between currents that are equal in motion, and likewise conversely.

<summary>Leonardo investigates why lightning moves in a zigzag pattern, favoring the theory of air resistance over internal explosions, and discusses the impossibility of "flat" water on a spherical Earth.</summary>

# FOLIO 52 (recto).

<margin>
If it

</margin>

<note>Folio 52 recto: Leonardo's notes on atmospheric optics and the density of air.</note>

Why the air is denser in wet places than in dry ones.
Why the air gathers in wet places rather than in dry ones.
Why the air contains humidity within itself.

This air can never in any way place itself between the eye and the object unless it is of such thickness <term>grosseza: density or physical volume</term> capable of multiplying that quantity of light which the surface of said object [reflects], so as to hide from the smoke <note>original: "fumo," likely referring to the visual obscurity or "sfumato" effect of the atmosphere</note> the point of the pupil, and from there hide it against the object. If the object is weak in light, it will be overcome by the air that is between the eye and it; and if it is luminous, the opposite will happen, because the air will be overcome by the light of said object, whereby its true form will be recognized. But if the object is in the distance and is of weak light, the air will be stronger than its light, because there the air is in a great sum and the light of the object is small. Therefore, the object, through weakness, remains overcome by the air and is not seen. And if the object is of great light, it will be seen over a great distance, because through its strength it will be powerful enough to penetrate the air and make itself known to the eye across long distances. The reason for this is as follows: light penetrates through the air because the air across great distances is weak, and weakness allows itself to be overcome by strength. And because of this, we see the stars, which although they are far away, are of great light, and for this reason they penetrate the air of the earth, which is thick, and make themselves seen. Therefore, we shall conclude that the air overcomes the object when it is weak, and the object overcomes the air when it is strong. And yet a weak object will still be seen if it is placed in the midst of a great light, just like the spots on the sun <note>original: "machule del sole." Leonardo was an early observer of sunspots, which appear dark only in contrast to the sun's brilliance.</note>.

# FOLIO 52 (verso).

<note>Folio 52 verso: Further studies on the atmosphere, including notes on why the sky is blue and how air density varies with altitude.</note>

Why the air will be clearer <note>or brighter</note> at the summit than at the base, because the air at the base is denser than that of the summit.

If the air is clearer at the summit of mountains than at the base, this arises because the air below is thicker and more full of vapors <note>original: "fumi," literally fumes or smokes</note>, and for this reason, it will be whiter in color; and the air of the summit, being thinner, will be more blue <note>original: "azura"</note>. And that blue color arises from the supreme darkness <note>original: "somma tenebra"</note> of the cosmic space <note>original: "spatio mundano"</note> which shines through the air, which is a very thin body.

<margin>
Why the air
bordering
the sun will
be clearer
to give off

</margin>

<note>Geometric diagram of an arc representing the atmosphere above a circular body (Earth or Sun), with light rays or observation lines.</note>

Why the air that is closer to the earth is thicker: because the air gathers in cold and humid places, and there the vapors and mists are made; therefore the air of high places will be thinner.

Why the air will be thinner at a high summit than at the base of mountains: because the air above is less burdened <note>weighted down</note> than that below, because the air supports itself.

Why the air is thicker in humid places than in dry ones: because wet air has water mixed with itself, which two things together are thicker than simple air.

Why the air overcomes the weakness of the object: because the air is weak in distant places, and for this reason, it will be penetrated by a great distant light, such as the stars and the sun.

Why the air is thicker in wet places than in dry ones: because wet air has water mixed within itself, and air is by itself thin.

### FOLIO 53 (recto). —

->[MEASUREMENT OF WATER]<-

53. — | Fig: ] a b c d e
THE QUANTITY OF THE TRUE OUNCE OF WATER <term>onca: a Renaissance unit of measure for water flow, usually defined by the amount of water passing through a specific aperture</term> --
— For water that does not lack a steady height at its surface, the quantity of water that flows through a given aperture in a given time will be proportional to the given height above that aperture. —
I say that if **b** pours a certain quantity of water in a given time, **c** will pour twice as much water in the same time, because **c** has twice as much weight of water above it. In this case, the proportions of the weights do not behave like dense, unified objects falling through the air; as for the water, in striking the air, it makes a continuous hole in it. However, a dense and unified object that descends through the air successively has to open the air which offers some resistance, and consequently condenses a little, so that it does not allow the passage of a moving body of a fixed length as easily as it does for water, which is of indefinite length <note>Leonardo distinguishes between a solid falling object, which must constantly displace new air, and a continuous stream of water, which maintains a path through the air.</note>.
— IF THE CANAL DECREASES IN HEIGHT WHILE POURING WATER THROUGH ITS APERTURES PLACED AT DIFFERENT DISTANCES FROM THE BOTTOM, THEN THE UPPER APERTURE LOSES MORE OF ITS REGULAR EMISSION OF WATER THAN THE ONE BELOW IT. —
Let us say that above the two apertures **d** and **c**, the entire height of the water **a-b** is decreased; in this case, **b-c** loses half of its power, because **a-b** is set as equal to **b-c**. And the aperture **d** loses a third of its power, because **a-b** fits 3 times into **a-d**, and so it follows --
<margin>[In the margin:] It follows that in the same amount of time, by taking away the height of the water **a-b**, the aperture **c** (losing **3 d**) only loses one [unit], because if **c** has a power of 6, by removing **a-b**, **c** will remain with a power of 3, half of its height having been taken away. And in such a case, **d-c**, which was at a power of 9, by losing **a-b** which was 3, remains at a power of 6; therefore, when **a-b** is missing, **c** loses half and **d** loses a third <note>This is a mathematical exercise in fluid pressure: the deeper the water, the more pressure—and therefore more "power" or flow—at the opening.</note>.</margin>

->[IMPACT OF WATER (FOUR MOVEMENTS)]<-

54. — Any water striking an object <note>Leonardo is describing how a stream of water reacts when it hits a flat surface or an obstacle</note> divides into four various and principal movements: namely, right and left, up and down; and the downward movement is harmful to the bottom <note>This refers to the erosion of a riverbed or channel floor caused by the downward force of the current</note>.
Of the four principal movements made by water that divides upon its reflection <term>reflection: in this context, the way water "bounces" or redirects after hitting an obstacle</term>, the one that reflects at a more acute angle will be the fastest.
[Figure 2:] a b a, acute angle; b, obtuse angle.
AS THE ANGLE OF INCIDENCE OF THE WATER IS CREATED BETWEEN MORE DISSIMILAR ANGLES, THE DEPTH OF THE CAVITY FORMED BENEATH THE ANGLE OF INCIDENCE WILL BE LESSER.
[Figure 4:] a b c d e
As if the incidence of the water’s course were made along line d-e, upon the bank a-c. The angles a-b-d and d-b-c are very dissimilar; therefore, the impact is weak at b, the angle of incidence, so that it is not reflected upwards, and it neither strikes nor carves out the bottom.

->— FOLIO 54 (*recto*). —<-

<note>Folio 54 (recto) contains notes on the movement of water and air, specifically regarding circular motion and impact (percussion).</note>

Every circular motion of water is caused by the impact <term>percussion: Leonardo uses the term 'perchussa' to describe the physical shock or impact of one element striking another</term> of water falling through the air. This motion, [traced as if] by a compass <note>original: 'in sesta'. Leonardo refers to the 'sesta' or pair of compasses to describe a perfect geometric circle</note>, occurs when it strikes still water and will be as circular as the force of the impact.

Such circular water motion dissipates along with the harmony <note>Here, 'harmony' refers to the mathematical regularity and sequence of the expanding ripples</note> of the circles created by the impact; for just as air striking water creates circularity, so too does the air when it is struck.

Such circulating motion of pressurized air from an impact will have circular dimensions and slow circular motions when struck in the air; however, they will be shaped by considerations of distances and forms.
Such motion of air striking air occurs close by and with less curved movements in the figure <note>original: 'dja'. Leonardo often uses 'dja' as a shorthand for 'diagram' or 'differentia' (difference)</note> at certain distances; the boundaries diminish according to the form of the motions, and in the distance they lose their height; in the distant form they lose the definition of their boundary and are consumed within the motions.

->[RESERVOIR OUTLETS. — CENTER OF GRAVITY].<-

55.— [Figure 1:] a b — Regarding outlets of equal length, shape, and height: the one that will pour more water in the same amount of time is the one with the thinner wall <note>original: 'sottile pariete'. That is to say, **a** will pour more water than **b**.

**a**, having its opening lower on the outside than on the inside, will pour more water than **b**.

ON THE CENTER OF GRAVITY:
Every irregularly shaped body <note>original: 'corpo disforme'. Leonardo refers to bodies that are not perfectly symmetrical</note> has three centers: that of its magnitude <note>the geometric center</note>, that of its accidental gravity, and that of its natural gravity. But if one were to incorporate the center of the world <note>In the Renaissance, the 'center of the world' was believed to be the center of the Earth, where all heavy things naturally tend to fall</note>, the center of accidental gravity would be missing.

Regarding irregular bodies that have a center of magnitude and a center of natural gravity: they can only align with the center of the world at the center of [natural] gravity, and the center of magnitude will remain separate.

<meta>Following the previous discussion on Folio 55 regarding hydraulic flow and the centers of gravity in irregular bodies, Leonardo now shifts his focus toward optics and the physics of light, specifically how celestial bodies like the Earth and Sun cast shadows and how the intensity of a shadow varies based on its exposure to light.</meta>

->— FOLIO 55 (recto). —<-

->### [ON THE ILLUMINATION OF SPHERES]###<-

That part of the ball which sees <note>Leonardo often uses the verb "to see" (vedere) to describe a surface’s exposure or orientation toward a light source</note> more of the sky will be more luminous, and that part which sees less of it will be less luminous; provided that the ball is of uniform material and has a polished surface.

That part of the ball which sees more of that part of the sky that sees the sphere of the sun will be more luminous than if it saw the part of the sky opposite to the sun.

If the sphere of the sun were of the size of the sphere of the earth, the shadow of the earth would be a cylindrical cone <note>original: 'cono cilindrico'. Here, Leonardo describes a shadow that does not taper, projecting a uniform column of darkness into space</note> and would extend to infinity, and the other part of the earth would be forever illuminated by the sun, and this shadow would never be of greater or lesser length.

If the sphere of the sun were larger than the sphere of the earth, the shadow of the earth would be a pyramidal cone <note>original: 'cono piramidale'. Leonardo is correctly identifying that a larger light source creates a tapering shadow that eventually ends at a point</note> and would be of a finite length.

---

->— FOLIO 55 (verso). —<-

->### [ON THE VARIETY AND INTENSITY OF SHADOWS]###<-

All shadows created by the same body and the same light will be equal among themselves if the objects <note>the surfaces upon which the shadows fall</note> of the said shadows are equal and at an equal distance from the light.

A very beautiful "fixed" white paper <note>Fixed (fisso) likely refers to a matte or permanent finish that does not bleed or change</note> is made from a mixture and the milk of the colocasia <note>original: "gichero." -> [ THE FRICTION OF THE HEAVENS ]. <-

**ON THE FRICTION OF THE HEAVENS; WHETHER IT MAKES A SOUND OR NOT**

Every sound is caused by air being struck by a dense body, and if it is made by two heavy bodies [striking] against each other, it is by means of the air that surrounds them; and this friction consumes the bodies that are rubbed. It would follow, therefore, that the heavens, in their friction—having no air between them—would produce no sound. And if such friction were indeed a reality, in the many centuries that these heavens have turned, they would have been consumed by such immense speed produced every day. And even if they did make a sound, it could not spread, because sound made under water by a strike is heard very little, and it would be heard even less, or not at all, in dense bodies. Furthermore, in the case of polished bodies, their friction makes no sound; the same would happen regarding the contact or friction of the heavens. And if these heavens are not polished at the contact of their friction, it follows that they are globular and rough; therefore their contact is not continuous, and if this were so, a vacuum would be generated, which it is concluded does not exist in Nature. <note>Leonardo invokes the classical principle "horror vacui" (Nature abhors a vacuum) to prove the heavens must be smooth</note>. Therefore it is concluded that friction would have consumed the boundaries of each heaven; and as much as it is faster toward the middle <note>the celestial equator</note> than toward the poles, it would be consumed more in the middle than at the poles; and then there would be no more friction, the sound would cease, and the dancers would stop <note>The "dancers" may be a poetic metaphor for the planets or stars in their orbits</note>—unless one heaven turned toward the East and the other toward the North.

<summary>Leonardo argues for the Earth's status as a celestial "star" and details complex recipes for creating composite, marble-like decorative papers. On the reverse, he uses the physics of friction, sound, and the vacuum to disprove the ancient theory of the 'Music of the Spheres.'</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, Earth as a star, papermaking, colocasia, sardonyx, celestial mechanics, acoustics, friction of the heavens, vacuum, music of the spheres</keywords>

— FOLIO 56 (verso). —

The motion produced in a movable object by a push will involve as much greater effort as that object is further from the prime mover. <note>Leonardo is discussing the principle of the lever: the further a weight is from the point of support or power, the more force is required to move or hold it.</note>

If there is a weight of 200 pounds <note>original: "libre"</note> which is supported by a man standing on the tips of his toes, and his leg is extended outward 1/4 of a cubit <note>term: "braccio" (literally "arm"). A common Florentine unit of measurement approximately equal to 23 inches or 58 cm</note> relative to its perpendicular line, then the calf muscle <note>original: "muscolo poppa della gamba." Leonardo uses the term "poppa" (stern) to describe the bulging back part of the leg</note> of the leg supports 400 pounds; and if it were extended 1/2 a cubit, then it supports 800 pounds; and if it were extended as far as the length of the sole of the foot, then it would support 1200 pounds.

But if the man stands on the middle of the sole of the foot with his whole person perpendicular to the middle of that sole, then that calf muscle supports no weight nor any effort.

From this it follows that the more a man leans and the further he moves from his perpendicular line, the more he loads the calf muscle of the leg.

The perpendicular line of a man is that which falls from the middle of the nape of the neck to the middle of the toenails. <note>Leonardo is defining the center of gravity and the vertical axis of the human body in balance.</note>

If a man who is falling weighs 150 pounds and his imbalance is 1/4 of his height, and his leg which must support him is 1 cubit away from his perpendicular line, then the calf muscle will support 300 pounds; and if it is 1/2 a cubit away, it will support 600 pounds.

It is said that if a man falls due to an imbalance of 1/4 of his height, the force that the leg must exert is double the weight of that man.

And if the imbalance is 1/2 of his height, the force will be four times the weight of that man.

<summary>Leonardo explores the efficiency of hexagonal structures in honeycombs as a balance between geometry and nature, followed by a mathematical analysis of how the human calf muscle supports increasing weight as the body moves out of vertical equilibrium.</summary>

## [LIGHT OF THE STARS].

57. — WHETHER THE STARS HAVE LIGHT FROM THE SUN OR FROM THEMSELVES [their own light].
Some claim that the stars possess their own light, arguing that if Venus and Mercury did not have their own light, they would darken as much of the sun as they cover from our sight when they pass between our eyes and the sun. This is false, because it has been proven how an opaque object placed within a luminous one is surrounded and entirely covered by the lateral rays of the remaining part of that luminous body, and thus remains invisible. This is demonstrated when the sun is viewed through the branches of leafless trees at a great distance; the branches do not block any part of the sun from our eyes. The same thing happens with the aforementioned planets, which, although they are without brilliance <note>original: "luce"</note> of their own, do not—as has been stated—block any part of the sun from our eye.

<margin>Second proof.</margin>

<note>[Figure showing:] Sun, Earth, Moon, Star</note>

They say that stars appear most brilliant at night the higher they are above us, and that if they did not have their own light, the shadow cast by the earth—which interposes itself between them and the sun—would darken them, as they would neither see nor be seen by the solar body. But these people have not considered that the <term>pyramidal shadow</term> <note>Leonardo refers to the cone-shaped shadow cast by a sphere like the Earth when illuminated by a larger sphere like the Sun</note> of the earth does not reach very many stars. Even for those it does reach, the pyramid has diminished so much in size that it covers very little of the star's body; the remainder of the star continues to be illuminated by the sun.

<note>1. Reference to J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, 912.</note>
