— FOLIO 58 (recto). —

<note>Leonardo's notes on optics, specifically how light and shadow behave when passing through small apertures, and the effect of atmospheric perspective on the clarity of shadows.</note>

### Of the shadowy body of air

**Seeing through apertures or narrow slits**
It is a matter of <term>necessity</term><note>Leonardo uses "necessity" to describe a mathematical or physical law that cannot be otherwise.</note> that what the eye sees is less than a <unclear>small</unclear> part of the sun than the aperture is; because the eye [must] <unclear>traverse</unclear> the space through which it [the light] exists.

For every shadowy body, the shadow will appear clearer—assuming it is of equal width—when seen by the eye if the air that is interposed between the eye and the shadow is greater in one part than in the other; thus, the greater volume of air will be that which **brightens** <note>original: "rinfrescha". Leonardo uses this term to describe how the atmosphere "washes out" or dilutes the darkness of a shadow, making it appear lighter and bluer with distance.</note> the part of the **face** <note>original: "uiso". This can mean "face" or, more generally, the "visual object" or "sight."</note> that is between the eye and the shadow; because the air, being thicker [at a distance], overcomes the shadow and robs it of its true darkness; and to maintain itself, the <unclear>old</unclear> shadow will be brightened by the sun.

<margin>
This seeing of the light of the sun will be of so much more **luminosity** as more of the sun itself is seen through the said aperture by the aforementioned eye; this seeing will be in the first part.
</margin>

### Of the same body

If the eye is between two shadows, one will be darker than the other.

The true darkness of a shadow of small width will be that which is seen by the eye when between the shadow and said eye there is less air than there is between the other eye and the other true shadow of equal darkness; by necessity, the air that is between the eye and the shadow will be thicker near the distant shadow than that which is between the eye and the nearby shadow.

---

— FOLIO 58 (verso). —

<note>Studies on the visual perception of objects and light/shadow intensity based on distance and the intervening atmosphere.</note>

### Of everything seen by the eye

Every part of a **face** seen in the sun: it is not true that it must necessarily be seen in the same way if the eye sees it through the interposition of air, in which the eye will see it in the first part, through which the eye will see the air within the sun itself.

If of the same face seen by the eye, one part is seen in the sun, it will be of one quality of clarity seen by the eye; the other part will be seen through another quality of air and the true shadow.

For every shadowy body seen within the air, if one is seen through one quality [of air] and the other through another, the air that is between the eye and that shadowy body will be less; the light will be in the same quality of shadow as a shadow of true width seen between the eye; the air that is interposed between the eye and the shadow will be greater in one part than the other; because if the eye is in one of those [points] and it is seen by the eye through [the distance], it overcomes the shadow and robs it of its true darkness; this will be true when it is seen through said less dense air; because the air being thicker overcomes the shadow; by necessity the nearby shadow will be less **brightened** than the distant shadow.

<margin>
The shadow will be so much more **brightened** the more air is interposed between the eye and the aforementioned shadow. The eye being at **d**, where the [remnant/edge] of the sun is seen through the aperture **b**.
</margin>

<gloss>seen through less dense air</gloss>

**Technical Vocabulary:**
*   **Aperture** (*spiraglio*): A small hole or slit through which light passes.
*   **Shadow** (*onbra*): The area where light is blocked by an object.
*   **Brightened** (*rinfreschata*): Literally "refreshed"; Leonardo’s term for the atmospheric lightening of shadows.
*   **Air** (*aria*): The medium through which light travels, which Leonardo treats as a physical substance that affects vision.
*   **Necessity** (*neciessità*): An inevitable physical or geometric law.
*   **Perspective** (*prospettiva*): The science of representing three dimensions on a two-dimensional surface.
*   **Mazzocchio** (*mazzocchio*): A ring-shaped, multi-faceted geometry (often a headgear) used as a complex perspective exercise.
*   **Shadowy body** (*corpo onbroso*): An opaque object that casts a shadow.

Leonardo also analyzes the behavior of light rays passing through narrow apertures, a key component of his studies on vision and the camera obscura.</summary>
<keywords>aerial perspective, atmospheric density, optics, apertures, shadow intensity, luminosity, visual perception</keywords>

### ->[CUBES AND QUADRATURES. — PLATO].<-

59. — [1st fig.:] a b d c [Under the 1st fig.:] — Double the square that is generated in the diametral section of the given cube, and you will have the diametral section of the cube that is double the given cube. | [Above the 2nd fig.:] Double one of *the squares* of the 2 square surfaces that are generated in the diametral section of the cube.

[Lower down:] The other proof that Plato gave <note>Leonardo refers to the "Delian Problem" or the doubling of the cube. Legend says the citizens of Delos consulted the oracle to stop a plague, and were told to double the size of their cubic altar.</note> to those of Delos is not geometric, because it proceeds with instruments—with compasses and a ruler—and experience shows this to us; but this [proof] is entirely mental, and consequently geometric.

[At the top:] d. d. Extend the line d n <note>This refers back to a diagram on the previous leaf, folio 58 verso.</note> tangent to the angle of the long quadrilateral; then, in the space that remains under that long angle, make another long quadrilateral as large as the space allows, and let it have 2 sides tangent to the 2 squares. Thus, you will have made a long quadrilateral that will be in the same proportion to the other long quadrilateral above it as the smaller perfect square is to the larger perfect square above it. And these two smaller long quadrilaterals have the same proportion between them as the cubes of which they will be the diameters.

These double squares placed here in the margin should be examined to see if they are in the same proportion as the 2 squares p s t placed in the **angle of proportions**; if this were so, you would not have to make so many figures to double the cube; but it would suffice for you only to find the square of the diametral section of the cube—which you know is long [oblong]—and to give that quadrature its double square. This, being made long again with the angle of proportions, would recreate the double cube and the sub-double of the other given cube.

Turn the page.

### ->[CUBES AND QUADRATURES].<-

[1st, 2nd, and 3rd figs.:] a b c

**TO MAKE A CUBE DOUBLE OR SUB-DOUBLE TO ANOTHER**

Let the large cube **a** be cut from the diameter of the upper part to the diameter of the lower part, and a long square [rectangle] will remain; this will be **b**, which you will make equidistant to the base, and the part will be **c**, from which you will proceed in the **angle of proportions** as you did on the reverse of this page.

[Fig. between the texts:] n p g o a m b

**GIVEN THE DIAMETER A B, FIND ITS SQUARE.** — Draw the perpendicular line **n m** in the middle of its length; then, from this perpendicular, cut a part equal to half of said diameter, which is made with the fourth part of a circle. Draw the line from **a** to **b**, and you will have made the triangle **a m b** which will be the fourth part of the square of which the given line **a b** will be the diameter.

[Final figs.:] a b c d e

**FOR THE DUPLICATION OF THE CUBE.** Let **a** be the cube for which another sub-double cube is to be made; I will proceed in this way: I will divide this cube in half by a cut that will divide it from the upper diameter to the lower diameter, made along the same line as above, and I will place half of this cube in **b**. With the "fifth" <note>Likely referring to a specific proportional rule or a numbered step in his geometric system.</note>, I will make the perfect square **b**, which will become **c**; then I will take half of **b**, which will be **d**, and with the "fifth" I will make it square, and it will become **e**. And because **c** has the **b** which is the diameter of cube **a**, and it is born from **d**, it does not have <margin>this **d** of a figure proportioned to itself as **c** is to its **b**; therefore it will be done with the angle of proportions.</margin>

### [APPARENT SIZE OF THE CELESTIAL BODIES].

60. — Why the planets appear larger in the east <note>The "East" here refers to the horizon as the planet rises.</note> than when they are above us, which should be the contrary, since they are 3,500 miles closer to us when they are in the middle of the sky <note>The "middle of the sky" refers to the zenith, directly overhead. Leonardo calculates that an observer on the Earth's surface is closer to a star overhead than one on the horizon by approximately the radius of the Earth, which he estimates at 3,500 miles.</note> than when they are on the horizon.
[ Fig. :] d a b c c
All the layers of the elements through which the species <term>species: in Renaissance optics, the "species" (Latin: *species*) were the visual images or "forms" of objects that traveled through the air to reach the eye.</term> of celestial bodies pass to reach the eye are curved, and the angles of the central line through which the central line of these species enters are unequal, and the distance is greater, as shown by the excess of **a b** over **a d**; and by the ninth [proposition] of the sixth [book] <note>Likely referring to a specific proposition in a treatise on optics, possibly by Witelo or Euclid.</note>, the size of these celestial bodies at the horizon is proven. ¹

### [PERSPECTIVE. — CELESTIAL BODIES].

PERSPECTIVE

Of things moved away from their position at an equal distance from the eye, that one will appear to be less diminished which was previously the most diminished <note>Leonardo is exploring the proportional change in size relative to starting distance.</note>.
Of things moved away from the eye at an equal distance from their first position, that one diminishes the least which was initially more distant from that eye.
And such is the proportion of the diminution as was the proportion of the distances they had from the eye before their movement.
For example: let there be body **t** and body **e**, such that the proportion of their distances from eye **a** is fivefold; I move each from its position and make it more distant from the eye, one of them by one of those five parts into which the proportion is divided. It happens then that for the one closer to the eye, the distance is doubled, and by the second-to-last [proposition] of this [treatise], the body is diminished by half of its whole; and body **e**, by the same movement, is diminished by 1/5 of its whole. Therefore, by the said second-to-last [proposition], what was proposed in this last one is true; and I say this for the movements of the celestial bodies which, although they have 1,500 m 3,500 miles of distance more when they are in the east <note>original: "inoriente"</note> than when they are above us, they do not increase or diminish <margin>[In the margin:] in a perceptible way ¹.</margin>

[2nd fig.:] a d n c b o m p

I will set down 4 here as an example: let first *o d n* [o n d] be equal to its correspondent *m n c* [p n c]; these 2 angles are equal because each has one curved side and one straight side, and the curves *d n* and *c n* are of equal curvature as they are placed upon a <term>cylindrical body: 'corpo colonale'</term> of uniform thickness; the other 2 angles are *n m a*, *m n a*, and *m n b* which have their sides straight, but they are not equal, because *m n b* is smaller than its correspondent; therefore the angle will be lower.

## [LIGHT RAYS]

62. — [Fig. 1:] n d c b e
**PERSPECTIVE**
The luminous ray creates an angle of incidence <note>The angle at which light hits a surface.</note> between four equal angles, which is to say, the axis of that angle.

[Fig. 2:] n m or ecodb [Fig. 3 (Between texts):] n m o e a c b d
Here, since the angle *a c m* is not equal to its opposite *m c b*, the eye *o* does not see *n* at point *c*.
The axis of the angle of incidence always falls between four right angles.

[Fig. 5:] c b d e f a h g
*C a d* is the angle of incidence upon the cylindrical object *e g*, and the axis of such an angle, *b a*, terminates at *a* between four equal right angles. This means that each of these angles is equal to its corresponding angle; thus *d a f* is equal to *c a h*, its correspondent, and likewise *b a e* to *b a g*.

## [LIGHT AND WATER — THE SPHERE OF WATER (EXPERIMENT)]

---

[Fig. 1:] Sun [and] Eye
If the shape of the waves were semi-spherical, like water bubbles, the convergence of the reflections <note>original: 'simulacri', meaning the reflected images or likenesses</note> of the sun that emanate from these waves and reach the eye would form a very wide angle when the eye is on the shore of the sea that lies between it and the sun.

[Fig. 2:] a Lead, Dewdrop
In a perfectly round dewdrop, many different cases regarding the function of the "sphere of water" can be considered; specifically, how it contains within itself the body of the Earth without destroying the sphericity of its surface. <note>Leonardo is using a dewdrop as a laboratory model to understand a larger cosmological question: how the heavy Earth and the water of the oceans coexist as a single sphere.</note> First, let a cube of lead be taken, the size of a grain of millet <note>original: 'panico', a type of small-seeded cereal</note>, and let it be submerged into that drop by a very fine thread attached to it. One will see that the drop does not lose its original roundness, even though it has been enlarged by the volume of the cube enclosed within that dew.

---

->[THE SUN IN THE WATER].<-

If you hold your eye as close as you can to the surface of the sea, you will see the image of the sun in a single wave of water, which you will be able to measure and find to be very small.

If you hold your eye near the surface of the water of that sea or pond which is situated between your eye and the sun, you will find that the image of the sun on that surface appears very small; but if you move away from that sea for a distance of several miles, you will see the image of the sun become several miles in size. And if the first image retained the true shape and light of the sun—just as mirrors do—this second one will preserve neither the shape nor the light of the sun itself, but rather a shape with broken boundaries and with light diminished from the first.

The shape of the image with interrupted and confused boundaries is generated by a composition of many images *of suns* <note>Leonardo emphasizes that the large reflection is actually a cluster of many smaller ones</note> of the sun reflected to your eye by many waves of the sea; whereas the first small figure was similar in shape and brightness. And the diminished splendor arises because the dark and light likenesses of the waves reach the eye mixed together, whereby their light is altered by their shadows; this cannot happen on the surface of a single wave which I proposed was near to the eye.

<summary>Leonardo explains how the reflection of the sun on water expands and becomes less distinct as the observer's distance increases, attributing this to the blending of reflections and shadows from multiple waves. He also notes the need to calculate the varying lengths of days on Earth and the Moon based on geographical and celestial position.</summary>
<keywords>optics, reflection, sun, sea, waves, perspective, Earth, Moon, solstices, light and shadow</keywords>

# — FOLIO 63 (verso). —

Why the air at dawn is reddish below.
This happens because the rays of the sun pass through the mist that is positioned above the horizon; and looking at that sun through the mist, it appears red, like a glowing coal in the smoke. And if the air is pure and without mist, it appears blue, and pink toward the horizon. This is similar to what is seen if you go atop a high mountain: then the sun appears red to you, as mentioned. And this is because if the air were without vapor and mist, it would be entirely black, because you would see nothing but a single sun in the midst of the infinite darkness of the air. 

This air is illuminated by the rays of the sun, and these strike within the tiny particles of moisture that are in the first region of the air <note>In the science of Leonardo's time, the 'first region' was the lowest layer of the atmosphere, closest to the Earth's surface and filled with vapors</note>, which, by being vivid <note>original: 'viva'</note> and reverberating, create the blue to our sight—just as is seen in gold leaf <note>original: 'oro mese', likely a variant of 'oro mèsso', meaning applied or burnished gold</note>, and precisely as a contrast to that color at the edge of very humid air, even more so now after the setting of the sun.

<vocab>luminous, mist, air, sun, dawn, horizon, blue, reverberating, sunset</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo investigates the physics of atmospheric color, explaining that the blue of the sky is caused by sunlight reflecting off moisture against the "infinite darkness" of space, while the red of dawn is caused by sunlight passing through thick mist.</summary>
<keywords>atmospheric optics, blue sky, scattering of light, sunset colors, moisture in air, Renaissance physics, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<header>— FOLIO 64 (recto). —</header>

# [SUN, MOON, EARTH. — LUMINOUS BODIES].

64. — When the intersection of the solar rays that *pass by* the moon, touching its edges, forms a right angle <note>original: 'rettangula'</note> with the intersection of the rays reflected from the earth that pass the moon touching its edges, then...

Why does every luminous body of an elongated shape appear round at a great distance?

It is never perfectly round, but it happens to it as it does to a lead die when, having been struck and heavily flattened, it takes on a circular shape. Thus, this light at a great distance acquires so much width in every direction that, the expansion being equal to the original source of the light, the first core of light becomes insignificant compared to that expansion; therefore, the uniform expansion makes it appear round.

And this serves to prove that the points <note>original: 'corni', literally "horns"</note> of any star are not perceptible at a great distance.

---

64. — <note>The following is a French translation of the Italian text above, provided in the source manuscript transcription.</note> When the intersection of the solar rays which pass beyond the moon while touching its extremities is rectangular with the intersection of the rays reflected from the earth which pass the moon while touching its extremities, then...

Why does every luminous body of a long shape appear round at a long distance?

It is never perfectly round, but it happens as it does for a lead die when, beaten and strongly crushed, it takes on a circular form. Thus this light at a long distance acquires so much width in all directions that what has been acquired being equal [to the rest], the original fund of light remains as nothing relative to this acquisition, and for that reason, the acquired width uniformly makes it appear round.

And this is good for proving that the horns of any star are not perceptible at a long distance.

<header>— FOLIO 64 (verso). —</header>

# [SUN, MOON, EARTH. — ECLIPSES, DAYS AND NIGHTS].

->OBSCURATION OF THE SUN, MOON, AND EARTH<-

The moon has day and night just like the earth; night in the part that does not shine, and day in the part that shines.

Here, the night side of the moon sees the light of the earth being obscured—that is, the light from its water <note>Leonardo believed that the Earth's oceans acted like a giant mirror, reflecting sunlight back toward the moon—a phenomenon we now call Earthshine</note>; and the obscured water sees the obscuration of the sun, and the moon's night lacks the reverberation of the solar rays that were reflected to it from the earth.

In this other figure, it is shown that the day of the moon is obscured, and the night of the earth remains deprived of the solar rays reflected by the moon.

When the moon is in the east and the sun is in the west, *the part of the* whole day that the moon had when it was with the sun *was in the west and is now entirely changed into night.*

The day that the moon has, which from the east looks toward the sun in the west, will be entirely night when that same moon is with the sun in the west.

---

->OBSCURATION OF THE SUN, THE MOON, AND THE EARTH.<-

<note>The following is a French translation of the Italian text above.</note> The moon has days and nights like the earth; the night in the part which does not shine, and the day in that which shines.

Here the night of the moon sees the light of the earth obscured, that is to say, of its water; and the obscured water sees the obscuration of the sun, and the moon lacks the reverberation of the solar rays which are reflected there from the earth.

In this other figure, one shows that the day of the moon is obscured, and that the night of the earth remains deprived of the rays reflected by the moon.

When the moon is at the rising [east], and the sun is at the setting [west], *the part of the* whole day that the moon had, such as it was when the sun was at the west, *is all changed into night.*

The day that the moon has, which from the east looks at the sun in the west, will be all night when the moon is with the sun in the west.

63. — ON THINGS CARRIED BY WATER
Of the things carried by the flow of water, that which has a greater part of itself in the air obeys the movement of the air more than that of the water; and conversely, that which has a greater part of itself in the water will obey the flow of such water more than that of the air. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of windage versus current—how a vessel or object is steered by whichever element it occupies most.</note>

[Figure 1: ] c a b e f d
See in the bends of the channels where the water is faster below, in the middle, and above; and of this, make a book. <note>Leonardo frequently reminded himself to "make a book" or compile a treatise on specific subjects he was studying.</note>
The pipe from which water is drawn upward receives less damage than the pipe where the water is pushed; and this occurs because for the first, the motor <note>the source of power or pressure</note> is above, and for the second, that motor is below.
Where the water is faster, it wears away <note>original: "consuma"</note> the bottom rubbed by it more.
Where the water constricts most, it becomes faster, and through its passage, it erodes the bottom more.

65.— ON THINGS CARRIED BY WATER.
Of things carried by the flow of waters, that which has a larger part of itself in the air obeys the movement of the air more than that of the water; and, reciprocally, that which has a larger part of itself in the water will obey the course of that water more than that of the air.

[ 1st Fig.: ] c a b e f d
Observe in the bends of the channels where the water is fastest—below, in the middle, and above; and from this, create a book.
The conduit from which the water is drawn upward receives less damage than the conduit from which the water is pushed; and it is so because for the former, the mover is above, and for the latter, this mover is below.
Where the water is faster, it wears down the bottom over which it rubs.
Where the water narrows most, it makes itself faster, and by its passing, erodes the bottom more.

**Of the motion of descent**

If there is a weight of 2 pounds, as is *f*, and it is spread over a marble plane, as is *s p*, and it is pulled by a weight of one pound; we wish to know how much force <term>fatha <note>original: "fatha," a variant of "fatica," meaning effort or force</note></term> it will take to overcome its stickiness <term>uischosità <note>Leonardo uses "viscosity" here to describe the resistance we now call friction</note></term>. And if the same weight is pulled over the same plane by its smaller surface *s*, we wish to know if it will be overcome with greater force.

<note>Mechanical diagram: This illustrates one of Leonardo’s most significant contributions to physics. He is testing whether the friction of a block changes if you flip it onto its narrow side. He discovered that friction is independent of the contact area—a principle now known as Amontons's Second Law, which Leonardo anticipated by two centuries.</note>

Every heavy body that moves over an extended plane, and not directly perpendicular to the center of the world <note>original: "cientro del modo," referring to the center of gravity or the center of the Earth</note>, will be partially resisted by its contact with that plane.

If a weight is placed upon an extended plane, as is *m n*, and it is pulled by a force *f*, as the sixth [figure] shows, let it be spread over a plane of another, rougher substance.

<note>Small sketch of a water vortex or whirlpool, showing the spiral nature of turbulent flow.</note>

-> — FOLIO 65 (verso). — <-

If the ring *f d* is descending from the height *p r*, and it descends moving away from the piston <term>stanpilio <note>piston or rod</note></term> *f*, it is due to the motion of the air which comes to strike it on the outer edge at part *p*. Because such air strikes the edge perpendicularly, the ring, by its opening *d*, will be distant from that piston.

Why the falling water spreads out, like the water *n m* which falls through the vent <term>sspiracholo <note>an orifice or small opening</note></term> *n*: because if its velocity is 10 pounds, the spreading <term>djstendjmeto</term> will be 10 fingers; and if the velocity of the fall is double, the spreading will be 20 fingers; and if it is 30, it will be 30.

The water that descends through the air from the same vent, if it is of a sustained velocity, will be in greater quantity at the end than at the beginning if it is of the same thickness; and it will be of greater thickness at the end than at the beginning if it is of the same velocity. <note>Leonardo is observing the relationship between the speed of a falling stream and its volume or density as gravity accelerates it.</note>

### [WATER EDDIES].

66. — <margin>[Under the 1st figure:]</margin> Eddies <term>retrosi <note>original: "liretrosi," referring to backflows or whirlpools where water turns against the main current</note></term> are always composed of two waters, that is, incident and reflected <note>Leonardo uses terms from optics—incident and reflected—to describe how water strikes a surface and bounces back</note>.
<margin>[At the top:]</margin> All the water in river currents that slows down behind objects in those courses has no other exit than through contact with the main current of these rivers.
The eddies that turn backward are always those of the fastest water.
And the eddies turned toward the *flow* <note>original: "fuga," literally 'the flight' or escape of the water downstream</note> of the river are those of the water that slows down in its course.
The law of waters in its eddies does not fail here, because the water that is slowed turns backward and creates eddies contrary to its motion, just as the eddies of faster water do; for this reason, these eddies—those of the slow water as well as the fast—mix together and double their power, though not entirely. This is because the slow eddy, in mixing with the fast, *becomes* <note>original: "fac sifa," a correction in the manuscript</note> faster than before, and the fast eddy, in uniting with the slower one, acquires slowness.
The submersion of eddies in fast waters will be against the arrival of the waters, and in slow waters, it will be toward the flow of those waters.
<margin>[2nd figure:]</margin> a b c d &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; a b fast &nbsp;&nbsp; d c slow

<note>Footnote 2: Idem, book four, chapter XLVIII, p. 354.</note>
<note>Footnote 3: Idem, chapter LI, p. 355.</note>

— FOLIO 66 (verso). —

### [TREATISE ON WATER (BEGINNING OF THE BOOK)].

->Beginning of the book.<-
A drop is that which does not detach itself from the rest of the water unless the power of its weight is greater than the power of the adherence <term>collegation <note>original: "collegation," referring to the surface tension that keeps a drop attached to its source</note></term> with the water to which it is joined.
That drop forms more slowly which has a slower movement of water at its creation.
All movements made by water at its surface are also made at every degree of depth, and likewise in every part of its length; and this is learned from the weeds attached to the bottom of rivers.
<margin>[Fig.:]</margin> b n a &nbsp;&nbsp; m o
Because every impetus <term>inpeto <note>A key concept in Leonardo's physics, "impeto" is the force transmitted to a moving body</note></term> is consumed by the movement of the object over time and the length of the movement made in any direction. If the weed *n a* had consumed its impetus and remained slanted, the wedge of water *n m a o* pushes it and drives *a* from its position, moving it with impetus toward *b*; it moves as long as that impetus lasts, and when it is consumed, the wedge of water does on this side as it did on the other. Thus it continues as long as the moving objects are accompanied.
The same occurs from the surface to the bottom, and likewise in any direction.

<note>Footnote 1, 2: F. Cardinali, book one, chapter XLII, p. 290.</note>
<note>Footnote 3, 4: Idem, book two, chapter XVII, p. 300, plate 6, fig. 27.</note>

### [RAINBOW AND THE SOLAR SPECTRUM].

->CONCERNING THE RAINBOW<-

*Whether the rainbow is generated by the eye (that is, its roundness [curvature]) or by the sun, by means of the cloud¹.*

*The mirror captures nothing but the images <term>species <note>original: "spetie," a term from Renaissance optics referring to the formal likenesses or "shadows" of objects that travel through the air to the eye</note></term> of visible bodies, and these images are not produced without those bodies; therefore, if this arc is seen in the mirror and the images that originate from this rainbow concur there, it follows that the arc is generated by the sun and by the cloud.*

<margin>If 2 metal spheres send solar rays into a dark place, the sprayed water <note>original: "acque soffiate," literally "blown water" or vaporized mist</note> will create the 'iris' arc [the solar spectrum] in a long shape.</margin>

*The rainbow is seen in fine rains by eyes that have the sun behind them and the cloud in front, and there is always an imaginary line, continuously straight, starting from the center of the sun, passing through the center of the eye, and ending in the center of the arc. And such an arc will never be seen by one eye in the same spot where the other eye sees it; rather, it will be seen in as many places on the cloud where it is formed as there are eyes that see it. Therefore, this arc is entirely throughout the cloud where it is generated and entirely in each place that can contain it, and thus it will appear larger or smaller, half, whole, double, or triple.*

<margin>This can also be done with water sprayed into a solar ray that passes into a dark place, having the sun at the back of the neck, and also with the light of torches, or the moon.</margin>

---

CONCERNING THE RAINBOW.

Whether the rainbow is produced by the eye (that is, its roundness [curvature]) or by the sun, by means of the cloud¹.

The mirror takes no images [likenesses] except those of visible bodies, and the images are not produced without these bodies; therefore, if this arc is seen in the mirror and the images concur there which have their origin from this rainbow, it follows that the arc is generated by the sun and by the cloud.

<margin>If 2 metal spheres send the sun's rays into a dark place, the sprayed [vaporized] water will make the rainbow arc [the solar spectrum] in a long shape.</margin>

The rainbow is seen in thin rains by eyes that have the sun behind and the cloud in front, and always an imaginary line, continuously straight from the center of the sun, passing through the center of the eye, will terminate in the center of the arc. And such an arc will never be seen by one eye in the same place as it is seen by the other eye; it will be seen in as many places of the cloud where it forms as there are eyes that see it. Therefore, this arc is all in all the cloud where it is produced, and all in each place that is capable of it, and thus it will appear larger or smaller, half, whole, double, triple.

<margin>This can also be done with water sprayed [vaporized] into the solar ray that passes into a dark place, having the sun at the nape of the neck, and also with the light of torches, or of the moon.</margin>

# Folio 67 (recto)

The cords of the muscles <term>cords <note>original: "corde," referring here to tendons</note></term> possess as much strength as the force of the muscle itself, and the eye demonstrates this to us; for this reason, the nerve <term>nerve <note>original: "nerbo"; in Leonardo’s time, this could refer to a nerve, a sinew, or a tendon, often viewed as part of a single mechanical system</note></term> is part of the cord, and the muscle is part of that same cord, and the nerve is the beginning of that cord and the end <unclear>of the muscle</unclear>.

# Folio 67 (verso)

->concerning circular motion<-

That part of a weight describes a perfect circle in each of its revolutions.

<image-desc>A mechanical diagram showing a horizontal balance beam or lever. On the left side, a circular weight is attached. The system appears to be a study of pendular or circular motion, with lines indicating the path or tension of cords. To the right of the main text block, there are small marginal sketches of hooks and circular motifs.</image-desc>

Just as the circle is a line that has neither beginning nor end, so every body that moves circularly has neither end nor beginning among the parts of its motion. But if you consider the motion in relation to the center line <note>original: "linea del mezo," referring to the vertical axis of equilibrium in a pendulum</note>, then that motion acquires a beginning and an end. Thus, if the pendulum <note>original: "pēdulo"</note> is in line with that center, that weight will be at the end of its descending motion and will be at the beginning of its ascending motion; and the further it is from the <unclear>center</unclear>, the more powerful the motion toward the center will be, because the further it is from that center <unclear>...</unclear>

### [RIVERS, LAKES AND SEAS. — SEA OF AZOV, GIBRALTAR].

68. — [Continuation from folio 68 verso:] Since the width of the exit is, as stated, equal to the width of the entrance, it is necessary that the entire river passing through the lake should also have a drop <term>drop <note>original: "calo," referring to the gradient or slope of the water's flow</note></term> of one braccio <term>braccio <note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally "arm," roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note></term> per mile, and thus the surface of such a lake will be at varying distances from the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the Earth's center of gravity; Leonardo is arguing that for water to flow, it must be moving "downhill" toward this center.</note>. But the water will have such a course—

That part of the lake water will have the slowest motion which is found furthest from the shortest line connecting the entrance and the exit of the river passing through that lake.

From this it follows that the Sea of Tana <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, which borders the Tanais <note>The Don River</note>, is the highest part of the Mediterranean Sea, being 3,500 miles away from the Strait of Gibraltar, as shown by the nautical charts; it has a drop of 3,500 braccia, which is one mile and 1/6. This sea is therefore higher than any mountain in the West <note>Leonardo concludes that because of the cumulative slope required for water to flow from the Don to the Atlantic, the sea level in the east must be physically higher than western mountains.</note>.

68. — [ Continuation from folio 68 verso : ] the width of the exit being, as said, equal to the width of the entrance, it would be necessary that the entire river passing through the lake also had a braccio of descent per mile, and thus the water of such a lake would be at its surface at a varied distance from the center of the world. But the water will have such a course...

That part of the lake water will be of slower motion which is located further from the very short line that goes from the entrance to the exit of the river passing through this lake.

Here it follows that the Sea of Tana [Azov], which borders the Tanais [Don], is the highest part of the Mediterranean Sea; now it is distant from the Strait of Gibraltar by 3,500 miles, as shown by the navigation chart, which has a descent of 3,500 braccia, that is to say, one mile and 1/6; this sea is therefore higher than any mountain of the West.

How the water rises above the level of the river by that same increase as the river; and if a river rises by one braccio <term>braccio <note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally "arm," roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note></term> of water on a level, in a fixed vessel that same water will rise on a level by more than one braccio—one is the increase of the water by itself, the other is the increase of a part of the water through the river.

I say that if a river's water rises by one braccio, the water of a vessel fixed within it will rise more than one braccio. And if in a vessel of water from a river, consider how it will rise more than one braccio in a vessel [due to] one braccio of water.

If the water in a river rises by one braccio, the water of the vessel of that river which sits at the bottom will rise by the same height; but if that vessel is filled with one braccio of river water and is set against the rise of one braccio, the water in the vessel will be one braccio and another braccio and a half-braccio <note>Leonardo is calculating a cumulative effect of water pressure and displacement</note>, and the height of that water will be two braccia and a half at the same time that the river has risen one braccio. And this arises because the river occupies one braccio of depth and the vessel occupies one and a half braccia of depth because air was occupied there for another half-braccio.

### [CENTRE OF THE EARTH AND THE SPHERE OF WATER].

70. — Because the center of natural gravity of the Earth must be at the center of the world, the Earth is always becoming lighter in some part, and the part that is lightened pushes upward, submerging as much of the opposite side as is necessary to join the center of its said gravity to the center of the world ¹; and the sphere of water keeps its surface constantly equidistant to the center of the world ¹.

Where the sun is directly overhead, the Earth lightens; being covered by air, it has lost the waters and the snows; on the opposite side, the rains <insert>alourd: make heavy</insert> and the snows make the Earth heavy, pushing it toward the center of the world and moving our lightened parts further from that center; thus, the sphere of water preserves the equality of distance from the center of its sphere, but not from the center of gravity.

Water *that flows, that flows* through a concave angle into the air is paniculated <term>paniculate: water that spreads into thin, leaf-like sheets or films resembling the branching of a panicle flower</term>, *and this, and it* continues to be more paniculated on the side of the angle where such water will have greater contact; on the opposite side, these panicles will spring back and form a junction in the manner of an open sheath ².

<note>original: "guaina aperta" - an open sheath or casing, describing the shape of the water film.</note>

> 1. <note>References to Venturi, p. 12; and Dr. M. Jordan, p. 76, "Bibliogr."</note>
> 2. <note>Reference to F. Cardinali, book five, chapter XIV, p. 360, plate 18, fig. 102.</note>

### [WATER OF THE SEA AND OF THE RIVERS].

The sea beneath the equinoctial <note>The equator</note> rises due to the heat of the sun and takes motion from every part of the "hill" <note>Leonardo views the thermal expansion of the ocean as a physical mound or hill of water</note> or part of the water that rises, in order to equalize and restore perfection to its sphere ¹.

If an opening of water *gives me* 16 measures of water at a 16-ounce drop for every mile, how much will the same opening give me at an 8-ounce drop per mile?

The revolutions of transverse eddies <term>retrosi: backward-flowing currents or vortices</term> acquire width and slowness at every degree of their length ².

*The, the* upwellings <note>original: "bollori," literally "boilings"</note> of reflected motions of the water from the bottom of rivers destroy the circulations of longitudinal eddies ³.

The water of the sea and of turbid <note>Muddy or silt-heavy</note> rivers is heavier than other waters, and consequently offers more resistance to the weights carried by them [ it ].

But the water of the sea resists more because the weight of the salt mixed with it is liquefied and is inseparable from it without heat that dries the water; but the turbid part of the water <note>The silt or mud</note> separates itself with heat and when that water is at rest.

# FOLIO 71 (recto)

### [MOVEMENT OF WATER IN AIR AND IN WATER].

71. — The movement of water made through the air follows for some distance the lines of the sides of the openings from which it descends; this does not happen with a discontinuous quantity, such as is shown by a stone thrown by the circular motion of a man's arm, which follows a straight line. The water does not do this because of its <term>paniculation<note>original Italian: *panniculatione*; Leonardo uses this term to describe the cohesive "skin" or membrane-like quality of water that allows it to stay in a continuous stream or sheet rather than breaking apart instantly like solid debris.</note></term>, which over a long distance of motion joins all parts of the water together.

The impressions of movements made by water within water are more permanent than the impressions that the same water makes within the air. This happens because water within water does not weigh anything, as is proven in the fifth [book], but only the <term>impetus<note>original: *impeto*; the force or momentum possessed by a moving body.</note></term> weighs, which moves that water without weight until that impetus is consumed.

The impressions of the movements of water will be more permanent where the water, carried by its impetus, enters into a <term>pool<note>original: *pelago*; refers to a large, deep, or slow-moving body of water or a basin.</note></term> of slower motion, and likewise the opposite.

The impressions made by water within the air are destroyed in the first movement they make toward the earth, because the impetus is consumed in the natural movement that is generated in the water.

### [WATERFALLS AND SPOUTING WATER].

The falls of water that intersect within the air fill with air in their reflected motion.

Regarding falls of water that strike each other in the air: being of equal thickness, the one that descends from a higher point of its reservoir will join the course of the lower one and will end its course with it.

THE FALL OF WATER THAT RUNS OVER PLANKING GREATLY BREAKS THE BOTTOM AT THE END OF SUCH PLANKING. This occurs because when the current of water reaches the edge of such boards, it falls and rises from the bottom; the longer it falls, the more deeply it hollows out the ground, because the fall becomes more powerful in greater depths than in lesser ones. <note>Leonardo is observing the "scour" or erosion that occurs at the edge of a man-made spillway or wooden dam.</note>

### [MOVEMENTS OF WATER].

72. — Regarding the <term>surges<note>original: *bollori*; literally "boilings," referring to the turbulent, bubbling upwelling of water after it hits a surface.</note></term> of water reflected from the bottom of the <term>deep pool<note>original: *pelagho*; a deep basin or large body of water.</note></term>, one part returns to the surface of the water, and *one part* there creates several incident and reflected movements. Another part turns back toward the initial fall, submerging itself there with it, and returning upward with lateral <term>eddies<note>original: *retrosi*; whirlpools or back-currents.</note></term>. Another part falls back into the middle of the surges and spreads with a slow motion around the center of its fall.

Simple motions of water are those which, with their single motion of whatever kind it may be, act simply.

Compound motions are created from various motions, and these are very powerful in various functions.

The wave is slower at its summit than at its sides.

The incident motion <note>The downward or striking motion.</note> is faster than the reflected motion <note>The upward or bouncing motion.</note>.

<margin>Joined together, the greatest and the least slowness of the waves—that is, of the wave itself with its sides and summits—becomes equal to the common course of its river; and this is to be cited in the conclusions, which is to say, to prove them.</margin>

### [ELEVATION OF WATER, NATURAL AND ARTIFICIAL].

If the water that springs from the high summits of mountains comes from the sea—whose weight supposedly pushes it up there because the sea is higher than those mountains—why is such a particle of water permitted to rise to such a height, and why does it not stay, instead of penetrating the earth with such difficulty and time? And why has it not been granted to the rest of the element of water to do the same, since it borders the air, which offers no resistance to prevent the whole mass from rising to the same height as the aforementioned part? 

To you who have found such an invention <note>Leonardo is likely addressing a contemporary theorist or a specific text he disagrees with.</note>, return to learning from nature, for you will be found lacking in such opinions, of which you have made a great collection along with the <term>capital of the friar<note>original: *capitale del frate*; likely referring to a collection of notes or a manuscript by a monk that Leonardo had acquired or was studying, which he here finds insufficient.</note></term> that you possess.

Water falling in a channel of width equal to the width of the falling water will create a deep concavity within the surface of the water.

Water falling into a width greater than the said fall will not create much concavity within the "skin" of the water, because of the eddies that reflect the water back toward the hollow of that fall. Water that is narrower than that which falls upon it will rise up.

<margin>Water clearing the bottom where it falls with speed or slowness, in width, depth, or narrowness. Book 9.</margin>

<header>- FOLIO 72 (recto). -</header>

### [THE IMPACT OF WATER AND AIR]

If water, through a high fall, is struck against its bottom, it will leap upward with many inverted branches of its descent. These are longer or shorter depending on whether the bottom is more or less slanted, and whether the water is more or less fast. This arises from the <term>impact<note>original: *percussione*; Leonardo uses this term to describe the physical strike or collision of one element against another.</note></term> that the air receives from the water, which, in leaping upward, carries the air with it, trapped between itself and the other water.

At the bottom of the water's fall, the air is enclosed by the falling water and by that which bounces back up due to the <term>rebound<note>original: *ripercussione*.</note></term>.

Water does not bounce back except because it is pushed by the air which it encloses between itself and the other weight <note>meaning the mass of the water itself</note>.

This impact of the water at the bottom will be much greater the more unified the impact is. And the impact is more unified when air is not mixed in with it.

<margin>
Because the water that bounces upward carries much air with it, the air is what divides it into minute parts and dissolves it into **mist**.
</margin>

<header>- FOLIO 72 (verso). -</header>

### [WAVES AND AIR CURRENTS]

All circular waves originating from the blow of the water's impact at its bottom create a larger circle the higher the point of its impact <note>Leonardo likely refers to the height of the fall increasing the energy and thus the spread of the ripples</note>.

I say that if a secondary wave is generated in the air by the motion of the water wave, the air wave will be much faster in motion than the water wave. This arises from the lightness of the air compared to the heaviness of the water, and because the air occupies more space than the falling water. The wave that the water makes in its fall through the air is smaller than the wave the air makes in the water, for the stated reason of the difference in their weights and lightness.

If the water wave is moved by an air wave, its motion will be much slower because of its weight compared to the lightness of the air.

The air moved by the fall of water at the bottom "smokes" <note>original: *si fuma*; refers to the plume of spray that looks like smoke</note> and rises toward the top, seeking a higher and freer place. Carrying the water with it, it is **atomized** into mist amid the falling water.

<margin>
Because the air wave is pushed by the water falling through the air.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how falling water traps air at the point of impact, creating a "rebound" effect that shatters water into mist and spray. He also compares the relative speeds of waves in water versus air, noting that air's lightness allows it to move and expand much faster than the heavier liquid.</summary>

### [TANGENCY AND PROPORTIONS. — OPTICS (SEA AND LAND)].

73. — <gloss>[1st fig.:] a c b d e f</gloss>
**ANGLE OF TANGENCY** —
If from proportionate things you remove a part in the same proportion, the remainder does not vary from its first proportion.
It follows that if from *c f* (which is double to *a e*) you remove *c d* and *a b* (which are also double parts), the remainders *d f* and *b e* remain double as before. And if the line *b d* is <term>tangent<note>original: *contingente*; Leonardo is referring to a line that touches a circle at a single point without crossing it.</note></term> to the circle, such a contact will form the said **angle of tangency**.

<margin>OF THE SEA WHICH TO MANY SIMPLE PEOPLE SEEMS HIGHER THAN THE LAND THAT FORMS ITS SHORE</margin>

<gloss>[2nd fig.:] a c b d</gloss> Naturally, no part of the land uncovered by water will ever be lower than the surface of the sphere of that water.
*D b* is a plain where a river runs to the sea; this plain has the sea as its boundary. Because, in truth, this uncovered land is not in a position of perfect equality <note>meaning a perfectly level horizontal plane</note>—for if it were, the river would have no motion—since it moves, this location should rather be called a **slope** than a plain. And so, this plain *d b* terminates in such a way with the sphere of the water that if one were to extend it in a continuous straight line from *b* to *a*, this *a* would enter beneath the sea. From this arises the effect where the sea *a c d [b]* appears higher than the uncovered land.

<header>— FOLIO 73 (verso). —</header>
<page-num>f. 73v</page-num>

### [MIXTURES. — PLATES RESEMBLING GLASS, CARNELIAN, AND AGATE].

**ON MIXTURES**
Take a natural or accidental branching and coat it with a stroke, then fix it upon a flat copper plate so that it does not bend. Once this is done, you coat it with as many layers as you see fit; let these be very thin, and each time you must let them dry well.
After you have coated them to your liking, you shall provide thicker "barks" <note>layers or coatings</note> and then thinner ones of fixed whites and transparents, and likewise of fixed blacks and transparent whites, and of fixed yellows and transparent yellows. These are made of <term>saffron<note>original: *zafferano*.</note></term> or <term>turmeric<note>original: *curcuma*.</note></term> dissolved with vinegar and then distilled—not through an <term>alambic<note>A chemical still used for distillation.</note></term> but through a filter—and partly with other fixed or transparent colors. Fill the final spaces with fixed white and let it dry well.
Once everything is reduced to a flat surface, smooth it with oil and sand, and then with oil and <term>Tripoli<note>A fine powder used for polishing metal and stone.</note></term>. Then have it sawn into tablets as thick as a book board. Have them polished and shined, and then varnished as thinly as you can, cleaning the excess with your hands. Clean your hands often on the edge of a knife so that no mark of the rubbing of the hands is seen on the surface. Do this six or eight times; it will not take long, as everything can be done in 2 or 3 days in summer, or in winter by the wind. In this way, it will appear to be glass.
But remember: if you have it sawn, coat the surface of your mixture two or three more times so that one does not see the "dryness" <note>aridita</note> and roughness of the materials. And if you wish to make large <term>paternoster beads<note>Prayer beads, similar to a Rosary.</note></term>, turn this material on a lathe, then polish and coat its surface 2 or 3 times as described above, and varnish.

<margin>"Verdino" <note>likely referring to a type of fig or green pigment</note> and saffron make carnelian, or use turmeric or <term>celandine<note>original: *celidonia*; a yellow-flowering plant.</note></term>. Fig milk makes chalcedony. Soot or smoke makes agate. No simple black or white was ever transparent.</margin>

## [OBJECTS MOVING THROUGH THE AIR].

74. — The movement of the air is less in front of the moving object that penetrates it than it is behind that object. —
The air that fills the vacuum left by the moving object as it penetrates the air <insert>has its</insert> has its total speed equal to that of the object; but the parts of that air, because they are <term>revertiginous<note>original: *reverticinosa*; describing a swirling, vortex-like, or turbulent motion.</note></term> (that is, of circular motion in the form of eddies), are in themselves much faster than the movement of the aforementioned object. —
Here it appears that because the object has more air-speed behind it than in front, such air might be the cause of the movement of that object; but by the seventh [rule], that cannot be.
*Every <insert>No</insert> moving object will ever be faster than the speed of the power that moves it. —*
The wave that the air makes in front of the object it penetrates does not pass much in front of that object; because that would be against the seventh rule, here the <term>penultimate<note>Referring to the previous rule mentioned in Leonardo’s sequence of propositions.</note></term>. —
The air behind the moving object returns backward in those parts of the circulation that border those that run behind the object. —
The air that runs behind the moving object that passes through it is moved by the <term>impetus<note>original: *inpeto*; the momentum or force imparted to a body.</note></term> attached to it by that object; this air, striking the other air through the large, spreading wave, returns backward with a great circulation which diminishes at its extremities, finally stopping and not following that object. —

74. — The movement of the air is less in front of the moving object which penetrates it than it is behind this object.
The air which fills the vacuum left by the moving object which penetrates it <insert>has the</insert> has its total speed equal to that of this object; but the parts of this air, because it is "revertiginous" (that is to say, of circular movement in the form of eddies), is much faster in itself than the movement of the aforesaid object.

The air from behind the object returns backward in those parts of the circulation which border those which run behind the object.

## [OBJECTS MOVING THROUGH THE AIR. — DUST PARTICLES IN SUNBEAMS].

Why the moving object follows the movement started by its motor. —
No <term>impetus<note>original: *inpeto*</note></term> can end immediately, but is consumed by degrees of movement.
The air that was first behind the gap made by the moving object in the air accompanies that object very little, according to the eighth rule. —
<margin>Eighth.</margin> The air that successively surrounds the moving object that moves through it creates various movements within itself. This is seen in the <term>atoms<note>original: *attimi* / *atomes*; Leonardo refers to tiny dust motes or particles visible in light as "atoms."</note></term> found in the <term>sphere of the sun<note>original: *laspera delsole*; likely referring to the volume of a sunbeam.</note></term> when they penetrate through some window into a dark place; if a stone is thrown through the length of such a sunbeam, one sees the particles swirling around the place where the path made in the air by the object was refilled by the air, as proven in the fifth rule. —
<margin>Fifth.</margin> No senseless thing moves by itself, but its motion is caused by others. —
The motion generated operates for a very short time and space as required by necessity, *as the fourth rule shows.*
<margin>Fourth.</margin> The air that moves to fill the vacuum made within it by the moving object has various speeds, densities, and movements within itself. —

And if the smoke is seen between the sun and the eye, it will be of a dark color toward the eye, and on the other side it will be light.

### [PAINTING (WHITE IN THE AIR)].

75. — <term>PAINTING<note>original: *PICTURA*</note></term>
Because white is not a color but is in a <term>state of potentiality<note>original: *in potentia ricettiva*; a Scholastic philosophical term meaning the capacity to receive or be changed by something else.</note></term> to receive every color, when it is in the open countryside, all its shadows are bluish. This occurs because of the fourth [rule of optics] which says: "The surface of every opaque body partakes in the color of its object." Therefore, as this white is deprived of the light of the sun by the interposition of some object placed between the sun and the white, all that part of the white that sees the sun and the air continues to partake in the color of the sun and the air; but that part which does not see the sun remains in shadow, partaking only in the color of the air. And if such a white surface did not see the green of the countryside all the way to the horizon, nor see the whiteness of that horizon, it would without doubt appear to be of the same simple color that the air shows itself to be.

---

75.— PAINTING.
Because white is not a color, but is in a state of potential to receive all colors, when it is in "high company" <note>Leonardo uses *incanpagnia alta*, which the French translator interprets as "deep air" or the open atmosphere.</note>, all its shadows are azure-tinted.

This arises from the fourth principle which states: "The surface of every opaque body partakes of the color of its object." Therefore this white, being deprived of the sun's light by the interposition of some object placed between the sun and this white, every part of it that sees the sun and the air continues to partake of the color of the sun and the air, and the part that does not see the sun remains in shadow, partaking <gloss>partaking only</gloss> of the color of the air. If this white did not see the greenness of the countryside as far as the horizon, and did not see the whiteness of that horizon either, it would undoubtedly appear to be of the simple color which the air shows itself to be.

### [WATER AND MOVEMENT].

— The circular wave born on the surface of the water contained in a struck vessel ends along the line by which it was created by the movement of its mover, and so —
— EVERY MOVING BODY THAT PRODUCES REFLECTION <unclear>was</unclear> ENDS ITS COURSE ALONG THE LINE OF INCIDENCE. —
This happens because the <term>incident motion<note>The initial movement or strike toward a surface before it bounces back.</note></term> is of greater power than the reflected motion, and that which is more powerful has more durability than the less powerful. —
The movement of the incident body will be more powerful than its reflected movement, because the impact of the incidence made upon the dense object <gloss>consumes</gloss> diminishes a part of the <term>impetus<note>original: *inpeto*; the force or momentum of a moving body.</note></term> joined to that body. This diminution does not leave the reflected movement as powerful as the aforementioned incident movement. Although at every degree of movement the impetus of the moving body diminishes by itself without hitting a dense object, it remains true that such an impact diminishes it much more. Indeed, if you measure the movement that the body would have made without the incident [impact], and you measure the movements born from many bounces between high and low, you will find that the movement continued in a single place <note>Meaning a single, uninterrupted path.</note> will be longer than that which is interrupted so many times by the incidences — 
Even if the beginning of the impetus in each of them were of equal power among them. —

The movement of the incident body will be more powerful than its reflected movement; because the percussion of the incidence made on the dense object *consumes* diminishes by one part the impulse given ["the joined impetus"] to this body, and this diminution does not leave the reflected movement as powerful as it was when called incident. ->— FOLIO 75 (recto). —<-

**Equivalence** <note>original: *giustitia*; in this context, Leonardo likely refers to "mathematical justice" or the proportional balance of physical forces.</note>

Because knowledge can be given of every motion, since they are compared by means of proportion. And if you say that the air has such a lack of power <note>original: *inpotenza*; referring to a lack of resistance or density.</note> that it resists every motion for the reasons stated above: because the air below is always the same as the air above, and that in front is the same as that behind. Because there would be as much force in front [resisting] as there would be air behind pushing it, and there would be as much force below pushing it upward as there is from above [pushing] it downward. For the bouncing of a ball within the concavity <unclear>in the air</unclear> would occur with the same lack of power; because the air would be perfectly uniform <note>original: *rito rito*; literally "straight straight," implying a direct or constant state.</note> above, and below it would be such that it pushes upward, and in front it would be such that it pushes from behind.

->— FOLIO 75 (verso). —<-

Weight, by its own logic, does not dissolve itself infinitely, because every volume makes itself known through itself. It is continuous in its members <note>original: *mēbris*; Leonardo uses the Latin term for parts or limbs of a body.</note>, or rather, the dissolving of members into all its points—a continuous whole where every point would be mobile. Therefore, since it has been demonstrated that the air is continuous through all its points, one must conclude whether it is true that the air—like every other body—is composed of mobile and immobile points. By the joining of these mobile points into continuous points within a framework <note>original: *cassa*; literally a "chest" or "case."</note> of immobile points, it would follow that it would be much changed in its continuous points, both immobile and mobile. 

Therefore, if it gives knowledge of itself in all its continuous points, the conclusion must be that it is [made of] points, both mobile and immobile in every part. For it would be more mobile and immobile in every part, air being mobile everywhere and everywhere mobile in its points. Therefore, if it is mobile in every one of its points, it gives knowledge of itself within its point. Air, then, would be resolved into air, from mobile points into mobile points. And if all the points are mobile in every one of its points, then the air would be mobile in every one of its points, just as it is mobile in every one of its points. Consider not the whole together, [to see] if it would go away into itself, or if it would become the sum of itself.

<summary>Leonardo explores the physics of air as a medium, arguing that its resistance is balanced on all sides of a moving object, and meditates on whether air is composed of infinitely divisible mobile points.</summary>
<keywords>motion, air resistance, proportion, physics of fluids, points, mobility, equilibrium, atmospheric mechanics</keywords>

### [MARTESANA CANAL DEPLETING THE ADDA; SPRINGS].

->**ON THE MARTESANA CANAL**<-

By constructing the Martesana canal, the water of the Adda is diminished, as it is distributed to many districts for the service of the meadows. There is a remedy for this, and it is to create many resurgence springs <term>fontanili: man-made irrigation springs typical of the Lombardy region, where groundwater is collected as it resurfaces to be reused</term>; for the water that is "drunk" by the earth performs no service to anyone, nor does it cause any harm, because it is taken from no one. By creating such springs, the water—which was previously lost—returns once again to be of service and utility to men. And where such canals were not previously conducted, one could not make these springs in the lower-lying lands. Therefore, we shall say that if such canals are made in the Martesana, the same water "drunk" by the soil of the meadows will be placed again upon other meadows by means of such springs—water which was previously lost. And if water is lacking in the gravelly bed of the Adda and in the silt, the locals will be able to make springs, seeing that the same water, "drunk" by the meadows multiple times, serves this purpose <note>Leonardo is describing a sustainable water cycle where irrigation water filters through the earth and is captured again via man-made wells (fontanili) to water fields further downstream.</note>.

---

->**OF THE MARTESANA CANAL.**<-

In making the Martesana canal, one diminishes the water of the Adda, which is distributed in many lands [localities] for the service of the meadows. A remedy for this is to make many springs <note>See manuscript K (3rd volume of the publication), folio 97 recto.</note>, for the water which is drunk by the earth neither renders service nor does harm to anyone, since it is taken from no one; and by making such springs, the water which at first was lost begins again to render service and be useful to men. And where at first such canals were not conducted, one could not make these springs in the lower lands. Therefore we shall say that if such canals are made in the Martesana, the same water which was drunk by the bottom of the meadows will be put back on other meadows by means of the springs, water which was at first lost; and if the water is lacking to the gravel [banks] of the Adda, in the mud <note>original: *mucha*; likely referring to the silt or sludge in the riverbed. Cit: Amoretti, Mem. stor., p. 104; J.-P. Richter, Vol II, 1010.</note> the peasants will be able to make springs, seeing that the same water, drunk by the meadows several times, serves this function.

The effects of one and the same weight upon different positions of the **balance** are of as much variety as the diversity of the positions in respect to the center of that balance.
Weight is understood, in every motion, to be in respect to the center of the world <note>original: "centro del mondo"; Leonardo follows the Aristotelian view that the Earth is the center of the universe, and gravity is the "desire" of objects to reach that center.</note>, in respect to which the weight weighs that much less.

-> the experience of seeing if it is <-

In every motion, experiences are given of every sort of occurrence <note>original: "accidẽti"; referring to physical phenomena or properties observed during an event.</note> that water makes in running within the banks of a clear brook over the meadows of a valley near the sea.
In this way, you will see the experiences far more clearly: the waters of a brook, which gladden the eye with their clarity, allow the stones of the bottom to be seen. These stones are moved, as if by one water through another, without any impediment of the water coming to your sight—which would be otherwise if the water were turbid, whether it were in the sea or elsewhere.

This is clearly seen when you observe that the stone which is closer to the center of the sea <note>Leonardo likely refers to the "center" or deepest point of the water's flow or the bed of the water body.</note> is moved with much more violence than that which is closer to the surface of the sea; these things have provided me with the answer.

### [RIVERS (THINGS CARRIED)].

78. — [3rd figure:] n a b c
A wide object carried by the current of a river between the surface and the bottom of the water—if it encounters water slower than that which carries it, and if it is positioned at that time at an angle <term>angle|original: "obliquo"; Leonardo is studying how the tilt of a submerged object causes it to rise or sink based on the pressure of the current.</term> toward the oncoming flow of the river, it will immediately jump from the bottom to the surface of the water. And if such an angle faces behind the retreat of the water, upon encountering the slow current, it will immediately throw itself toward the bottom. And if such an angle faces to the right or left across the width of the river, it will throw itself to that right or left side of the river, and so it will follow for every orientation.

That part of the depth of the water will delay its course by as much depth as that of its impediment, and it will not slow down at the contact of that impediment, but as far away from it as the "rule of the fifth" <note>The "rule of the fifth" likely refers to a mathematical proportion Leonardo used to calculate hydraulic resistance.</note> dictates. For example: if the surface impediment is one finger thick, the water *a b* will stop or turn backward (the motion being slow) for the entire space *a b*, and at its edge it will meet the current and go beneath it. Apply the rule for how long *a b* should be.

-> — FOLIO 78 (verso). — <-

### [SEA SILT AND FOSSILS. — RIVERS].

If the mountains had not remained in large part uncovered by the waters, the rivers—the courses of the rivers—could not have carried as much silt <note>original: "lita"; referring to the sediment or mud deposited by water.</note> into the sea as that which is seen at a great height, mixed with the animals <term>animals|Leonardo uses "animali" to refer to fossilized sea creatures, like shells and corals, found high in the mountains.</term> that were enclosed within it.

The revolutions of reflected water <note>original: "acqua riflessa"; water that has bounced off an obstacle or bank.</note>, in returning to the current of its river, always penetrate more into its lower parts than at the surface; and this arises because the current, according to the seventh <note>A reference to Leonardo's 7th proposition on water, which states that surface water moves faster because it lacks the friction of the riverbed.</note>, is faster above than below and, consequently, is more powerful above. For this reason, it is less penetrated by the impact of such reflected water above than it is below.

[1st figure:] h g e a c f b d
*a b c d* is the thickness of the current with its width; *c a f b* are the thickness and width of the water reflected backward.

The eddies <term>eddies|original: "retrosi"; back-currents or whirlpools.</term> created by the impact of the reflected water in the course of the oncoming water are of two kinds: one kind is generated toward the bottom and turns between the top and bottom along the length of the river; the other is at the surface and turns here and there across the width of the river. The lower one is produced by the falling back of the "boilings" <note>original: "bollori"; the churning or bubbling action of turbulent water.</note> toward the bottom, and the surface one by the circular motion which strikes the surface current.

</margin>

<meta>Folio 79 shifts from the mechanical and hydraulic principles discussed on the previous page to Leonardo’s pioneering observations in paleontology and geology. ### [FORMATION OF FOSSILS (SHELLS)].

79. — **ON ANIMALS THAT HAVE THEIR BONES ON THE OUTSIDE, SUCH AS SHELLS, SNAILS, OYSTERS, SCALLOPS, "BUOOLI" <note>The term "buooli" likely refers to a type of sea snail or whelk common in Italian coastal waters.</note>, AND SIMILAR ONES, WHICH ARE OF INNUMERABLE SPECIES —**
When the floods of rivers, clouded with fine mud [silt], discharged it upon the animals that inhabit the waters near the sea shores, these animals remained imprinted by such mud. Finding themselves buried under a great weight of this mud, they were forced to die, lacking the animals they were accustomed to feeding upon. With the passage of time, as the sea level lowered, this mud—the salt water having drained away—was converted into stone. The shells of these mollusks, their internal soft bodies having been consumed, were filled in their place with mud. Thus, during the creation [transformation] of all the surrounding mud into stone, the mud that was enclosed within the "skins" <note>Leonardo uses the word "scorze" (bark or rinds) to describe the hard outer shells.</note> of the shells (which were somewhat open) also turned to stone, having joined with the external mud through the opening of the shell. Thus, all the "skins" of such shells remained enclosed between two stones: that is, between the stone that served as their mold and the stone that filled them. These are still found in many places today. Almost all the shells petrified within the rocks of mountains still retain their natural shell material around them, especially those that were old enough that their hardness allowed them to be preserved; the younger ones, being already largely turned to lime, had been penetrated by the viscous and petrifying humor <note>Leonardo uses "humore" to describe the mineral-rich fluids he believed were responsible for turning organic matter or silt into solid rock.</note>.

<margin>
[In the margin:] Of imprinted shells that are not petrified and do not have the surface shape [form] that their shell [envelope] once had.
</margin>

79. — **OF ANIMALS THAT HAVE THEIR BONES ON THE OUTSIDE¹, SUCH AS SHELLS [(or: testaceans)], SNAILS, OR OYSTERS, SCALLOPS, THE "BUOOLI" [?], AND SIMILAR ONES, WHICH ARE OF INNUMERABLE SPECIES.**
When the floods of the rivers, muddied with fine silt, discharged it upon the animals that lived under the waters of the sea shores, these animals remained imprinted by this silt; and being found deep under a great weight of this silt, they necessarily had to die, the animals on which they were accustomed to feed being missing. The sea lowering with time, this silt—the salt waters having flowed away—came to change into stone, and the shells of these mollusks, whose animals had been consumed, were found, in place of the latter, filled with silt; thus, in the midst of the creation [transformation] of all the surrounding silt into stone, the silt also which had remained enclosed in the "barks" [surfaces] of the shells, being somewhat open, having joined, through this opening of the shell, to the other silt, also came to be converted into stone, and thus all the barks of such shells remained enclosed between the two stones [petrifications], that is to say between that which enclosed them and that which they contained. One still finds them in many places, and almost all the shells petrified in the rocks of the mountains still have their natural "bark," especially those which had aged enough so that they were preserved by their hardness; and the young ones, being already reduced to lime for the most part, had been penetrated by the viscous and petrifiable humor².
[In the margin:] Of imprinted shells which do not have, and petrified ones which do not have, the superficial figure [form] that their bark [envelope] had.
