### [FORMATION OF FOSSILS (FISH)].

**ON THE BONES OF FISH FOUND WITHIN PETRIFIED FISH —**
All animals that have their bones inside their skin and have been covered by the mud of river floods far from the ordinary beds of such rivers, have had their impressions made in detail by the mud. Over time, the beds of the rivers having lowered, these animals—imprinted and enclosed in such mud—had their flesh and intestines consumed. Only the bones remained, and these, having fallen out of their natural order, settled at the bottom of the cavity of their impression. When the mud dried out (due to its elevation above the river's course) and lost its watery moisture, it took on a viscous moisture and turned into stone, enclosing within itself whatever was found there and filling every void. Finding the cavity of the impression of such animals, the moisture subtly penetrates it through the tiny pores of the earth. The air that occupied that space flees through the lateral parts, because it cannot escape from above (as those pores are occupied by the humor descending into the void) and it cannot flee from below because the humor that has already fallen has sealed the lower pores. There remain the lateral parts, which are open so that the air—condensed and pressed by the descending humor—escapes with the same slowness as the humor descends. Once this humor dries, it becomes stone without weight <note>Leonardo likely means "without great density" or referring to the porous nature of some sedimentary rocks.</note> and preserves the same form as the animal that left its imprint there, and inside it, the bones remain.

**OF THE BONES OF FISH THAT ARE FOUND IN PETRIFIED FISH.**
All animals having the bones inside their skin which have been covered by the silt of the waters of rivers having left their ordinary beds have received in an instant the imprint of this silt. And with time, the beds of the rivers being lowered, these animals having the imprint of this silt which enclosed them—their flesh and organs being consumed, only the bones remaining, their organization being decomposed—fell to the bottom of the concavity of their imprint. And in this concavity, the silt, when it dried (by its elevation above the course of the river) of its aqueous humidity and took on a viscous humidity, turned into stone, enclosing in itself what was found there, filling every hollow with itself. And finding the concavity of the imprint of such animals, it penetrates subtly into the small porosities of the earth through which the air that was there escapes, [that is to say] through the lateral parts, for it cannot escape above because this porosity is occupied by the humor which descends into this vacuum, and it cannot flee below because the humor already fallen has closed the porosity. There remain the lateral parts, which are open so that the air, condensed and pressed by the humor which descends, escapes with the same slowness with which the humor descends there; this humor drying, makes itself stone without weight, and preserves the same form as the animals which left their imprint there, and it encloses the bones within.

> 1. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, p. 491: "Bibliography."

— FOLIO 80 (recto). —

# [THE FORMATION OF SHELLS, STONES, AND FOSSILS].

<margin>80. — THE HOUSE OF SHELLS</margin> ->SHELLS AND THEIR NECESSARY FORM.<-

The animal that lives within the shell builds its own dwelling with joints, seams, lids, and other parts, just as a man does for the house where he lives. This animal grows its house and its lid by degrees, following the growth of its own body. It is attached to the sides of these shells; at this attachment point, the interior of the shell—which is otherwise clean and delicate—remains somewhat spotted and rough. This roughness is suited to receive the connection of the muscles with which the animal pulls itself inside when it wishes to shut itself within its house.

When nature begins the formation of stones, she produces a sort of viscous humor <note>Leonardo uses the term "humor" (humeur/omore) to describe a mineral-rich fluid or "juice" that he believed acted as a binding agent to turn sediment into stone.</note> which, as it dries, solidifies everything trapped within it. It does not change these objects into stone, but preserves them inside itself in the exact shape it found them. This is why leaves are found whole inside stones formed at the base of mountains, mixed with various substances left there by river floods during the autumn seasons. There, the mud from subsequent floods covered them, and then this mud bonded with the aforementioned humor and turned into layered stone, forming strata according to the layers of mud.

<note>original: "faldata agradi" — referring to the sedimentary layers or "steps" seen in rock formations.</note>

<margin>80</margin>
**On visual rays**

Why veils seen through one another do not obstruct each other, and why one veil seen through another shows its texture <note>Leonardo is exploring the "moire" effect or the transparency of layered fabrics.</note>. And this occurs between the eyes by reason of the rays that depart from the angles born in the parts inside the veil, which is tinted with mist <note>original: "tinto di nebbia" — referring to the hazy or translucent quality of the fabric.</note>. This misty veil, when placed before an object, does not allow the eyes to see the fabric of the veil itself, but instead allows what is outside to be seen through it. Conversely, it allows the eyes inside to be seen by those outside. If you wish for the veil itself to be seen, it must be viewed against a bright light near a shadow.

If the eye is positioned between the light and the eye of another man whom it is watching, it will see within that man's eye the sphere of the eye itself, the air, and the <term>depth-clarity<note>original: "sacetudine" — a difficult archaic term used by Leonardo to describe the deep, clear quality of the darkness within the eye's anatomy.</note></term> of the air inside that pupil. This happens because the observer sees his own shining eye reflected in the clear eye of the man or animal watching him; and because the bottom of the pupil is black, it allows the light coming before it to shine within itself. Thus, it creates within that pupil the likeness of the thing that the light, with its visual rays, regards.

<margin>80. — THE HOUSE OF SHELLS [OR TESTACEANS]</margin>
The animal that lives in the shell makes its own dwelling with joints, commissures, covers, and other parts, as man does for the house where he lives. When nature comes to the formation of stones, it produces a quality of viscous humor which, in drying, congeals with the things that are enclosed there without changing these things into stone, but by preserving them in the form in which it found them. It is for this reason that leaves are found whole inside the stones formed at the base of mountains with a mixture of various species [a mix of different substances] that the floods of rivers left there in the autumn times; there, the mud of the following floods covered them, then these muds aggregated with the aforementioned humor and changed into layers of stone by degrees, according to the levels of mud.

### [THE MOTION OF AIR]

Every motion in its particles

Whenever air is moved within still air, it will always be moved in a straight line until it finds other air that is firmer <note>Meaning denser or more resistant.</note> than itself, along which it bends at angles; so that a point of percussion <term>perchussione: the impact or strike of one body (or air mass) against another</term> of said air with the other will form an angle throughout the length of the motions, of which one is inclined toward the other with angles similar to the length of the motions along a point, and this will be only in one way; and such a motion will be as much longer as the motion is more rapid.

<margin>Why the air</margin>

<note>Small diagram of two bean-shaped structures, possibly heart valves or sound/air pulses, with faint lines indicating flow or reflection.</note>

The moved air will be of such length as is one of the sides of an angle, so that said air will be called of such length as it is through the other said air; so that the point of percussion will be in the middle of said air. Just as if the said moved air were of the same length as the still air, and said air were called through the middle of the still air, and the said air will run through said air through the middle of the still air.

### OF THE VOICE

If the air is broken by the voice of a concave <note>Likely referring to a hollow instrument, a vessel, or the anatomy of the throat.</note>, the air will be of one point in one way; said voice will be radically called at that point; as much as the air is at a point of one motion, so much would be the moved air; as much will be the air, it will not be of such length as one of the [parts] of the unmoved air. The point of percussion will be in the middle of said voice; it will be of such length as the still air; said voice will be called through the middle of the still air.

the air</margin>

The moved air will be of such length as is said voice; the moved air will not be called [so], [but] said voice will be called through the other said voice, so that the point of percussion will be in the middle of the said voice; it would be of such length as said voice as much as the moved air.

## [WATER (MOTION AND CARRIED OBJECTS)]

->Of the surfaces that surround the water which pours from a pool <term>pelago: a deep basin, pond, or body of standing water</term> into the air, and their contacts, and also what the water does within those surfaces.<-

->Of the motions of things falling together with the water that moves through the air, and also what they do in that pool.<-

Of things that float upon the middle water, and how they are submerged when they find themselves between the center of that middle water and the fall; they are submerged along with that fall which pours into the pool, and they strike the bottom and break into pieces; therefore, write down all the effects of things that are submerged as far as any extremity of this middle water, which always submerges its extremities because it stands in the middle of all the reflected motions <note>Reflected motions refer to the water bouncing back from the bottom or sides of the basin.</note> directed toward the bottom of its pool.

<summary>Leonardo examines the dynamics of falling water, describing how thin sheets of water rebound upon impact and how the resulting turbulence creates a mill-wheel rotation that can submerge and destroy floating objects.</summary>

*The man who walks on flat ground*

IF TWO TOWERS ARE BUILT IN A CONTINUOUS STRAIGHT LINE, AND THE SPACE ENCLOSED BETWEEN THEM IS PARALLEL, WITHOUT DOUBT THE TWO TOWERS WILL COLLAPSE AGAINST EACH OTHER, PROVIDED THE CONSTRUCTION ALWAYS CONTINUES WITH AN EQUAL HEIGHT FOR EACH OF THE TWO TOWERS.

Let the two central lines of the two angles **b c** [Fig. 2] continue in a straight line. If they cut one of these towers at **c g** and the other at **b f**, it follows that these lines do not pass through the center of gravity of their length; therefore **k l c g p**, a part of one, weighs more than its remainder **c g d**. Between unequal things, one prevails over the other, so that, by necessity, the greater weight of the tower will pull the entire tower against the opposite tower. And the other tower will do the same, in reverse to the first. <note>Leonardo is arguing that on a spherical Earth, "vertical" lines are not parallel because they all point toward the center of the Earth. If a builder tries to keep the space between two towers perfectly parallel (Euclidean geometry), the towers' centers of gravity will eventually pull them inward toward each other.</note>

->### [WORLDS AND ELEMENTS — GRAVITY AND MOTION]<-

Given that there was contact between two terrestrial bodies <note>original: "corpi terresti," referring to planets or Earth-like spheres.</note> with their elements, what shape would those elements take at the point of contact?

Given a spherical weight <term>grave: a heavy body or weight, used in the study of gravity</term> at the contact point of the element of fire with the other element of fire, which weighs as much toward one of the centers of such elements as toward the center of the other elements—this weight would descend obliquely and would settle upon the contact point of the two terrestrial bodies, as the figure shows, and its movement would be oblique.

[Fig. 2:] c d e a g b f

GIVEN THE CENTERS OF TWO WORLDS WITHOUT ELEMENTS, VERY DISTANT FROM ONE ANOTHER, AND GIVEN A UNIFORM WEIGHT WHOSE CENTER OF GRAVITY IS EQUALLY DISTANT FROM THE TWO SAID CENTERS, IF SUCH A WEIGHT WERE THEN DROPPED, WHAT WOULD ITS MOVEMENT BE?

It will move for a long time, moving with a motion in which every part of its length will always be equally distant from each of those centers, and finally, it will stop at an equal distance from each of the two said centers at the nearest point reached by the line of its motion; and thus, this weight will not approach either center of the two worlds. <note>This is a sophisticated thought experiment on gravitational equilibrium, predicting that an object placed between two equal gravitational pulls would eventually settle in a state of balance between them.</note>

### Regarding seeing below
Fish under the water will not be seen in the place where they actually are, because the air moves more rapidly than the water. <note>Leonardo is observing the effects of refraction, though he attributes the displacement to the relative 'speed' or density of the mediums of air and water.</note>

### On sleep
Every motion is refreshed by the rest of its motor, as is seen in the eye, which rests between one opening and another during the blinking of the eyelid; and similarly the heart, which refreshes itself in the rest it takes between one beat and the other; and likewise the lungs. And so it is with all the movements of the members: one cannot exist without the other.

### On dreaming
Regarding sleep: how it seems that the eye of a sleeper sees, as if it sees without the eye or any other sense, except by the <term>imaginative power</term><note>original: "virtū imaginativa"; the faculty of the mind that produces images.</note>. This power, from a single point, directs itself throughout the whole spirit of the man, going to strike through the optic nerve even to the sense, just as it appears to be in a light that is not real. Nor is it by any other sense that the imagination shows it sees, but like a cord that is stretched in the water which, when shaken, creates many circles; so it directs from the eye even to the sense. And thus it happens from a single point of the imagination to the eye of the sleeper, by way of the optic nerve.

## [THE SPOTS ON THE MOON. — THE EARTH. — GRAVITY AND WATER. — CITATION].

<margin>84. — THE SPOTS ON THE MOON</margin>
Some say that vapors rise from the moon like clouds and interpose themselves between the moon and our eyes. If this were so, such spots would never be stable in either position or shape; and when seeing the moon from different aspects, even if these spots did not change, they would appear to change shape, as does any object seen from different sides <note>Leonardo is applying the principles of parallax and perspective: if the spots were clouds floating above the surface, their appearance would shift as the moon moves relative to the observer.</note>.

<margin>ON THE WORLD</margin>
Every <term>heavy body</term><note>original: "graue" (grave); in Renaissance physics, this refers to any object with weight that seeks its "natural place" at the center of the world.</note> tends downward, and high things will not remain at their height, but with time they will all descend; and thus, in time, the world will become spherical. Consequently, it will be entirely covered by water, and the *subterranean veins of the earth will remain motionless.*

<margin>On the convex wave and the concave wave</margin>
Whether a <term>convex wave</term> created by the fall of water into the water of a canal of uniform width and depth will have a long-lasting motion or not.
Whether a <term>concave wave</term> created by water that falls suddenly from an open canal beneath a <term>sluice gate</term><note>original: "cateratta" (cataract/sluice); a gate used to control water flow in a canal.</note> will have a long-lasting motion in a canal of uniform width and depth.

<margin>—</margin>
Every heavy thing tends downward, nor can it be sustained upward forever; wherefore the entire earth would already have been made spherical. <note>original Latin: "Omne grave tendit deorsum nec perpetuo potest sic sursum sustineri quare iam totalis terra esset facta sperica." Leonardo often used Latin for scientific axioms.</note>

## [THE SPOTS ON THE MOON].

<margin>ON THE SPOTS OF THE MOON</margin>
Others said that the moon was composed of parts that were more and less transparent, as if one part were like alabaster and another like crystal or glass. It would follow from this that when the sun strikes with its rays the less transparent part, the light would remain on the surface; thus the denser part would remain illuminated, and the transparent part would show the shadows of its dark depths. Thus they compose [explain] the nature of the moon; and this opinion pleased many philosophers, especially Aristotle. And yet, it is a false opinion, because in the various aspects that the moon and the sun often present to our eyes, we would see such spots vary, sometimes becoming dark and sometimes light.

They would become dark when the sun is in the west and the moon is in the middle of the sky, because then the transparent concavities would take on shadow even *to the tops of the edges of these transparent concavities, because the sun could not make its rays penetrate into the mouths of such concavities.*

These spots would appear bright during the full moon, when the moon in the east faces the sun in the west; then the sun would illuminate even to the bottom of such transparent parts, and thus, no shadows being generated, the moon would not show us the aforementioned spots at that time. And so they would be now more, now less, according to the changes of the sun relative to the moon, and the moon relative to our eyes, as I have said above. <note>Leonardo refutes the "transparency" theory by noting that if the moon were like a jagged glass or crystal ball, the shadows within its "depths" would disappear when the sun hit them directly (Full Moon), but the spots remain visible regardless of the phase.</note>

<summary>Leonardo refutes contemporary theories that the moon's spots are clouds or caused by varying levels of transparency, instead treating the moon as a solid, opaque body. He also posits a geological future where gravity eventually pulls all land into the sea, resulting in a perfectly spherical, water-covered Earth.</summary>
<keywords>lunar spots, gravity, planetary formation, hydrodynamics, Aristotle, optics, lunar topography, erosion</keywords>

# FOLIO 85 (recto).

### [THE SPOTS OF THE MOON].

85. — ON THE SPOTS OF THE MOON
It has been said that the spots of the moon are created within the moon itself by being of varying <term>rarefaction</term><note>A state of being less dense or "thinner" in substance.</note> and density. If this were so, during an <term>eclipse</term><note>An astronomical event where one celestial body is obscured by the shadow of another.</note> of the moon, the solar rays would penetrate through some part of the aforementioned rarefied areas. Since such an effect is not seen, the said opinion is false.

Others say that the surface of the moon, being smooth and polished, receives within itself the likeness of the Earth, just like a mirror. This opinion is false, because the Earth, when uncovered by water, presents different shapes from different points of view. Therefore, when the moon is in the East, it would reflect different spots than when it is directly above us, or when it is in the West; yet the spots of the moon, as seen during the <term>full moon</term><note>original: "pleni lunio"</note>, never vary during the motion it makes across our hemisphere.

A second reason is that an object reflected in a <term>convexity</term><note>The outward-curved surface of a sphere.</note> occupies only a small part of that mirror, as is proved in <term>perspective</term><note>The mathematical study of how objects appear to the eye based on distance and position.</note>.

A third reason is that at the full moon, the moon "sees" only half of the illuminated sphere of the Earth, in which the Ocean and other waters shine, while the land creates spots within that brightness. Thus, one would see half of our Earth surrounded by the brightness of the sea illuminated by the sun, and on the moon, such a likeness would be a tiny part of that moon.

And the fourth is that a shining object does not reflect itself in another shining object. Therefore, the sea, catching the brilliance of the sun just as the moon does, could not reflect the Earth; otherwise, one would also see the reflection of the body of the sun and each of the stars positioned opposite to it.

[2nd figure:] t a g

# FOLIO 85 (verso).

### [LIGHT AND HEAT. — SUN AND MIRRORS].

The very rapid friction of two dense bodies generates fire.
[1st figure:] a e c b
Therefore, such effects participate in the primary cause and not the intermediate one.

It is proved that the sun is by its nature hot, and not cold as has been previously stated.
[2nd figure:] c d g f
A <term>concave mirror</term><note>A mirror that curves inward, which can focus light into a single point.</note>, despite being cold, upon receiving the rays of a fire, reflects them even hotter than the fire itself.
A glass ball filled with cold water sends out the rays it catches from the fire even hotter than the fire.

WHETHER GREATER LIGHT WITH LESS HEAT CAUSES CONCAVE MIRRORS TO REFLECT MORE POWERFUL RAYS OF GREATER HEAT THAN A BODY OF GREATER HEAT AND LESSER LIGHT.
In such an experiment, let a "loaf" of copper be heated until it glows. Let it be viewed through a round hole of the same size and at the same distance from the mirror as the heated copper. Here you will have two bodies equal in distance, varying in heat and varying in <term>splendor</term><note>original: "splendore"; refers to the intensity of light or brightness.</note>. You will find that the greater heat here will cause the mirror to produce a reflection of greater heat than the aforementioned flame. Therefore, we shall say it is not the brightness of the sun that heats, but its natural heat.

From these two experiments, it follows that the heat of the rays issuing from the mirror or the cold water ball is hot by <term>virtue</term><note>original: "per uiurtu" (per virtù); refers to the inherent power or focused energy of the source rather than the temperature of the lens itself.</note>, and not because the mirror or ball is hot. The same happens in the case of the sun passing through those bodies: it heats by virtue. Because of this, some have concluded that the sun is not hot; whereas, by these same cited experiments, it is proved that the sun is extremely hot. This is shown by the experiment of the mirror and the ball which, despite being cold, take the rays of the heat of the fire and return them as hot rays because the primary cause is hot. The same happens with the sun, which, being hot itself, reflects great heat when passing through such cold mirrors.

# FOLIO 85 (recto).

->to straighten the sail with the wind<-

<margin>85</margin>

If the motion of the sail is equal to the motion of the wind, the sail will be entirely still; and if it is one degree less, it will be moved by that degree of difference; and if the wind is one degree greater, the sail will be moved by that degree. And if the motion of the wind is one <term>braccia</term><note>A Florentine unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> per hour and the sail flees at one braccia per hour, the wind will not strike it, because the motion of the one and the other is the same. And if the wind is 2 degrees and the sail is one, the sail will be moved by one degree; and if the wind is 3 degrees and the sail is one, it will be moved by 2 degrees.

Therefore, to straighten the sail, it is necessary that the wind be many degrees faster than the motion of the sail, because the motion of the sail is always being lost while the wind remains of the same force. Hence, if the sail is fluctuating in its changes, it is necessary that the wind comes to strike the sail to straighten it with as much more force as has been lost from the velocity of the sail; and the surplus of that force will act to straighten it.

And if the sail is one braccia and the wind is 2 degrees, the sail will flee at one degree of velocity. And if it [the wind] is 10 degrees, the sail will flee at 9 degrees.

And if the sail is 5 degrees and the wind is 6, the sail will flee at 1 degree.

In the time that the sail turns to straighten itself, it loses its velocity, and this will always happen if the force of the wind remains the same; because the more it turns to face the wind, the less it offers itself to the wind, and therefore it is pushed less by the wind; and through such loss of motion, the wind strikes it with more force and is more powerful to straighten it.

And this would happen because of the sail clashing in its fluctuating movements with the opposing <term>percussion</term><note>The physical impact or strike of the wind against the surface.</note> of the wind, which percussion is of as much velocity as the velocity of the sail added to the velocity of the wind. So, if the sail is one degree of velocity and the wind is 2 degrees, the percussion will be 3 degrees, because the sail, clashing with the wind with its motion of one degree, will come to strike with one degree of the wind, and the other degree of the wind will come by itself to strike the sail with another degree of motion; because if the motion of the wind and the sail were of equal velocity, one thing would not come to strike the other. This thing is the clashing of the velocity of the sail with the velocity of the wind.

### — FOLIO 86 (recto). —

### [SOLAR RAYS — PEAKS OF THE CAUCASUS].

86. — Solar rays pass through the cold region of the air and do not change their nature; they pass through glasses full of cold water and do not lose their nature; and through whatever transparent place they pass, it is as if they were penetrating that much more air.
And if you were to argue that the cold rays of the sun incorporate the heat of the fire while penetrating its element <note>In the Aristotelian worldview, the "Element of Fire" was a sphere located above the atmosphere and below the moon.</note>, just as they incorporate the color of the glasses they penetrate, it would follow that in penetrating the cold region, they would incorporate such cold after the incorporation of the said heat; and thus the cold would cancel out the heat, whereby the solar rays would reach us deprived of heat. Since this is not confirmed by experience, such an argument—that the sun is cold—is vain.
But if you were to say that the cold through which the burning rays of the sun pass tempers somewhat the excessive heat of those rays, it would then follow that on the high peaks of Mount Caucasus <note>The Caucasus Mountains, located between the Black and Caspian Seas.</note> in Scythia <note>An ancient region of central Eurasia; Leonardo uses it to refer to the remote North/East.</note>, one would feel greater heat than in the valleys, because that mountain rises above the middle region of the air, and near the summit there are never clouds, and nothing grows there.
And if you say that such solar rays push the element of fire towards us through the places they pass by local motion <note>The physical displacement of matter from one place to another.</note>, this cannot stand; because the local motion of such air does not happen without a length of time, and all the more so when the sun appears at the horizon, where it is further from us by 3,500 miles <note>Leonardo’s estimation of the atmospheric or orbital distance at the horizon compared to the zenith.</note> than when it is in the middle of our sky. If it were so, it would cause the opposite at our horizon, because it would carry away with its rays the opposite part of the element of fire that it penetrated.
<margin>If a smaller fire is attracted and bends toward a larger fire, as is seen in experience, it is necessary that the sun draws the element of fire to itself rather than chasing it away and pushing it toward us.</margin>
And the heat of fire does not descend unless it follows burning igneous matter; in doing so, it is material and consequently is visible.

---

### — FOLIO 86 (verso). —

### [WATER IN A CANAL AND IN THE AIR. — MOTION AND GRAVITY].

-> Water that flows through a canal of equal capacity and fills all its first flat part will fill all the other parts, straight or oblique, and will move with equal velocity. <-

The movements of heavy elements <note>referring to 'elementi gravi,' or substances like earth and water that naturally seek the center of the world in ancient physics.</note> are not toward the center simply to go to that center, but because the medium where they are cannot resist them; and when they find resistance in their own element, that body no longer has weight, nor does it seek to go further toward the center.
Water in the air has weight and descends by the shortest path; it divides and opens the air that stays beneath its center of gravity with all its parts equally, and it does not divide the air that stays at its sides because it is not situated above it. Because of this, a hole is made through the air of very short length until it reaches that which resists it; and this resistance being water, the water which falls through the air into this water no longer seeks to go toward the center, because it no longer divides the water as it did the air. Therefore, a heavy body moves downward where it finds no resistance, and not merely to go to the center.

<summary>Leonardo argues that solar heat is intrinsic to the sun's rays rather than gathered from the atmosphere, and posits that gravity is a movement driven by a lack of resistance in a medium rather than an innate pull to the center of the Earth.</summary>
<keywords>solar rays, atmospheric heat, Caucasus Mountains, Scythia, element of fire, hydrodynamics, gravity, resistance, fluid motion</keywords>

# FOLIO 86 (recto).

<margin>86</margin>

Because the water that departs from the bottom pushes ahead of itself an equal weight of water, and if said water is of a low nature <note>Leonardo likely means water moving at a lower velocity or under higher pressure near the bed.</note>, it is because the water at the bottom of the river is slower than that at the surface; this is because it bears the weight of the water above it and the friction against the earth below.

---

The friction (*frotamento*) <term>frotamento: Leonardo’s term for friction or the "rubbing" of water against the riverbed.</term> against the bottom will be the reason why the river moves more slowly at the bottom than at the surface; because the water that strikes the bottom is, by that percussion, deflected upwards, whereby its transverse <note>That is, the horizontal flow of the river toward its mouth.</note> motion must necessarily be diminished. And even if the water were not deflected upwards, the friction of said bottom would still necessarily diminish its motion; so, the transverse motion being diminished by the percussion it makes from bottom to top, it follows of necessity that the motion toward the sea will be diminished for the reason stated above.

---

That river will have a slower motion which has a lesser slope (*pendenza*) and a rougher bottom; and if such roughness is equally spread throughout the entire bottom, that river will necessarily be of slow motion because the water rubbing against the bottom is greatly hindered. Conversely, that river will be faster which has a smoother bottom and a greater slope.

<margin>
That part of the river will be faster which has a smoother bottom and a greater slope; and that will be slower which has a rougher bottom and a lesser slope.
</margin>

---

If a wave has a small base and a wide base <note>Leonardo is likely comparing waves of different proportions.</note>, its motion will be fast; in the internal friction (*atito*), it is divided into bases above or below or in the middle. The water will be of slow motion at the bottom due to the percussion it makes against the bed; if it is of slow motion at the surface, it is due to the percussion against the air; and if in the middle the water opposes the motion, it will be of slow motion at the bottom, slow motion at the surface, and slow motion in the middle.

# FOLIO 86 (verso).

The water that strikes against the earth will have greater force, and its motion will be more diminished. The water that is confined in a narrow space (*angustia*) will have a greater motion than the water that is in a wide space.

<note>Geometric diagram at top right showing water flow through a constricted or angled channel.</note>

---

Every motion of a slope will be that much faster as the slope is greater. This is proved because everything that hangs along the line of its gravity <term>line of gravity: The vertical path an object would take if falling freely; the steeper the slope, the closer the water's path aligns with this vertical pull.</term> will have a greater motion the more it approaches said internal line. Because the line of slope will be that much faster as it is longer, being joined at the height <note>Leonardo is comparing different slopes starting from the same height; the longer the diagonal path relative to the height, the less steep the slope, yet here he explores the relationship between the angle and the speed of the fall.</note>, the water will be of faster motion because its line has a greater slope.

And if the line has a greater motion, it is necessary that the water of such a line has a greater motion; it follows that the water will have a greater motion because of the greater slope. Water of a greater slope will have a greater motion because the water that has a greater slope will have a greater motion because the water that has a greater slope will have a greater motion... <note>Leonardo repeats this phrase several times, a common habit in his notebooks when he is ruminating on a physical law or seeking the perfect rhetorical formulation.</note> the water that follows the line of its gravity.

# FOLIO 87 (recto).

->[WATER. — MOVEMENTS IN THE AIR, CONDENSED AND RAREFIED].<-

---

<margin>87. —
OF THE AIR</margin>
[Figure:] a, b. The faceted object placed at an angle in the middle of a stream of water; even though the water strikes its flat face, the water will flow in greater quantity toward the side of the lower slope, *that is, more at point 'a' than at point 'b'.*

And because—as proven in the seventh proposition—it is not contrary to the nature of air to condense and rarefy almost in an instant (which is not possible for water, which maintains its primary shape), it is easier for the air at the sides and above a falling object (*mobile*) to fill the vacuum left by that object above itself, than it is for the air below to bend and move along a long, curved line to fill such a vacuum. Furthermore, it is impossible, according to the 8th proposition—which proves that every impulse <term>impeto: Leonardo's term for the force or momentum imparted to a medium.</term> created in the air moves that air along the line of the impulse’s creation, just as the wind moves as much air as its impulse moves (as seen with dust moved by winds, or the "atoms" <note>original: "atimi"; Leonardo refers to the tiny dust motes visible in a shaft of sunlight.</note> in the sphere of the sun when one blows on them). Therefore, for these reasons: the air pushed by the impulse of the heavy body (*grave*) descending through it flees along the line of motion made by its mover; the air at the sides turns into lateral eddies; and the air from above descends to fill the vacuum that the moving body leaves behind it at every stage of its movement.
The air beneath the moving body as it descends becomes dense, and above it, the air becomes rare <note>A mark in the manuscript indicates this line should have been placed before the preceding paragraph.</note>.

The impulse is much faster than the water because many are the times that the wave flees the place of its creation, while the water does not move from its site; similar to the waves made in May in the grain fields by the course of the winds, where one sees the waves running through the countryside while the grain does not change its place.

When a heavy body <term>grave: any object with weight that is subject to gravity.</term> descends through the air, and that air moves in the opposite direction to continually fill the place left by that heavy body, the movement of the air is curved. This is because, while wanting to rise by the shortest line, it is blocked by the heavy body descending above it; thus, by necessity, it must bend and then return above that body to fill the vacuum left by it. And if it were not so, the air would not condense under the speed of the heavy body; if this were the case, birds would not be able to support themselves upon the air struck by them. But one must say that the air condenses under that which strikes it, and rarefies above to fill the vacuum left by what has struck it.

# — FOLIO 88 (recto). —

->[BOOK OF THE TREATISE ON WATER. — AIR.]<-

88. — BOOK 9: ON THE ACCIDENTAL RISING OF WATER <note>original: "surgimenti accidentali"; refers to water rising or splashing due to obstacles rather than natural flow.</note>

<margin>Air I</margin> If, by means of a sluice gate <term>caterata: a gate or barrier used to control water flow in a canal</term>, the wider body of water is divided from the narrower, and the movement of the water is from the *wider* narrower to the *narrower* wider <note>Leonardo appears to be correcting himself here regarding the direction of flow through the gate.</note>, the water that surges under the sluice gate will leap over the wider water, and its fall will hollow out the bottom of the canal in several places with various leaps.

<margin>Air</margin> The movement of air within air condenses itself and the air it strikes.

<margin>Air</margin> Air moved within a body denser than itself condenses more than when moving through other air.

Air moved within a body lighter than itself rarefies <note>original: "rarefa"; becomes less dense or occupies more space.</note>.

Water moved within a body lighter than itself becomes rarefied—not in its quality <note>its essence as water</note>, but in quantity, through spreading and "paniculation" <term>paniculatione: a term Leonardo used to describe water breaking into a thin, branching film or droplets, like a panicle (a cluster of flowers).</term>.

Smoke that penetrates the air, if it is thick and born from a large flame fed by damp wood, does not mix with it, but appears denser on its top than in its middle; this is more evident when the air is cold. Subtle light always penetrates warm air, becoming increasingly refined (and the dust that penetrates the subtlest air rises the highest).

# — FOLIO 88 (recto). —

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's mirror writing on folio 88 recto, describing the behavior of water jets in the air.</note>

### Why the motion of water through the air divides into many tiny droplets.

Let the mass <note>original: "palla," literally "ball" or "sphere." Leonardo often envisions a volume of water as a geometric solid before it is acted upon by external forces.</note> of water be struck by the air and made thin within that air by the great force of its motion. Because its forward movement is impeded by this motion, it dilates and spreads out, taking the form of a skin <note>original: "pelle." Leonardo uses this term to describe a thin, continuous film of liquid.</note>; and because this skin is so thin, it breaks apart into various minute pieces.

**If the water that leaps through the nozzle <term>spiraculo: a small opening or aperture through which a fluid is forced</term> of the basin <term>conca: a vessel or pressurized container used in hydraulic experiments</term> is of a large quantity.**

**If the water that leaps through the nozzle of the basin is of a small quantity in respect to the void of that basin.**

**If more water leaves that basin than enters it.**

**If less water leaves that basin than enters it.**

**In what way the water leaps through the nozzle of the basin into the air, and how it divides and in what quantity, and how one part is hindered by the impediment of the other.**

These same natures are observed in the lights that are lit, and in smokes, and in winds, and in every fluid thing. And note that what is said of the basin of water is also said of that nozzle of water which is thrown by impetus into the air; this water also thickens, and because of the impediment of the air, it slows its motion and spreads into a skin.

AIR

## [CYLINDRICAL WAVES]

92. — [Figure 1:] a b
— The semi-cylindrical wave, the further it moves, the more it lowers, the more it widens, and the faster it becomes. <note>Leonardo is observing that as a wave spreads out, its energy is distributed over a larger area, causing its height to decrease while its speed increases.</note>
When there are unequal cylindrical waves *of different degrees* <note>original: "digra," likely a contraction of "di grado" or "of degrees," referring to their relative sizes or stages</note> where the larger one is born before the smaller one, the smaller one intersects and passes over the larger one. This happens because the larger one, which was born first, has already widened and lowered by the time it meets the smaller one; the smaller wave, being higher when it strikes, hits the low point of the larger wave, and finding no obstacle as high as itself, it runs over the other, collapses on the opposite side, and continues with its initial momentum.
But if, among unequal cylindrical waves, the smaller one is born higher in the river than the larger one, then the larger one follows its natural course, and the smaller one follows the course of that larger one.
— The wave produced by an object moving against still water will be of the same size and nature as the wave produced by water moving against a still object. <note>This is an early observation of the principle of relativity in fluid dynamics.</note>

92. — [Figure 1: ] a b
<note>The following text is a French translation of the Italian above, included in the original manuscript's transcription.</note>
The more the semi-cylindrical wave moves, the more it lowers, widens, and becomes rapid. <note>original footnote: F. Cardinali, Book 4, Ch. 76, p. 339, plate 12, fig. 60. Francesco Cardinali was an 18th-century editor who compiled Leonardo’s writings on water.</note>
If of two unequal cylindrical waves the larger is born before the smaller, the latter cuts the larger and passes over it; this happens because the larger, born first, has widened and lowered when it faces the smaller, and the smaller which strikes it, being high, hits the depression of the large one and, finding no obstacle as high as itself, runs over the other, rushes to the other side, and follows its initial momentum. <note>original footnote: Idem, Ch. 77, plate 12, fig. 61.</note>
But if of unequal cylindrical waves, the smaller is born higher in the river than the larger, then the larger follows its natural course, and the smaller follows the course of the larger.
The wave is the same whether the object moves against still water, or the water moves against a still object.

## [CYLINDRICAL WAVES]

[Figures:] colliding semi-cylindrical waves [Figure 1:] a b d c [Figure 2:] f g i k [Figure 3:] n m o p [Figure 4:] a b c d
If cylindrical waves strike each other and do not intersect as far as the middle, the middle part that strikes leaps backward and passes over the part that did not strike.
When two cylindrical waves strike each other entirely with equal size and power, they both return entirely backward without any penetration of one into the other.
But if the cylindrical waves are of unequal size, the larger and the smaller will not observe their law, because the larger does not bend, and the smaller unites with that larger one.
And if for equal waves the birth of one occurs *at a greater height* before the other, their collisions will not be made with equal power; consequently, the course of the second will bend before that of the first.

[Figures:] Colliding semi-cylindrical waves. [Figure 1:] a b d c [Figure 2:] f g i k [Figure 3:] n m o p [Figure 4:] a b c d.
<note>The following text is the French translation of the second Italian section.</note>
If cylindrical waves strike each other and do not cut through to the middle, the colliding middle part jumps back and passes over the part that did not collide. <note>original footnote: F. Cardinali, Book 4, Ch. 72, p. 337, plate 11, fig. 56.</note>
When two cylindrical waves strike each other fully with equal magnitude and power, they then return backward without any penetration of one into the other. <note>original footnote: Idem, Ch. 73, p. 338, plate 12, fig. 57.</note>
But if the cylindrical waves are of unequal sizes, the larger and the smaller will not observe their law, because the larger does not bend, and the smaller joins with the larger. <note>original footnote: Idem, Ch. 74, plate 12, fig. 58.</note>
And if for equal waves *that are higher* the birth of one takes place before the other, their collisions will not be made with equal powers; therefore, the course of the second will bend before that of the first. <note>original footnote: Idem, Ch. 75, plate 12, fig. 59.</note>

<note>Glossary of technical terms:
**cylindrical waves** (ondes cylindriques / onde colunnali): waves that form a tube-like or column shape.
**semi-cylindrical** (semi colunnale): half-column shaped waves.
**intersect** (intersega): to cross or cut through.
**momentum** (inpeto): the force or energy of movement.
**unequal waves** (colunnali inequali): waves of different sizes or heights.
**collision** (urto / vrtate): the impact of waves hitting each other.
**power** (potentia): the force or intensity of the wave.
**origin/birth** (nasscimento): the point or time where the wave is created.</note>

He also notes the law of relative motion, stating that a wave's behavior is identical whether an object moves through water or water moves against an object.</summary>

How the grass bends by the wind

<meta>Following the observations on Folio 92 regarding the movement of grass and shadows in the wind, Leonardo shifts his focus here to the properties of light reflection on spherical bodies (the Moon) and the mechanics of wave formation in flowing water. ## — FOLIO 93 (recto). —

->[THE MOON. — REFLECTION OF THE SUN].<-

93.— ON THE MOON. IF IT IS POLISHED AND SPHERICAL, THE IMAGE <note>original: "simulacro," meaning the reflected image or representation</note> OF THE SUN WITHIN IT IS POWERFULLY LUMINOUS, BUT ONLY ON A SMALL PART OF ITS SURFACE.

And you will see the proof of this by taking a ball of burnished gold placed in the darkness with a light positioned far from it; although it illuminates about half of that ball, the eye sees it only on a small part of its surface, and all the rest of such a surface reflects the darkness that surrounds it. For this reason, only the image of the light appears in it, and all the rest remains invisible, the eye being distant from the ball. This same thing would happen on the surface of the moon if it were polished, lustrous, and dense, like the bodies that reflect.

<margin>Prove [explain] how, if you were on the moon or on any star, our earth would appear to you to perform the same function for the sun as the moon does. And prove how the same image of the sun in the sea cannot appear as one sun, as it appears in a flat mirror.</margin>

<note>The notes in the original manuscript margin refer to Jean-Paul Richter’s 19th-century compilation of Leonardo's works, volume II, section 893.</note>

## — FOLIO 93 (verso). —

->[WAVES].<-

[Figures: a b c d] [2nd figure: simple semi-cylindrical wave n m a b o q p] [3rd figure: m c s q r f]

— THE WATER WHICH MOVES BETWEEN STRAIGHT AND SMOOTH BANKS AND BOTTOM WILL NOT CREATE ANY SORT OF WAVE. —

What is stated happens because a wave is not generated except by reflected motion, and reflected motion arises from the impact <note>original: "percussione," the striking force</note> of the incident motion, which is made against a particular object on the bottom or the sides of the canal. If in these places there are no particular objects, for the reason stated, no wave will be generated, such water being made of minute uprisings <note>original: "surgimenti," small upward flows</note> that rise little from the bottom, so that upon coming to the surface they do not create waves.

— THE SIMPLE SEMI-CYLINDRICAL WAVE IS GENERATED BY ANY MINUTE OBJECT JOINED TO THE BANK; THE WATER THAT STRIKES IT MAKES A LONG WAVE IN THE FORM OF A HALF-COLUMN WHICH DIRECTS ITSELF OBLIQUELY TOWARD THE OPPOSITE BANK, AND THERE IT DIES AND IS REBORN. —

Let the object *a* be placed on the bank *a-o* of the canal *n-o-m-p*; I say the water that strikes that object will make a wave which, by its continual creation [reforming itself without ceasing], will also make itself continual, and it would always be so if it were not interrupted by the common course of the water in the canal, which strikes entirely upon that wave and pushes it constantly at every degree of its length, until at the end it directs it according to its ordinary course.

These 2 figures below are interchanged in the description and in the drawing; arrange them correctly later in the principal book <note>original: "libro principale," likely referring to his intended treatise on water</note>.

<meta>Leonardo continues his exploration of physical forces on Folio 93. ## [CURRENTS AND WATERFALLS]

94. — In water of moderate speed <note>original: "dimediocle velocita"</note>, the middle water will have small ripples.
The water that *is beneath* [original: *sta sotto*] and interposes between the middle surface water and its bottom is not of the same nature as the middle water. This is because the surface water receives the percussion from the incident [falling] water and the reflected water; both, being in contact with the air, fall upon the other water, creating an impact as if they were a heavy object, and they penetrate like a heavy object into the other water struck by them.

The water falls first, then resurfaces and rises with its semi-cylindrical wave <note>original: "semi collona ondosa," literally a "wave-like semi-column"</note> above its opposite semi-cylindrical wave, which made the fall more oblique. —
[4th fig.:] a b   u c d
Why does the water a-u-c fall in a more *ob*-direct line than the water b-d?

---

94 — In water of moderate speed, the middle water will have [will show] small ripples.

Indeed, the surface water receives the percussion of the incident and the reflected water; both, by bordering the air, fall upon the other water, creating a percussion like a heavy object, and penetrate like a heavy object into the other water struck by them.

## [BOOK ON LIGHT (SUN, EARTH, MOON, EYE)]

<margin>
The Moon is cold and humid.
Water is cold and humid.
Our sea provides such influence to the moon as the moon does to us.
</margin>
My book extends to show how the Ocean, with the other seas, by means of the sun, makes our world shine in the manner of the moon, and to those further away it appears as a star; and this I prove.

[Figure:] a b c
First, demonstrate how every light distant from the eye creates rays which appear to increase the size of such a luminous body. And from this it follows that...

The eye does not diminish the light at any distance because the likeness of the light that is imprinted on the surface of the eye illuminates the interior, just as paper windows do <note>In Leonardo’s time, windows were often made of oiled paper rather than glass; they diffused light, making the entire surface of the paper appear to glow.</note>, which spread the light they have received through the places that see that paper; previously, those places could not see the cause of the illumination of that paper when the paper was not there. The sun, which is seen in mirrors, causes the image <note>original: "simulacro," referring to the reflected likeness or "ghost" of the object</note>, not passing inside, to reflect outward like a real light. If the lead <note>The reflective backing used in mirrors.</note> were not behind such mirror glass, the image of the sun that is imprinted on the surface of the glass would pass inside and would illuminate the interior or the back of such a mirror. So it is with the eye, which receives the light of such an image within, which spreads greatly into the visual faculties <note>original: "virtu visiua," the medieval and Renaissance concept of the power or "virtue" of sight.</note>.

Thus does the eye, which receives within the light of the image, which spreads much into the visual faculties.

# — FOLIO 94 (verso) —

<margin>
The wind moved from within and through the air, and it will be turned upon itself and consequently turned.
</margin>

Air does not move by itself unless it is pushed or pulled or turned upon itself by the motion of bodies that strike into it.

If the air is without any motion, it will be moved in various ways; the air moved by various [means]...

<margin>
<note>Small diagram of a "star" or radiating lines representing air movement.</note>
</margin>

If the air swirls within itself from many motions of bodies that turn or swirl within it in various ways, and if it be the weakest or most wandering, the moved air will be weaker than that moved from still air; because still air is more resistant to the motion of whatever wishes to flee it or swirl within it; because still air is more compressed than moved air is, because moved air is more dilated <term>dilatata (expanded or thinned)</term> and consequently it will be easier to overcome it.

<margin>

</margin>

# — FOLIO 95 (recto). —

## [WATER FLOWS. — DISTANT LIGHTS AND REFLECTION.]

95. — [1st fig. :] b o a b c s t
ON THE PROPORTION OF THE MOVEMENT OF THE WATER THAT POURS FROM THE BOTTOM OF A VERY LONG DITCH, THE EXIT OF WHICH IS A HUNDRED TIMES NARROWER THAN THE WIDTH AND DEPTH OF THE DITCH.
The question is asked: how much slower will the movement of the upper water of the ditch be than the movement of the <term>rozza (a rushing stream or gush)</term> made of the same width as the mouth through which the water exits that ditch?

Why, when the image of the light of a torch or candle diminishes at a great distance from the eye, the size of that light does not decrease, but only the power of its <unclear>s</unclear> and the lucidity of its splendor is lost.

[4th fig. :] a b c d e [Last fig. :] q l a n o p
A light that diminishes in quantity also diminishes in illuminating power, but by not moving from its position, it does not lose its original amount of illumination in all those places it previously illuminated. This is proven: the light given by the sun onto the surface of the water is reflected backward and radiates like a material light, both inside and out, and it actually illuminates things placed opposite to it, and also within.

— One cannot define [explain] this here due to a lack of paper, but go toward the beginning of the book to page 40; the definition is there.

## [ANATOMY. — PREPARATIONS (SLEEVES AND PAPERS).]

ANATOMY.
Which nerves or cords <note>Leonardo used "corde" (cords) to refer to tendons.</note> of the hand are those that bring the fingers of the hand and feet closer together and further apart from one another?

<margin>
To make sleeves <note>original: "maniche" (sleeves or tubes)</note> coated with the ramification of <term>bole (a reddish clay used as a pigment base)</term> and orpiment <term>orpiment (a bright yellow mineral pigment)</term>, and then all the rest with transparent [layers], or in a filtration of fixed and fine white, which you shall do in winter, dipping the very fine ramification and immediately pulling it out into the cold air; it will have no cause to run <note>original: "colare" (to flow or drip)</note>, and it will be uniform and fine, and it will be clearly seen in the transparent layer, and the broken fronts [edges] will be beautiful.

Pass the dissolved bole through wine and you will make the ramification; and cook it, and coat it with black, and then with burnt orpiment, and then with azure.
It is better to imitate nature.
Therefore, make the ramification of passed bole, and coat it with a transparent layer, then with black-white, then with black, and then with transparent white, in the manner of <term>chalcedony (a translucent, clouded gemstone)</term> made from the milk of <term>gichero (the cuckoopint plant, Arum maculatum)</term>.

You shall also make papers of your material in various colors, and then wrap them randomly, and then press them, tied tightly, and make a cut across them; then loosen them and let them expand as much as you like (but above all, ensure that such papers are somewhat moistened again so that in pressing them they do not form sharp angles). This done, coat these expanded papers several times with fixed and transparent coatings so that you close every void; and if you do as [shown] here in the margin, you will be able to see all the levels of coatings above.

[Under the 1st fig. :] If you do it quickly and pull out the well-dried ramification, it will not be spoiled; and make it black, and coat it with white, and place it in a transparent layer.

[Under the 3rd fig. :] Do this in winter for the sudden freezing, and dry it without fire by suspending the thread so that it turns.

->FOLIO 96 (recto).<-

->[PREPARATIONS, CAUSTIC SOLUTIONS, AND MIXTURES]<-

<note>This page contains 19th-century printed transcriptions of Leonardo da Vinci’s Italian mirror-script, followed by translations and scholarly commentary from the same era. Leonardo often used his notebooks to record "recipes" for art supplies and engineering materials.</note>

96. — <margin>Varnish it 6 or 8 times the thickness, very finely, letting it dry well each time; it will appear like glass and will not fear humidity.</margin>

Very fine papyrus <note>original: "Palpiro"</note> without glue, soaked in a mild, warm fish glue with vinegar; when pressed with the greatest force, it will become so dense that it will appear to be made of bronze.

<margin>CAPITELLUM <note>original: "capitel". In Renaissance chemistry, a *capitellum* or "capitel" was a caustic solution or lye used to dissolve substances.</note>: Made of distilled vinegar,</margin> ram’s horn, egg white, and fish glue; but this egg white falls apart with humidity. <note>Leonardo notes the fragility of the binder.</note> It will become so dense it will appear to be bronze.

CAPITELLUM: Oil of distilled tartar, salt, ammonia, and mustard.

MIXTURE — Branched bole <note>original: "bolo ramificato". Bole is a soft, fatty clay used as a base for gold leaf or as a pigment.</note> by the piece, mixed with cinnabar <note>original: "cinabrese"</note>; cook it enough so that it does not fall apart when wetted; then coat it with three layers of transparent [glaze], then one layer of yellow, and then whatever color you like. But remember that the branched cinnabar mixture must be cooked, otherwise it will not dry at all even with very strong glue. These coatings should be done in the sun, or in a very hot oven; or, one may take the branched moss from trees, give it strong glue and whatever color you like, then dry and coat it.

Egg white and a little glue, so that it does not crack while drying; or if you prefer: *Egg white, gum, and glue.*

Lapis lazuli <note>original: "Ilapis"</note> dissolves in wine, in vinegar, or in aqua vitae <note>original: "acqua vte". This refers to concentrated alcohol.</note>, and can then be recombined with mild glue.

Dissolve shellac <note>original: "lacha goma"</note> with distilled urine, and experiment with dissolving feathers, horn, or claws; but the ram’s horn is the most transparent.

Turn your cups made of these mixtures on a flat lathe, just like potters do.

<note>1. Reference to J.-P. Richter, The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci, Vol. I, 613.</note>

->FOLIO 96 (verso).<-

->[THE WEALTH OF DOCTORS. — COLORS. — MAN AND ANIMALS. — BONE FLASK.]<-

Every man desires to make a fortune <note>original: "far capitale"</note> only to give it to doctors, the destroyers of life; therefore, they must be rich. <note>Leonardo often expressed a skeptical or satirical view of the medical profession of his time.</note>

Distilled human blood is very powerful.

Man has a great capacity for speech, the majority of which is vain and false; animals have a small capacity, but it is useful and true. Better is a small certainty than a great lie. <note>A famous Leonardo aphorism prioritizing observation over empty rhetoric.</note>

Verdigris <note>original: "Verde rame"</note>, aloes, and gall, or turmeric, make a beautiful green; also saffron or burnt orpiment <note>a yellow arsenic sulfide pigment</note>, but I doubt they will not soon turn black.

Ultramarine blue and glass yellow <note>original: "giallo diuetro". Likely a lead-tin yellow or antimony yellow used in glassmaking.</note> mixed together make a very beautiful green for fresco—that is, for walls.

Lacquer and verdigris make a good shadow for blue in oil painting.

<margin>[Illustration of a vessel] Bone: this does not fear impact.</margin>

Take bone in the form of lantern plates <note>thin, translucent sheets of horn or bone used in lanterns</note>; soften it, then squeeze it into the shape of hot embers [?]. When you have squeezed it, cut away the excess while it is still fresh; then let it dry well and hollow it out. Then do the same for the other half and join it to this one, attaching it with liquid varnish and glass, and let it dry for 15 days. But before you join these shells together, gild the inside <note>original: "doratura di dentro"</note> and clear out all the hollows. Then varnish it three times; or rather, apply verdigris, varnish, and aloe everywhere. Then attach them, let them dry, and put on one or two rings to hold the cord of the flask.

## Folio 96 (recto)

<margin>
the motion,
the movement
imparted by the
motion of the water
that is poured
from above through
the air moved
along a line
formed below
</margin>

Those [bodies] which are within,
moved by the motion
of the water that
is poured from above
through the air,
moved along a line
formed below;
and similarly the motion
of the air which shall be
moved within the water.

Weights that lower themselves shall be moved
by the weight of a single force;
they shall be moved through equal
spaces in equal times,
and this will occur when the line
along which they descend has reached
the perpendicular motion, or through spaces
proportioned to their obliquity <note>original: "obliquisstà". This refers to the slant or inclination of the path of descent; Leonardo is observing how the angle of a slope affects the speed of a falling object.</note>;
which weights shall be of equal weight
and shall move equal weights in equal spaces
in equal times;
as will be the case with two equal weights, one within the other,
moving from one another for equal times
and through equal spaces.

The motions of bodies shall be of equal
velocity <note>original: "velloçità"</note> when the motions of their movers
shall be equal, and the
line of their motion is similar, or when
their paths are equal.

## Folio 96 (verso)

The water that is moved through the air
shall have as much velocity
as the air moved within
the water.

Weights that move
through the air: the heavier
weights shall be so much faster,
provided they are
of equal volume.

For every weight within
the limits of its
velocity and slowness,
its motion shall be equal
through equal spaces...

Here for the (6th) I say that it amounts to the same to multiply <note>original: "avltiplicare"</note> **d b** against **a d** by the part **d b** and add above the sum the square of **b c**, as to multiply **d c** by itself —

| | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | | | | 10 | | | 16 | | | | | | |
| | | 4 | | | 6 | | | 6 | | | | | |
| d | | | b | | | c | | | | a | | | |

| | | | | | | | | | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | | | | | | | | | | | | 64 | |
| | | | | | | | | | | | | 36 | |
| | | | | | | | | | | | | --- | |
| | | | | | | | | | | | | 100 | |

From 4 times 16 makes 64 for **a d b** against **a d**; then for **b c** you will say 6 times 6 makes 36; add it with 64. It makes exactly 100; then multiply **d c** by itself, which is 10 times 10, it makes likewise 100 —

<note>Diagram 1 labeled: e d b a c. Diagram 2 labeled: o e d b n a h m c. These represent the geometric construction used to prove the Pythagorean theorem.</note>

These two triangles [in the first figure] are equal because the base **e a** of the one is equal to the base **a b** of the other, because they are sides of the square **a b o e** below [in the second figure]; and likewise the sides **d a** of the one are equal to the side **a c** of the other, because they are sides of the larger square **d a c h**, and the angle **e a b** and the angle **d a c** are right angles. If one adds the triangle **e a n** to both, they will be as much more than right angles as is the size of the said triangle **e a n**; and by the fourth [proposition] of the first [book], the side **d b** will be equal to the side **e c**.

And the squares <note>Leonardo uses "quadrati" (squares) here, but he is likely referring to the rectangles formed within the larger construction.</note> **n a**, **m c**, and likewise **a b**, **e o** are equal because each of them is double its triangle by the 23rd [proposition], <note>Likely referring to the theorem that a parallelogram is double a triangle on the same base and between the same parallels.</note> which shows their bases to be common to the triangle and to the square [rectangle].

<header>— FOLIO 14 (recto). —</header>

### [WATER CONDUITS].

-> b <-
-> a <-
-> c <-
-> d <-

> It is in the nature of things that a single conduit can throw [water] an infinite distance from itself, because the height occupied by the water that presses down upon such an outlet can be infinite; as does the conduit **b a q**, which can be imagined to be of infinite height. And at every degree of height, the conduit **a c** gains degrees of distance in its outward throw. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of "head pressure," where the height of a water column determines the velocity and distance of the stream at the bottom.</note>

---

<header>— FOLIO 14 (verso). —</header>

### [MOVEMENT AND IMPACT].

<note>The following text is written upside down in the original manuscript.</note>

-> ON MOVEMENT AND IMPACT. <-

> If someone descends step by step, making a jump from one to the next, and you add together all the powers of the impacts <note>original: "percussioni"</note> and the weights of such jumps, you will find them to be equal to the total impact and weight that such a man would produce if he fell in a straight vertical line from the head to the foot of the height of the said stairs.
> 
> Furthermore, if such a man fell from a height, striking level by level upon objects that would bend like a spring, so that the impact from one to the next was small, you would find that by the final part of his descent, the man would have his impact diminished compared to that which he would have made in a free vertical line, by as much as the sum of all the impacts combined that were given at each step of the said descent upon the aforementioned springs. <note>Leonardo is exploring the conservation of energy and momentum, observing that many small impacts can dissipate the force of a single large fall.</note>

---

<header>— FOLIO 15 (recto). —</header>

### [GUNS. — MAXIM. — EXPERIENCE].

> Test the strength <note>original: "valitudine"</note> of the thinnest gun barrel <note>original: "canna di scoppietto" — a scoppietto was an early type of hand-cannon or light firearm.</note> that you can.
> 
> He who does not value life does not deserve it. <margin>Cited in J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, No. 1140, note 19.</margin>
> 
> A man throws a loop of rope 25 cubits <note>original: "braccia" — a measurement of roughly 23 inches / 58 cm.</note> to the horns of an ox and catches it. I ask in what manner this man twirls the whole rope and holds the binding in the other hand...

<note>The term "braccia" refers to a common Florentine unit of measure. The ox-roping question appears to be a study of mechanics and human movement.</note>

<summary>Leonardo investigates the physics of water pressure in pipes and the mechanics of impact, concluding that the sum of multiple small impacts equals one large vertical fall. The page also includes a famous moral aphorism on life and a practical observation on firearm strength.</summary>

<keywords>hydraulics, water pressure, percussion, impact force, gravity, mechanics, ethics, firearms, measurement</keywords>

--- FOLIO 14 (verso). ---

<note>Textual study of the physics of the circle and the architectural properties of the arch.</note>

The circle is of such a nature
that in whatever part of its circumference
a force reaches, that force travels
toward the center, and from there it <unclear>directs itself</unclear> through
the diameter of said circle to that part
of the circumference which is opposite the first
point of impact. And this is caused because every
ball of glass or other solid material strikes
from whatever direction it may hit within a circle
that is hollow within itself; such is the truth.

But if, however, the stones <note>original: "sassi"</note>
were arranged along the circumference of the circle
so that the inside were empty, I say for this reason
that it is true [they hold], because every stone supports
its neighbor with its shoulder <note>original: "spalla", referring to the lateral surface of a wedge-shaped stone in an arch</note>; and because of this, such motion
toward the center meets and they impede
one another. They cannot move toward the center, so that
by remaining in such a state of motion, the arch stands
with great resistance.

### [MECHANICS].

Whether a thing is to be lifted or pulled makes a great difference in difficulty for its mover; in fact, if it is a thousand pounds, in lifting it—simply pulling it up <note>original: "sen consenpli ce", likely meaning "semplicemente" or "simply"</note>—it shows itself to be **one thousand** pounds. But if it is dragged, [the resistance] decreases by 1/3; and if it is pulled with wheels, it decreases by as many degrees as the size of the wheels, and also according to the number of wheels multiplied. And one can, with the same time and power, make the same journey with different quantities of time and power; and also in the same time and motion. This increase [in efficiency] is achieved only with the wheels where the poles <note>original: "poli", referring here to the axles or pivots of the wheels</note> are placed, which are to be multiplied.

---

Whether the object is raised or pulled gives a great difference in difficulty to its mover; indeed, if it is a thousand pounds, when one raises it by simply pulling it, it shows itself with these thousand pounds, and if it is dragged, it decreases by 1/3; and if it is pulled with wheels, it decreases by as many degrees as are the sizes of the wheels, and also according to the number of wheels multiplied. And the same journey can be made with various quantities of time and power, as well as in the same times and movements; and it only increases with the wheels, where the poles are placed which have to be multiplied.

# [BACKGROUNDS — CONTRASTS]

### ON COMMON PERSPECTIVE

->ON COMMON PERSPECTIVE.<-

An object of uniform thickness and color that is seen against a background of non-uniform color will appear to be of non-uniform thickness. <note>Leonardo is describing an optical illusion where a high-contrast background makes the edges of an object seem to "bleed" or recede, changing its perceived width.</note>

And if an object of uniform thickness and various colors is seen against a background of uniform color, the object itself will appear to be of varying thickness.

The greater the variety in the colors of the background or of the object seen against that background, the more varied their thicknesses will appear to be, even if the objects seen against the background are actually of equal thickness.

<margin>Notes 1, 2, and 3 refer to the J.P. Richter edition of Leonardo's notebooks, volume 1, section 241.</margin>

---

# [THE LAWS OF NATURE — OBJECTS ON A BACKGROUND]

Nature is full of infinite laws <note>original: "ragioni"; in this context, Leonardo refers to the logical principles or governing "reasons" behind natural phenomena</note> that were never part of human experience.

A dark object seen against a light background will appear smaller than it actually is.

A light object seen against a background will appear larger in shape than when it is seen against a background of a darker color. <note>This is the phenomenon of irradiation: bright light seems to spread beyond its physical boundaries into the surrounding darkness.</note>

<margin>
1. Richter, vol. 2, section 1151.
2, 3. Richter, vol. 1, section 242.
</margin>

->EXPERIMENT ON THE INCREASE AND<-
->DECREASE OF THE PUPIL THROUGH THE MOVEMENT OF THE SUN<-
->OR OTHER LUMINOUS BODIES —<-

(The darker the sky, the larger the stars will appear to be.) And if you illuminate the surrounding air <note>original: "il mezo," referring to the medium or environment through which one sees</note>, those stars will appear smaller. This change arises solely from the pupil, which expands and contracts according to the brightness of the environment between the eye and the luminous body.

Let the experiment be performed with a candle placed above the head at the same time you look at such a star; then, gradually lower the candle little by little until it is near the line of sight that travels from the star to the eye. You will then see the star diminish so much that you will almost lose sight of it. <note>This is a classic demonstration of "glare" or "disability glare," where a nearby bright light source causes the pupil to constrict, making it harder to see a faint distant light.</note>

— The pupil of the eye, being in the open air, changes its degree of size with every degree of movement made by the sun. <note>Leonardo notes that as the sun moves and light intensity changes, the eye constantly adapts.</note>

### [ELEMENTS — CENTER OF GRAVITY — SCREWS]

According to the ninth [proposition] of the 2nd [book] of the *Elements* <note>Leonardo likely refers to a medieval edition of a work on statics, such as the *De ponderibus* attributed to Jordanus de Nemore or Euclid's work on geometry.</note> which says the center of every suspended gravity stops beneath the center of its support—therefore:

— The "central line" is defined as that which is imagined as a straight line from the object to the center of the world <note>In the Aristotelian view, the "center of the world" was the center of the Earth, the destination of all falling things.</note>.

— The center of every suspended gravity desires to unite with the central line of its support.

— And that suspended gravity which by accident is further removed from the central line of its support will acquire more force <note>term: "force" (forza). In this context, Leonardo is describing leverage or torque—the tendency of a weight to cause rotation when placed far from its pivot.</note> in addition to its natural weight.

Now, to conclude, I say that the water in the screws places the center of its gravity on the central line of its pole, and every tiny weight added to one of the sides will be the cause of its motion. Therefore, $a$, which has the weight above its poles and always touches at a point, will move more easily than $c$.

<margin>always at a point will be of easier motion than c</margin>

## [MECHANICS (SCREWS AND GEARS)]

### FOLIO 25 (verso)

When the wheel turns its <term>pinion<note>original: "carello"; translated as "coussinet" in the French transcription. In this context, it refers to a small gear or roller that meshes with a larger wheel.</note></term> with the same ease that the pinion turns its wheel, then their motor <note>the source of power</note> provides no mechanical advantage. But the greater the difference [between them], the more advantage the motor will have, specifically when that which moves is able to move the other but cannot be moved by it in return—such as the **worm gear** <note>original: "vite sanza fine" (endless screw)</note> with which the motor moves the wheel, while the wheel will never be able to move such a screw.

---

When the wheel turns its pinion with the ease with which the pinion turns its wheel, then their motor is without advantage. But the greater the difference, the more advantage the motor will have, when that which moves shall move and cannot be moved by the other; like the worm gear with which the motor moves the wheel, while the wheel will never move such a screw.

## [MECHANICS (GEARS)]

### FOLIO 26 (verso)

The closer the <term>pinion<note>original: "rochetta"</note></term> is situated to the diameter <note>the centerline of the wheel</note>, the less <term>friction<note>original: "confregatione"</note></term> the tooth of the wheel will create along the length of the <term>spindle<note>original: "fusello"; the rods or rungs of a lantern gear.</note></term> of said pinion; and conversely, there will be greater friction the further the pinion is removed from the said diameter of the wheel.
The simple, direct turn made by the screw is that which will be turned by the wheel further from the diameter than any other kind of pinion.
But such a pinion can never provide motion to the wheel with the same ease that the wheel provides a turn to it.

---

The closer the pinion is situated to the diameter, the less will be the friction that the tooth of the wheel makes on the length of the spindle [the rods] of said pinion, and reciprocally there will be a greater friction the further the pinion is from said wheel diameter.
The simple direct turn made of the screw is that which will be made by the wheel further from the diameter than any other kind of pinion.
But that pinion can never give motion to the wheel with the ease with which the wheel makes it turn.

<note>Leonardo's notes here are written in his famous mirror script, where he writes from right to left. In these passages, he is investigating optics—specifically how the distance of a mirror affects the perceived speed of a reflection or the visual ray itself.</note>
