one must ask: the more the motion 
of the mirror approaches that of the

it will be, and the slower it will be,
because of the breaking of the motion 
of the sight from the 
mirror.

> Here, one only takes into account the force of the friction <note>original: "confregatione" — an archaic term for the rubbing or friction between two surfaces.</note> created by the pivot <term>polo: the pole or pivot point around which a mechanism rotates</term> against the place where it rubs; therefore, you shall make the pivot thin and the support easy to rotate.
>
> The bell <note>original: "lacanpa nada" — a dialectal or idiosyncratic spelling of "la campana."</note> distributes its weight equally along the central line of its pivot. For this reason, it is demonstrated that if the thickness of such a pivot were reduced to a mathematical line <note>Leonardo refers to a "mathematical line" as an idealized geometric line with no physical width, which would theoretically eliminate friction.</note>, a weight of almost infinite smallness would set such a weight in motion to balance equal weights around its pivot. Therefore, with the water being of equal weight relative to pivot **a**, as shown at **m** and **f** with the central line **a-n**, a small weight placed at **t** moves the water casing from its original position; it does so successively, leaving the water in its position, equally heavy around its pivot — 4.

--- FOLIO 45 (recto). ---

[The Knife-Grinder's Wheel].

The axle <note>original: "polo", literally "pole," referring here to the central pivot or spindle.</note> is worn down more during the stroke where its motor <note>The "motor" in Leonardo's mechanics is the source of power—in this case, the grinder's leg.</note> exerts greater force—as is shown by the knife grinders <note>original: "arrotatori" / "rémouleurs". Traveling craftsmen who sharpened blades on a foot-pedal-powered stone.</note> who travel through the cities.

Every axle is worn down on the side where its motor gives it more force. See the one who turns the wheel for knives with his feet; where he pushes his foot downward, he gives the beginning to the force, which then generates the motion of an entire turn. It is clearly understood that as this motion becomes more distant from its cause, it becomes slower and wears its support less. Every time the motion is re-caused and the force is renewed by the foot with an impulse <note>original: "impeto". Leonardo uses this to mean the kinetic energy or momentum provided by the physical push.</note>, the support is worn down again under that impulse, and thus that axle goes on wearing unequally.

<summary>Leonardo examines the mechanics of friction, impulse, and proportion, using the example of a traveling knife-grinder's wheel to illustrate how uneven force causes uneven wear on an axle. He also calculates the flight of rockets based on their physical dimensions and the deformation of wheels under weight.</summary>
<keywords>dynamics, reflected motion, ballistics, proportions, mechanical wear, friction, knife-grinder, physics of motion, braccio, impetus</keywords>

## [LANDSCAPE (DISTANT COLORS)]

->ON LANDSCAPES.<-

The dark colors of the shadows of mountains at great distances take on a more beautiful and purer azure <note>original: "azzurro"</note> than their illuminated parts. From this it follows that when the rock of a mountain is reddish, its illuminated parts appear brownish-gray <note>original: "bisa" or "bise", a dark, neutral color</note>; and the more it is illuminated, the more it will take on its own natural color.

---

<margin>Besides the non-original pagination, this page bears the number 11, and at the bottom, upside down: 20.</margin>

## [TIN PLATE. — PICTORIAL ACTIONS]

->Method for making a thin and even tin plate.<-

These must be made of bell metal <note>a hard bronze alloy used for casting bells</note> to ensure they are harder, and fitted onto square iron shafts so they do not twist. Thus, as one turns, the other will rotate, and they will flatten a tin plate about half a <term>braccio<gloss>An Italian unit of measurement based on the length of an arm, approximately 23 inches</gloss></term> wide.

The movements <note>or poses</note> for painters are best observed in players, especially those of ball, tennis, or <term>pall-mall<gloss>A historical game where a ball is struck with a mallet through a hoop</gloss></term>, when they are competing together; these are better than in any other place or action.

---

<margin>The words on this page differ from Leonardo da Vinci’s ordinary handwriting; if they are by his hand, perhaps they are related to the strange words found here and there in some of his other manuscripts (for example: later, folio 122 [74] verso, and the Codex Atlanticus, folios 4 recto and verso, 19 recto), which bear an analogy to oriental scripts whose meaning has not yet been determined, and which might well have belonged to some secret writing. (Cf. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, 1379, note.) See also Manuscript B, folio 3 verso.</margin>

How to make these 4 teeth or <term>rungs<gloss>vertical rods in a gear, often called "pioli"</gloss></term> of the <term>pinion<gloss>original: "rondegnio," a cylindrical gear consisting of two discs joined by rods or rungs, common in mill machinery</gloss></term> descend into the channels <note>the grooves of a screw or worm gear</note>; what ratio <note>original: "ragione"</note> is maintained in such a way that, by moving from one side to the other, it can stop without hindrance. ### — FOLIO 49 [1] (verso). —
[DATE. — OPTICS. — THE BEE AS FRAUD. — CARNIVAL COSTUME].

Monday I bought 46 <term>braccia<gloss>An Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm, literally "arms."</gloss></term> of cloth for 13 lire 14 <term>soldi<gloss>A subunit of the lira currency.</gloss></term> and 1/2 on the 17th day of October 1497.

The closer an object comes to the eye, the larger the angle it presents; and the image of that thing does the opposite; for the closer it is measured to the eye, the smaller the figure it appears. <note>Leonardo is exploring the geometry of perspective and how the perceived size of an object changes relative to the distance from the pupil.</note>
The <unclear>wasp</unclear> <insert>bee</insert> can be compared to fraud, because it has honey in its mouth and poison in its behind. <note>original Italian: "Laue pechia" [l'ape] / original French: "l'abeille". This is a classic Renaissance "Bestiary" style moralization.</note>

->CARNIVAL COSTUME<-

To make a beautiful garment, take fine cloth and give it a scented varnish made of turpentine oil and <term>kermes<gloss>original: "vernice in grane," a red dye derived from insects, used here as a coloring agent for the varnish.</gloss></term>; then use a perforated stencil, which should be wetted so that it does not stick. This stencil should be made with patterns of knots which are then filled with black millet, and the field with white millet.

2. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, 1524. ".... 13 lire 14 s 1/2..."
3. Idem, vol. I, 704 ".... and of varnish in grain, with a pierced stencil.... this stencil may be made in a pattern of knots.... "
</margin>

### FOLIO 49 [1] (verso)

<note>Study on mechanics and force. Originally written in Leonardo's famous mirror script, here translated from the transcribed Italian.</note>

<note>A small diagram at the top illustrates a line of motion, likely representing a weight being pushed.</note>

Because every motion is made in a straight line.

If r + 1 be motion in a straight line:

As much as the force is, so is the resistance.
The reason is this: if you
push a weight along a flat plane,
the resistance of the weight 
combined with the resistance of the surface will be 
equal to the power of the force that
pushes it in that same manner.

If you push a weight along a straight line,
in which line is created as much resistance
as there is force pushing it
in that same manner:

As much as the force is, so is the resistance.
The reason is this: if you
push a weight along a flat plane,
the resistance of the weight 
combined with the resistance of the surface will be 
equal to the power of the force that
pushes it.
<note>Leonardo is exploring the balance of forces. He suggests that for an object to move at a constant rate, the force applied must precisely overcome the opposing friction (the "resistance of the site") and the weight of the object itself.</note>

## [DOG RINGING A BELL].

And if you wanted the pivot <note>original: "polo"</note> of the bell to have no point of leverage in its movement, but for the weight of the bell to place that pivot in the center, and for it to be balanced by as much weight as that of the bell with as much distance above the said pivot, one pound of force with the movement of an ounce <term>once; a unit of weight or measurement</term> will move a weight of 746,480 in the same movement and time that is usually used to ring another bell for a good ordinary occasion; and with a thread of thin twine to make it, as a game, be rung by a dog trained for that—

[Continued from folio 57 [9] recto:] and if you wanted the pivot <note>original: "pôle"</note> of the bell to have no lever at its movement, but for the weight of the bell to put this pivot in the middle, and for there to be compensation for the weight the bell has by an equal distance above this pivot, one pound of force with the movement of one ounce will move a weight of 746,480 in the same movements and time as one is accustomed to ring for a good ordinary occasion. Another bell is with a thread of fine twine, [in such a way] as to make it be rung for a game by a dog accustomed to it.

### [Wonderful Movement. — Bells, Mechanics].

[1st figure (at the bottom:)] m

This rule will produce a circular motion of such durability that it will appear marvelous and beyond nature <note>original: "fori di natura"; Leonardo often uses this to describe phenomena that seem to defy common experience, such as perpetual motion or extreme efficiency</note>, because it will continue to move long after the movement of its motor [has stopped]. ### — FOLIO 57 [9] (*verso*) —

Water
— The fish in the water does not weigh as much [as it does in air], as it lacks [weight] in proportion to the deficiency caused by the measurements <note>original: "mātichon", likely a contraction for "menticioni" or "misurazioni" (measurements/calculations)</note>... 18.

I say that if air is inside a gold ball, that ball in the air will weigh less because of the air [inside it]; [but] over the water it will weigh [less] because of its included air—that is, because of the air that is inside that ball. I maintain that it does not weigh less because of the parts [of air] inside it, but because of the air that is missing <note>Leonardo is grappling with the concept of displacement: the weight of the object is reduced by the weight of the fluid it displaces</note>... the weight of the air that is missing... the manner of the missing air.

<margin>
If you pull a weight upwards, as it gradually comes out of the water, it will weigh more as it leaves the water, as the help of the water is gradually lacking.
</margin>

### — FOLIO 58 [10] (*recto*) —

Every heavy body <note>original: "grave"; a technical term for an object with mass</note> moves along the shortest line toward its universal center <note>original: "ūiuersale cētro"; the center of gravity, which Leonardo identifies with the center of the world</note> in the air; and through the universal mind <note>or "universally," referring to a general physical law</note>, a heavy thing does not rest except at one center. ### [Proportions of Powers and Resistances]

->ON THE PROPORTION OF MOVEMENTS<-
->OR POWERS AND RESISTANCES<-
<note>original: "DE PROPORTIONE DIMOTI O POTENTIE O RESISTENTIE"</note>

If upon a soft or liquid body two moving objects are placed or joined, one being double the weight of the other and both of equal shape, I ask which will sink further in—the larger or the smaller?

One will not go further than the other, because every power <term>power: in this context, the downward force or pressure exerted by the weight</term> finds a resistance equal to its point of contact.

It is true that I might perhaps contradict myself; indeed:
If one cube is eight times another in shape and weight, the larger one has a base four times greater than the smaller; so that, taking a fourth part of the base of the larger, it is equal to the base of the smaller. But the quantity [of weight] that is above the base of the larger is twice as high as the small cube, and it will sink twice as much. Therefore, the whole larger cube [will sink more than] the smaller, the smaller having a diameter half that of the larger...

### [THE MEETING OF THREE WATERS]

Where three waters meet together, a sudden depth will be created because they rise up and acquire weight; then, moving with great force, this weight is broken as it strikes against the bottom.

<note>original: "Dove 3 acque sisconteranno..." — Leonardo is describing how converging currents create turbulence that scours the riverbed, forming deep pools.</note>

---

### [RIVER FALLS]

If the bottom of the riverbed from which the water falls is hollow in the middle, the water moving from the sides will direct itself toward that center and will rise up before it falls.

If a flowing river is hindered by some reef, it will leap upward, and the place struck by its fall will take on the nature of a well.

<margin>1. See below, folio 72 [24] recto, 7th line of the manuscript; F. Cardinali, book one, chapter 1, p. 273, line 21.</margin>

<note>The "nature of a well" refers to a plunge pool, the deep basin carved out at the foot of a waterfall or obstacle by the sheer force of the descending water.</note>

— Men will pursue the very thing they fear most. — <note>That is to say: they will live in misery (frugality) so as not to fall into misery (poverty).</note>
— Disunited things will unite and receive such virtue within themselves that they will restore lost memory to men. — <note>That is to say: sheets of paper (or papyrus) which are made of separated fibers and keep the memory of the deeds and facts of men.</note>
— One will see the bones of the dead, with swift motion, determine the fortune of him who moves them. — <note>Dice (traditionally made of bone).</note>
— The horns of oxen. The oxen will defend the fire from its death with their horns. — <note>Lanterns; in Leonardo's time, the transparent panes of lanterns were often made of thin, shaved horn.</note>
— The forests will give birth to children who will be the cause of their death. — <note>The wooden handle of the ax.</note>

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1301.
2. Mr. Richter, in publishing this passage and a similar one from the Atlantic Manuscript, explained them by noting that lanterns were formerly made in Italy out of horn (vol. II, nos. 1295, 35, note, p. 357).</margin>

->— FOLIO 63 [15] (verso). —<-

**An extreme matter**
In that same time, a great part of the human race will be destroyed, proceeding from one to another.
The food shall be taken from many of those who were the cause of their life <note>original: "uita"; likely referring to children taking nourishment from their parents, or perhaps the harvest.</note> — or the food shall be taken from those who were the cause of their death.
Those who were bones shall come out of their graves and shall be seen walking, making no movement of their own through long fatigue. <note>This riddle refers to **leather shoes** or **clothing** made from animal skins; the "bones" are the human feet moving within the dead skins.</note>
Those who were placed under the earth with great toil shall emerge from beneath the earth.
Those who were placed under the earth with the greatest love shall be seen. <note>This refers to **sowing seeds** or **planting crops**, which "die" in the ground only to be reborn as food.</note>

->— FOLIO 64 [16] (recto). —<-

**Bodies that have no [soul]**
Of those who from great glory shall arrive at ill repute, whose works shall be one within the other with ill repute. <note>This may refer to **books** or **writings** that are criticized or suppressed.</note>
These are those who will die while alive; the soul will be dead within the flesh. They will leave a stench behind them. The smoke shall be the skins of animals. <note>A description of **ignorant people** or perhaps **parchment** (animal skins) being burned.</note>
A way shall be given to men to speak and respond to one another from the farthest countries, and one to the other without a voice. <note>This refers to **writing letters** or correspondence on parchment.</note>

**A matter of those who eat**
Many things shall be given to eat to those which have no feeling. <note>This refers to **ovens** being fed wood or **purses** being filled with coins.</note>
A human voice shall come out through the mouth of a man. <note>This refers to **musical instruments**, such as flutes or whistles, which produce sound through human breath.</note>

Appropriate [things] which have no [feeling].
There will be men, one of whom will be... they will be dead for "flowers of wines." <note>original: "fior uini". This is a pun on **florins** (fiorini), the gold coins of Florence. Leonardo is describing people killing or dying for money.</note>
And they shall not smell the stench of the dog because of the "flowers of wines."
**Of the speech of animals**
Those which are placed [in hand] will be struck by many verses, and many will be seen running to the aid of one another with "flowers of wines." <note>This refers to **writing with quills** (from animals) to conduct business or trade.</note>
And it shall be extended among many; it shall be without words; one sign of love shall be extended from one to another and shall be understood without a word.

**An extreme matter**
Many shall have arrived under the earth; they shall be seen in the limbs of those who see them; it shall be through the love of those in whose limbs they shall be. <note>This likely refers to **ancestors** or the **dead** whose traits or "limbs" are seen in their living descendants.</note>

Those shall be seen killed by those who cannot break the limbs of those who shall be seen; through smoke and through flame, many killed shall be seen. <note>This describes the effects of **firearms or artillery**, where men are killed from a distance by fire and smoke.</note>

**The flowers of wines** <note>Florins/Money</note>
They shall come in one; many shall be dead, the "flowers of wines." <note>The spending or loss of gold coins.</note>

### — FOLIO 65 [17] (verso) ¹. —

## [ ALLEGORICAL PREDICTIONS ].

[Upside down:]

->OF BEATEN WALNUT TREES<-

Those who have done best will be beaten the most, and their children taken and flayed or stripped, and their bones broken and shattered. <note>Leonardo is describing the harvesting of walnuts, which are beaten from the tree with poles, husked, and then have their shells cracked.</note>

->OF SCULPTURES<-

O woe is me! Whom do I see? The Savior crucified once again! <note>A reference to the act of carving or casting a crucifix.</note>

->OF THE MOUTH OF MAN, WHICH IS A TOMB<-

Great noises shall come forth from the tombs of those who died a wretched and violent death. <note>This riddle suggests that the human mouth is a "tomb" for the animals we eat; the "noises" are the sounds of human speech or perhaps indigestion.</note>

->OF THE BEAUTIFUL SKINS OF ANIMALS WHICH RETAIN THE SENSE OF TOUCH, WHICH ARE UPON WRITINGS<-

The more one speaks with skins, the garments of feeling, the more wisdom one shall acquire. <note>Referring to parchment—made from animal skins—used for writing books.</note>

->OF PRIESTS WHO HOLD THE HOST IN THEIR BODIES<-

Then almost all the tabernacles where the Body of the Lord <note>original: "Corpus Domini"</note> resides shall be seen clearly to go of their own accord through the various streets of the world. <note>A literal description of priests walking through the streets after having consumed the consecrated bread during Mass.</note>

### — FOLIO 66 [18] (recto) ¹. —

## [ ALLEGORICAL PREDICTIONS ].

[Upside down:]

— And those who feed upon the air <note>original: "l'aria"</note> shall turn night into day. — Tallow. <note>This refers to candles or lamps made of animal fat (tallow) which "consume" air to produce light.</note>

— And many terrestrial and aquatic animals shall rise among the stars. — The planets². <note>A clever pun: "Pianeta" in Italian means "planet," but it is also the name for a priest's chasuble, a vestment often embroidered with stars and images of animals.</note>

— The dead shall be seen carrying the living to various parts [of the earth]. — Chariots and ships. <note>Carts and ships are made of "dead" wood but transport living people.</note>

— From many, food shall be taken from their mouths. — The ovens. <note>Bread being pulled out of the "mouth" of an oven.</note>

— And from those whose mouths are filled by the hands of others, the food shall be snatched from their mouths. — The furnace.

2. "Pianeta" has, besides the meaning of planet, that of a chasuble, and perhaps some other meaning.
</margin>

I see Christ crucified and sold once again, and his saints martyred! <note>A critique of the commercial trade in religious art and relics.</note>

Men shall reach such a state of vileness that they will be grateful that others triumph over their ills, or over the loss of their true wealth, which is health. <note>Leonardo often expressed skepticism toward the medical profession of his day.</note>

Those who have been dead for a thousand years shall be the ones who pay the expenses of many of the living. <note>Refers to religious orders that were funded by donations and endowments established in the names of ancient saints.</note>

Many who were undone by fire *long before this time* shall take away the liberty of many men. <note>Lime is created by burning limestone in a kiln; the resulting mortar is then used to build the walls of prisons.</note>

### — FOLIO 67 [19] (recto). —

<note>A fundamental observation on inertia and the external causes of motion. Leonardo notes that objects in nature do not move themselves, but are acted upon by elements like wind or water.</note>

Nothing shall be moved by itself, if not
by the movement of another force, and this arises
either through the movement of the wind or the movement of the water,

by a weight it shall be moved by a force,
it shall be moved by another force,
it shall be moved by another force,
by a weight it shall be moved by a
force of the wind.

<term>mossa (movement/impulse)</term>: Leonardo uses this to describe the act of being set in motion.
<term>rinchontro (opposition/encounter)</term>: Refers to the resistance or the meeting of two forces.
<term>polso (impulse/pulse)</term>: A term for a sudden or rhythmic application of force, like the beating of a heart.

<summary>These folios document Leonardo's observations on the physics of motion, specifically how external forces like wind, water, and weight act upon objects, and how different environments offer varying levels of resistance.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous notes on the mechanics of motion and impulse (Folios 65-66), these pages apply those principles of physics to the natural world—specifically the behavior of rivers (hydraulics) and the movement of wind (aerodynamics). Leonardo shifts from abstract mechanical balls to the concrete study of how water and air interact with physical obstacles like rocks and mountains.</meta>

## — FOLIO 67 [19] (verso). —
->[A ROCK IN A RIVER].<-

[Figure: a]
If a rock in the river rises above the flow and divides the course of the water, which then reunites after this rock, the interval found between the rock and the point where the water reunites will be a place where sand is deposited. <note>Leonardo is describing the formation of a sandbar in the low-pressure zone (wake) behind an obstacle.</note>

But if the rock that divides the course of the water is covered by the flowing water only on its lower parts <note>i.e., it is partially submerged or the water flows over the top</note>, the water that passes over it will fall behind it, carving out the ground at its base and causing it to turn; and the water that plunges into this hollow rotates vertiginously beneath and above, because the reunification of the two streams—previously divided by the rock—does not immediately allow the water to continue on its journey. <note>original: "non lasscia subito scorere lacacq assuo viago"</note>

---

## — FOLIO 68 [20] (recto). —
->[MOTION. — RIVERS].<-

— Every natural and continuous motion desires to preserve its course along the line of its origin; that is, in whatever place it varies, it seeks its original principle. <note>This is an early observation of inertia: the tendency of an object or fluid in motion to continue in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force.</note>
This aforementioned motion occurs in the courses of rivers, which always fight against and consume whatever opposes the straightness of their course.
— But if the rivers were straight, with equal width, depth, and slope, you would find that in every degree of motion they would acquire degrees of velocity.
Hence, where there is a change or variety in the slope, there will be a variety in the flow—and where it flows less in equal width, it becomes deeper—and where the slope is equal, where it widens more, it slows down more. Therefore, the waters which desired a straight course and to become faster in every part of their motion, finding the places through which they pass wider and deeper, slow down and break the bottom and the bank.

---

## — FOLIO 68 [20] (verso). —
->[WATER. — WIND. — AUGUSTUS IN GAUL].<-

— The movement of the water's rebound will be faster than that of the initial strike when the water that strikes is heavily mixed with air. <note>Leonardo is observing how aeration—bubbles in the water—affects the force and speed of a splash.</note>
The water that issues with impetus from its waterfall onto the ground, the more it moves, the more it becomes...
[Continued from folio 69 [21] recto:] 4 — but being able to exhale [escape] above with great ease, because the intervals between the mountains are wide, the wind [?] below willingly and easily flees upwards. Note that Augustus made a vow in Gaul to the wind *Circius* because, by a similar impetus, he was on the verge of losing his army, and he built a temple there. <note>The "Circius" is a violent North-Northwest wind, known today in France as the Mistral. The Roman Emperor Augustus Caesar reportedly built a temple to this wind in the province of Gallia Narbonensis after it nearly destroyed his camp.</note>

---

## — FOLIO 69 [21] (recto). —
->[WATER. — COMPRESSIBLE AIR, MOUNTAIN WIND].<-

This eddy carves into its bottom
the entire grotto and the floor.
Passage of wind.

[Continued from folio 69 [21] verso]. Because air can be compressed, and the more it is compressed, the more it weighs compared to other air; and the more it weighs, the greater the strike it gives upon its object, as is seen with the winds that are forced from a great width to pass through a narrow mountain gorge; if they did not have an opening above, they would not fill the spaces of the things before them. <note>Leonardo is describing the Venturi effect or "canyon effect," where wind increases in speed and pressure as it is squeezed through a narrow opening.</note>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion of fluid dynamics and air flow around obstacles (Folios 67-68), Leonardo now applies these principles of "percussion" (impact) and "violent motion" to the behavior of water in canals and rivers. He explores the interaction between trapped air and water, and how the energy of currents erodes embankments and shapes riverbeds.</meta>

### — FOLIO 69 [21] (verso) —

->[WATER THAT JUMPS BECAUSE OF AIR]<-
<note>original: "EAU QUE FAIT SAUTER L'AIR"</note>

Water will jump much higher than its point of fall through a violent motion caused by the air found enclosed within the bubbles <note>original: "vessciche"</note> of the water. This air, which rises and is seen in the bubbles on the water's surface, returns to the place of impact and is once again submerged by that impact. Finding itself trapped between the water that strikes it from above and the water it pushes against below, and being compressed by such fury and percussion, the air suddenly breaks through the water that served as its cover. Like a lightning bolt <note>Leonardo compares the escape of air to a "saetta" or thunderbolt emerging from clouds.</note> exiting the clouds, this air bursts out of the water, carrying with it part of the water that originally covered it.

---

### — FOLIO 70 [22] (recto) —

->[WATER OF THE CANALS]<-

<margin>To spring forth <note>original: "scatorire"</note></margin>
<margin>
[2nd figure:] b a s
</margin>
The hump <note>a swelling or surge in the water</note> at *a* will always cause the bank to collapse at *b*. The coarse gravel will remain at *s*, followed by the fine gravel, then the sand, then the silt <note>original: "lalita," referring to fine river mud or ooze</note>; finally, the wood, roots, and leaves will remain in the places specified in the general propositions.

Water that passes from a narrow channel *p* into a wider section immediately becomes thinner and faster and strikes with impact because it finds a slope where it moves forcefully. With its momentum established, it directs itself toward the base of its bank and strikes it; after this impact, it turns upward and, with a whirling motion <term>revertiginoso <note>Leonardo's term for the turbulent, circular motion of water—eddies or vortices—that acts as an erosive force.</note></term>, goes about scraping the foundation of the bank until it returns to the surface. This scraping takes the shape of a ship's hull, beginning and ending narrow and becoming deep and wide in the middle.

<margin>
[2nd sources/figure:] b a s
</margin>
The swelling at *a* will always cause the dike to crumble at *b*, and the large gravel will remain at *s*, then the small gravel, then the sand, then the mud; then the wood and roots and leaves will remain where stated in the general propositions.

The water that becomes wider in some part of a narrow canal immediately becomes more subtle and rapid and strikes, because it finds a declivity where it moves strongly. With its course begun, it directs itself toward the foot of its bank and strikes it; then after this impact, it turns upward and moves with an "eddying" motion, digging out the foundation of the bank until it returns upward. And this digging is in the shape of a ship's keel, beginning and ending narrow, and in the middle deep and wide.

---

[2nd figure:] a b
</margin>
*A-b* represents an oblique line across the river; the falling water strikes and hollows out the area beneath the bank in the shape of a cave.

[2nd figure:] a b

*A-b* is an oblique line across the river, and by the line of the fall, it strikes and digs under the bank, in the shape of a grotto.

### — FOLIO 71 [23] (recto) —

->[WATER WHIRLPOOLS]<-

Here arise the bubblings or the upward splashes of water in the midst of the upper eddies. The question is asked whether the motion of the eddies arises because the water runs backward toward the impact of water that is lower than in any other nearby part; or whether the push of the running water in the middle of the surface's width is what, by striking the other waters, raises them and creates a "hill" of water, which then returns toward its entry into the pool; or if the water, struck by the other running water and compressed, leaps and jumps back to the place from which the current comes.

-> — FOLIO 69 [21] (verso). — <-

<note>Drawing of turbulent water or a whirlpool at the top of the folio, showing swirling currents and foam.</note>

Water that is pushed through a narrow <unclear>nozzle</unclear> or pipe will have a louder whistling sound and more foam, and will possess greater force in proportion to the greater weight of water pushing it. This is because every weight <term>weight: Leonardo uses "peso" to describe the gravitational pressure or potential energy of a body of water</term> is transformed into motion; and the greater the cause of motion, the greater the effect of motion in said water. The reason for this arises because the said water, within a narrow pipe, has no place to expand except into the air; and because the said water is heavier than air, the said air cannot support it. Thus, the water will have a greater frequency <note>referring to velocity or the intensity of flow</note> in proportion to the greater weight pushing it. Because the said water strikes against the said air, the whistling sound and the whiteness of the foam are born. This air is pushed by the force of the said water and has nowhere to go, and for this reason, it becomes trapped within the said water; the foam is born from the said air which is enclosed within the said water.

## — FOLIO 72 [24] (verso). —
### [THE BOOK OF WATER (DEFINITIONS)].

BEGINNING OF THE BOOK OF WATER.
A pool <note>original: "pelago"</note> is what is called a place that has a wide and deep shape, in which the waters remain with little motion. A whirlpool <note>original: "gorgo"</note> is of the nature of a pool, except for the variation in one part, which is that the waters entering a pool are without impact <note>original: "percussioni"</note>, and those of the whirlpool have great falls and boilings and springings made by the continual revolutions of the waters. A river is that which occupies the position of the lowest part of the valleys and flows continually. A torrent is that which flows only because of rains, and it too leads itself into the depths of the valleys and joins with rivers. A canal is said of waters regulated <note>directed</note> within embankments by human aid. Sources <note>original: "fonti"</note> is the name given to the births of rivers. A large embankment <note>original: "argine"</note> is that which, with its sudden height, resists the spreading of rivers, canals, and torrents. A high bank <note>original: "ripa"</note> is higher than an embankment. A low bank <note>original: "riva"</note> is lower than an embankment. A shore <note>original: "spiaggia"</note> is at the ultimate low point of the places that limit the waters. A lake is where the waters of rivers take on great width. -> If a barrel contains wine four cubits <term>cubit: "braccia," a traditional measurement roughly equivalent to the length of an arm, about 23 inches</term> high and it throws the wine four cubits away from itself; if, when the wine is lowering, it has descended to the height of two cubits in the barrel, will it then throw the wine through the same spout another two cubits? That is, whether the lowering of the level and the force of the jet from the spout decrease in equal proportion or not.
And if the barrel, being full, fills two jugs per hour through its spout, when the barrel was half full, it should, by this reasoning, fill only a single jug per hour—using the same spout that was pouring.
This rule, along with all others similar to it concerning waters that pour through a conduit, should be placed at the beginning of the study of instruments, in order to be able to proceed better with several rules in the testing of such instruments. <-

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's glossary of hydraulic terms, Leonardo now applies these definitions to the physical behavior of air trapped in water. ### — FOLIO 71 [23] (verso). —

Just as a club hitting <note>original: "maza della percussione," referring to a mace or heavy stick used to strike something with force</note> tree branches strips them of all their tenacity, so the impact made by air in water strips it and drives it away on every side. It is imaginable like a stone thrown into soft mud, which, splashing high, leaves a void from its impact within the water; this opening closes in a short time because of the moisture splashing upward and that which gushes from the sides of the hole, and thus it falls back and refreshes the same impact.

---

### — FOLIO 72 [24] (recto). —

The small ball of air that is submerged by the force of water is driven upward by it. The ball receives more force and velocity the greater the weight of water that stands above it. Furthermore, the air within the water becomes short and thin, growing long toward the direction in which it moves—that is, upward. This arises from the resistance the water offers to the movement of such air; thus the air, which is by nature like a club <note>Leonardo uses the analogy of a "maza" (club/mace) to describe the cohesive force or momentum of the air column</note>, is flattened between one resistance and the other—namely, the water that awaits it and the water that follows it. A ball of lead would do the same inside water, as would a ball of gold if it were not for its great hardness; or a ball of wax or other weak body within air that has great motion. And as soon as it stops, such air inside the water becomes spherical again.

---

### — FOLIO 72 [24] (verso). —

If air is pushed into water by force, that air opens up and occupies a larger space within the water than it would if it moved by its own nature downward or sideways. Thus, a large space is created inside the water that is void of water—that is, filled with this air. This air will create an equal impact in every direction through the small spaces between the small and large motions depicted within it. Or rather, within the large motions are the small ones, whereby such air moves within itself and the parts open from one another, receiving no impact from the surrounding water until that air is stopped on every side by the resistance of that same air.

---

### — FOLIO 73 [25] (recto). —

Air that opens into air is weightless, so the small motions created within it by the larger ones do not feel any weight. Thus, such air remains within the water inside its surrounding motions, which move the water within the impact between one resistance of water and the other.

<note>Drawing of a hydraulic phenomenon, possibly air bubbles rising or moving within a body of water, depicted inside a rectangular vessel or channel with a curved shaded area showing displacement or pressure gradients.</note>

All air is filled with <term>vortices</term> <note>original: "vertigine," meaning eddies, whirlpools, or circular turbulent motions</note> of movements surrounding one another. No motion can be drawn from this air that does not pass through infinite motions. Thus, like branches of a single ball of air within water or air, if it moves, it creates innumerable vortices which turn one through the other, moving faster toward the center of each vortex.

<vocab>impact (percussione), air (aria), water (acqua), vortex/whirlpool (vertigine), strips/bars (sbarra), gushes (schatunisce), greater (mazzior), spherical (spericha)</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of air bubbles and vortices in water, using mechanical analogies to describe how pressure and resistance shape fluid movement. He concludes that all air is composed of infinite, interlocking vortices that increase in speed toward their centers.</summary>
<keywords>fluid dynamics, air bubbles, vortices, percussion, resistance, hydraulics, physics of water</keywords>

### [RIVER COURSES AND FALLS]

[Continued from folio 75 [27] recto:] — Along every line starting from the center of the upwelling <note>original: "surgimento," referring to the rising or welling up of water, often after a fall or hitting an obstacle</note>, the further they descend from that upwelling, the more they spread out. And a part moves with the course of the river; consequently, it is necessary for 3 movements to occur, each of which greatly consumes the foot of the bank. Because that which descends from the height of the upwelling throws itself toward the bottom, and because such a descent is oblique, it acquires movement toward the base of the bank; and because the descent partly follows the universal [general] movement of the river, the upwelling falls by a movement tripled in descent: one [going] downward, the other toward the bank, and the other toward [following] the course of the river. And all three consume the foot of the bank by the greatest removal that can be done by such momentum; for if the river ran straight, coasting along the bank, it might find some stone that would defend a piece of that bank behind it; but this movement goes down toward the bottom, forward toward the bank, and down toward the course of the river, so that every stone is struck by three different movements and from 3 different sides. Therefore, it is necessary that if the ground is prone to being consumed, it will collapse in a short time. —

->**[Continued from folio 75 [27] recto:] along every line starting from the center of the upwelling, and the more they descend from this upwelling, the more they widen. And a part moves with the course of the river; consequently, it is necessary that 3 movements occur, which each greatly consume the foot of the bank. Because that which descends from the height of the upwelling throws itself toward the bottom and because such a descent is oblique, it acquires movement toward the bottom of the bank; and because the descent follows in part the universal [general] movement of the river, the upwelling falls by a tripled descent in movement; [going:] one downward, the other toward the bank, the other toward [according to] the course of the river. And all three consume the foot of the bank by the greatest removal that can be done by such momentum; indeed, if the river ran lengthwise, coasting the bank, it might find some stone that would defend a piece of this bank behind it; but the movement goes down toward the bottom, forward toward the bank, and down toward the course of the river, so that each stone is struck by three different movements and from 3 different sides. Therefore it is necessary that if the ground is fit to be consumed, it collapses in a short time.**<-

---

### [NARROWING AND FALLS OF RIVERS]

When the universal [general] course of rivers is narrowed at their exit from valleys and their entry through mountain gaps, then the water will surge into the width and cause a great drop and movement through said mountain narrowness; and after this, having passed the middle of this narrowness, it will create a great cavity, and then having re-entered the wide part, the depth will decrease in the same proportion as the width increases, so that they [the waters] become of equal flow. And the aforementioned depth will decrease after the leap of the waters because the gravel will accumulate under the greatest elevation of the leap <note>original: "pe salto," likely referring to the peak or primary arc of the waterfall</note> of said waters. —

[Under the 1st figure:] Let such depth be made at the exit from the narrow part and the entry into the wide part.

[Under the 2nd figure:] If the fall is of the same width as the river, the water that strikes the bottom will jump back up, and then fall back [Continued on folio 74 [26] verso].

->**When the universal [general] course of rivers is narrowed at their exit from the valleys, and at their entry through the mountain gaps, then the water will engorge itself in the width and will have much lowering and movement through the said narrowness of the mountains, and after this and having passed the middle of this narrowness it will make a great cavity, and then having re-entered the wide part, it will lack depth in such proportion as the wide part grows, so that they [the waters] become of equal flow. And the aforementioned depth will be lacking after the leap of the waters because the gravel will accumulate under the greatest elevation of the leap of the said waters.**<-

# — FOLIO 75 [27] (verso). —

## [WATERS OF THE FLORENCE MILL].

<margin>[Below the figure:] little mill of Florence <note>original: "molinuzo di firenze"</note></margin>
<margin>[At the top:]</margin> This water, in its general descent, turns at a right angle; but during floods, it moves in a straight line. And the impact <note>original: "percussione"</note> is so powerful that, by gouging, it carries away stones with its current, rolling them over the bed of other stones. Thus the water, following its leap beyond its surface, leaves the stones it has pushed at the edge of the mound. 
But when the depth decreases or the floods fail, the water cannot pass over the mound that was formed from gravel; thus it turns back into its original course, created by the fall of the other water which overflows at the weir <note>original: "pesscaia", a dam or embankment used to direct water or catch fish.</note> that creates such a hollow in the place where it falls.

### Little mill of Florence.
<margin>[At the top:]</margin> This water, in its general descent, takes a right angle; but in floods, it goes straight. And the impact is so powerful that by digging it carries away the stones with its flow, rolling other stones onto the shore; and thus the water, following the jump out of its surface, leaves the stones pushed to the extremity of the mound.
But when the bottom or the floods have failed, the water cannot go beyond the hill that had been made of gravel, so that it turns into its first course, made by the fall of the other water which overflows at the weir that such a hollow makes at the place where it [the water] falls.

## [CONTINUOUS AND DISCRETE IMPACTS].

The lines of movements made by bodies that strike one another are transformed into each other after the said impact, as much in <term>continuous quantity</term> <note>A term from Aristotelian physics referring to unbroken mass or flow, like water.</note> with continuous impact, as in <term>discrete quantity</term> <note>Referring to separate, individual units or objects.</note> and discrete impact.
> But if the discrete quantity is six times as much as its concurrent, the leap of the sub-sextuple <note>One-sixth the size.</note> will be 6 times more remote from the median line f-g than that of 6 times as much weight.
> And in the continuous quantity of impact, there will never be anything but equal impacts, even if the bodies moved by the waters were very unequal.
> But if in equal bodies there is unequal velocity or unequal movement before the impact, inequality will still arise from it.

The lines of movements made by the bodies that strike each other are transmuted one into the other after the said impact, as much in continuous quantity, with continuous impact, as in discrete quantity and discrete impact.
But if the discrete quantity is six times as much as its concurrent, the leap of the sub-sextuple will be 6 times further from the median line f-g than that of 6 times as much weight.
And in the continuous quantity of impact, there are never anything but equal impacts, even when the bodies moved by the waters are very unequal.
But if in equal bodies there is unequal speed or unequal movement before the impact, inequality will still be born.

Where one sees mounds rising in flowing waters, rising in the manner of eddies <note>original: "bollori", literally "boilings", used by Leonardo to describe turbulent upsurges.</note>, it is a sign of great depth from which such eddies jump back after the impact the water makes upon the bottom; and by the speed of its leap, it bores through and penetrates the other water and turns toward the surface of the running water and passes through it. ### [AIR AND WATER].

Water that, with little movement, encloses a small amount of air beneath its surface—which submerges with it—returns out of the surface with little momentum, carrying with it such a "clothing" of water <note>This refers to the thin liquid film that creates the bubble's surface.</note> that, being of equal weight to that air, stays above it in the form of a hemispherical shape.

### FOLIO 80 [32] (*verso*)

Because the moon has no light of its own, except for what it receives from the sun; if it has any [light], it is from that which the earth and the sea reflect back upon it. And that part which faces the earth receives it for itself.

### [CIRCULAR WATER — BENDS IN THE CURRENT]

If the entry of the water into the pool <note>original: "pelago," referring to a deep basin or stretch of water</note> is circular in shape, the concavity of its bottom will be lunar <note>crescent-shaped</note>, receiving the gravel within the body—or rather, between the two horns—of such a figure.

I ask whether the current will create any "elbow" <note>a sharp bend or "gomito"</note>, whether it will hollow out the bottom, the middle, or the top, and likewise regarding the "leaps" <note>surges or small falls</note> that subsequently follow against the banks of rivers, assuming the bottom is of uniform material, as well as the bank and its defenses <note>original: "ripari"</note>, and where it rises and settles; and how to apply remedies <note>to improve or repair it</note>.

---

### [WATERFALLS]

A bottom that is high in the middle, from which the water then falls from its height.

I ask what shape the water makes in various angles of descent in each of these falls, and what shape the concavity will take as the water strikes <note>original: "percotento"</note> a bottom of uniform material; and I ask what shape the gravel will take which lies after the impact <note>percussion</note> of each of these descents, and its remedies against damages <note>and how to repair the harm caused</note>.

---

### [DIRECTING RIVERS]

### ON THE METHOD OF STRAIGHTENING RIVERS THAT HAVE SLOW COURSES
Because the straighter a river is, the swifter it becomes, and it gnaws strongly and consumes the bank and the bottom; therefore, it is necessary to widen such rivers significantly, or else send them through many windings <note>tortuosities</note>, or divide them into many branches. And if the river, through many windings, becomes sluggish and marshy because of its many turns, then you must straighten it in such a way that the waters take on sufficient motion, but not so much that they ruin the cliffs or banks.

And when there is a depth near any bank, then one must <note>original: "bebe," likely "debbe"</note> fill such a place with gabions <term>gabions: wicker baskets or cages filled with rocks and earth used for erosion control</term>, along with fascines <term>fascines: bundles of sticks or brushwood used to reinforce banks</term> and gravel, so that the water does not scour <note>hollow out</note> while in motion beneath the bank. If it were to collapse the bank, the river would then create an "elbow" <note>a bend</note> in your property or villa and direct its course there.

### [LAND STRIPPED BY WATER]

When water, during floods, begins to find a place where it can run, it starts with its weak inundation to skin <note>original: "ascorticare," to strip or scour</note> and remove the lightest things, and it discharges them where the course becomes weak. As it grows, it removes heavier things like sand, and conducts them over the first materials and leaves them there. And even if the water does not grow further, yet by its perseverance <note>its continuous flow</note>, it continues to remove things bit by bit from the place where it runs; but because of their weight, it does not carry them as far forward as the first, lighter things. If it then removes even heavier things, it discharges them proportionately near to the place from which it took them.

### ON RESTORING LAND TO PLACES DISCLOSED AND STRIPPED BY WATER CURRENTS ON HILLS, MOUNTAINS, OR OTHER SHORES.
One should use the rains, or else have the convenience of other waters, to make canals or river mouths pass through places where they run with great force; these should be managed so that they become clouded <note>turbid</note> with the earth they remove. These should be adapted so that when they reach the place where you want them to discharge that earth, such water canals are divided into many small branches or "furrows" <note>original: "solchi"</note>. In this way, their fury is slowed, and the water will become clear again <note>as the sediment settles and restores the land</note>.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the erosion and sedimentation patterns of rivers, detailing how water flow creates crescent-shaped basins and how engineers can use gabions and siltation to protect and restore land.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, river management, erosion, sedimentation, gabions, fascines, alluviation, water engineering, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

The faster the object seen is moved, the less it will be recognized by the sight; and the more slowly it is moved, the better it will be recognized. And the more quickly it is moved, the less it will be recognized and seen. Slowness and speed are lacking to the sight just as they are lacking to the hearing; as if a strike <note>A sudden blow or impact</note> [were heard].

If a branch of a tree moved by the wind appeared to be a single branch when it is still, and if it is moved it will appear as many; and if it should be extremely fast, it will appear to occupy the entire space through which that branch moves. <note>Leonardo is describing the "persistence of vision," where a fast-moving object leaves a trail or seems to be in multiple places at once, like a vibrating string or a spinning wheel.</note>

---

Of those things seen by the eye, that which is closer to the central line <note>The central axis of the cone of vision</note> of the visual rays <term>visual rays<note>Leonardo followed the medieval optical theory that "rays" of light or spirit traveled between the eye and the object.</note></term> will be better seen. And of two objects that are at an equal distance from the eye, that one will be better recognized which approaches more closely to the said central line.

And of the same figure, that part will be better recognized which is closer to the said central line; and of two [parts] that are at equal distance from the central line, that one which is closer to the eye will be better recognized. And that one will be more recognized which is close to the said central line and is moved more slowly.

---

Because if the eye is immobile and the object moves before the eye, it will appear to that eye that the object moves so much faster the closer it is to that eye, and more slowly the further away it is. And this arises from the deficiency of the sight; because if the object is very far away, one cannot discern that it moves, because the image of the object moves on the sense <note>The "sense" refers to the optic nerve or the point in the brain where Leonardo believed images were processed.</note> only as much as the width of a line of the visual ray <term>visual ray<note>original: "uisuale uiso rāmo," referring to the smallest unit of the field of vision.</note></term> in the sense.

---

<note>Two diagrams showing cross-sections of water channels with variations in the bed profile.</note>

When the water descends along the bottom of some canal and encounters some irregularity <term>irregularity<note>original: "rōsura," literally an "erosion" or "gnawing" in the bed of the channel.</note></term> of the bottom, it swells up through certain spaces [above] that bottom, and then it fills it and levels it throughout, if it has no other way to pass but over a bottom...

### [RIVERS. — WATER IN A VASE (EXPERIMENT)].

By the aforementioned reasoning, it is demonstrated how rivers of equal depth and width, which collapse at their end <note>Referring to the point where a river bed drops off or forms a waterfall</note>, flow faster at the surface than at the bottom. This is because, at the drop, the water on top is faster in its fall than the water beneath it; consequently, as the upper water rests successively upon the other, it is necessary for it to move in such a way as was described—

**EXPERIMENT**
The front is made of glass; the front-facing side is the same; behind it is a wooden board.

To experiment with which part of the water—whether from the top, middle, or wherever you wish—is the water that actually reaches the exit when an opening is made at the bottom of a reservoir <note>original: 'bottino'</note>, make a vessel of straight glass plates as you see. Cloud the water with mashed paper <note>Leonardo suggests using macerated paper as a "tracer" to visualize the flow of water, a precursor to modern fluid dynamics techniques.</note> and note the movement of such particles as it pours out.

---

But if the plane were oblique, you will find that as much as one extremity is higher above the center of its base than the level one, so much more weight does it acquire beyond that center.

### [WATERFALL].

Water which falls from a narrow channel into a wide one moves with a speed that is faster in proportion to the height from which it falls relative to its own thickness.

### FOLIO 89 [41] (verso)

**[ON DISPLACEMENT AND AIR PRESSURE]**

Why as much water rises in the vessel as the volume of the stone that is placed within it. The reason is that the water which is displaced <note>original: "concaccia," meaning driven out or displaced</note> from its place by the stone will be equal to the volume of that stone; and if the stone weighed as much as its volume of water, then the water would rise as much as the weight of the stone. But because the stone weighs more, the weight of the water that rises will be less than the weight of the stone.

<margin>
Ensure that air is not lacking in the vessel, because while the water exits through the spout <note>original: "ramiuolo," a small pipe or outlet</note>, that air would become rarefied by being pulled by the weight of the water, and that weight of the water would decrease by as much as the resistance made by the pulled air, and you would not obtain the true measure of the water from the sluice <note>original: "catteratta"</note>. See also that the water from the spout does not enter into a vacuum, so that the compression of air does not come to interfere with said measurement.
</margin>

Why the water that comes from the sluice gate <note>original: "cateratta"</note> divides itself: because the part in the middle, which is without obstacle, will be faster than the lateral parts. ## [MOVEMENT AND WEIGHT]

MOVEMENT INCREASED WITH IMPETUS
AND WEIGHT

This movement is first increased with impetus <note>original: "impeto," referring to the momentum or force an object gains through motion</note> because the further the stone that moves it falls, the more it becomes rapid and heavy; secondly, the more the cord that unwinds from the part of the circle unwinds, the further it becomes from the center of the movement; therefore, the further it becomes, the more it weighs and the more impetus it acquires.

---

MOVEMENT INCREASED WITH IMPETUS
[or: lively impulse ("impeto")] AND WEIGHT.

This movement is first increased with impetus, because the further the stone that moves it [makes it go] falls, the more rapid and heavy <note>original: "grave," meaning having weight or gravity</note> it becomes; secondly, as the cord that unwinds from the side of the circle continues to unwind, it moves further from the center of motion; hence, the further it moves, the more it weighs and the more impetus it acquires.

# FOLIO 99 [51] (verso) <note>Towards the middle of the page, there is a cross, likely a reader's mark.</note>
## [Motion and Percussion. — Engines, arms and hands].

-> On Motion <-
There are some movements of movers that, in the course of achieving their motion, receive the percussion <note>In this context, "percussion" refers to the strike or impact that initiates or affects motion.</note> in the middle of their movement; and these are of great power.
<margin>[2nd figure:] b a</margin>
I ask why "field-throwers" or "whip-slings" <note>original: "lancia-campi" and "caccia-frusti"; these refer to types of staff-slings or mechanical siege engines designed to hurl projectiles.</note> have a greater range of motion than the arm alone. I say that this happens because the hand describes a much larger circle while the arm moves than the elbow does; and consequently, being moved in the same amount of time, the hand travels twice as much distance as the elbow. Therefore, the hand can be said to have double the speed of the motion of the elbow, and because of this, it throws objects further away from itself. Thus, you clearly see the elbow making half as much travel and being half as slow. It is true that if you subtract from the movement made by the hand as much as was made by the elbow, they are of equal slowness.

---

# FOLIO 100 [52] (recto).
## [Motion and Percussion].

-> On Motion <-
If the object moved by the blow of its mover received its motion from simple percussion alone, without any following-through of the motion of that striker, the object that moves would have a very short motion.

-> On Motion <-
If the act of percussion is the greatest power to be found among us, why does it not immediately drive away the thing it moves, and why does the mobile object then wait for the push <note>original: "sospinta"</note> after the percussion has been given and received?

-> On Motion <-
If a stone moved by the power of its engine <note>original: "machina"</note> follows, at the start of its motion, the total power and speed of its mover, why does it not continue with that same equality of the first motion without immediately beginning its deceleration? And if it does indeed separate immediately, what benefit is it to be so closely accompanied by such power?

---

# FOLIO 100 [52] (verso) <note>After the second paragraph, there is another cross mark.</note>.
## [Motion. — Bombards].

-> On Motion <-
The power that moves, which accompanies the mobile object for a longer time, will remove it further <margin>from that limit from which it separates itself.</margin>

-> On Motion <-
Almost universally, everything that is the cause of motion diminishes its power before it separates from the thing it moves.

-> On Motion <-
The bombard <note>An early type of cannon or mortar.</note> only increases its force because, during the longer travel the ball makes within its body <note>The barrel of the gun.</note>, more powder is ignited. It must be admitted that such catching of fire takes place over a divisible amount of time; the more parts of time it lasts, the more powder ignites, and the more the fire is compressed within such an instrument, and with more impetus and fury it expels the ball from itself.

-> On Motion <-
The question is asked: for the same travel of the mover, when does it remove the moved object further—starting with slow motion and always increasing the impetus, or starting fast and gradually slowing down, or perhaps something else?

---

# FOLIO 101 [53] (recto).
## [Motion. — Bows and Crossbows].

to plummet
-> On Motion <-
I ask if two mobile objects of equal shape, weight, and material, if they have double the speed, whether one will travel twice as far as the other or not.

-> On Motion <-
Because one sees bows or crossbows with long arms making great but slow reaches, and one sees crossbows with short, thick arms making fast but short reaches. The strikes <note>original: "percussioni"</note> of the short ones make a great [rapid] passage at the third part of their motion, while the long ones make little. In this distinction <note>original: "discretione"</note> it is necessary to demonstrate all the mathematical forces, since in these crossbows various causes occur that produce many different effects. Among them, one finds those with a great rise, those with a short one, some long and thin, others thick and short, some wide, others narrow; thus they go on varying in shapes and effects in many ways.
-> *Therefore we shall say that the more a single mover accompanies the mobile object, the further it removes it from itself.* <-

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of motion, specifically how the "accompaniment" (follow-through) of a mover affects a projectile's speed and distance. He applies these principles to human anatomy (the arm), ballistics (bombards), and archery (bows and crossbows).</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, percussion, impetus, ballistics, cannons, crossbows, lever action, velocity, acceleration</keywords>

# FOLIO 99 [51] (verso)

-> Motions <-

If the weight is equal to the force that pulls it, that weight will remain in balance; and if the weight is increased, it will lower itself; and if it is diminished, the weight will rise.

<margin>
<note>Drawing of a cross-shaped lever or balance system with weights at the ends.</note>
</margin>

By increasing the weight at the pole <note>The "pole" here refers to the pivot point or fulcrum of the scale.</note> of the balance, the balance will not be changed in the equality of its position. By increasing the weight on the arm of the balance, it will lower itself, and by decreasing it, it will rise. But if the equality of the position is to be perpetual, it must be by reason of equal weights; however, if there are both equal and unequal weights, then there will not be equality of position.

<margin>
<note>Circular diagram showing an arc with radial lines and a central point, likely analyzing angular motion or the relationship between a pivot and weights.</note>
</margin>

If the center of the circle is the pole of the balance, that balance will never be in an inequality of position by whatever weight is placed in the circle, unless the balance is removed from the pole.

<margin>
<note>Triangular geometric figure with a central vertical line, potentially a study of centers of gravity.</note>

# FOLIO 100 [52] (verso)

-> Motions <-

The reason why <term>natural motions</term> <note>In Renaissance physics, "natural motion" refers to an object moving toward its natural place, such as a heavy object falling toward the Earth.</note> go on accelerating, and <term>accidental motions</term> <note>Also known as "violent motion," this refers to motion caused by an external force, like a ball being thrown.</note> go on slowing down.

-> Motions <-

The accidental motion will be so much faster as the force that moves it is greater, and it will be so much slower as the weight that resists it is greater.

-> Motions <-

The reason why the movement of a fish in the water is faster than the movement of a bird through the air is because water is denser than air, and for this reason, it is more powerful [...] <note>Leonardo is exploring the relationship between the density of a medium and the "grip" or resistance it provides for propulsion.</note>

-> Motions <-

Air moved by force will have a uniform motion if the weight of the bird is equal to its effort.

# FOLIO 101 [53] (recto)

-> Motions <-

Why water that falls from a distance becomes thin toward the end of its motion, and why that water then falls in drops, and why the water that falls does so in a perpendicular line, and why the air that is beneath it is driven away in a straight motion and not along a twisted path. And if it wanted to flee along a twisted path, it could not flee with such speed [...] and because of this, the water opens into drops and the air interposes itself there, and the air that is inside the drops ensures that the water cannot flee in a straight line [...] <note>Leonardo provides a remarkably modern observation on fluid dynamics, noting how air resistance breaks a continuous stream of water into droplets.</note>

## — FOLIO 102 [54] (recto) —

### [BOMBARDS, PROPORTIONS. — THE AUTHORS AND EXPERIMENTS].

[Continued from folio 102 [54] verso:] 3. Saying if one thousand pounds of stone are thrown to me in 2 units of time, while you hold yourself still in your imagination at the 3-mile mark; saying also if 1,000 pounds of <term>cannonballs</term> <note>original: "ballotte"; refers to projectiles for a bombard.</note> are thrown to me, at the said limit, in 20 units of time, in how many units of time will the same power throw me a one-pound ball? And suppose if 1,000 gives me 20, what will one give me? You will find that it will give you 20/1,000 [1/50] of a unit of time, which makes about 3/50 of a unit of time. Now if one shoots the weight of a small grain of powder, experience would not send it any further than the <term>bombard</term> <note>A large-caliber medieval/Renaissance cannon.</note> sends its smoke when it begins to fire; and this reasoning would send it a million miles in the time that the thousand-thousand pounds of balls go 3 miles. Do not trust then, you speculators, the authors who have, with their imagination alone, wished to make themselves interpreters between nature and man, but [trust] only those who have exercised their intellects <note>Continued on folio 101 [53] verso.</note> [to recognize] the effects of her experiments.

## — FOLIO 103 [55] (recto). —

### [MOTION, WEIGHT. — PROPORTIONS, AUTHORS].

[Continued from folio 103 [55] verso:] And besides this, when you have found a weight that removes itself furthest from the beginning of the motion, using every diligence [going as fast as possible], by way of percussion, since you act with the simple weight without percussion, one can see what difference there is between the causes of motions—being a simple weight, or else [with] percussion. And likewise you will go on varying the moving objects for this weight until you find a weight that is proportioned to such a power of such a motor, that is, the ball that will be shot furthest from its motor. Then you will weigh one of the moving objects and the other, and you will consider the distances they have moved, and you can truly make a general rule between those 2 powers. Then you will diminish the moving object by half, as those who have written on proportions agree [to do], and you will see that it cannot be that half the weight is moved twice as fast by the same power; that is, [because] if it went twice as fast, it would go just as much [further (which does not happen)], because such is the proportion [Continued on folio 102 [54] verso].

<summary>Leonardo investigates the physics of ballistics and motion, arguing through mathematical thought experiments that physical force and speed do not scale infinitely or simply. He famously critiques theoreticians who rely on imagination over physical experience, asserting that laws of proportion must be tested against the actual behavior of objects like cannonballs and gunpowder.</summary>

### Folio 105 [57] (recto)

<note>Hydraulic study sketch showing the turbulence and flow patterns of water falling over a horizontal weir into a basin, creating bubbles and sediment mounds.</note>

Water that falls upon other water with an <term>oblique impact</term> <note>original: "percussione obliqua"; an impact occurring at an angle rather than perpendicularly.</note> penetrates along the line of its motion down to the bottom, and with that same obliquity, it bounces back toward the surface of the water; and upon exiting the water, it leans somewhat toward the center of the place of its origin. The water that is moved at the bottom by such an impact creates circular motions, and in its circles it <term>whirls</term> <note>original: "ravolgle"; to revolve or churn in an eddy.</note>; and if the water is muddy, it creates a small mound of that same mud in the center of each of its circles, and there it settles.

->[WAVES OF SMOKE. — WATER].<-

ON SMOKE
— Smoke enters the air with a wave-like form <note>original: "figura dondatione"</note> just as surging water does with its momentum <note>original: "inpeto"</note> into other water. —

ON WATER
— Rivers flow, when they are straight, with a much greater momentum in the middle of their width than they do at their sides. —

ON WATER
After water has struck the sides of rivers with equal impact <note>original: "percussione"</note>, finding some narrower part of the river, it will leap toward the middle of the stream and such waves will create a new impact between them; consequently, they will return again toward the banks equally. The water of a pyramidal shape <note>Leonardo is describing the triangular or wedge-shaped currents formed when water is redirected from the banks toward the center.</note> that is enclosed between the first impact made on the bank and the second made in the middle of the river will slow down at its base, and near its tip, it will be fast. Striking the bottom, they will then rise equally to the height [Continued on folio 105 [57] verso].

### [MOVEMENT OF WATER].

[Continued from folio 109 [61] recto: ] toward its surface with a momentum that creates a movement almost as fast as that of its descent; but it will not be as fast, for the reason stated in the 2nd [proposition] of the 7th [book] <note>Leonardo often cited numbered propositions from his own planned treatises.</note> (which says that the movement of a rebound will never be as fast as the descent of the object that bounced; or: a subsequent rebound will never be equal to its predecessor). Thus, the leap made by the water starts from the bottom where it was naturally <note>original: "per na"; likely "per natura."</note> produced, with nearly the same velocity as the descent that gave it birth. In addition to this, a second velocity is added which increases this movement: that is, the air that was submerged along with the falling water. This air, "clothed" in water, surges up with fury and leaps into its own element <note>Air's "natural element" is the atmosphere above the water's surface.</note> like wind forced out by a bellows; it carries with it the water near the surface and makes it leap much higher than its nature would otherwise require.

<margin>A word under the first two lines (heat?) and further down, some short red pencil marks; further to the right, a cross.</margin>

You shall conduct an experiment on this with a vessel made of four plates of glass, and observe from the side.
**ON MOTION**
Water falling from a height of one cubit <term>braccio: an Italian unit of measurement, literally "an arm," approximately 23 inches</term> will never return to the same height except in small droplets, which will leap much higher. This occurs because the movement of the rebound is much faster than that of the descent; for when the water falls, it submerges a great quantity of air with it; then, after the water has struck, it leaps back toward [Continued on folio 108 [60] verso].

<header>— FOLIO 109 [61] (verso). — — FOLIO 110 [62] (recto). —</header>

### [MOVEMENT AND PROPORTIONS (AIR AND WATER)].

->ON MOTION<-
<note>original: "DE MOTO"</note>
If you set a bellows with a long pipe and with such a bellows you push the air all the way to the bottom of the water, all the power produced by such compressed air as it returns to its own element <note>In Leonardo’s time, "elements" sought their natural place: air above water, water above earth.</note> shall be equal to the weight and force that presses upon said bellows; and if the weight was immeasurably greater than what was appropriate for such a submersion of air, the fury of such air becomes more powerful and lifts more weight.
a m $\frac{3}{2}$

If two rivers <note>original: "fivmi"</note> of water flow through equal widths, depths, and slopes, from one beginning to the same end with an equal sum of water, there will be the same proportion between their courses as there is between their lengths; that is, if the short one is six times <note>original: "secvplo"</note> the speed of the long one, the long one will be six times the length of the shorter one.

---

->ON MOTION<-
<note>The following is a French translation of the Italian text above, now rendered into English.</note>
If you hold a bellows with a long tube and with such a bellows you push the air down to the bottom of the water, all the power created by such compressed air as it returns to its element is equal to the weight and force pressing the bellows; and if the weight has been immeasurably more than what was suitable for such a submersion of air, the fury of the air becomes more powerful and lightens more weight.

### [DIVIDED FORCES (RIVERS, BELLS, ROPES)].

->ON THE DISUNITING OF THE POWER OF RIVERS<-
If the excessive greatness of rivers wastes and breaks the maritime shores, one must—since these rivers cannot be turned to other places—break them into tiny streams <note>original: "minvti rivicelli"</note>.

->COMPARISON<-
If a bell rings and is heard for six miles, and weighs 6 thousand pounds, and 6 miles are 18 thousand braccia.... But so as not to extend myself into too much calculation <note>original: "ragione"</note>, I say that if you break it into tiny bells <note>original: "sonagli"</note>, it will not be heard even 1/8th of a mile, even though all that metal rings in the bells at one and the same time. And if a rope supports a hundred thousand ounces, if you break it into a hundred thousand threads, each thread by itself will not support $\frac{1}{\text{  }}$ of an ounce. And so it follows in all divided <note>original: "disunite"</note> powers.

---

->ON DISUNITING THE POWER OF RIVERS<-
If the excessive greatness of rivers spoils and breaks the maritime shores, one must, from the moment one cannot turn these rivers elsewhere, break them into small brooks.

->COMPARISON<-
If a bell rings and is heard at 6 miles, and weighs 6 thousand pounds, 6 miles being 18 thousand braccia.... But so as not to extend myself in too much calculation, I say that if I have broken it into small bells, it will not be heard at an 1/8th of a mile, even though all the metal rings in the bells at the same time. And if a rope supports a hundred thousand ounces, if you break it into a hundred thousand threads, each thread by itself will not support $\frac{1}{\text{  }}$ of an ounce. And thus it follows for all disunited powers.

<summary>Leonardo explores the physics of displaced air and the proportionality of river currents, while introducing the principle of "disunited power"—the idea that a single great force (like a bell's sound or a rope's strength) loses its cumulative effect when divided into smaller parts.</summary>
