## [INTERSECTIONS OF WATER STREAMS]

If the courses of two lines of water cross each other in the middle, or in part of the flow of rivers—crossing to pass one through the other or one over the other—do they each bounce back <note>original: "rinbalzi," to recoil or rebound</note> after the impact? Certainly they bounce back—because it is impossible for two bodies to pass through one another —

But after the two waters have struck together, they will spread out at the contact point; and once they have been struck, they will want to move away at equal distances from the center of the impact. That part which goes *down* up follows its nature, and the other part below the center of the impact—which would want to go down but cannot—increases the water above.

---

## [WATER JUMPS (EXPERIMENTS)]

->EXPERIMENTATION ON THE JUMPS WITHIN A UNIFORM CANAL<-

What you see the water doing here, between up and down, it will also do here and there, striking the banks—except that the water that jumps will fall back upon itself.

Let one side of the canal be made of glass and the rest of wood; and let the water that strikes there be mixed with millet or paper pulp <gloss>1. See above, folio 89 [41] verso.</gloss> <note>Leonardo suggests adding small particles to the water so the internal currents and "jumps" become visible to the eye.</note> so that one may better see the course of the water by their movements. When you have performed the experiment of such jumps, fill the bottom with sand mixed with fine gravel; then see to it that you level this bottom and make the water jump over it, and watch where it lifts [the sand] or deposits it —

Then make the bank near the wood out of mud <note>original: "lita," likely referring to clay or silt</note> and watch its effects through the glass, and do this with a continuous flow of water.

<margin>1. See above, folio 89 [41] verso.</margin>

# FOLIO 115 [67] (verso)

->[MOVEMENTS OF WATER]<-

Movements and leaps of discontinuous quantity —

Movements and leaps of the continuous quantity —

[Continued from folio 116 [68] recto:] the continuous quantity <term>continuous quantity: a substance where all parts are connected, like a flowing stream, as opposed to a "discrete" quantity like a pile of stones</term> has equal movements when its river is of equal width and depth. This is because, since the water is all joined together, it is necessary that in every part of its motion, every part pulls and is pulled, and pushes and is pushed—or chases and is chased. It is necessary that this occurs with equal motion and power; if it were not so, the water would "multiply" <note>Leonardo means the water would pile up or congest</note> more where it slowed down, and would be lacking where it moved faster.

---

# FOLIO 116 [68] (recto)

->[MOVEMENTS OF WATER]<-

If water were a discrete quantity <term>discrete quantity: a collection of separate, individual parts (like grains of sand) rather than a unified flow</term> rather than a continuous one, the motion it makes between the high and low points of its waves would be unequal. In such a case, the part that rises would gain degrees of slowness at every stage of its motion, so that at the highest point of the wave it would be at its maximum slowness. Then, in descending, at every stage of motion it would acquire degrees of speed, so that at the lowest point it would acquire the greatest motion. Therefore, the percussion <term>percussion: the force of impact where the water strikes the riverbed or an obstacle</term>—the resistance that ends the descent—is what receives the damage [erosion], while the point that ends the height of its elevation receives no damage at all.

But if the quantity is continuous: [Continued on folio 115 [67] verso].

---

# FOLIO 116 [68] (verso)

->[MOVEMENTS OF WATER]<-

Where the water divides, it rises; then, in falling back, it reinforces its course because of the increased momentum of the subsequent descent.

Where waters join together, they rise up; then the neighboring motion that follows becomes slow. <note>Leonardo observes that when two streams merge, they briefly surge upward and lose their forward velocity before smoothing out.</note>

---

# FOLIO 117 [69] (recto)

->[MOVEMENTS OF WATER]<-

When in the courses of rivers there are two currents of water which, starting far from each other, converge at a point where they strike one another: after such an impact, they will rise upward. The riverbed beneath them will be little eroded <note>original: "consumato," consumed or worn away</note> because the water moves away from the bottom as it surges upward. Then, the waters fall back down, breaking apart and separating; as they fall again, they strike and scrape the bottom. Because of this percussion which beats and scrapes the bed with its motion, a deep pool will be created there. This occurs in the great currents of rivers.

[2nd figure:] <a>

**A** is the place of the aforementioned percussion. You can see that the elevation of the riverbed (which is eroded very little at the point of impact) is what causes the water to rise even higher at the point of junction; thus, when it eventually falls, the impact of the fall is even stronger.

<summary>Leonardo examines the fluid dynamics of rivers, arguing that water acts as a "continuous quantity" where every part affects the next, and explains how converging currents create specific patterns of erosion and surging.</summary>
<keywords>fluid dynamics, continuous quantity, discrete quantity, river erosion, percussion, wave motion, hydraulics, currents</keywords>

### [HIGH AND LOW POINTS OF WAVES].

-> ON THE SUMMIT OF WAVES <-

**The wave.** The greatest height of the waves will not wear away the bottom beneath it; in fact, they touch it very little, according to the 5th [proposition] of the 6th [book] <note>This likely refers to a specific theorem in a treatise on mechanics or geometry known to Leonardo, possibly Euclid’s or his own collection of rules</note> (which says that every thing weighs along the line of its motion). Therefore, we shall say that such a wave moves toward the air, which flees from its percussion <note>original: "perchuasione," meaning impact or striking</note>, and it weighs toward the air. And if there is indeed a little friction, it will be of little force and will wear away the bottom very little.

-> ON THE LOWEST DEPTH OF WAVES <-

— That thing which is the primary cause for breaking the straightness of the water’s established course will be the most worn away and removed by said water. —

We shall say, then, that if the air were the cause of breaking the straightness of the wave’s elevation, the air would be worn away by such a percussion of water. But this air is not the cause of such a course being broken; the only cause is the weight the water acquires as it leaves its element <note>In Renaissance physics, water's "element" is its natural resting level; when it rises above this as a wave, it gains weight that pulls it back down</note>. And it would slow down in such a position if it were a discrete quantity; but, being a continuous quantity, it is necessary that the waters being joined, one pushes and the other pulls.

***

## FOLIO 118 [70] (recto).

### [MOVEMENT OF WAVES].

<margin>(Waves, eddies, surges, boils.)</margin>

WHETHER THE WATER MOVES FASTER AT THE FALLING OF THE WAVE THAN AT ITS RISING, AND IN WHAT PLACE SUCH WATER SLOWS DOWN THE MOST.

[Regarding] the water that moves in the formation of waves, it will be found that its speed at its elevation is the same as that of its descent; and there will be as much speed in the middle of the *valleys <note>the troughs of the waves</note> as there is at the extreme descent, which is the same as at* its extreme height. And if it were not of equal movements, it would not be of equal depths or widths; and even if it were of equal lengths and depths, *it [the water] would* not be of equal movements, and it would form a great height in the place where it slowed down the most.

[Figure:] Surface.
Bottom.

### — FOLIO 117 [69] (verso). —

-> ON THE WEIGHTS AND MOTIONS OF WATER <-

If the water that exits through the vent <note>original: "spiracholo," a small opening or orifice</note> of the mouth of a wineskin <note>original: "otre," a bladder or leather bag used to hold liquids</note> is of the same weight as the weight that presses upon it, it will exit through the air with a velocity that increases the more it is lighter than the air itself.

But if such a wineskin were submerged under water, that water would exit with a velocity that increases the more it is heavier than the surrounding water.

The water that is forced out of the wineskin will move with a velocity that increases in proportion to the greater weight that moves it. Therefore, if such a wineskin is pressed by a weight of 100 lbs, the water will exit with a velocity greater than if the skin were pressed by 50 lbs, following the same proportion that the weight of 100 lbs has to the weight of 50 lbs.

And if such a wineskin is pressed by a weight that is lighter than the water exiting from it, that water will exit with less velocity than if the said weight were equal to the weight of the water.

---

### — FOLIO 118 [70] (recto). —

<margin>
gold
lead
silver
copper
</margin>

**On the motion that water makes within itself due to the impact caused by the fall of other water.**

The velocity of the first exit of water from the wineskin will be in the same proportion as the weights pressing it are to the weights of the air through which it moves.

But if this water exits through other water, then the difference in velocity from one exit to the other will be in inverse proportion to the density of the mediums <note>Leonardo is noting that the resistance of the surrounding environment—the "medium"—changes the speed of the fluid's motion</note> through which these waters move.

-> — FOLIO 120 [72] (*recto*). — <-

### [MOTION (CROSSBOWS, ALBERT OF SAXONY)¹].

[Figure:] &nbsp;&nbsp; a b c
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a b c
Ask the crossbowmen what difference there is in holding the hand at a, or at b, or at c, so that the arrow is shot higher or lower, and where it comes from.
ON MOTION
Albert of Saxony <note>original: "alberto di sassonia"</note> says in his *On Proportions* that if a power moves a moving body <note>term: "mobile" refers to any object in motion</note> with a certain velocity, it will move half of that body twice as fast. This does not seem so to me; because he does not consider that such a power might be employing its ultimate strength. For if it were to do so, the thing that weighs less would not be in proportion to the force of the mover, or of the medium through which it passed; hence it would be a thing fluttering in the wind and not a direct motion, and it would go less [far]. <note>Leonardo argues that air resistance and the limits of the mechanism prevent a lighter object from simply doubling its speed.</note>

---

> [Figure:] &nbsp;&nbsp; a b c
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;a b c
> I ask the crossbowmen what difference there is in holding the hand at a, or at b, or at c, so that the arrow is shot higher or lower, and from where it originates.
> ON MOTION.
> Albert of Saxony says, in his "On Proportions," that if a power moves a moving body with a certain speed, it will move half of that moving body twice as fast. It does not appear so to me; indeed, he does not account for the fact that this power employs its ultimate strength, for if it did not do so, the thing that weighed less would not be in proportion to the force of the mover, or the medium where it passed; therefore it would be a thing floating in the wind and not of a straight path, and it would go less [far].

<margin>
1. Albert of Saxony <note>original: "Albertus de Saxonia"</note>, Bishop of Halberstadt (14th century), author of a treatise on proportions and commentator on Aristotle. — See Fabricius, and, above, the 1st page of the Table of Contents of Manuscript F, note.

### — FOLIO 122 [74] (recto). —

### [RIVERS. — BALLISTA].

[Figure 1:] n m

If a river strikes the opposite bank with its straight course between two angles, and turns to the right and partly to the left, the line of motion will turn more crookedly to the right than to the left in proportion to how much faster the right side moves, that is, *m n*.

[Figure 2:] a f g n

The more you want the <term>cimitrilla<gloss>a small catapult or stone-throwing device, likely named for its curved, scimitar-like shape</gloss></term> to throw far across, the more you must hold it at a slant, as shown at *a n*; and if you want it to throw higher, hold it at the opposite slant, as shown at *g f*.

### — FOLIO 123 [75] (recto). —

### [MOVEMENTS OF WATER. — REEFS].

*I ask how high the water will throw when made to emerge as low as possible, and how high when made to emerge at various heights, and in various thicknesses, and at various slants, and at various distances from the foot of the vessel, and elevated...*

The water runs faster at the sides of a submerged rock <note>original: "scoglio coperto," a hidden reef or obstacle</note> than above it; once it has passed it, it twists the waves of its surges, creating crescent-shaped <note>original: "lunali," lunar-like or crescent-shaped</note> figures on the surface.

---

*I ask how high the water will throw in making it rise as low as possible, and how much in making it rise at various heights, and how much in various thicknesses, and how much in various slants, and how much at various distances from the foot of the vessel, and elevated...*

The water runs faster at the sides of the covered reef than above [it], and after it has passed it, it therefore twists the waves of its leaps, making lunar figures on the surface.

---

## — FOLIO 127 [79] (verso). — FOLIO 128 [80] (recto). — FOLIO 128 [80] (verso). — FOLIO 129 [81] (recto). —

### [TWO KINDS OF WATER LEAPS]

The leaps of water are of two natures—that is, composed of two causes. One is due to the unevenness of the bottom over which the water passes; the other occurs when the parts of the water that strike against the protruding parts of the bank bounce back toward the opposite bank. These quantities of water, which strike and rebound to the opposite shore, press and push against the first wave they encounter, swelling and leaping toward the sky. Each part flees equally from the point of impact until another wave drives it back, and then another forward. Thus, successively, they fill the surface of rivers with a <term>gridded pattern</term> <note>original: "digraticolata figura," referring to a lattice or mesh-like appearance on the water's surface</note>, always rising at the points of these impacts.

---

### [RULE OF LEAPS, AN EXPERIMENT]

<margin>Raging</margin> <note>original: "Furibonda"</note>
. to the other [?]

->I ask about the leap<-

Tell me, if the first leap is ten <term>braccia</term> <note>a "braccio" or "arm" was a common Italian unit of length, roughly 23 inches or 60 centimeters</note>, how long will the second be? Dye the ball so that it marks the place where it strikes the marble or another hard surface, and follow the rule of all successive leaps, and make a general rule of it.

<margin>Raging ¹</margin>
. . . . . [?]

->I inquire about the leap<-

### [TRAJECTORIES OF BOMBARDS]

If a <term>bombard</term> <note>a heavy, early type of cannon used for hurling large stone balls</note> fires at a target in a straight line for 10 cubits, how far will it fire at its maximum range? And conversely, if it fires 3 miles at its maximum range, how far will it fire in a straight line?

If a bombard fires at various distances with various arcs of motion, I ask at what point of its range will the highest point of its arc be located?

---

### [TRAJECTORIES OF BOMBARDS]

[Figure:] r a   f e d c   g n m h b

If the bombard, using its ultimate power, throws its ball from **b** to **g** while the bombard is at **c r**, and I want to fire to **n**, I will raise the bombard **m** to **d r**, and I will fire to **n**. If I want to throw to **m**, direct the bombard to **o r**. Thus, through experience, go on testing cubit by cubit the ranges that the bombard achieves. Create its scale marked with degrees, so that each is 100, and each degree is divided into 10 minutes of 10 cubits each, and each minute is divided into 10 <term>minims</term> <note>the smallest unit in this scale</note> so that each minim is one cubit. In this way, mark your scale based on experience. And I remind you that the final range of the arched trajectory of the bombard should be marked when the ball makes a hole of its own size without bouncing.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of water turbulence caused by obstacles and transitions into ballistics experiments, attempting to calculate cannon ranges and trajectories through a system of degrees and minutes.</summary>
<keywords>fluid dynamics, water flow, ballistics, bombard, geometry of motion, measurement scales, physics experiments</keywords>

### FOLIO 127 [79] (verso)

<note>Decorative sketches of swirling clouds or waves are present at the top and bottom of the text block, reflecting Leonardo's study of atmospheric turbulence.</note>

If an appearance of one sort appeared to me as another, the nature of that thing would deceive me; therefore, it should not be said that the same surface appears to be of several colors, but that the very same shadow which is upon that surface reveals itself through the air that exists between the eye and it. For this reason, it seems to be of several colors, but if it were close to the eye, it would appear to be of a single color. <note>Leonardo is discussing "atmospheric perspective," the way air and distance change how we perceive the color and clarity of objects.</note>
The reds of the clouds at the setting of the sun are caused by the thickness of the air that stands between the sun and the eye; and the eye sees the same thing looking toward the east at the rising of the sun—that is, seeing the air red. And so it happens in every transparent thing, but not in every opaque body without the light of the sun.

---

### FOLIO 128 [80] (recto)

The reason why the sight of the eye is obscured when taking in the rays of the sun is because it is harmed, and thus <unclear>distressed</unclear> <note>original: "affretto," which can mean hurried, pressed, or constrained</note> is the <term>visual power</term> <note>original: "virtù visiva," a Renaissance term for the physiological faculty or "spirit" that enables sight</note> so that it no longer has the strength to perform its duty until the harm is purged; and it is not purged except by the time that the eye stays in the shadow or until the sun sets.

### FOLIO 128 [80] (verso)

I say that the motion made by a weight descending along an oblique line is slower and lasts for a longer time than that which falls along a perpendicular line; and this arises because the oblique line is longer than the perpendicular over the same site.

<note>Mechanical diagram showing a series of curved paths (trajectories) originating from a single point on a horizontal line, reaching different heights and descending at different angles.</note>

If you shoot an arrow with a bow along a perpendicular line, it falls back into the same place from which it departed; and if you shoot it along an oblique line, it does not fall back into the same place.

### FOLIO 129 [81] (recto)

<note>Geometric diagram at the top illustrating optical principles, possibly showing light rays entering an eye or interacting with a curved surface. Points are labeled with letters (e.g., a, b, c).</note>

On the proportion of the movement of the eye in looking at things distant from each other by various widths: if the movement of the eye is fast, the judgment of the motion of the thing that moves will have little truth; and if the movement of the eye is slow, the judgment will have great truth. But between these extremes is a middle state which has more truth than either of the aforementioned. Furthermore, if it is possible to have the same duration for the movement of the eye, it will have great truth; and further, if it is possible to have the same duration for the movement of the eye as the movement of the thing seen, then the judgment will be of the highest truth. <note>Leonardo is observing that tracking an object at the same speed it moves allows for the most accurate perception of its motion.</note>
Let this be proven: let **a** be the eye and **b** **c** be the thing seen which moves from **b** to **c**. I say that if the eye is still...

### DISTANCES OF THE ECHO

**VOICE OF THE ECHO**
[Figure:] b c d e f g 30 to 100
If an echo’s voice at 30 braccia <note>original: "braccia," an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or an arm's length</note> responds in 2 time-beats, in how many beats will one respond that is 100 braccia away?

If an echo’s voice responds to me in 2 beats across a distance of 30 braccia, with 2 degrees of noise intensity, at what degree of noise will it manifest to me at 100 braccia?

### BOMBARDS — SCIENCE AND PRACTICE

If a bombard <note>An early type of large-caliber cannon used for throwing heavy stone balls</note> throws a ball of 100 pounds 3 miles with its maximum power, how far would it throw a ball of 200 or 300 pounds, or of any other weight different from 100, whether more or less?

If a bombard with 4 pounds of gunpowder throws a 4-pound ball 2 miles at its maximum power, how much must I increase the powder to throw it 4 miles?

If a bombard with 4 pounds of powder drives a 4-pound ball 2 miles, how far will 6 pounds of powder drive it?

**Science is the captain, and Practice are the soldiers.** ¹ <note>This famous aphorism emphasizes Leonardo’s belief that theoretical understanding must guide manual application.</note>

### ON MOVEMENT IN GENERAL

->ON MOVEMENT IN COMMON [GENERAL]<-
What thing is the cause of movement? What is movement in itself? What thing is most suited to movement? What is impetus <term>impeto: the momentum or "force" stored in a moving object</term>? What is the cause of impetus and of the medium in which it is created? What is percussion <note>impact</note>? What is its cause? What is rebound? What is the curving of a straight motion, and its cause?

...they cannot ¹ know what wind is blowing; that is to say: those who live beneath the hills of the shores do not know if the wind is a back-draft or a direct wind.

Aristotle, in the 3rd book of *Physics*, and Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher</note>, and Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, and others, on the rebound, in the 7th book of *Physics* and *On the Heavens and the Earth* ² <note>original: "de Cœlo et Mundo," a Latin title of a work by Aristotle</note>.

### WEIGHT AND MOVEMENT

There are two balls of the same material and shape, but one is double the weight of the other. I want to let them fall through 2 channels situated in such a way that, at the end of these channels, the balls collide. I ask how far each of them must be from the meeting point of these channels at the start of their movement.

If the weight of the beam **m n** is carried by 4 people at the ends, moving it backward or forward gives weight to or lightens the load of those in the back or those in the front; and likewise, by being moved sideways, it will increase the weight for those on one side or the other.

### FOLIO 129 [81] (*verso*)

<note>A geometric diagram at the top depicts a horizontal line (the object or plane) with several points labeled connected by rays to a single point 'a' below, representing light rays or lines of sight.</note>

The shadow that exists between the light and the object <note>original: "obbiello", an archaic term for object</note> will be of so much less darkness as it is further from the object and closer to the light.

The shadow will be of the same darkness in all its parts when it is caused by light of the same quantity, at the same distance, and in the same position.

---

### FOLIO 130 [82] (*recto*)

The shadow will be of so much more clarity as it is struck by more light, and of so much more darkness as it is struck by less light; the air that surrounds it will be of so much more darkness as it is deprived of light.

If the shadow is struck by illuminated air <note>this refers to ambient or reflected light from the atmosphere</note>, it will be of so much more clarity as that air is of greater quantity; and it will be of so much more darkness as the air is of lesser quantity; and it will be of the same darkness and clarity in all its parts if it is surrounded by air of the same clarity.

If the shadow is struck by air of the same clarity, it will be of so much more clarity as it is struck by a greater quantity of such air; its darkness will be of the same clarity in all its parts if it is surrounded by air of the same clarity.

The shadow will be of so much more darkness as it is struck by air of lesser clarity.

---

### FOLIO 130 [82] (*verso*)

Primary shadow, secondary shadow.
If the shadow is seen by an eye placed between the object and the light, that shadow will be seen in such a smaller part as it is more remote from the eye; and it will be seen in such a larger part as it is closer to the eye; and it will be seen in such a smaller part as it is closer to the light, and seen in such a larger part as it is further from the light.

Between the eye and the light, the shadow can be placed in such a way that it is entirely seen, and it can be placed in such a way that it is entirely hidden.

<note>A small sketch at the bottom illustrates a curved shape with shading, possibly a landscape or an anatomical detail viewed in perspective.</note>

If the eye is placed in the center of the shadow, it will not see any part of that shadow; but if it is placed outside the central line of that shadow, it will see so much more of that shadow as it is further from that line.

---

The opening of the dividers <note>original: "sesta", a tool used for measuring and drawing circles</note> is as much wider for 4 degrees as it is for two degrees.
</margin>

<margin>
Eat and drink with moderation <note>original: "temperamento"</note> and do not sleep immediately after a meal.

If the opening of the dividers is 4 degrees and one of the legs is diminished by one-tenth, its opening will diminish by one-tenth of that opening; if it is diminished by half of a tenth, its opening will diminish by half of a tenth; and so it will be for the remaining parts: if they are diminished by one point, one point of its opening will diminish.

->[PROJECTILES FROM CANNONS]<-

— The more quickly the gunpowder catches fire <note>original: "sapiglia" from "s'appiglia," to take hold or ignite</note>, the more it drives out its ball, provided the instrument is made of copper; because if made of other materials, it breaks immediately. —

What difference is there in igniting the fire in several places along the length of the breech <note>original: "coda," literally "tail," referring to the powder chamber of a breech-loading bombarde</note> of the cannon?

— If another cannon were fired from within the barrel of the first cannon, casting its weight at the same time it moves itself, that would be a rapid movement; but it would be like a feathered iron stake <note>original: "palo diferro inpenato"; Leonardo is theorizing a two-stage projectile or a dart-like bolt launched with extreme velocity.</note>. —

### — FOLIO 132 [84] (verso). —

->[ON THE DYNAMICS OF RIVERS]<-

<note>Text in Leonardo's mirror script concerning the dynamics of river currents and bank erosion. Transcribed left-to-right from the original Italian.</note>

If the water that flows through the middle of the river strikes a bank that is oblique <note>slanted or angled</note> to its force <note>original: "uirtu," meaning the kinetic power or momentum of the flow</note>, it rebounds toward the other bank, and so it will continue rebounding from bank to bank until the end of its course.

If the water running through the middle of the river strikes a straight bank, it doubles its height at that point of said bank, and then it turns and flows through the middle of the river, divided into two branches.

This is the cause of scouring <note>original: "cauare," to hollow out or excavate through erosion</note> beneath the bank; because the water that rises <note>original: "mota" for "monta," to climb or rise</note> over the bank and then falls back strikes the root of that bank and keeps diminishing <note>wearing away</note> it; and thus the bank falls and the river grows through such widening.

---

### — FOLIO 133 [85] (recto). —

->[ON THE IMPACT OF WATER UPON THE RIVERBED]<-

<note>Text in Leonardo's mirror script discussing the impact of falling water on riverbeds and the formation of eddies. Transcribed left-to-right from the original Italian.</note>

**On the impact of water made against the bed of the river**

The impact <note>original: "percussioe"</note> that the water makes against the bed of the river destroys and scours <note>hollows out</note> that bed, if such water in its fall does not find other waters to support it.

Water that falls with great motion onto other waters causes that motion to penetrate down to the bottom and it goes on scouring it.

Water that falls between the banks of the river with great impact causes that impact to divide into many parts; because, in striking other still waters, it creates from itself a great multitude of circles <note>eddies or vortices</note> which go on wearing away the embankment <note>original: "argine"</note> and go on destroying it.

That part of the embankment will be destroyed most quickly which is found to be near the circumference of said circles.

<note>Leonardo's technical vocabulary for this section includes: water (laqua), river (fiume), bank (ripa), rebound or impact (ripercussioe), bed or bottom (fondo), embankment (argine), circles or eddies (circuli), force/power (uirtu), and scouring/excavating (cauare).</note>

<summary>These folios document Leonardo’s transition from mechanical engineering and pulley systems to hydraulic studies, specifically how river currents erode banks and scour riverbeds through "rebounding" forces and the creation of eddies.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, river dynamics, erosion, scouring, pulleys, mechanics, fluid mechanics, eddies</keywords>

-> — FOLIO 133 [85] (verso). — <-

Lack of light in the sphere <note>original: "tondo"; referring to a spherical body or the geometry of light on a curved surface.</note>
because the eye does not see the surface
of shaded bodies unless they are illumi-
nated by the sun or by another light.

It cannot be that the <term>sphere of the air</term> <note>The atmosphere surrounding the Earth.</note> is
of the same density everywhere for
the reasons stated in [section] 11; but however it may be,
the eye that sees through the air does not perceive
its quality except as that quality
interposes itself between the eye and the object seen.

If the air were of the same
density throughout, the eye would not see distant things
except with that same knowledge of fi-
gures and colors as those nearby.

Because the air is of varying densities, the eye
cannot see the boundaries of distant things except
with great confusion and uncertainty,
which, though appearing more uncertain, still maintain
their true figures.

The air is more luminous.

The air is more luminous toward the earth

<summary>This sequence of notes explores the principles of atmospheric perspective, explaining how the varying density of air causes distant objects to lose clarity and color contrast. Leonardo concludes that air is more luminous near the ground because its density allows it to reflect more light, a fundamental observation for his painting technique.</summary>

### [LATIN GRAMMAR. — ARITHMETIC PROBLEM, RULE OF THREE].

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's Italian and Latin notes</note>

The other, of many.
<note>Latin declensions for "another"</note>
Nominative: another [masculine, feminine, neuter]
Genitive: of another
Dative: to another
Accusative: another [masculine, feminine, neuter]

Say again: if 8 were 12, what would 4 be?
It would be 6, that is
half a soldo <note>A soldo was a silver coin; Leonardo is practicing calculating proportional values.</note> $\frac{4}{8}$

$\frac{5}{7}$ If you want a method close to the truth, indeed the very truth of a fraction, to know what part it is of a whole, even though you cannot simplify <note>original: 'scifare', meaning to reduce or clear a fraction</note> it, do this: Let us say it is $\frac{5}{7}$, which cannot be simplified. You know what $\frac{5}{7}$ means, whether of a soldo, or a pound, or a lira, or whatever it is; it is enough that it asks for $\frac{5}{7}$ of a whole. Let us say it is one soldo, which is 12 denari; then by the rule of three <note>A mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known ones based on proportions.</note> you will say: if 7 were 12, what would 5 be? That is $\frac{5}{7}$. Put it in form and you will say: 5 times 12 is 60; divide it by 7, the result is 8 and 4 remains . . . . . .

---

<note>Printed French commentary and translation</note>

The other, of many.

Nominative feminine: another, another, another.
Genitive feminine: of another.
Dative feminine: to another.
Accusative feminine: another, another, another.

[Continuation of the text placed below:]
Say again: If 8 were 12, what would 4 be? Which would make 6, that is to say, a half-sou <note>sou: a French coin equivalent to the Italian soldo</note>, $\frac{4}{8}$?

$\frac{5}{7}$ If you want a method approaching the truth, giving even the very truth of a fraction, to know what part of a whole it is, even though you cannot avoid it <note>In the sense of simplifying the fraction further.</note>, do this: Let us say it is $\frac{5}{7}$, which cannot be simplified. You know what $\frac{5}{7}$ means, or $\frac{5}{7}$ of a sou, or $\frac{5}{7}$ of a whole. Let us say it is a sou, which is 12 denari; by the rule of 3, you will say: If 7 were 12, what would 5 be, that is to say $\frac{5}{7}$; place them as they should be, and you will say: 5 times 12: 60; divide it by 7, the result is 8 and the remainder is 4 . . . . . .

---

### [PROPORTIONS OF MOTION].

<note>Transcription of Leonardo's Italian notes</note>

If a power <note>referring to physical force or energy</note> moves an object with its greatest strength *a thousand cubits* <note>original: 'braccia', an Italian unit of length</note>, [if] one pound [moves] a thousand cubits, how much will 11 ounces of those 12 ounces move, up to one, so that each time you move one pound? And if the power of 'd' <note>likely a label for a force in a diagram</note> which moves 10 pounds 100 cubits, how much will it move those 10 pounds separated into 10 parts, and each part being one pound? And how much will it move 5 and 4 pounds separated? And if from 10 pounds you make 4 parts, of which the first is one pound, the 2nd: 2, the 3rd: 3, the 4th: 4, how much will it move them thrown together at one time, and what proportion will the spaces of their first strikes <note>original: 'percussioni', referring to the point where a projectile hits.</note> have? And how far will one go from the other? If you then throw only 4 and 3 pounds together, what difference will there be between the intervals of 3 and 4 when 1, 2, 3, 4 were thrown together, and when it was then [just] 3 and 4?

---

<note>Printed French translation</note>

If a power moves a mobile object with its greatest strength *at a thousand cubits*, one pound, at a thousand cubits, how much will it move 11 ounces of those 12 ounces down to one, that is to say, each time you move one pound. And if the power of 'd' which moves 10 pounds [does so] at 100 cubits, how much will it move these 10 pounds separated into 10 parts, each part being one pound, and how much will it move 5 and 4 pounds separated? And if from 10 pounds you make 4 parts, of which the first is one pound, the 2nd: 2, the 3rd: 3, the 4th: 4, how much will it move them thrown together at one time, and what proportions will the spaces of their first strikes have? And at what distances will they go? If you then throw only 4 and 3 pounds together, what difference will there be for the intervals of 3 and 4, when 1, 2, 3, 4 were thrown together, and when afterwards it was 3 and 4?

---

<meta>This page follows the publisher's imprint and acts as a bibliographic appendix to the multi-volume facsimile series of Leonardo da Vinci's manuscripts. # BIBLIOGRAPHICAL SUMMARY

### ->ANCIENT EXTRACTS FROM LEONARDO’S MANUSCRIPTS<-
->AND PUBLISHED TREATISES<-

The most complete of the compilations made in the 16th and 17th centuries, based on the manuscripts of Leonardo da Vinci, is kept in Rome (*Vatican Codex* <note>original: "Codex vaticanus"</note>) and bears the name and notes of Francesco Melzi <note>Francesco Melzi (c. 1491–1570) was Leonardo’s favorite pupil and the primary heir to his notebooks and artistic estate.</note>. Several collections of the same kind can be found in various libraries¹.

It was from the copies of two of these collections that R.-Tr. Dufresne published in Italian, in 1651, in two folio volumes, the *Treatise on Painting* <note>original: "Traité de la peinture"</note>, along with a biography of the author (which was immediately translated into French by Roland Fréart de Chambray). The first copy (based on manuscript H 227 in the Ambrosian Library) came to him from Cassiano dal Pozzo <note>A celebrated 17th-century Italian scholar and patron of the arts.</note> via de Chanteloup; the other came from Thevenot (*Barberini Codex* <note>original: "Codex barberini"</note>), featuring line drawings by Nicolas Poussin <note>A leading French Baroque painter who illustrated Leonardo's concepts of anatomy and motion.</note>, with touch-ups and additional figures by Errard and Gil Alberti. More than twenty editions of this treatise have appeared since then, in six different languages. The main ones include: that of 1792, in quarto, in Florence, by Abbot Fontani (*Riccardian Codex* <note>original: "Codex Riccardianus"</note>), in Florence, with copies of Leonardo's drawings by Stefano della Bella); that of 1803, in octavo, in Paris, by Gault de Saint-Germain, with a life of Leonardo; that of 1804, in octavo, in Milan, by Carlo Amoretti, with *Historical Memoirs of Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: "Memorie storiche di L. da V."</note>; that of 1817, in quarto, in Rome, by G. Manzi (*Vatican Codex*), with a life of Leonardo; then, in 1882, in Vienna, the scientific Italian and German edition by Mr. Heinrich Ludwig, in four octavo volumes, followed by a fifth in 1885 (*New Material* <note>original: "Neues material"</note>), in Stuttgart; and in Rome, the quarto edition by the Cooperative Union of Typographers, with a preface by Mr. Tabarrini, the life of Leonardo by Vasari, and notes by Mr. G. Milanesi.

From the compilation in the Barberini library, the quarto edition was produced by Fr. Cardinali: *On the Motion and Measurement of Water by Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: "Del moto e misura dell' acqua di L. da V."</note>, in Bologna, in 1828².

<meta>This page concludes the series of publications of Leonardo da Vinci’s manuscripts by the French Institute. It links current French efforts with the new, ambitious publication projects starting in Italy and expresses hope for future work in England.</meta>

# ->CONCLUSION<-

At the very moment our French undertaking is being completed, Italy is solemnly inaugurating the full publication of the *Codex Atlanticus* <note>original: "manuscrit Atlantique"</note>. Gilberto Govi was surprised by death while dedicating himself to the comprehensive work that Mr. Gustavo Uzielli had proposed in 1872¹; however, a worker of great merit, both scholar and artist, Dr. Giovanni Piumati, has been granted the opportunity to resume and realize this great task under the auspices of the Academy of the Lincei <note>A prestigious Italian science academy; the name refers to the lynx, known for its sharp sight</note>. He has shrunk from no effort to bring it swiftly to completion. Already one installment has appeared, featuring superb phototypes <note>an early photographic printing process</note>²; others are to follow soon, until the five or six mismatched manuscripts that form the 395 folios <note>individual leaves of a manuscript</note> of this enormous collection³ are completely brought to light. On the other hand, a distinguished architect from Milan, Mr. Luca Beltrami, recently published, also in its entirety and with 94 excellent facsimiles and their literal transcriptions, the manuscript of Prince Trivulzio⁴, which is the same size as our manuscript A. We may hope that the manuscript of Count Manzoni in Rome, with its 16 pages of the same size⁵, from which Mr. Uzielli has printed important extracts⁶, will also be completely reproduced; and likewise, the annotations by Leonardo da Vinci on the seven-page *Treatise* by Francesco di Giorgio Martini, which passed from Lord Ashburnham’s collection to the Laurentian Library in Florence. We are happy to hail this new dawn here! Thus, the native country of Leonardo da Vinci will raise toward its crowning achievement the work begun on the soil that saw his final days.

May England follow these examples! The autograph papers of Leonardo—

4. *The Codex of Leonardo da Vinci in the Library of Prince Trivulzio in Milan, transcribed and annotated by Luca Beltrami.* <note>original: "Il Codice di Leonardo da Vinci nella Biblioteca del Principe Trivulzio in Milano, trascritto ed annotato da Luca Beltrami."</note> — Reproduced in 94 heliographic plates by Angelo della Croce. — Milan, 1891. — Dumolard Brothers, publishers.

    Despite the knowledge and care of the Italian author, the transcriptions in his beautiful book are not entirely free of inaccuracies. For example, on the front of folio 90 alone, which I had to study specifically (*Museum Bulletin* of April 25, 1891, p. 122), I encountered several; indeed, in the 1st, 4th, 9th, 13th, 19th, 24th, 25th, and last lines, one reads: “pezi, sacheto, Ma, in dirieto, sc[a]rpe, Anchora, ancora, guastassi, sola,” while the original text carries: “pez, sachetto, ma, jndirieto, s[c]arpe, An chora, A ncora, guastassi, solo”; to which I add that the words on the 3rd line: “of battle note” <note>original: "di bataglia nota"</note> are not by Leonardo’s hand, and nothing warns the reader of this. The accuracy of the facsimiles, moreover, leaves such details with no real importance and makes their critique easy; if I have made the preceding remark, it is only to prove how truly difficult it is to avoid even the slightest errors in such a genre of work.

5. These pages, written in the common direction <note>meaning left-to-right, unlike Leonardo's usual "mirror writing"</note>, which were owned by Libri and which seem to come from manuscript B of the Institute (Appendix S, in-quarto), treat the flight of birds, with a view toward the flight of man. I stated (Volume II) that people were wrong to claim this was pursuing a chimera <note>an impossible dream</note>. The day is near when science will take possession of the air as it has conquered the water. Furthermore, it was not so much a matter of inventing as of perfecting, with the help of parachutes, a system recently tested.

    In 1460, Giovanni Battista Dante of Perugia had flown by flapping wings, as others have flown since. From the fact that all were victims of accidents, one must not conclude that the problem of aviation is scientifically insoluble (see: G. Uzielli, 1884, p. 401-408: *Flight and Alchemy* <note>original: "Vol et Alchimie"</note>). Not long ago, the winged boat of Mr. Pompéien Piraud, recalling the studies in Leonardo’s manuscript B and some of his drawings published by Gerli, had given new hope; and today it is announced that Mr. Ader, author of one of our telephone systems, has just successfully traveled three to four hundred meters with a winged mechanism, by means of an electric motor (see the *Small Journal* <note>original: "Petit Journal"</note>, *The Illustration* <note>original: "l'Illustration"</note>, etc., late June, and *The Lightning* <note>original: "l'Éclair"</note>, issue of July 7, 1891, “The Bird-Machine” <note>original: "La Machine-Oiseau"</note>).

6. G. Uzielli, *Research concerning Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: "Ric. int. a L. da V."</note> 1884, pages 256, table no. 3, 301 and 389.

<meta>This page concludes Charles Ravaisson-Mollien’s multi-volume effort to publish Leonardo da Vinci’s manuscripts held in Paris. <page-num>52</page-num>
# ### CONCLUSION. ###

The manuscripts held in that country <note>Referring to England, mentioned on the previous page</note> are numerous and still partially unpublished; the beautiful pages that have been photographed and the sections already printed show how important it is to know the entirety of them, which totals more than 1,660 pages¹.

For our part, with the 2,178 facsimiles reproducing the fourteen manuscripts of the Institute <note>The Institut de France</note> and the National Library, we have completed nearly half of the general unearthing of this material. I said at the beginning, and I repeat in conclusion, that such a work must be carried through to the end to give definitive satisfaction to those preoccupied with the majestic figure of the rival of Michelangelo <note>original: "Michel-Ange"</note>, for it is through the disclosure of the whole that one will understand the intrinsic value of the tiny details in his writings. Nevertheless, the effort taken so far has provided more than just hope; the fruits have exceeded expectations, and already a brand-new light has shone upon the strange genius of Leonardo da Vinci. We are beginning to understand him better; we recognize that the alleged aridity, incoherence, caprice, and childishness of his studies hide, within a profound unity of genius, a poetic enthusiasm for the mysteries of life and creation. These are the inspiring sources of his superhuman imitations and marvelous inventions. We see that the prodigious extent of his knowledge is explained in part by a passion for Art that always goes beyond form to discover its principle, beyond the materiality and essence of things to contemplate their primary cause. Finally, we see that those somber allegories, crude jests, and skeptical maxims—where some believed they saw an enemy of God and men—are merely the outbursts of a spirit often diverted from its most ardent aspirations, struggling against all sorts of difficulties, primarily calumny <note>slanderous false accusations</note>, and irritated by living in a time of extreme moral disorder. He lived in a transitional society that was partially corrupt, in which a splendid elite had to fight step by step against prejudice, routine, pride, and intrigue. Those whom Leonardo da Vinci lashes most with his epigrams are the hypocrites, the envious, and the vain—all those with narrow, low, petty, or false minds. He targets vicious people, unless, in a sentiment of a different order, he contents himself with laughing at them and observing them with curiosity, as Mr. Lévêque* has shown regarding the misdeeds of Jacques André, and for those individuals from whom the author of the sublime Last Supper <note>original: "la sublime Cène"</note> wished to borrow the features of Judas². The enigmatic and gently ironic *Mona Lisa* <note>original: "Joconde"</note> offers a reflection of this soul, so simple and complex at once, in his happy days; and the principal portrait he made of himself in his old age shows, beneath grandiose features, the elevated character of his sorrows. This character likely did not weaken toward his final days, for the paralysis that had affected his right hand did not prevent his writing and drawings from retaining all their firmness.

CHARLES RAVAISSON-MOLLIEN.

June 1891.

### FOLIO 135 [87] (verso)

<margin>

and 4 remain;

equal parts, equal parts, equal parts <note>original: "ana ana ana"</note> 4
</margin>

If the water is pushed through a round conduit <margin> 1/2 </margin>
and said conduit is of equal width
in every part of its length, from which
I conclude that as much water enters through the mouth
as leaves through the other; and if one mouth
were doubled, the other would double
because of the velocity of the water, whereby being
the velocity doubled, it would come to do
the same in the reflected motion; that is, if the velocity
of a [stream of] water is 10 and the motion is 10, the doubled motion
shall be 20, whereby the leap <note>the height of a jet or splash</note> of the water,
if it were 10 braccia <note>A Florentine unit of measure, approximately 23 inches</note>, it would leap 20 braccia,
because the velocity increases by 2 and the height increases by 4. <note>Leonardo is observing the relationship between kinetic energy and the height of a water jet.</note>

### FOLIO 136 [88] (verso)

If one of the vessels is 1/2 the size of another and they are filled
with water to the same height, the exit
of the water from the mouth shall be of equal velocity,
even though the thicknesses <note>the diameter of the openings</note> are one 1/2 of the other;
whereby from one there will exit, in the same amount of time,
half the water as from the other, because one mouth is
half the size of the other; and for this reason, if they
were emptied while turning at an equal height,
one vessel would empty itself
in the same time as the other.

<note>Small sketch of a vessel with a water jet emerging from its base.</note>

However, if 10 comes out through the wide [opening], 
10 still comes out through the narrow [opening], but much more
rapidly.

The water is pushed by force into a narrow pipe,
and moved from above with force, it shall be of so much
greater velocity as its pipe is made more narrow,
provided it is done with equal force.
